president-in-office of the council.– mr president, the european union is not only a market, it is also a union built on common values. the eu treaties are eloquent and crystal clear. article 2 states the values on which this union is founded and reaffirms that these values are common to all member states. membership of our union entails not only benefits, but also responsibilities. among the foremost responsibilities of each member state is respect for the union’s fundamental values, not least the rule of law, democracy, and fundamental rights. it is what makes us as member states, and also as a union, unique in the world. these values are shared not only because they are written on paper, but because they have been brought to life in pluralistic and open societies over the last decades, sometimes against stiff opposition. they are fundamental because they provide essential guarantees for the freedom of our citizens and the functioning of our democracies. however, neither the rule of law nor other fundamental values can be taken for granted. this continent brought forth the three most deadly and venomous political doctrines that we have known. our ancestors fought over these doctrines and finally overcame them. we have learned our lessons the hard way, and we have vowed countless times that we would never return to those dark days, but would build a new community on this continent where freedom and peace would reign. we have been successful in this endeavour and the secret of that success is that we put democracy and the rule of law first. it was crucial then and it remains crucial today that we continue to do so. ensuring respect is a constant challenge that governments have to live up to, and yet we must be honest. no one country has a monopoly on virtue and no one country has a monopoly on vice. we all have deficiencies, but the true strength of our democracies is that we can identify these deficiencies, debate them, acknowledge them and fix them. that is what democracy is all about. this also implies that we are ready to have open discussions about the best way to protect these values in times of change. today’s debate in which the council – and i thank you for that – has been invited to speak, has been triggered by the most recent measures introduced by the newly democratically elected polish government, including the position of the constitutional tribunal, and the governance of public media. both the independence of tribunals and the freedom and pluralism of our media are indispensable elements in ensuring the rule of law in a democratic society. the council has repeatedly stressed that media freedom and pluralism are fundamental values and essential pillars of democracy. this is due to their important role in ensuring transparency and to their impact on public opinion and on the participation of citizens in decision-making processes. on several occasions the council has also highlighted the independence of the judiciary as a core value emerging from the constitutional traditions of member states. it is not for the presidency to pass judgment, especially not at this juncture in time. the council has not discussed the situation, but i do want to briefly say something about poland. not many countries have suffered from european history as poland has, divided, occupied, purged and ravaged, but the polish spirit has never died. it has fought for its independence and its identity even under the soviet yoke, and while its government was in exile, polish soldiers helped to liberate my country in 1945, and for that i will be eternally grateful. (applause) and now in 2016, 11 years after poland joined the european union, it has thrust itself forward into the circle of big powers. it has succeeded in establishing itself as a confident and successful european political and economic power, and it has grown into a democratic state with strengthened institutions. and the polish people have been able to do this because they could build upon a tradition, having had one of the earliest enlightened constitutions in europe as its constitution of 1791 attests. the polish people deserve huge respect for what they have accomplished and in their quest for sovereignty they have found themselves at the heart of the european union. the presidency is grateful for being given the opportunity to participate in this debate. parliament has always shown great dedication to the protection of rule of law, democracy and fundamental rights in the union. it is no secret that my country, the netherlands, home to grotius and host to many international tribunals, feels it must embed fundamental rights and the rule of law in its foreign and european policies. in 2013, together with germany, finland and denmark, we sent a letter to our partners arguing the need for a platform to debate the rule of law. if we can talk about fish and finance, why not also talk about fundamental rights and the rule of law? that is also why we are organising a rule of law seminar on migration in strasbourg on 2 february. we hope to have many participants from the relevant institutions. already two months ago the council held its first annual dialogue on the rule of law in the union. we will organise a second rule of law dialogue in the may general affairs council. we will use the outcome of the february seminar as a basis for this discussion. our presidency is thus committed to ensuring respect for these core values. of course, the council is not acting alone in these matters of fundamental importance. on the contrary. the commission plays in our view a vital role in monitoring developments in this field across the union, especially in its role as guardian of the treaties. i also wish to highlight the role played by the council of europe and its venice commission in these questions. both the european commission and the venice commission, in accordance with their roles, are looking into the developments of our discussion today, and we would suggest that this debate is carried out in an impartial and cooperative spirit, and that progress can be made after a thorough analysis of the facts. the vice-president of the commission will update us on the work of the commission and the next steps after the college’s decision last week to launch a structured dialogue with the polish authorities, and prime minister szydło, with whom i had the honour to talk today, will have the opportunity to address this chamber and share her government’s position. i welcome her participation today which can only contribute to the necessary dialogue within our european democracy.
first vice-president of the commission.– mr president, on behalf of president juncker and my colleagues in the commission, i want to set out for you the reasons why the commission has decided to assess the recent developments in poland, and how we hope to move forward in a constructive and facts-based dialogue with poland to prevent the emergence of a systemic threat to the rule of law. the main reason for beginning this assessment under the 2014 rule of law framework is the situation concerning the polish constitutional tribunal, and in particular the dispute about the nomination of a number of judges of the tribunal. in principle, this should be an issue for the constitutional tribunal itself to resolve. however, as things stand, the other institutions of the polish state have not complied with the judgments rendered by the constitutional tribunal on the matter. this has given rise to uncertainty regarding the functioning of the constitutional tribunal. furthermore, the polish parliament has decided to shorten the mandates of the president and vice-president of the tribunal. on 28 december last year, an amendment to the law on the constitutional tribunal entered into force which appears to render the functioning the constitutional tribunal considerably more difficult. given the central position of the tribunal within the polish judicial system, we risk seeing the emergence of a systemic threat to the rule of law. concerns have also been raised as regards the new media law. the rule of law, as defined in our rule of law framework, requires the respect for democracy and fundamental rights. media freedom and pluralism are also closely connected with fundamental rights, in particular the freedom of expression. this is why the commission considers it necessary to assess this law in the light of the rule of law. the european union is founded on a common set of values enshrined in article 2 of the treaty on the european union, which include, in particular, the respect for the rule of law. mutual trust among eu member states and their respective legal systems depends on the confidence that the rule of law is observed in all member states. when national rule of law safeguards seem to come under threat, the eu needs to act. i would also note that the constitutional tribunal in poland has a key role to play in ensuring that the legislative reforms currently envisaged in poland comply with the constitution. for this reason as well, it is essential to resolve the present dispute concerning the constitutional tribunal as a matter of urgency, so that the tribunal can fully play its role as a national rule-of-law mechanism. i wrote to poland twice on these matters on 23 and 30 december last year. however, the replies we received then were not complete and not sufficient to dispel our concerns. the rule of law framework allows us to assess the matter in a structured manner together with the polish authorities. we should make use of the rule of law framework in an open and constructive manner, in a spirit of cooperation, not of confrontation. we have just received, i think an hour or so ago, another letter in answer to the letter i sent last week and we will assess it, indeed, in a constructive and cooperative manner to see what the answers are to the questions we sent last week. obviously, i cannot go into that already now, we need to assess it carefully, as we just received the letter an hour ago. i would like to stress firstly that we are at the beginning of the process under the framework. the framework has a preventive nature, and the start of a detailed, factual and legal assessment in no way implies any automatic move to decisions at later stages. that will depend purely on the facts – and answering us so quickly will help to stimulate that dialogue and to have a constructive dialogue with the polish government. we will engage in this dialogue in an impartial, evidence-based and cooperative way. it goes without saying that the commission fully respects the sovereignty of the republic of poland, and carries out its duties in an objective and non-partisan manner, as for any other member state in line with the duties imposed on the commission by treaties, signed and ratified by sovereign states – the members of the european union. finally, we will conduct our assessment in close cooperation with the venice commission of the council of europe. i welcome that, following my suggestion, the polish government has itself asked for an opinion of the venice commission on the reform of the constitutional tribunal. i want to repeat, this is the spirit in which we wrote to the polish government last week, and i have a feeling this is also the spirit in which the polish government has responded to our letter of last week. we will make a careful analysis of the response and then enter into further dialogue with the polish government to hopefully solve this issue shortly.
prime minister of poland. - mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. mr. president, i would like to thank you for your service. minister! ladies and gentlemen! i thank you very much for allowing me to speak about poland in the european parliament today. thank you for inviting me, for allowing, i hope, a substantive, good, substantive debate. it's very important to me that we can clear your doubts today, if any, about the changes we're making in poland. and we are introducing them because as a result of the democratic elections that took place in october 2015, the polish citizens in that democratic electoral act decided that they wanted exactly the changes that were proposed by my ruling camp by law and justice to be implemented. this is the decision of the polish people. i am grateful to be able to speak to such a distinguished group here today on behalf of the polish government, but above all on behalf of the polish people, for whom freedom, equality, justice and sovereignty are inalienable values. these are the values that poles have fought for for many years and that we value above all else. freedom, sovereignty, equality and justice are the values on which we base the development of our country. i would like you to be convinced that poland is part of a united europe in the same sense and in the same dimension as the countries you represent. ladies and gentlemen! i think that these voices, which we very often hear with pain in poland, are unjust voices, voices that judge poland, the polish state, but also the polish government in an unjustified way, that they are only the result of lack of information or are voiced by those who simply have a bad will, but i also believe deeply that they are in the minority, because we, europeans, should build our community precisely on the basis of trust, respect for diversity and building within this diversity of ours the unity that is the european union. we have taken up this challenge, we have taken it up because we value security and unity and we know full well that only a united europe, with the strength of its states, is capable of facing the challenges that we are facing today, and that we must all discuss together with an open mind. poles are open to supporting europe in difficult decisions. poles are open to supporting europe in meeting these challenges. we are part of a united europe. this is a huge asset to us. the polish history, which was also discussed here, which mr henderson spoke about, and for which i thank you very much, is a very difficult history. it's a story that has defined our journey to this day. our fathers, our grandfathers, shed their blood so that we could enjoy freedom today, so that we could be part of an equal and united europe, but they also shed their blood for the freedom of other european nations. for many years, for decades, we had to fight for the right to express our own opinions, to build our own statehood. we won this and we will not let it be taken away from us, because this is the idea that united europe has taught us. we are europeans. we're proud of that. the polish people in the elections that took place last autumn chose the program with which we went to the elections - we, the representatives of the ruling law and justice group today. they chose a programme that is primarily aimed at those citizens who today, after years of transformation, including participation in the european union, do not live well in poland. it may seem strange to you, but poland, although it is in the european union, although it is a large country, still faces problems such as high unemployment among young people, low wages among young people. many polish children still dream of having the only hot meal at school. there are pensioners in poland who spend half their pension on medicines and very often have to make dramatic choices: whether to buy a prescription or pay the bills. that's the reality in poland, too. many poles feel that they have been left out of this transformation process. we want to build a poland today that is the european union a poland of equality, of equal opportunities. we want poland to develop even faster on this path to equal opportunities. we have a programme where we have proposed solutions that are being used in many european countries. we have taken good examples from different european union countries because we believe that we have to learn from those who have succeeded, who can do it, but we also know that many polish citizens today feel that they must finally have equal opportunities and the programme we are implementing is exactly such a programme. this election, which is the decision that we are forming a government today, the decision of our citizens, has committed us to making good change. the good changes we agreed to in the elections with our voters, we agreed with the poles. and since the beginning of our government, we've been doing that. we have realized these postulates, which according to the poles should form the basis and foundations of polish development and the state. we do this in accordance with the law, respecting the constitution, respecting the laws, and finally respecting the european treaties, because i will say it again: we are part of the european union, we were, we are and we will be part of europe, this europe of development, this europe of equal opportunities. we have a vision of europe that respects all europeans, that cares for the development of all the countries that make up the continent. this is our future and we want to be an active member of such a european union. poland has for centuries respected the rule of law and the rule of law. yes, we are the first country in europe to introduce a constitution, and for poles, a constitution is sacred. and there has been no violation of the constitution in poland recently. so i have to say that while i am happy to be here today, to speak to you, to present the polish position, i see no reason why we should spend so much time and so many words on polish issues, because it seems to me that there are many important, very important issues and problems that deserve to be addressed and our attention that exist in europe today. but i'm here because i want to take up the dialogue that we were talking about. i want to tell you about poland, i want to clear up all the doubts, and i believe deeply that with the goodwill i will meet here, we can all come out of this debate convinced that poland is a strong, well-developed member of the european union and that we are all proud of it. ladies and gentlemen! there are two doubts that have been raised here: regarding the constitutional court and regarding the media, the media law. the constitutional court, ladies and gentlemen, is doing very well in poland. it's working. even today, just a few hours ago, he made one of his resolutions, he's working, nothing bad is happening. the amendments we have made to the constitutional tribunal in the constitutional tribunal act are in line with the standards in force in europe and do not differ in any way from the regulations applied by other countries of the european union. we had to change the law on the constitutional tribunal because in june 2015 the previous sejm, the previous ruling coalition, passed the law on the constitutional tribunal, which was, moreover, challenged by the constitutional tribunal on 3 december 2015 ruled to be unconstitutional in part. and this aforementioned judgment of the constitutional court, questioning the law adopted, i will remind, by the previous sejm, by the previous ruling coalition, and numerous expert opinions ordered the correction of these errors. in breach of the constitution, the judges of the court were elected prematurely and were to take office after the new parliamentary elections. we had to correct this 14 of the 15 judges were to be nominated by the outgoing ruling coalition, whereas the venice commission, which i will refer to here, in its 1997 opinion clearly states that the system for selecting judges to the constitutional court should be geared towards ensuring more democratic representation in its composition, and the ruling party should not be able to fill all the seats of its choice. this was done, however, despite the fact that during this transitional period the president-elect also asked that such decisions not be taken. the president's decision to refrain from accepting the oath of office from persons elected to judicial positions in violation of democratic standards has enabled the new sejm to adopt resolutions correcting these abuses. the constitutional tribunal has also ruled that the constitutional law of the republic of poland does not allow for the appointment of judges. from a legal point of view, there are 15 sworn judges in poland - exactly the number required by the constitution. the constitutional tribunal is composed of a president, a vice-president and a president. only five of the 15 judges are those elected by the parliamentary majority supporting my government. law and justice has never sought to dominate the court. moreover, we never wanted a majority in the tribunal. we were just trying to keep the balance. i also want to tell you that we agree that 8 of the 15 judges will be nominated by the opposition. this is a positive change in the perception of opposition rights that radically differentiates us from our predecessors. we respect the opposition and their rights. we want dialogue, we want to solve together issues important for poland and for poles. in order to ensure the pluralistic nature of the court's decisions, the present parliament has decided that, as in many other countries of the union, the court will, in principle, adjudicate in full. it should be beyond doubt. this is also the case in some countries of the european union, where the court must always sit in plenary. in addition, and this is questionable to some, it was decided that decisions should be taken by a qualified majority of two thirds. since the decisions taken by the constitutional tribunal de facto determine the shape of constitutional amendments, it was considered that they should be adopted by the same majority as the national assembly adopts the constitution. in many countries, judges of the constitutional court are elected by a two-thirds majority. there are countries in europe where some cases before the constitutional court require a two-thirds majority. and you know this very well, because many of you represent these countries. it is also worth stressing that this requirement will encourage judges to seek compromises and will give their decisions a more pluralistic and inclusive character. finally, it is necessary to clarify the misunderstandings that have arisen around the implementation of the constitutional tribunal judgments that were handed down last december. it is worth emphasising that the ongoing controversy surrounding the court is political, not legal. the constitutional court is a court of law, not a court of fact. it assesses the constitutionality of legal norms and therefore decides whether the contested norm will continue to apply. the constitutional tribunal is not a court of law, but a court of law. the rules that the court ruled unconstitutional in december are no longer valid and will not be applied. they have been permanently eliminated from the legal system and this is the only legal consequence of these judgments. so there's no need to do it in any extra way. however, i would also like to stress to you once again that the dispute over the court is at present a political issue in poland, not a substantive one, and as such, in my view, it should be resolved on the basis of an agreement and a political compromise in poland. this is an internal polish matter and that's why we should solve this case ourselves. i'm willing to do that and i'll talk to the opposition to make sure they accept our solutions. ladies and gentlemen! as regards the changes to the public media, they were introduced by a parliamentary majority and do not in any way violate european standards for public broadcasters. moreover, the changes we have initiated are an attempt to restore the authentic nature of apolitical and impartial public media in poland. until now, many circles in poland have claimed that impartiality, neutrality and objectivity are not preserved. public media, in our view, requires changes that restore pluralism and equal access to all parties and introduce standards of neutrality and reliability. that's the only reason we're making these changes. three weeks ago, the polish parliament passed an amendment to the radio and television act, the first step in the reform of public media. the association of polish journalists called for reforms at its extraordinary congress. in the first stage of the reform, we have streamlined the issues of ownership control over public media, which until now has not only been inconsistent with european standards, but has also proved ineffective, leading to the financial collapse of public media. it was therefore necessary to separate the function of the media market regulator, namely the national council for radio and television, from the exercise of the state treasury's proprietary powers, which are expressed in the appointment of the boards of directors of the media market operators. the need for such a model is clearly stated in the 2010 venice commission opinion. none of the constitutionally guaranteed functions of the national council as the media market regulator has been violated and will remain unchanged. the government is currently working on another amendment to the radio act, which will give a new form of organisation to public broadcasters and ensure a stable basis for their funding. in the case of changes in public media, we are following the approaches used in many eu countries. ladies and gentlemen! the government of the republic of poland is open to dialogue and debate. we want to build an understanding in poland with all the parliamentary clubs, both with the opposition clubs and with those clubs that today support the polish government in introducing changes that are good for poland. we are open to dialogue and conversation, we are open to solving polish problems together. i think it is important for all of us to feel supported by the european union in these activities, to feel that poland, as a free and sovereign member of the european union, can always count on support and that our community, our sovereignty, is preserved in decisions concerning internal affairs. ladies and gentlemen! i'm ready to answer all your questions. i'm prepared to share any information, as are all representatives of my government. poland is a beautiful country, poles are a proud people. we want to be the leader of the european union. these are our dreams, these are the dreams of poles. we have waited too long to enjoy freedom, justice and sovereignty to throw away the values that are so important to us today. it's priceless to us, to all poles. thank you very much for listening to me. i am confident that my explanations will give you a new quality of information about poland. i am firmly convinced that it is through dialogue and agreement that we will build a good future for the european union.

vice president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– madam president, these are very important times for colombia. let me say that, for once, among many different difficult situations in the world around us and far away, this is a place in the world where we have signs of hope and change. i am very glad that you decided to organise this debate on the peace process because i am convinced that this year can be the year where we have good news after an armed conflict that has lasted for over half a century. two hundred and twenty thousand people have died and over six million have been forcibly displaced. countless others have been kidnapped, and these appear to have been victims of violence. the first peace negotiations were held more than 30 years ago, and today in havana we finally see the chance of a breakthrough. let me say that this opportunity for peace, for good news – sometimes we do have good news, as happened a few days ago in vienna on iran – cannot be missed. personally, i had been following the colombian peace process even before becoming the union’s high representative. i was already in bogotá as an italian prime minister and, since i started my role in the european union institutions, i have supported, on behalf of the european union, my friend president juan manuel santos’s courageous efforts. over this year, our relationship with bogotá has grown stronger in many different ways, from the visa waiver agreement to colombia’s engagement in our mission, atalanta. just a few months ago i decided to appoint eamon gilmore as my special envoy for the peace process to demonstrate and strengthen the eu’s active commitment to it. i was particularly glad that this decision was taken with the full support of president santos. eamon gilmore’s direct involvement in the peace process in northern ireland and his political experience made him a perfect, ideal candidate who, as i said, has already been very well received in these first months with all the contacts he had among the parties, even in recent days. he is currently in bogotá, and i know that he is looking forward to meeting the members of the committee on foreign affairs (afet) later this month to explain his role, share his views on the prospects and the remaining challenges of the peace process and discuss with the members of afet the way in which the european union can better contribute to supporting this process. let me give you an update on the state of play. we have all seen the landmark agreement that was reached last december on the victims. this agreement offers a sound basis for truth, justice and reconciliation. we all know that reconciliation is the only possible real base for any peace process to move forward in a sustainable way. this agreement can ensure that the truth about the conflicts, its roots and each actor’s responsibilities is known and acknowledged. it can bring justice and guarantee the non—repetition of crimes, can make it possible to move beyond the conflict and look to the future and can ensure that the disappeared are accounted for. it is crucial to heal the wounds and, for those who have lost their loved ones, to grieve the loss and cope with it. the agreement can also guarantee appropriate reparations to the victims, either individually or collectively. this is probably the first time a peace agreement has given such a central role to victims. there is no other way towards reconciliation, and the culture of political divergences can be solved peacefully through politics and elections. the agreement walks a thin line – we know that very well and the colombians know it very well – between preventing impunity and making peace possible. it was not an easy task, but the deal has managed to strike a good balance. the two sides have also committed to making the effective protection of human rights a top priority. this includes a strong focus on human rights defenders. their extremely precious work too often makes them the target of threats and violence. colombia started from a difficult position in this regard, but it has also made very good progress over the past few years. in spite of a security situation that remains challenging in a number of regions, such commitments by the two sides will help consolidate progress. of course, the havana negotiation is not over yet. we are talking about a process that is still ongoing. important issues still need to be addressed. just to quote a number of them: the modalities for a definitive ceasefire and its verification, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of former combatants, the arrangements for guaranteeing their physical security, and how to implement the agreement. still, i am confident that the negotiation can not only be concluded, but can be concluded rapidly in line with the commitments taken by president santos. as an agreement comes close – hopefully – we must also think of what comes next on how to support the peace that it is now possible to build. experience shows that implementing a peace agreement is often the most challenging part of it. vested interests may stand in the way. a new mentality will need to replace the old ways of doing things and all parties will have to confirm their dedication to peace, well beyond the signature of a deal or even its ratification through a plebiscite. this is why our work and eamon gilmore’s mandate is focused very much on the implementation phase and how we can support it with all the different means that we have. european union engagement will not decrease once an agreement is signed and ratified – on the contrary. on land and rural development, political participation or human rights, we will keep encouraging deep change in the country along the lines that will be agreed in havana. it is these reforms that can bring sustainable peace and not just peace in colombia. the european union will be with colombia all along the way. we are together with colombia today, we will be there at the moment when the peace agreement is signed – soon, hopefully– and we will be there to help the parties implement it fully. my colleague neven mimica and i have been working together to set up an eu trust fund which will pool contributions from the eu budget and from willing member states. we are already seeing contributions coming in. we are currently finalising the preparatory work for this fund in close contact with interested member states and, as i said, there is a growing interest in this. the trust fund will have to be ready by the time the peace agreement is concluded. it will complement colombia’s own financial efforts in close coordination with other donors and partners of the country. we are not just offering good intentions but constant political support that is very much needed and concrete means to make this work in a sustainable way, for when the agreement is signed, for when it starts to be implemented and for future decades. through our political support, our work with international partners and our financial assistance, the european union is making, and will continue to make, a crucial contribution to the success of the peace process in colombia. these are days that are very important for latin america, days of change, days of new challenges, and – potentially – days of reconciliation. such change needs to be driven, encouraged and accompanied. when the opportunity for positive change arises for once, our european union has a specific interest in playing a key role. that is what we are also doing in colombia – and not only there – and i know that i can count on you for support in doing this because, as we focus on managing the crisis in the conflicts around us, we cannot afford to lose sight of the positive and encouraging steps that can be taken around the world, helping us stabilise, as in this case, a conflict that lasted for 40-50 years or prevent further destabilisation and conflict. even when they look far off, they do affect the stability and the security of the world, so it is our primary interest in the european union to support and facilitate them with the maximum of our efforts and, as i said, our political and also financial support.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's energy policy is not undermined by the fact that the european union is not able to meet the demands of the world market. the european industry maintains a dominant position in the global market for cable transport facilities accounting for 60% of the world market, with the ski industry being the main market for cable transport technology. we are talking about four thousand jobs directly linked to cable transport installation companies and millions of users in europe and the world. these figures highlight the importance of ensuring a high level of consumer protection and full harmonisation of technical requirements, as well as clear and detailed rules that are uniformly applicable throughout the union, creating a true pan-european framework that will set a global standard and creating common standards. the harmonization of the internal market is a challenge which the members of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection and myself take very seriously. since the creation of the european coal and steel community in 1951, the process of economic integration has been the main engine around which progressive political integration has been built. a harmonized internal market allows for greater economic integration and greater growth of our enterprises. today, more than ever, in the face of anti-european rhetoric, we must highlight the benefits of the union and the length of the road we still have to travel to generate growth and wealth for our businesses. with these three reports we are discussing here today, we are taking another step towards a more efficient internal market, which is friendly to businesses and consumers. the market for cable transport installations is characterised by a high degree of specialisation. that is why we are dealing with a report of very technical content. the 2000 directive, which we are replacing today with a regulation, has given rise to a number of differences in transposition, which we will remove tomorrow. the regulation we are going to adopt tomorrow actually allows for full harmonisation and allows us all to fulfil the general political commitment to work towards better regulation and simplification of the european regulatory environment. the proposal harmonises the conditions for placing on the market of subsystems and safety components intended for cableway installations and ensures the free movement of these products within the european union. to this end, uniform application throughout the union is ensured, full harmonisation, as member states cannot impose new or stricter requirements in their national legislation. this gives the industry the assurance that its goods meet the technical requirements for sale in all european countries and, on the other hand, unnecessary transposition costs are avoided. however, member states will remain competent to regulate other aspects of cableway installations, such as land use, land use planning and environmental protection. improving legal clarity was another of the fundamental objectives of this regulation. the new regulation indicates its scope and lists clearly the exclusions. the proposal provides for more precision, particularly as regards cableway installations for the transport of persons and for leisure activities. facilities used for leisure purposes in fairs or amusement parks and historic facilities more than 30 years old are excluded from the scope. this is in response to a request from many member states, which will be responsible for safety standards for these facilities. finally, the integration of subsystems into the conformity assessment procedures used for safety components is also to be noted. treating subsystems differently from systems would lead to market distortions and differences in treatment. the proposal thus maintains the conformity assessment procedures for safety components, extending them to subsystems.
member of the commission.– madam president, i would like to thank the members very much for all their comments on this package. this is the first time in my short (one-year) experience in the commission that i have heard so many unanimous positive opinions, so i want once again to warmly thank the rapporteurs for cooperating so closely and ensuring consistency throughout the three texts, as well as with the new legislative framework package. let me just very shortly stress three key points. with those three regulations, we will have a simpler, fairer and more modernised legal framework. replacing the directive with regulations will make life less burdensome for companies and we will be better equipped to fight non-compliant and potentially unsafe products, which is essential for our citizens and for protecting honest companies. members, i therefore call again on your strong support for this package and would like to thank you very much, especially the rapporteurs, for your efforts.
the rapporteur. madam president, i think i am as pleased as everyone else about this joint work with mrs stihler and mrs ford. i think we have all done a good job, all the components, although there are always some exceptions; there is always someone who does not want to participate in this, but well, it is normal. in our case i think we have made a huge step forward in the internal market, which is why i joined this committee. i am new to this and i am very proud that i have been able to work with both speakers on this report and i think i have learned a great deal from both of them. i would simply like to make four points on the final report on which i had the honour of being rapporteur. there is more information for consumers, with a reinforced mention of the producers' website in the recitals and articles; the wording of the article on the braking system for cable transport systems remains true to the principle of technological neutrality and will allow fair competition between all players in this market; a new recital on penalties - i would like to mention here an alternative rapporteur, lucy anderson, who has been very insistent on this issue - which has succeeded in reinforcing the penalties system of the proposal for a regulation; and, finally, we have addressed the concerns of the member states regarding historic installations, which are usually of high tourist interest. as the european people's party group leader responsible for this report, i also thank the alternative rapporteurs for their collaboration on this package on the harmonization of the internal market, which allowed all the amendments that were in line with the competence of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection to be positively assessed, leading to a very satisfactory result of which all the members of the imco committee can be proud.

madam president, i have supported this report. i explained yesterday in the debate why i think it is important that we have a uniform basis of criminal procedural law in europe, because we have a european arrest warrant and we are extraditing citizens across europe. but i did not have time to say, and that is why i have joined the debate today, that it is good that the version of the proposal prepared by the european parliament has been adopted and that some of the shortcomings in the original proposal, which came from the commission, have been removed. i consider it particularly important that the commission proposal was omitted, which allowed for an exception and a breakthrough in the principle that the burden of proof in criminal proceedings must always be on the defendant, that is to say, on the state and not on the citizen. i do not know why the commission wanted to break this fundamental principle. there has also been a refinement of some concepts, such as the understanding of criminal procedure, as each country has slightly different rules on its scope. so it's good that the european parliament's version passed, it's certainly better.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this proposal for a directive because we think it is very important to introduce minimum criteria at european level which force member states to respect the presumption of innocence and other rights of persons detained, such as the right to be present at trial. one of the main ideas introduced in this proposal for a directive is to safeguard the right of all detained persons to access some form of legal aid, even if only provisionally. we are pleased that, in the face of the regressive changes under way in the judicial systems of various european countries, the presumption of innocence is being protected and trials in absentia are being prevented. some of the key issues for us have not been included, such as the inclusion of the right to remain silent or some measures relating to the safeguarding of evidence, which are often violated in the spanish state in cases related to the persecution of social activists. however, we believe that the final result introduces improvements by safeguarding rights and introducing measures to protect the rights of detainees.
in writing. ‒ the rapporteur welcomes the proposal for a directive which strengthens certain aspects of the presumption of innocence and the right to be present at the trial itself in criminal proceedings, but considers that the commission has taken a too limited approach and questions the lack of ambition of the initial proposal, which carries the risk of downward harmonisation of national provisions. the commission is therefore proposing amendments aimed at improving the protection of suspects and accused persons in europe. the amendments tabled by various groups extend and clarify the aspects relating to the presumption of innocence, the burden of proof, the right not to incriminate oneself and not to cooperate, the right to remain silent, the right to be present at one's own trial and the right to a retrial, substantially amending the commission proposal, which contained unacceptable aspects such as the inversion of the burden of proof, the admission, in certain circumstances, of the use of coercion to obtain information or the admission of the 'tactical' waiver of being present at one's own trial. we voted for the resolution.
in writing. ‒ my congratulations to nathalie griesbeck for the excellent work and the agreement reached in the libe committee on the presumption of innocence and the right to be present at the trial itself in criminal proceedings. the directive shall apply to all stages of criminal proceedings until the final determination as to whether or not the person concerned has committed the criminal offence in question has been made. in addition, member states shall ensure that suspects and accused persons are presumed innocent until proven guilty in accordance with the law.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this agreement at first reading reached with the council on the proposal for a directive presented by the commission in november 2013 on the presumption of innocence and the right to be present at the trial itself in criminal proceedings. this proposal, which forms part of the package of procedural guarantees, contributes to strengthening the right to a fair trial in criminal proceedings by establishing minimum standards on certain aspects of the presumption of innocence and the right to be present at trial, and to ensuring that suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings in the member states enjoy, throughout the union, a high common level of protection and full respect for procedural guarantees, without prejudice to the application in a given member state of rules which offer greater protection. by establishing such minimum standards on the protection of the procedural rights of suspects or accused persons, the confidence of member states in the criminal justice systems of other member states will be strengthened and thereby contribute to facilitating the mutual recognition of judicial decisions in criminal matters.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this agreement reached at first reading with the council on the regulation on gaseous fuel appliances and equipment which are new to the union market at the time of their placing on the market. this regulation, which adapts the current legislation to the provisions of the product package adopted in 2008, and in particular to decision no 768/2008/ec on a common framework for the marketing of products, applies to domestic and non-domestic gaseous fuel appliances intended for a number of specific applications and to equipment designed to be incorporated into such appliances. the new legislation establishes harmonised rules for the placing on the market of these products and for the protection of consumers when using these products, in particular the prevention of gas poisoning and the leakage of any substance harmful to health and safety.
in writing. ‒ i have supported the proposal for a regulation on gaseous fuel appliances, which is intended to replace directive 2009/142/ec. the change in legal instrument from a directive to a regulation is in line with the general political commitment to work towards better regulation and simplification of the regulatory environment and is aimed at ensuring the proper functioning of the internal market for gas appliances. it lays down clear and detailed rules which will be applied uniformly and simultaneously throughout the eu. we should also not forget that the gas sector plays an important role in the eu economy and, in the gas appliance sector alone, employs 476 000 people.
in writing. ‒ the regulation adapts the current legislation to the provisions of the product package adopted in 2008, and in particular to decision no 768/2008/ec on a common framework for the marketing of products. it applies to domestic and non-domestic gaseous fuel appliances intended for a number of specific applications and to equipment designed to be incorporated into such appliances. it concerns the placing on the market of these products and the protection of consumers when using these products. my group considers the final agreement reasonable, and i have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ the generalised system of preferences (gsp) is a key trade instrument of the community's development aid policy, through which the european union provides preferential access to the community market for products originating in developing countries and territories by granting full or partial exemption from customs duties. with this instrument, the eu aims to contribute to reducing poverty in developing countries, while guaranteeing fundamental human rights and promoting sustainable development. the inclusion of a country in the generalised system of preferences requires an individual assessment of compliance with the requirements of the regulation, including ratification of a number of international conventions, as well as monitoring of compliance with such requirements. kyrgyzstan is currently a beneficiary of the generalised system of preferences (gsp) but on 25 november 2015 the commission decided to propose granting its access to gsp+ and i therefore voted against the proposal to object to its granting.

madam president, according to the eurobarometer survey of may 2015, citizens' trust in the european union is only 40%, and this is due to many reasons: the refugee crisis, the troika's austerity policies, the abandonment of rural areas, the defence of 'fracking' and above all the lack of support in such serious issues as thalidomide or hepatitis c. we in the committee on petitions are very familiar with these problems and that is why we are calling on the european commission to get more involved, to give appropriate answers and to stop throwing balls, to be more agile. remember that our role is to listen and provide political solutions to real problems and not to be mere technocrats.
in writing. since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon on 1 december 2009, the charter of fundamental rights of the european union is a legally binding instrument. it allows citizens to raise concerns with the european parliament about the impact of eu policies and legislation on their daily lives. the main policies addressed by the petitioners are justice and fundamental rights, the environment and the internal market. the commission's initiative to bring together formal and informal complaint mechanisms on a 'your rights' page is an important step forward. however, the distinction between formal mechanisms (complaints to the commission, petitions to the european parliament and complaints to the european ombudsman) and informal mechanisms (solvit, ecsc network, fin-net) needs to be better clarified for citizens. on the other hand, an analysis of the statistics shows that the main reasons for declaring petitions inadmissible are that petitioners continue to confuse european union competences with national competences, and that they confuse the institutions of the european union with those of the council of europe, in particular the european court of human rights.
in writing. ‒ the stabilisation and association agreement between the eu and the self-proclaimed republic of kosovo establishes contractual relations between the parties in the field of political dialogue and trade relations. although five eu member states have not recognised kosovo, the region has been officially considered as a potential candidate for eu membership since the european council gave it a 'european perspective' in 2003. this eu-kosovo stabilisation and association agreement, which would enter into force upon completion of the ratification procedure, is considered a significant formal step towards kosovo's accession to the eu. however, i voted against the proposal to approve this agreement, because by this agreement the eu implicitly recognises kosovo as a state, as well as its unilateral declaration of independence, in violation of un security council resolution 1244/1999. it is intolerable that the european parliament should try to put pressure on member states, including spain, which do not recognise kosovo, which is a political interference in the powers of the states. in addition, this agreement implies the creation of a free trade area, which i also reject.
in writing. ‒ we abstain in this vote because, although the international court of justice concluded that the unilateral declaration of independence of kosovo did not violate international law or un security council resolution 1244/1999 and that the process of state-building in kosovo is irreversible, the opinion does not imply that the former province has a well-founded right to be recognised by third parties. the situation in kosovo has a complex political background and must therefore be addressed and resolved politically, by means of an agreement which in any case includes serbia, which neutralizes serbian and kosovar nationalism, which constitutes a permanent internal threat to peace, which safeguards the rights of ethnic minorities in the area and which guarantees the withdrawal of foreign military powers from the area in the medium term. the stabilisation and association agreement which the council proposes to endorse and which is mainly aimed at 'deepening economic and trade relations' is therefore premature and fails to prioritise actions leading to real and lasting stabilisation of the area.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the outcome of the vote on the eu-kosovo association agreement. it's an important step for the recognition of the country. i hope that today's vote will serve to convince the six eu member states which have not yet recognised kosovo to do so.
in writing. ‒ the stabilisation and association agreement (saa) between the eu and kosovo was negotiated between october 2013 and may 2014 and initialled in july 2014. in october 2015 the council agreed to its signature by 27 october 2015. the assembly of kosovo ratified it on 2 november 2015. since the unilateral declaration of independence of kosovo in 2008, spain has maintained the same position, defending the principles of territorial integrity of states and respect for the rule of law, principles on which the european union is also based. exercising the discretion allowed by international law, the spanish government did not recognise the unilateral declaration of independence, considering it contrary to international law, by violating the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity recognised to serbia and guaranteed by the helsinki final act. in line with the position of the spanish state and in the interests of a constructive attitude so as not to block an agreement which will introduce measures which will benefit the kosovar people, i have decided to abstain from voting.

in writing. ‒ the volkswagen emissions scandal has once again exposed the complicity of the commission and the member states with the large multinational groups, since leaks to the press have shown that they knew about the manipulation of emission limits long before the us environmental agency uncovered the scandal. these responsibilities and political connections need to be clarified urgently as the commission plans to legislate again on emission limits and to reformulate (downwards and with the participation of the multinationals themselves) transatlantic automotive regulation through ttip. i think this is a fundamental issue, not only because of the serious impact of emissions on the quality of life of europeans (especially in urban areas) but because the scale of the scandal is such that the future of the car industry and its workers in europe is at stake. the setting up of a committee of inquiry should make it possible to clarify responsibilities and lay the foundations for an environmentally and socially sustainable industrial policy. this is a technical vote to complete the appointments to the committee of inquiry, whose mandate was formally approved at the previous session.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament must work effectively to ensure that eu emissions legislation is complied with. that is why it is great news that a committee is being set up so that we can know everything that has happened in relation to the infringements by vehicle manufacturers and the role of the institutions in this whole matter. i support the list of members who will form this body and i hope that their work will help to clarify everything that has happened.

in writing. ‒ i voted against the resolution in favour of the association agreements and the deep and broad free trade agreements between the eu and georgia, moldova and ukraine, since i am convinced that the eu is pursuing a policy of expanding its geopolitical interests and the sphere of influence of the eu and nato in the area with a will to confront russia. such trade agreements in themselves pave the way for putting european business interests ahead of those of the peoples of the various countries. in the case of ukraine, much further afield, the drive to expand the eu's sphere of control has been the key factor in triggering the coup in ukraine and the civil war in the country. since i strongly condemn the escalation of tensions with russia and the presence of nato in the area, i have wanted to express my rejection of these agreements, which harm the local population and, moreover, endanger peace in the region, by voting against.

in writing. ‒ i voted against the european parliament's joint motion for a resolution in favour of the activation of the mutual defence clause requested by france on the pretext of the recent attacks in paris, since this move, if carried out, will reinforce the process of converting the european union into a military alliance. this is the wrong response to the paris attacks. france's interpretation is biased and intentional since a terrorist attack is not an act of war no matter how much they try. its interpretation is a fraud on international law and a return to the logic of the war on terror. in the face of terrorism, there is only civil response, police action, intelligence, cutting off the funding of terrorist groups and cutting off international support. in any case, the answer must always be within the rule of law and these acts cannot be used as a pretext for a collective curtailment of individual freedoms.
in writing. ‒ we reject the activation of article 42 (7) teu as an ineffective military response with a high risk of further innocent victims, further displacement of populations and further destruction of territories. we advocate diplomatic structural solutions, development cooperation and peaceful conflict resolution in the framework of international law outside the eu; within the eu, we advocate actions that prioritize investigation and police action with full respect for human rights and individual freedoms, as well as adequate and sufficient public policies of integration and intercultural building.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this resolution on the mutual defence clause which condemns in the strongest terms the heinous terrorist attacks perpetrated by daesh and conveys our deep sympathy and solidarity as well as our condolences to all the victims of the terrorist attacks and their families.
in writing. ‒ following the paris attacks of 13 november 2015, the french government activated the mutual defence clause of article 42 (7) teu, by which the member states of the union must provide aid and assistance in the event of armed aggression against one of them. this is the first time that this mutual assistance clause has been used and it is not clear what developments and consequences it will entail. in the absence of protocols setting out what to do, the assistance from the member states is in most cases undefined and has not translated into concrete operational measures, with some exceptions. this joint motion for a resolution seeks to strengthen the mechanism and to call for the establishment of a protocol and practical measures for more effective implementation in the future; it also recalls, as does the treaty itself, that all armed action must in any case respect the charter of the united nations, and also respect human rights and international provisions on humanitarian law. i therefore voted in favour of this joint motion for a resolution.

in writing. ‒ today, other political groups made the same strategic mistake as france and the eu member states: to link the terrible paris attacks, which were mainly committed by eu citizens, to military interventions abroad. the majority in the ep went even further than france and the member states: they presented and adopted a resolution which calls for using the terrorist attacks and the activation of article 42(7) teu for far—reaching institutional changes – the establishment of a permanent eu military headquarter, a defence union for collective defence like nato, the activation of the structured cooperation of article 44 teu and further aspects of military cooperation in the field of csdp. greens/efa would have preferred and supported the activation of article 222 tfeu, which is specifically designed for responding to terrorist attacks on the territory of an eu member state and which relies on a criminal justice approach to terrorism by making use of eu instruments, procedures and funds. the way chosen by france and the member states weakens eu institutions, values and principles, including cfsp and csdp.

in writing. ‒ i voted against the joint motion for a resolution on the eu's priorities for the sessions of the united nations human rights council in 2016 (2015/3035 ((rsp)) because, while there are important issues mentioned in the afterword of the joint resolution on mechanisms for the defence of international law and human rights, i do not agree that the european union should have an increasing role within the united nations, which would entail a decrease in the national sovereignty of the member states. i also do not share the analysis of the situation, the condemnation of venezuela and the exploitation of human rights by the european union, which prevents me from supporting this joint motion for a resolution.

mr president, since podemos we have always been a full-fledged defender of citizen participation. we are celebrating the right to petition by voting in favour, but above all we are celebrating the great involvement of european citizens in the political debate. i want to mention two facts: first, that spain is the country that sends the most requests (449 in 2014), which is a reflection of the social empowerment experienced after the 15 m, and secondly, the high number of requests on environmental and energy issues, especially on fracking and energy prospections in the canary islands. we are not, however, giving up our complaint that the current european institutional architecture is openly undemocratic. only three of the 31 european citizens' initiatives have come to fruition, and of these, only one has so far got the european commission moving. people have said it in every corner of europe: we want to build together a more democratic and fully participatory europe. it is possible, your honours.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i consider it to be a good reflection of the activities carried out by the committee on petitions during 2014, since, thanks to the fact that many of the amendments tabled by the gue/ngl group were approved, significant issues have been taken up which were the subject of numerous petitions: the rejection of the atci and the opacity of the negotiations, the citizens' opposition to 'fracking' or the complaints which moved dozens of europeans to the eu's migration, trade and foreign policies. i also welcome the fact that the report contains a number of specific requests for improvements in the handling of petitions, such as: increased resources for the secretariat of the committee on petitions, greater involvement of the european commission in analysing petitions or improvements to the website so that petitioners can have up-to-date information on the handling of their petitions. finally, i think it is important to note the call in the report for the regulation governing european citizens' initiatives to be revised so that it can truly be an instrument for greater participation by citizens in the european decision-making process.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it contains the main activities and data highlighted by the requests received. i would like to stress the special value and importance of the committee on petitions, because it is the real window open to the citizens. the fact that more than half a billion europeans can bring their demands directly to the house and set the political agenda is of unique value. it is worth noting that countries such as my own, spain, are leading the way year after year in terms of requests (as well as infringements and sanctions received) for breaching european legislation. the government should take note, as it is largely responsible for this. finally, i would stress paragraph 21, where we regret that the charter of fundamental rights has not been adopted in all the member states and that its application is confused. and i also regret the strict interpretation of article 51 of the charter, under which the european commission has repeatedly declared itself incapable of acting in the field of fundamental rights. we must enforce the charter and adopt a new approach to its interpretation, since by definition fundamental rights must be defended against all odds.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on the activities of the committee on petitions during 2014, but i disagreed with my group in two votes. i voted against amendment no 4 by the green group, because i think the original text is more appropriate, since it considers that parliament has an obligation to ensure that an unjustifiably long period of time does not elapse in order to declare inadmissible or to close the files on petitions that are not admissible. i also supported paragraph 44, which refers to the visit to this committee by a delegation from the scottish parliament, because this kind of collaboration can improve the exchange of good practice.
in writing. ‒ the committee on petitions acts as a bridge between citizens and the european institutions. the treaties of the union guarantee all european citizens the right to address the european parliament in writing to address the various problems they may face in their daily lives, provided that the issues raised are within the eu's sphere of competence. it also plays an important role in helping to identify problems in the practical application of union law. the european parliament has an obligation to ensure that all the rights and opportunities created by european legislation become a reality and benefit all citizens of europe. the report details the work of this commission and i voted in favour of it.

member of the commission, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– mr president, i would like to thank everyone for their contributions to this discussion leading up to the european parliament’s resolution today. we share the concerns raised by many of you. two years of uncertainty have contributed to the agony of all involved. we have followed closely the situation of the estonian and uk security guards, liaising with the estonian and uk authorities, as it pertains to the protection of eu citizens. this case has been raised by the eu with indian interlocutors several times over the last few months. this case has a negative bearing on the global fight against piracy at a time when we, the international community, should foster cooperation and focus on countering new threats. we have recently learned that a tamil nadu court has sentenced the guards to five years in prison and a fine, reversing the lower court’s acquittal. we understand that they are now considering an appeal to the court’s decision; this came as unexpected news. allow me to fully subscribe to what the estonian foreign minister, ms marina kaljurand, has said: ‘from a human standpoint, i was undoubtedly hoping for a positive outcome, but regardless of the verdict we will continue to act in the name of returning the men home’. a solution must be found at the earliest. we will continue to liaise with estonian and uk authorities in the coming weeks, during the next phases of the judicial process. as regards the case of the two italian marines, while fully respecting the content and scope of the european parliament resolution to be voted on today, i wish to reiterate that a solution must be found at the earliest. the european union has been regularly raising this issue for the past four years at all levels with indian interlocutors, always with the same message, advocating a rapid and consensual solution in respect with international law. respect of international law means not only full compliance with the un convention on the law of the sea (unclos), but also with the un conventions on human rights. the decision to initiate an international arbitration in the framework of unclos is consistent with international law and a step in the right direction. you can rest assured that we will continue to monitor the situation of all eu citizens under detention in india and coordinate further actions with the member states.
author. - mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate ourselves on the degree of consensus we have achieved in adopting this resolution. it is true that this is a long and complex resolution, and that is inevitable when we talk about ethiopia. there is a very clear starting point, which is what we want to denounce here: the government repression of peaceful demonstrations by farmers and herders protesting against the attempt to enlarge the addis ababa municipality, an attempt that fundamentally affected their way of life and that exposed them to being left out in the open. these demonstrations were brutally suppressed and, according to human rights defenders, resulted in at least 140 deaths. that is the urgent point that brings us here today. but it was also inevitable, and that's why the extension of this resolution, to contextualize, to talk about what is happening, in general, in ethiopia. and what is ethiopia right now? a country with a failed democracy, hijacked by a one-party regime. a country where the repression of various ethnic groups, such as the oromo and ogaden, is systematically practised. a country full of displaced people, of refugees, many of whom are fleeing to our europe. a country where anti-terrorist laws are applied which restrict freedom of expression, where arbitrary arrests are made, where members of ngos are persecuted and where citizens of the european union are also imprisoned. it is true that it has a key role in the region, but that should not be an excuse for our position, the position of the european union, which must demand attention and compliance with all the human rights provisions that are in the ethiopian constitution itself. ethiopia is also one of the poorest countries in the world. those of us who have been there have seen levels of misery that i don't think can be surpassed. and the european union is the first aid donor to ethiopia. we must use this role to force the ethiopian government to fulfil its commitments in defence of human rights. if we do not, we will be giving up one of the fundamental roles of the european union.

member of the commission.– mr president, the commission would like to thank parliament for the broad engagement – so many committees engaged in the tisa negotiations – and, of course the rapporteur, mrs reding, for the work she has done on this, as well as the shadow rapporteurs. it is very important for us to make sure that we negotiate this in close cooperation with the european parliament. as you know, services account for about 70% of our gdp, but they represent only 25% of our external trade. so tisa is a tool to try to redress that imbalance and open up foreign markets to eu suppliers. this week, as we speak, negotiators from 23 wto members are meeting in geneva for the 16th negotiation round of tisa. we welcome the progress achieved to date, especially in the autumn: a lot of progress has been made, and we hope to continue on this positive track. i had the possibility to meet almost all ministers whose countries are engaged in tisa in davos. we took stock of where we are. there was a positive atmosphere, and many countries wanted to bring these negotiations to an end this year. this is an ambitious, realistic tool, but, of course, for us the content is more important than speed. having a very ambitious work plan ahead of us, we appreciate the support and recommendations that the european parliament has included in the draft resolution to be voted on wednesday. we would certainly take your views into account, as much as possible, as the negotiations progress. as you point out in the resolution, tisa aims to unleash the untapped potential of more integral global services markets. it could give us a unique possibility to address the existing barriers to the international trade in services that are impeding the expansion of services export. we aim to develop strong, transparent and effective rules across the different sectors that are crucial in enabling global services trade in tisa. this is also an important contribution to the multilateral trade agenda, in particular in a situation where plurilateral deals are meant to play an increasing role in the post-nairobi context. so we fully agree with you – and this is important for me personally – that there should be as broad a participation as possible in tisa so that we can work towards future multilateralisation. as you know, today 23 countries participate in the negotiations, and that represents 70% of global services trade. but we should keep the doors open for more applicants, notably towards large, emerging economies such as china. it would bring tisa towards the critical mass required for the multilateralisation of the deal. with this in mind the eu has been leading the efforts to design the proposal and the architecture of tisa so it would be fully compatible with the gats agreement and thus facilitate future multilateralisation. i am pleased to hear that the european parliament has appreciated the efforts of transparency. thank you for pushing on this, and we will continuously try to enhance that. you now receive all negotiation documents, as does the council. the chief negotiator regularly delivers extensive briefings to the inta monitoring group led by the rapporteur mrs reding, and we are in regular dialogue with civil society. in addition we have ensured that all the reports from the negotiating rounds are available on the internet. i would like to reassure you on some of the points that you raised in the resolution and some of the concerns. the draft resolution calls for horizontal carve-outs accepted by all tisa participants on public services and an assurance that tisa parties subscribe to the ilo conventions. however, if we want to see tisa multilateralised in the framework in the future, we need to base it on the scope of the gats, and gats does not contain such broad carve-outs or requirements to subscribe to other international conventions or law which developing and emerging countries would want to see if they joined tisa, and they will have difficulties to subscribe to this. but that does, of course, not exclude us in other fora working with countries for them subscribing to the ilo conventions. secondly, and this is very important, public services, culture, labour rights – it is my firm intention, and this is for the whole negotiating team, to ensure that we remain able to unilaterally, here in europe, decide on the level of protection we want to have. in particular, the eu will never compromise on the essential role of the widest discretion of national, local and regional authorities in providing, commissioning and organising public services as guaranteed in the eu treaty. this is our approach and that will remain. third, i note that the draft resolution recommends limited trade liberalisation commitment in cross-border trade: the so-called mode 1. we will pursue a very cautious approach here, for instance, in some sectors such as financial services. however, in other sectors like digital services, which represent growth potential – especially for us, it is an offensive interest – the cross-border nature is so inherent to the technology that it would not be in the eu’s interest to limit our commitments. fourth, data protection is a fundamental right of the eu. tisa will not jeopardise it. finally, let me say that we have come to a compromise on the e-tisa architecture as a result of very difficult negotiations, and any changes to ratchet and standstill clauses here would bring us back to day one. but be assured that these clauses only apply to a right to discriminate between foreign and domestic companies – what we call national treatment – and not to liberalisation, meaning market access commitment. in addition, we also deploy broad carve-outs for sectors which we consider genuinely sensitive. so i consider this resolution as a strong signal of support by the european parliament to continue and to conclude tisa negotiations. you have clearly marked your red lines and your input here, so allow me to thank you for this and also for all the opinions given by the different committees and to pledge my full cooperation with the european parliament in the future as we push for a conclusion of this agreement.
