in writing. ‒ we socialists support the launch of trade negotiations with tunisia, as a show of support and solidarity to a neighbouring country which has made enormous progress since the arab spring and is immersed in a difficult transition process. we demand, in principle, that trade negotiations be used as a tool to regulate sustainable development objectives and respect for human rights at international level, promoting the highest standards of labour, social, health and environmental protection. as regards the economic conditions of the agreement, we demand special and differentiated attention to the circumstances of tunisia, with progressive and asymmetric clauses that allow it to be properly opened up internationally, by stages and sectors. we want a progressive trade agreement which brings clear benefits to all tunisian and european societies. we therefore call once again for maximum transparency, for the agreement to be linked to the fight against corruption and for the tunisian and european civil societies to be fully involved in the negotiation process. we will continue to advocate for debt relief for the former regime and the creation of a joint civil forum that allows citizens to evaluate and monitor compliance with human rights and sustainability clauses.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the recommendation in favour of opening negotiations on a free trade agreement between the european union and tunisia, since i am convinced that such agreements involve the liberalisation of trade not only in agricultural products but also in services, affecting basic social rights. the european union has also refused to promote an international audit of the odious debt of the ben ali regime, which the tunisian people are still bearing today. in addition, the negotiation of this agreement does not take account of the asymmetries and does not involve the participation of tunisian social organizations and trade unions. i therefore voted against this agreement, because i believe that it is only in the interests of large companies and has a negative impact on workers and small producers on both sides, both tunisian olive oil producers and those in southern european countries.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it supports the opening of a free trade agreement which can only push the current neoliberal model and its contradictions further. prior empirical experience shows that there is a great potential for fostering social imbalances in a country whose situation is already sensitive.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this motion for a resolution on the opening of negotiations on the eu-tunisia free trade agreement. it begins by strongly condemning the terrorist attacks in tunisia in recent months and by referring to the fact that the tunisian economy is facing major difficulties. the union and tunisia also have a clear demographic and economic imbalance which justifies the adoption of an asymmetric and progressive approach in the negotiations.

i supported this report, which describes the ombudsman's work in great detail. i must say that i welcome the fact that the ombudsman's activities are increasing. i also welcome the fact that the eu institutions generally respond positively to the ombudsman's initiatives, because the ombudsman is 'useless' if his recommendations and opinions are not taken seriously by the competent authorities concerned by his recommendations. here i think it is good news that 80% of the ombudsman's initiatives have been taken into account by the european authorities. there's still a 20% reserve, and that's what i think we need to work on, and hopefully that 20% number will decrease in the future. what i consider important is that citizens can contact the ombudsman electronically through the website, because easy access to the ombudsman is the basis for the success of this institution, and i therefore welcome the increase in initiatives and the ombudsman's electronic communication with eu citizens.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the annual report on the activities of the ombudsman's office as the work carried out by mrs o'reilly in 2014 deserves recognition for modernising the institutions and bringing them closer to the citizens in these times of political and social conflict. i would like to highlight the ombudsman's use of her capacity to conduct inquiries of her own motion as she has done in the revolving door cases, transparency in clinical trials and in the atci negotiations. special mention should be made of the push made in 2014 by both the ombudsman and the vice-president of the european commission, frans timmermmans, to register interest groups, where more than 7000 organisations have already been registered. this register provides transparency for the work of the european parliament and all the european institutions. the work of the ombudsman's office during this period has helped to improve the functioning of all the institutions by focusing on possible instances of maladministration and recommending solutions, solutions which have been adopted by 80% of the bodies investigated.
in writing. ‒ this motion for a resolution builds on the annual report submitted by the ombudsman. specifically, it refers to his work during 2014. the motion for a resolution stresses several positive elements of the ombudsman's work, in a general context of growing public distrust of the european union. this is the case, for example, of the investigation into the 'revolving doors' within the european commission, the breach of access to information by the european institutions or the recommendation to create a mechanism to deal with the infringement of individual rights by frontex. the need to increase resources for the ombudsman's office is also highlighted and that 20% of cases of non-compliance with recommendations still persist. however, i have decided to abstain as our amendments on such sensitive issues as the dual use (civil and military) of european funds to third countries participating in the horizon 2020 programme (such as israel), or the end of frontex's joint deportation policies have not been taken up. i also think it is wrong to congratulate the european commission on its transparency in the negotiations on the att, for obvious reasons.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it highlights the great work and enormous effort that the ombudsman's institution put into 2014. this work has highlighted the need to continue to improve and improve the functioning of european public administration, in such sensitive areas as revolving doors, improving the transparency of negotiations (including the atci) and the critical and constructive approach to the work carried out by frontex, as well as the permanent defence of the fundamental rights of europeans. through this report i also want to thank and acknowledge the ombudsman for her work on the migration and asylum issue, where she has highlighted the defence of european values and the need for a common response from the outset.
in writing. ‒ i abstained on this report. the report on the ombudsman's activities is quite positive, and we also assess positively the ombudsman's performance in 2014. but we disagree with certain views expressed in the report, such as 'the celebration' of 'the progress achieved on transparency' in the atci negotiations, or the lukewarmness with which it refers to frontex, the hot returns and the lack of rights for refugees in this crisis context. our group tabled amendments to this text on these issues, but they did not go through, so we are obliged not to give our full support to the report. however, we welcome the ombudsman's work in defending citizens' rights and her work in creating a network between the different levels of the eu.

in writing. ‒ the european parliament intends to continue to support and promote the ombudsman and his activities. the european objective is to ensure that the union's institutions provide the best possible public service to citizens and to ensure that their rights are respected. the ombudsman contributes to this by being empowered, as provided for in the tfeu, to receive complaints concerning maladministration in the activities of the european institutions. the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon extends these powers to include requests for possible maladministration in the framework of the common foreign and security policy, including the common security and defence policy. when we speak of maladministration, we mean cases where a public body does not comply with the rules that have been established or when it does not comply with the principles of the european union. in this sense, cases such as the blocking of the anti-discrimination directive in the council or the non-ratification of the marrakesh treaty could fall within the scope of the ombudsman's duties.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the annual report on the activities of the ombudsman's office as the work carried out by mrs o'reilly in 2014 deserves recognition for modernising the institutions and bringing them closer to the citizens in these times of political and social conflict. i would like to highlight the ombudsman's use of her capacity to conduct inquiries of her own motion as she has done in the revolving door cases, transparency in clinical trials and in the atci negotiations. special mention should be made of the push made in 2014 by both the ombudsman and the vice-president of the european commission, frans timmermmans, to register interest groups, where more than 7000 organisations have already been registered. this register provides transparency for the work of the european parliament and all the european institutions. the work of the ombudsman's office during this period has helped to improve the functioning of all the institutions by focusing on possible instances of maladministration and recommending solutions, solutions which have been adopted by 80% of the bodies investigated.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this annual report on the activities of the european central bank (ecb) because it supports the ecb's expansionary monetary policy, including the programme for the purchase of public debt of the member states, and the priority set in august 2012 to do everything necessary to ensure the financial stability of the euro area and the irreversibility of the single currency. i regret, however, that a negative coalition, made up of the far right, the eurosceptics, the radical left and the majority of the european people's party and the alliance of liberals and democrats, blocked amendment no 12, which was put forward by a pro-european coalition of meps from four political groups, including the author, and which called on the ecb to consider turning its profits (of the order of eur 1 billion a year) into a new resource of its own. it is in any case gratifying that the amendment has had the support of my group (socialists and democrats), and i shall therefore continue to work towards the objective of increasing the european union's own resources and, in particular, building up fiscal capacity in the euro area.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because the final result has diluted the important criticisms made by the rapporteur in the first version under discussion. the initial version of this report contained an explicit condemnation of the president of the european central bank, mario draghi, for his role in the financial extortion that this institution is subjecting the member states of the european union's periphery to. however, this initial text has been modified by the majority of the groups in this parliament, leaving an idyllic, uncritical and decaffeinated view of the activity carried out by this institution during the 2014 financial year. it is for all these reasons that i have decided to vote against this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report by the european parliament on the ecb's activity in 2014. the report contains some progressive elements, by pointing out the negative role the ecb has had in greece and the democratic deficit the ecb suffers from, and by emphasising the austerity policies the ecb has pushed. however, i voted against the report as a whole because it contains an implicit validation of the current structure of the ecb.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this report on the 2014 annual report of the european central bank. it also states that the modest, geographically unbalanced recovery forecast for the euro area in the coming years must be strengthened and that potential economic growth will need to be increased in order to reduce the high unemployment rates in many euro area member states and to alleviate the debt burden. i deferred my group's vote on amendment no 12, which asked the ecb to consider using its power of initiative to transform part of its net profits into a new own resource of the union, so as to ensure that only those member states which have adopted the single currency benefit from the net profits of the ecb. i regret that this amendment was not adopted.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this motion for a resolution because it seeks to deepen trade relations between australia and new zealand on the one hand and the european union on the other without warning of the harmful effects it will have on their economies. the agreement seeks to strengthen trade relations to offset the diversionary effect of the recent trans-pacific agreement. however, we believe that this agreement could have a fatal impact on our economy, especially on the european milk sector, which is already suffering from the disappearance of quotas and which, due to the contraction of chinese consumption, will see the milk market flooded with new zealand surpluses. this agenda of liberalizing international trade that is carried out for the benefit of multinational corporations without considering the real effect it will have on the real economy is at the root of many of our economic problems. it is for all these reasons that i have decided to vote against this motion for a resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it supports the opening of a free trade agreement which can only push the current neoliberal model and its contradictions further. the same report acknowledges the possible adverse effects that the agreement may have on social and workers' rights, but we do not find it convincing as regards the clause that would annul it if these adverse effects were to occur.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this report on the opening of negotiations on free trade agreements with australia and new zealand. i think it is very important to deepen relations with the asia-pacific region for economic growth in europe. i deferred the vote with my group on amendment no 11 by the gue/ngl group which calls for particular consideration to be given to human rights and labour, social and environmental standards. i wanted to vote for it and i was wrong. i have already made the appropriate correction in support of this amendment which differed from the line of my group.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution on the opening of negotiations on future free trade agreements with australia and new zealand which will serve to deepen trade and investment relations and contribute to economic development. although it is premature to assess the level of ambition of the agreements, we socialists demand rigorous prior impact studies, especially on the agricultural chapter, adequate public consultations, transparency in the negotiations, firm provisions on the protection of labour rights, the defence of the power of the eu and the member states to legislate in the public interest and the inclusion of a strong, binding and enforceable sustainability and human rights chapter. we also support multilateralism as a priority of eu trade policy. the commission's efforts to move forward with further bilateral negotiations should not be to the detriment of the resources it devotes to the multilateral agenda.

in writing. ‒ europe must continue to deepen relations between the eu and the asia-pacific region to foster their economic growth in europe. in this context, australia and new zealand are strategic partners and the promotion of dialogue and negotiations is necessary to improve existing bilateral agreements. i therefore consider it necessary to vote in favour of opening these negotiations.
i supported this motion for a resolution and i am very pleased that we have adopted today a declaration which will lead to the creation of common cat and dog registers in europe. this will go a long way in combating smuggling, illegal trade and the general mistreatment of these animals. for me, this is not another bureaucracy, for me it is the protection of animals and cats, which are today, unfortunately, especially in central europe, illegally artificially bred in so-called breeding houses and then smuggled into western europe. these are not isolated phenomena, but tens of thousands of poor animals that are captured, raised and then taken to western europe in cruel conditions every year. if animals are registered, then trade in animals as living creatures will be given clear rules and we will, i hope, treat animals as living creatures, not just as commodities and goods.
in writing. ‒ this motion for a resolution focuses on the harmonisation of the criteria for the registration of domestic animals and calls on the commission to put in place measures to stop the illegal trade in such animals. i have supported this motion for a resolution because i support the obligation to identify and register domestic animals to prevent their abuse and neglect, for reasons of public health and to prevent abusive practices among breeders. i also support the establishment of common criteria for the breeding and sale of domestic animals in order to guarantee minimum welfare conditions and to prevent illegal trafficking of such animals, which is often linked to organised crime. for all these reasons, i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this joint motion for a resolution to ensure that pet animals can travel in the necessary hygiene and safety conditions between the member states of the union and to prevent the illegal trafficking of exotic and wild animals.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this joint resolution on the introduction of compatible systems for the registration of pet animals in the member states. it highlights the positive contribution of pets to the lives of millions of individual owners and families across the eu. the improvements in the animal movement regime and the additional security features of the animal passport are welcome. and we must also take into account the increase in the trade, both legal and illegal, of wild animals commonly kept as pets.
in writing. ‒ a new regulation on the registration of pet animals and the conditions under which they may travel with their owners for non-commercial purposes (regulation (eu) no 576/2013) entered into force at the end of 2014. a new model passport was introduced for these animals and the requirements for vaccinations and the need for these to appear on the travel document were strengthened, which also apply to animals from third countries wishing to enter the eu. in view of the first results of the application of regulation (eu) no 576/2013, i support by my vote the proposals contained in this proposal for a european parliament resolution on the introduction of compatible pet animal registration systems in the member states.

in writing. ‒ the socialist group in parliament supports, by its vote, strong action in the face of the dramatic humanitarian situation in yemen, a crisis with enormous human consequences for 20 million people, with very serious violations of human rights, and to which the international community is not giving the necessary attention. we have voted to urge the parties to the conflict in yemen to allow immediate humanitarian and medical access and to resume peace negotiations as soon as possible in order to achieve a political solution to end the conflict. we also condemn the increasingly frequent attacks on the medical facilities of médecins sans frontières and call on the international community to ensure that medical facilities are respected as protected spaces under international humanitarian law. on the specific question of the arms embargo on saudi arabia, the socialist group has led the way in supporting its establishment. we therefore regret the vote against and the dubious ethics of the conservative part of the european parliament, which supports the transformation of wars into a macabre opportunity for commercial gain.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution on the humanitarian situation in yemen, as it clearly and unequivocally points to the military intervention led by saudi arabia as the cause of the humanitarian catastrophe. the saudi regime has used internationally banned cluster bombs and bombed civilian targets, including medical facilities, severely damaging basic infrastructure. despite attempts by the right wing of the house to prevent the vote on this motion for a resolution, i have strongly supported it, since my group also contributed to the adoption of an amendment calling on the european union to impose an arms embargo on saudi arabia for its breach of international humanitarian law. unfortunately, my country, thanks in part to the very close relations between the spanish royal family and the saudi dynasty, is one of the main suppliers of arms to the saudi regime. i will continue to denounce it and i hope that this resolution will help bring this arms sale to an end.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the joint motion for a resolution because i believe that the european union should strongly promote compliance with international humanitarian law, as provided for in the relevant eu guidelines, and that, in its relations with saudi arabia, it should give priority to the need to comply with international humanitarian law over other considerations (trade, geostrategic, etc.) and, should such dialogue fail to produce results, should evaluate other measures in line with the eu guidelines to promote compliance with international humanitarian law.
in writing. ‒ i would like to thank the members who negotiated this resolution on the humanitarian situation in yemen. i voted in favour of it, while supporting the amendment tabled by my group to impose an eu arms embargo on saudi arabia in view of the serious allegations of violations of international humanitarian law by this country in yemen.
in writing. ‒ the situation in yemen is becoming more dramatic by the day. according to the united nations, 80 percent of its population is in need of some form of humanitarian aid and 47 percent live below the poverty line. the conflict has already left 2.5 million people displaced, 14.4 million in need of food aid and almost 20 million in urgent need of access to healthcare. to address this situation, i voted in favour of both the amendment which envisages an eu arms embargo on saudi arabia and the joint resolution which stresses the importance of preserving the unity, sovereignty and integrity of yemen through the search for a negotiated, inclusive political solution.
in writing. ‒ the socialist group in parliament supports, by its vote, strong action in the face of the dramatic humanitarian situation in yemen, a crisis with enormous human consequences for 20 million people, with very serious violations of human rights, and to which the international community is not giving the necessary attention. we have voted to urge the parties to the conflict in yemen to allow immediate humanitarian and medical access and to resume peace negotiations as soon as possible in order to achieve a political solution to end the conflict. we also condemn the increasingly frequent attacks on the medical facilities of médecins sans frontières and call on the international community to ensure that medical facilities are respected as protected spaces under international humanitarian law. on the specific question of the arms embargo on saudi arabia, the socialist group has led the way in supporting its establishment. we therefore regret the vote against and the dubious ethics of the conservative part of the european parliament, which supports the transformation of wars into a macabre opportunity for commercial gain.

madam president, ports are a fundamental component of the creation of an integrated and efficient transeuropean network, serving the citizens and industry of the european union. the european commission is aware of this, and has therefore made two attempts - this will be the third - to improve its functioning. but what it initially sought (more competition, transparency, equal treatment, freedom of establishment, social protection and efficiency) has been transformed into a tailor-made suit, full of exceptions, opaque, designed for certain ports and disconnected from the reality of the logistics chain. the report also interferes with the member states' powers which are part of their essential economic constitution. in the case of spain, ports are part of the public domain. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the use of the internet is not subject to any restrictions. i'm sorry about that. the spanish delegation of the ppe will vote against this report tomorrow, because it leads to the isolation of ports from the transport network, it does not respond to the general interest and it does not respect the constitutional provisions of the member states. we're sorry about that. some people say that this third attempt will be the only one that will be viable, but, commissioner, it will not be because of your ambition, but quite the opposite. the modernisation of ports in europe will remain an open question and will not allow for commodity, i.e. symbiosis between different modes of transport.
madam president, the efficiency of european ports is one of the keys to the union's competitiveness. we therefore support this report, which adds efficiency, financial transparency and autonomy to the management of these infrastructures, promotes efficiency and competitiveness on equal terms for all, wants to lighten customs bureaucracy without losing control, better protects the rights of users and workers of ports and ensures that some essential services, such as piloting, fulfil their public interest functions without private interference. we hope that port autonomy, expressed in different management models, professionalism and free competition will encourage innovation and the creation of new and better services. we therefore oppose exceptions which allow some states to centralize price policy through fees, a practice which prevents ports, without losing their status as public authorities, from setting their rates with full autonomy. the european trade associations also consider that it is clearly detrimental to the competitiveness of those who suffer from this restriction and a threat to the autonomy and transparency of all ports in the union.
madam president, i would like to point out one element which is fundamental for our group and that is that the centre of gravity of this report has been shifted from the obsession with liberalization to the labour and social aspects. the liberalization - better called privatization - of ports, railways and public services in general does not free, on the contrary, condemns the social model, because the benefits are only obtained by deteriorating working conditions and the quality of service. when the interests of large companies are put before those of individuals, the result is that the social dumping of the most socially dumping competitors within europe is finally combated. that's not our model, that's not our solution. the way forward is to achieve more efficient, transparent and environmentally sustainable ports without degrading working conditions or the quality of service.
madam president, the commission must listen to the firm stand of this house and of the port workers against the liberalization of the sector and must act at once against those states which ignore the european norm when new social standards are defined. we believe that this proposal improves working conditions in ports, something we have already called for in the opinion of the committee on employment. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. but we must be careful: these rights must apply equally to workers in public and private ports. we are firmly opposed to the exclusions now being demanded by the right. and there are still problems to be solved, for example, the insufficient protection of workers in the event of transfer of service and the obstacles to public financing of ports. in this respect, we consider it particularly serious that the need to ensure public control of key infrastructures such as ports can be called into question.
madam president, this port regulation is a very good attempt to set a level playing field for all european ports and also to enhance their competitiveness. business as usual in some member states has until now protected the interests of the centralised port bureaucracy of some member states instead of the interest of consumers, enterprises and economic growth. europe needs to be successful in sharing best practices, like the ports’ fiscal autonomy, among the more reluctant reformers of the european union. as a catalan mep i welcome this report and i hope that this legislation makes it through with minimum changes in the negotiation with the council.
madam president, this is the third attempt to europeanise ports and i would like to ask what we mean by this. for commissioner kallas, who put the initial text on the table, it was a matter of applying competition rules within ports, imposing competition dynamics on the various port services, including vital services such as the drilling, which must meet safety, environmental and even labour exploitation requirements. that is why i agree with the rapporteur and parliament on this point. i am glad we excluded them from a rule that put everything in jeopardy. for the ports of the south it was also an opportunity to establish a system of transparency to avoid unfair competition between those in the north, which are historically rich because they are financed with heavy state aid, and those in the south, which do not have such aid. i was not surprised to see this morning that commissioner vestager has proposed exempting aid for port infrastructure, obviously for those who have the means. that is why my vote, also in view of the problems of the port charges in the spanish system, cannot be positive.
madam president, we are once again debating this year a budget which is becoming more and more precarious and increasingly pressing, more urgent and more ambitious. i should therefore like to thank mr javor in particular for the special emphasis he has placed on income protection, which i started some time ago. he has made it clear: in 2013 alone, vat fraud amounted to eur 168 billion, i.e. more than the entire 2016 budget. and it's absolutely impossible for that to continue. that is why it is so essential that, through olaf - but above all with the pif directive, which must include vat and must be adopted as soon as possible - there is this possibility of fighting this fraud which entails these multi-million dollar losses for a budget which needs more. madam president, assessing the impact of gender on public policy is not just a matter of modernising public policy. assessing how different public policies affect men and women differently and taking and promoting measures for equity, to achieve equal opportunities between men and women, is a fundamental human right and social justice. there are no neutral policies that are put in place without a gender perspective. that is why i welcome and celebrate this resolution which calls for all the work of the european parliament to be accompanied by a gender impact assessment and, of course, also budgets, because that is to understand society better: more efficiency, more transparency, better redistribution of resources and opportunity for greater participation and, above all, greater democracy.
madam president, hepatitis c is a silent disease affecting at least 14 million europeans, given the number of known cases, because only 25% of those infected know they are infected; the rest do not know it, but are at risk of transmitting the disease by blood, sex or mother-to-fetus. as you know, the consequences can be devastating, because this disease -- as i say, silent -- ends up in many cases developing liver cirrhosis or liver cancer. at present there is no european-level protocol to enable or enhance coordinated detection, registration, prevention and treatment by member states. in many cases, there is no such register in these member states. as you know, there is now a new drug that is able to end this disease in 97% of cases, but it poses a great challenge to health systems - in the case of spain, 18% of the pharmaceutical budget at the moment. therefore, and given that it is a devastating disease that can be eradicated, i would ask the european commission to coordinate an eradication plan to end hepatitis c in europe.
madam president, the neoliberal policies of the european primary sector are at the root of the suffering of the people of the agricultural and fisheries sectors in my country, galicia. the distribution of quotas in the encirclement, the proposed galician aquaculture law, the non-obligatory labelling of the country of origin on canned fish, as may be the case for mussels, the non-regulation of agricultural production and agricultural markets, as is currently the case for milk, the low prices of agricultural products are a good example of the deep and long crisis we are enduring in the agricultural and fisheries sectors. the european union can and must react. the common agricultural policy and the common fisheries policy must be changed urgently in order to safeguard the livelihoods of thousands and thousands of people and the future of the galician people and the poor of southern europe. there will be no future for the european union if we continue with these policies of annihilation of peoples.

member of the commission.– madam president, today is international women’s day and i happily take this occasion to discuss with you the situation of women and men in the european union. it is also described in the commission’s 2015 annual report on gender equality published today. equality between women and men is one of the union’s fundamental values; it has been present as a legal obligation in our treaties since the very beginning of the integration. our societies have progressed enormously in the past sixty years, and the position of women has advanced a great deal. women have more access to employment than ever before. there is no denying that we are moving forward. but there are still inequalities which persist. however, if we continue at this pace, it will take us another 70 years to achieve gender equality. still, for every hour of women’s work, they take home 16% less than men. still, fathers spend about an hour per day taking care of the children and the house, while mothers devote three hours. parents, and mothers far more than fathers, face such great challenges in combining their private life with their work. this threatens women’s economic independence and can lead families into poverty, especially, but not only, if the woman is the sole breadwinner of the family. this also has consequences on women’s pensions and risk of poverty in old age. nowadays, women’s pensions are 40% lower than men’s pensions on average, and this gap shows no sign of narrowing. we need to accelerate the positive changes of the previous decades, to create the kind of society where every boy and girl can thrive. please allow me to reflect on three key issues on how to move towards a more equal europe. women make up half of the european population. there are more men than women in most levels of management and supervisory positions, and there are more men than women in national parliaments in all member states, and also in this house. in the largest publicly listed companies registered in the eu countries, only a little over 20% of all board members are women. the commission’s proposal to achieve greater gender balance on boards of listed companies aims to tackle this inequality by ensuring that boards consist of at least 40% of both sexes. we must get this adopted, and you must help advocate it in the member states, which are still reluctant. secondly, we have to make it easier for european citizens to combine the responsibilities they have at work with the responsibilities they have at home. later this year, the commission intends to present a package of legislative and non-legislative proposals aimed at improving the work-life balance of employees. it will be well-rounded, dealing with the accessibility and affordability of high quality childcare, leave arrangements for fathers, mothers and carers, and flexible work arrangements. it will be an important contribution to the integration of women in the labour market, which is demographically and economically necessary. it is also an important contribution in the european growth process. and finally, there is a persisting gender-based violence. in the european union, one in three women has been physically attacked, sexually attacked or both. last week, the european commission proposed the eu’s accession to the istanbul convention, the first ever legally binding instrument to combat violence against women at international level. the accession of the eu to the istanbul convention is a key step under our ‘strategic engagement’. the convention’s holistic approach to this complex phenomenon is in tune with the eu approach. the accession of the eu will provide greater efficiency and coherence in combating and preventing violence against women where there are already common eu rules, as well as in the more effective use of eu programmes and funds. it will strengthen our common credibility and accountability externally. it will contribute to wider eu objectives of gender equality, anti—discrimination and economic growth. further, i have been working with commissioner thyssen to ensure the follow-up of the survey conducted by the fundamental rights agency (fra) in 2013. this survey on gender—based violence would be led by eurostat and carried out by national statistical offices with eu support and funding. eurostat will start working towards such a survey, as announced in its annual work programme. the strategic engagement for gender equality 2016-2019 clearly identifies all the above-mentioned areas as a priority within our work to promote gender equality, including on equal economic independence. the strategy sets out, in addition to the key actions, that gender equality will continue to be promoted through the integration of a gender-equality perspective into every aspect of eu intervention, such as the preparation, design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of policies, legal measures and spending programmes. let me conclude by underlining that improving the socio-economic situation of women and promoting actions to stop violence against women are the top priorities for the commission.

madam president, madam commissioner, i would like to express my sincere thanks to mrs honeyball and congratulate her on an excellent report, not only accurate and comprehensive but above all timely because, beyond its growing importance as a multifactorial phenomenon and the shameful paralysis of european governments to manage it in the only way possible with a common policy on borders, asylum and resettlement, something very important has changed in the refugee crisis. on the one hand, the european union, collapsed by this colossal flow, is facing, for the first time, a humanitarian crisis within its territory, which is illustrated by the commission's unprecedented initiative to allocate 700 million in humanitarian aid for this purpose. and on the other hand, now, 60 percent of the refugees and migrants who arrive are women and children -- in the middle of last year, 73 percent were men. the gender dimension of this massive displacement of people is therefore an essential factor to be taken into account. men and women are exposed to various types of vulnerability, but women and girls are particularly victims of discrimination and sexual and gender-based violence. 'illegal immigration is over' said mr tusk, president of the council, last night at the end of the umpteenth summit. and, yes, mr tusk, i was just about to say... but desperate legislation and policies to curb - not manage - irregular immigration must not prevent access to the right of asylum enshrined in article 18 of the charter of fundamental rights and which complements legal instruments such as the cedaf, the geneva convention and the istanbul convention, which we are finally going to sign as the european union.
madam president, commissioner, i would like to congratulate mrs honeyball on her courageous report. i think what makes it very clear is that refugee women are doubly victims and suffer all kinds of violence. the question is very clear: will we be heard outside this parliament? will the european council listen to us? will the member states listen to us? i'm afraid not, after the shameful deal they've made with turkey. what they want to do is close the doors to people who are suffering and who just want to survive. i would like to use these seconds to make a little vindictive memory. in 1939 - not so long ago - the swiss activist elisabeth eidenbenz founded a maternity hospital in the catalan village of elna, in southern france, to take in women fleeing the francoist terror and giving birth in the refugee camps on the beaches of algiers. children were dying of cold and infections, and it had to be these facilities that took in those poor women. in this same maternity ward, women fleeing the nazi horror later took refuge. we were the refugees not long ago. where is the historical memory? where is the european solidarity?
member of the commission.– madam president, due to the fact that we have run out of time and i gave all the important and essential information in my opening remarks, i would like to limit myself to thanking members for their comments and the discussion, and to assure this house again of the preparedness of the commission to do its best to take all efficient measures to make the life of vulnerable people coming to the eu with the wave of refugees easier, and to reflect this in all its legislation and all its steps which will follow, be it the istanbul convention, be it asylum procedures or other steps.
in writing. help us restore our dignity. this short, direct sentence was written on a small sign by a refugee in one of the thousands of refugee shelters in europe. dignity is linked to freedom and respect. women and girls make up about half of the world's refugees. they face threats on the journey of escape and risks that do not end when they reach the place they expected to be safe. refugee women, especially those with disabilities, the lgbtq community, and older women, are vulnerable at all stages of the journey, in the countries of origin, transit and destination. invisible because of her dual status as a woman and a refugee. asylum policy must be sensitive to this in order to protect the dignity on which the european construction is based.
in writing. highlighting the vulnerability of women and children in the current migration crisis is not a policy action on gender equality; beyond that, it is an awareness of an objective reality that has important implications for the management of migration flows by the european union. this report highlights the significant change in the demographics of the migration problem, with more and more women fleeing persecution in their home countries (in january 2016 the percentage went from 38% recorded the previous year to 55% according to unhcr data). but the dangers are not only there. once the journey to safety has begun, the risk situations continue and their vulnerability is accentuated, both on the journey and on arrival at the reception centres. the eu must therefore protect women, including by taking measures to take account of their situation in eu migration procedures and, above all, by creating legal and safe routes of entry into the eu to protect them from networks of exploitation and traffickers.
unhcr.– mr president, thank you for welcoming me here. it is an honour for me to be with you today to mark international women’s day and to speak about it from the perspective of the united nations’ refugee organisation. last month i was on the greek island of lesbos where i saw the hellenic coast guard bring in a boat it had just rescued at sea. the boat was carrying 200 people. most were women with children, some of them very small, many elderly and a few sick people. as they were disembarking, i spoke with several of them and they told me stories of the conflicts they fled from in syria or afghanistan, the dangers of their journey and worries about what the future would bring. they were just one of many examples of today’s global displacement crisis. over 60 million people worldwide have been forced to flee. on average, 42 500 are forced to flee their homes every day. half of them are women. even though the vast majority of these uprooted people, 86%, are in other continents, europe is now also seeing record numbers of refugees and migrants arriving on its shores. as you know very well, in 2015 a million people arrived in europe, crossing the mediterranean in unseaworthy dinghies and flimsy boats. we have all seen the images of the piles of discarded life jackets on the greek beaches of those who survived the perilous journey. more than 3 700 people did not make it: a tragic testimony of our collective failure to properly address their plight. this year, to date, 138 000 refugees and migrants have arrived in southern europe. in public opinion the image is often that of young single men arriving in europe to look for work. today, on international women’s day, i wish to report instead that nearly two-thirds are women and children, up from last year’s 41%. take for example fatima, who fled the war in syria. she was found in a state of shock in the port of the greek island of samos. she was severely traumatised and injured. she had suffered violence at the hands of the man she had been travelling with. she was taken to a hospital for treatment and there she revealed that her husband had entrusted her and their young daughter to a man she did not know to get her to a safe country in europe. during this journey the man confiscated all their travel documents, mobile phone and money. he abused fatima and denied her direct contact with her husband. fatima is just one of thousands of women and girls who are making the journey on their own, fleeing violence and persecution only to face a similar ordeal on their way to europe, a place where they had hoped and expected to find sanctuary. many desperate people worldwide view europe as a safe and prosperous place that stands up for human rights and welcomes refugees. most, for lack of better, safer alternatives choose the services of smugglers at their great risk. let me also be clear on an important fact that is often overlooked. the majority of the people arriving in europe, 88%, come from the world’s top 10 refugee producing countries, chief among them syria, afghanistan and iraq, but also eritrea and somalia. this has been, and essentially remains, a refugee movement. the number of women and children among them is increasing rapidly, as i have said, and many travel without male relatives. we also see a large number of pregnant women, or women with babies and small children, among the arrivals. a recent unhcr study found that 20% of the syrians arriving in greece were families headed by women, without husband or father. just as fatima, these women and children are exposed to abuse and sexual violence at the hands of unscrupulous smugglers or are at great risk when they travel along insecure routes, having to stay in places that lack basic security, such as parks, bus or train stations or at the road side. in greece we have seen a rapid build-up of stranded refugees and migrants, currently over 35 000, who as a result of border closures in the western balkans have been denied access into the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. this has had a direct impact on women and girls, who are suffering disproportionately and are at great risk of sexual exploitation and trafficking. we at unhcr, with our partners, support local authorities in all affected areas to improve reception conditions and to provide assistance to people in need. we have taken measures to reduce risks and help women along the way. many reception areas and transit points now have separate facilities for women and children. together with unicef and the international committee of the red cross, we have set up 20 child and family support hubs. these hubs, also known as ‘blue dots’, provide a safe place for women and children, where they can find all available services and information about their options in a single location. the hubs aim to help vulnerable women and children on the move and mitigate the risks of trauma, violence, exploitation and trafficking. however, we need more than a humanitarian response. on other continents, countries with far fewer means than europe have been responding to much larger movements of people forced to leave their homes and continue to do so. in this very chamber, exhortations to states around the world to treat refugees according to principles and in an organised manner have resonated many times. such exhortations now apply to europe. this emergency does not have to be a crisis. it can be managed. as you know, yesterday the european union heads of state or government met with turkey on the onward movement of refugees and migrants to europe. we were not party to these conversations and understand that discussions on the details are still ongoing. but as a first reaction, i am deeply concerned about any arrangement that would involve the blanket return of anyone from one country to another without spelling out the refugee protection safeguards under international law. (applause) an asylum seeker should only be returned to a third state if the responsibility for assessing the particular asylum application in substance is assumed by the third country, the asylum seeker will be protected from refoulement, and if the individual will be able to seek and, if recognised, enjoy asylum in accordance with accepted international standards, and have full and effective access to education, work, healthcare and, as necessary, social assistance. these safeguards would need to be set out legally and would need to govern any mechanism under which responsibility would be transferred for assessing an asylum claim. pre-departure screening would also need to be in place to identify heightened risk categories that may not be appropriate for return, even if the above conditions are met. turkey is already hosting nearly three million refugees and it is important for the international community to share this responsibility more widely. we welcome, of course, any initiative that promotes regular pathways of admission for refugees in significant numbers from all neighbouring countries in the region – not just turkey and not just syrian refugees – to third countries. we hope that this will happen and that it will also apply to other countries in the region that also host a considerable number of refugees, such as lebanon and jordan. in fact, unhcr has been calling on states to increase the different legal routes for the admission of syrian refugees so that they do not have to resort to people smugglers and to dangerous journeys. these pathways include resettlement, humanitarian admission, private sponsorship and refugee—friendly family reunion, as well as student scholarships and labour mobility schemes. a key opportunity to advance these solutions for syrian refugees will be on 30 march, in geneva, when unhcr will convene a high-level meeting on global responsibility sharing through pathways for admission of syrian refugees. states will be invited to pledge concrete commitments. we hope that up to 10% of the syrian refugee population in the region, which currently stands at 4.7 million, can benefit from these pathways. i still believe that to properly address the flow of refugees and migrants in europe we need a coordinated european response, based on solidarity, political leadership and the sharing of responsibilities to stabilise the situation and manage the movement of people more effectively. last friday, we presented a set of practical proposals to the european union and its member states that would help achieve that. these proposals remain valid. they focus on improving registration and referral processes, including the relocation schemes within europe. it remains imperative that relocation works and that the necessary places are made available. with the support of the commission, for which we are grateful, we also need to boost the emergency response capacity in greece. unhcr is on the ground with its partner, working closely in support of the greek authorities. finally and looking forward, we must build on the lessons we have learned. it is crucial to strengthen compliance with and uphold the standards of the common european asylum system, even in times of emergency. it is of paramount importance to prevent further suffering and loss of life and to strengthen protection safeguards for people at risk, in particular women and unaccompanied children. this includes improving search and rescue operations, developing coordinated systems to protect and help unaccompanied children, and establishing measures to prevent and respond to sexual and gender-based violence. we need a new approach to develop an effective european asylum system, not only to manage the current refugee and migrant movement, but also for the future. we have to ensure that member states located at the external borders of the european union will not continue to bear the disproportionate burden in addressing immediate reception needs. the solidarity that is so essential today for greece and italy may well be required for other states in the future. next week, the conflict in syria will enter its sixth year. more than 4.7 million people, as i have said, have sought asylum in the region and 6.5 million people are internally displaced. inside syria, it is estimated that 13.5 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance, including 4.5 million in hard—to—reach areas. with the cessation of hostilities now holding for 10 days, the united nations organisations, including unhcr, have been able to deliver some much-needed humanitarian aid to people who have suffered years of war and deprivation. meanwhile, in the neighbouring countries, despite the generosity of host governments and communities, syrian refugees are facing increasingly difficult living conditions after five years in exile. a recent study we conducted with the world bank found that in jordan and lebanon, 90% of the syrian refugees are living under the national poverty line, as they have little access to legal work and many, by now, have depleted any resources they had brought with them. at last month’s london conference, the international community pledged eur 10 billion for activities that are meant to help the refugees and the host communities in improving education and livelihood opportunities. states must now honour the pledges made at the conference. this is very urgent in stabilising the refugees in the region and we need to take advantage of the window of opportunity given to us by the cessation of hostilities in syria. but syria is not the only country in the region beset by violence. in 2015, the escalation of violence in iraq resulted in waves of new displacement. during the last two years alone, nearly 3.3 million people have been displaced across the country. sixteen percent of the people arriving in europe today are from iraq. and after more than three decades, afghans remain one of the largest refugee populations in the world, with some 2.6 million registered refugees. the vast majority of them live in pakistan and iran. an upsurge in violence in the second half of 2015 caused significant levels of displacement inside the country and across the border, including many unaccompanied children who try to reach europe. today, in afghanistan, 31 out of 34 provinces are affected by conflict, with more than one million people registered as internally displaced, an increase of 78% compared to last year. twenty-five percent of the people arriving in europe are afghans and many have urgent protection needs. elsewhere in the world, conflict continues to disrupt lives and uproot people. our refugee programmes in africa remain severely underfunded, while the number of wars and displaced people increases rapidly: northern nigeria, the central african republic, south sudan and burundi, just to name a few. the horn of africa remains the theatre of multiple displacement situations, especially somali refugees. in many of the protracted displacement situations in africa, however, we can hardly give the refugees more, and even sometimes we give them less than the bare minimum to survive. in many countries they are not allowed to work legally, so they remain dependent on very scarce aid. in south-east asia, in the bay of bengal, more than 33 000 refugees and migrants, mostly rohingya and bangladesh nationals took to smugglers boats last year. many died, the majority not from drowning as we see in the mediterranean sea, but from abuse at the hands of people smugglers, abandonment and disease. we also have a very specific refugee crisis in central america, where thousands of salvadorians, hondurans and guatemalans are fleeing deadly transnational gang violence. again, international women’s day is an opportunity to remember that most of them are women and children. they use the traditional migration routes, going north to find safety and a future, but many are indeed refugees fleeing violence, extortion and persecution. in a world riddled with conflict, mass population movement is a reality. building fences and walls to keep people out is not a solution. it will only increase the suffering of the people who have already suffered the unimaginable. (applause) and women everywhere are among the most exposed. in the face of massive displacement and arrivals, very often the first reaction of politicians is to resort to scaremongering. manipulation of public opinion and inciting hate against those who are different are unacceptable. a real response can only be based on solidarity and human rights, on responsibility sharing and respect for international law. today we celebrate the many achievements we have made on the road to gender equality and the participation of women in social, economic and political life since international women’s day was first observed in 1975. it is also a moment to think about the long way ahead to reach full parity. but it is equally a day on which to reflect on the fact that discrimination and exclusion, because of ethnicity, religion and gender, are among the main root causes of conflict and persecution and, ultimately, of forced displacement. in 27 countries, for example, women still do not have the same rights as men to confer their nationality on their children. many of the women arriving in europe come from these countries, including syria and iraq. that means that if the fathers are missing or there is no proof of paternal descent, their children will not have a nationality and are at risk of becoming stateless. this may affect access to healthcare and education, and affect their ability to return home when conditions allow. as we have said and heard countless times in the past 25 years, there are no humanitarian solutions to the political problems that are the root causes of massive forced displacement. there are no humanitarian solutions to the intractable wars, the upsurge in violence and the oppression and lack of governance in many parts of the world. we need political leadership and action, both to resolve the conflicts that cause displacement and to make sure that people like fatima and her little daughter can find the protection and safety they need without having to resort to criminal networks and smugglers who abuse and exploit them. these are not abstract concepts about which to make abstract statements. they are real, brutal facts which only courageous political leadership and considerate, forward-looking decisions based on international cooperation, respect for human rights, solidarity between states and a renewed sense of humanity can counter and redress. europe is facing a moment of truth. this is the time to reaffirm the values upon which it was built. (sustained applause)
member of the commission.– mr president, let me start by thanking the high commissioner for the wake-up call regarding the situation of women migrants today. the sheer number of people arriving on greek shores and travelling through the western balkans, and the numbers we read daily in the press, risk making us forget that these are individuals and human beings, many of them vulnerable and in need of protection: many women travelling alone despite the dangers they are facing, many mothers risking their own and their children’s lives. let me assure you that the european commission does not forget, and does not forsake its humanitarian duties. yes, we have to take control of the flows, make them more manageable and lower them. yes, we need to better manage our external borders, for the european union, for the member states and for their citizens, but also for the people arriving. yes, we need to stop – also with the help of europol – the business of smugglers that send people in their thousands every day to a possible death. instead of dangerous routes, it is our responsibility to create more legal pathways for people in need of protection to be able to come to europe directly, legally and safely. that is why i continue to call on member states not only to deliver on the resettlement commitments they made in july last year and for the turkey humanitarian admission scheme, but also to commit to more, and soon. all irregular migrants who have arrived through turkey will be returned to turkey in accordance with european and international law. for the people who are already here, we need to improve the situation. that is why we have proposed a humanitarian assistance scheme to be used within the eu. it is why we urgently need to proceed to large-scale relocations, and why we need to further develop reception capacities. and in all of these things, the unhcr is our steady and quintessential partner, and i look forward to continuing to work closely together with filippo grandi, a person who has come to lead the unhcr in the midst of the refugee crisis, and also a veteran on these issues: he is a man with commitment to the cause of refugees, and i count very much on his invaluable help. let me therefore once again welcome the close cooperation that we have established with the unhcr and express my strong appreciation of the work done by the unhcr in the current crisis. unhcr support is highly valued inside and outside europe. the european commission and the unhcr work closely together to help italy and, especially, greece in accommodating and relocating migrants, but also in resettling them from the outside. together with the unhcr we need now to ensure a quick implementation of the voluntary humanitarian scheme from turkey and to implement projects that will further improve the situation of syrians in turkey. as you know, our actions are not limited to the borders of europe. the fact that over 60 million people are refugees or internally displaced persons across the globe reminds us that we should not lose sight of the fact that migration is not a european issue only; it is a global challenge. everyone in the international community should take their share of the responsibility. all developed countries across the world should respond to the call of the united nations for resettlement from the affected regions. the pledging conference organised by the unhcr for 30 march will be the next opportunity. and we need to reflect together on how to positively address the phenomenon which characterises our era, our world: people’s mobility, a phenomenon which is expected to increase for many different reasons, to take different forms and to be directed on different routes. we cannot ignore people’s mobility. we can neither deny it, nor stop it. we need to prepare ways to respond to it without destabilising our societies, but rather by turning it into a two-way opportunity for the hosting countries and the migrants. we believe, therefore, that it is europe’s duty and in its interest to support key partners managing the migratory flows and addressing the roots causes of the displacements. dealing with the global migration crisis requires, therefore, solid partnerships, enhanced cooperation and coordination with third countries and with regional and international organisations. in other words, it needs a global strategy. in a multifaceted and complex refugee crisis like the one of today, there cannot be a one-size-fits-all approach, and it cannot be the responsibility of just one country or one stakeholder. we all need each other, and we need to work together. that is why the relationship and collaboration between the european union and the unhcr is of utmost importance. a lot of work awaits us in the coming days and months, and we are all ready and committed to do it.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, mr high commissioner, international women's day is not just about rights, it is about facts. being born a woman should be the same as being born a man, but it's not: that's a fact. in many countries of the world, women have fewer rights and fewer freedoms: that is a fact. in europe, women have the same rights and freedoms in law, but not in reality: that too is a fact. i myself, if i were a woman, would have had an infinitely more difficult time being able to come here today, on international women's day, to defend women's equality. that's a fact, too. there are many people who find the usefulness of having an international women's day debatable, but it is indisputable that there are millions of reasons, millions of facts that justify this international women's day. there are millions of girls who don't go to school because they're girls; there are millions of women who are paid less for the same work because they're women. there are millions of old women who will never retire because they are grandmothers. there are millions of women who are abused, beaten, injured, mutilated, humiliated because they are women, and many of them are even poor. in europe -- here in europe -- 3,500 women are killed every year by their partners, killed by men: eight every day, eight today. one in three women over the age of 15 has been sexually harassed at some point in her life. we have better intentions than the taliban, of course, but we have nothing to brag about. today, the un high commissioner asks us to look into the eyes of women refugees, the most vulnerable, those who flee not only from sexism, but also from war. the ones who always run away with their children - because it's so rare that it's a man who takes the children when he has to run away - the ones who are forced by the system and the mafias to be sexually exploited. those who have their own reasons for fleeing, such as genital mutilation or rape used as a weapon of war. in the last year, in the mediterranean, fleeing syria, 55 percent of the people who drowned were women and children. in the face of a humanitarian tragedy such as the one we are living through, the solutions we hear are increasingly inhumane. putting up barriers to make the inhumane flight of women with children difficult dehumanizes us, not them. a society that is incapable of feeling pity for a mother who pleads for asylum with her baby in a cardboard box is a heartless society, it is an inhuman society. it's definitely not ours. being a woman, being born a woman is a blessing. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work is a step in the right direction. in writing. ‒ i voted against the amendment proposing to reject the agreement reached between the council and parliament, thus supporting the recommendation for the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on transmissible animal diseases and amending or repealing certain acts in the field of animal health (animal health legislation). this agreement is a major improvement on the original text proposed by the commission on animal welfare and the control and eradication of diseases affecting animals, and i have therefore not supported its rejection.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the report on animal health because we think it is positive that measures are being taken to prevent and tackle outbreaks of animal diseases such as avian influenza and african swine fever, which are transmissible between animals and potentially also to humans.
in writing. ‒ i supported this report and voted against the amendment by the efdd group. i think that the agreement reached by the rapporteur, mr selimovic, from my group in this parliament is a good one. it approves new rules to curb animal communicable diseases such as avian influenza and african swine fever, which are transmissible between animals and potentially also to humans. the new rules also focus on prevention and clarify the responsibilities of farmers, commercial intermediaries, professionals, including veterinarians, and animal owners. farmers, animal owners and intermediaries shall be obliged to apply the principles of good breeding practice and prudent administration of medicinal products.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the new animal health regulation as it lays down the rules for the prevention and control of animal diseases and zoonoses. this applies to all types of animal species, both domestic and wild, and their products, as well as to means of transport and equipment which may be potential vectors of disease transmission. among the most important aspects of these rules are the creation of a system for the categorisation and prioritisation of diseases and the health actions to be applied to each disease, the strengthening of the role of each animal health actor by setting out the responsibilities of each (veterinarians, animal professionals, pet owners and competent authorities), the standardisation of requirements for the import and export of animals, animal products and by-products, the requirement that all operators participate in the reporting and surveillance systems and in the control and eradication programmes, as appropriate, and the introduction of mechanisms for farms, zones or countries to be progressively declared disease-free, thus facilitating safe trade in animals and products.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the amendment proposing to reject the agreement reached between the council and parliament, thus supporting the recommendation for the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on transmissible animal diseases and amending or repealing certain acts in the field of animal health (animal health legislation). this agreement is a major improvement on the original text proposed by the commission on animal welfare and the control and eradication of diseases affecting animals, and i have therefore not supported its rejection.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the amendment because i am in favour of the measures contained in the recommendation, as it is relevant for the eu as a whole to have a common policy on animal health. it is important, in order to develop a common set of measures in the eu, that member states collect and send to the commission the results obtained on antimicrobial resistance to medicinal products.

in writing. ‒ the committee on agriculture and rural development unanimously approved this proposal for a regulation laying down rules for the prevention and control of animal diseases which are transmissible to other animals or to humans. this proposal does not contain provisions specifically regulating animal welfare, although animal health and welfare are linked. the union has a well-developed animal welfare acquis covering different species (for example, broilers, laying hens, pigs or calves) or activities (for example, breeding, transport, slaughter, research). this animal welfare legislation must necessarily continue to be applied. the proposal invites member states to commit to collecting relevant, comparable and sufficiently detailed data on the actual use of antimicrobial medicinal products in animals and to submit these data to the commission so that more prudent use of antimicrobial medicinal products in animals can be ensured, thereby contributing to reducing the risks linked to antimicrobial resistance. for these reasons i am voting in favour of this draft legislative resolution.
in writing. ‒ my support for the new rules which will i am convinced prevent and tackle outbreaks of animal diseases such as avian influenza and african swine fever, which are transmissible between animals and potentially also to humans. we are facing a breakthrough in which we link animal and human health in a clear way, and that will mean major improvements in preventing and controlling situations that continue to produce great social and economic damage.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the new animal health regulation as it lays down the rules for the prevention and control of animal diseases and zoonoses. this applies to all types of animal species, both domestic and wild, and their products, as well as to means of transport and equipment which may be potential vectors of disease transmission. among the most important aspects of these rules are: the creation of a system for the categorisation and prioritisation of diseases and the health actions to be applied to each of them, the strengthening of the role of each of the animal health actors by setting out the responsibilities of each (veterinarians, animal professionals, pet owners and competent authorities), the standardisation of the requirements for the import and export of animals, animal products and by-products, the participation of all actors in the reporting, surveillance systems and in the control and eradication programmes, as appropriate, and the introduction of mechanisms for farms, zones or countries to be declared disease-free in a progressive manner, thus facilitating safe trade in animals and products.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this dossier because, among other things, there were key references emphasising the link between animal health and good standards of animal welfare, and the need to guard against antimicrobial resistance when carrying out disease prevention and control measures. the ‘master list’ of diseases subject to eu regulation will be put together by delegated acts and there is a commitment towards preserving biodiversity and valuable genetic resources. there is also a general requirement to avoid pain, distress and suffering when carrying out disease control measures.
in writing. ‒ we are talking about a regulation which unifies, modernises and simplifies legislation on a subject such as animal health, a highly technical but very important issue for consumers and producers. the regulation has a positive impact on the consumer and livestock sectors, but also on trade with third countries, and is the culmination of what has been agreed between producers, european bodies and national administrations in relation to the eu's animal health strategy. i therefore consider it necessary to vote in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ as statistics show, around 70% of current infectious diseases are common to animals and humans. this indicates that animal health needs to be controlled in order to safeguard the welfare of people. i believe that, as the committee on the environment has pointed out, this requires the elimination of all risk factors for disease and the adherence to the motto 'prevention is better than cure'. i therefore believe that it is necessary to study diseases from their origins and to use past events as a basis for learning, before carrying out mass sacrifices. i therefore support this report because of the benefits it brings to the health and welfare of european citizens and eu animals.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the report on the restructuring of school fruit and vegetable, banana and milk support schemes, which have a very positive impact on society in that they promote healthy eating at an early age and seek to establish direct links between the two ends of the food chain, producer and consumer, by empowering the local primary sector. in addition, indirectly, two productive sectors - milk and fruit and vegetables - account for about 30% of the union's agricultural production.
in writing. ‒ i have supported the report and the negotiation by mr tarabella on a new programme for the distribution of fruit, vegetables and milk in schools, with the aim of inculcating good eating habits in children and combating childhood obesity. the initiative will combine two existing schemes into one programme: one for the distribution of fruit and vegetables in schools and the other for the distribution of milk. as a novelty, it also provides for the education of minors so that they acquire healthy eating habits. the programme will have an annual allocation of eur 250 million, of which eur 150 million will go to the fruit and vegetables programme and the remainder to the milk and milk products programme.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the proposal for a regulation amending regulation (eu) no 1308/2013 and regulation (eu) no 1360/2013, as well as the agreement reached in the negotiations with the council, as regards the aid scheme for the distribution of fruit and vegetables, bananas and milk in school centres. issues such as childhood overweight and declining fruit and vegetable consumption are presented as being of major importance to the union, and the union should promote healthy eating habits and the consumption of local products, and continue and strengthen these school programmes. the power to adopt acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu shall be delegated to the commission in respect of the adoption of the multiannual financial framework for the period from 1 january 2017 to 31 december 2018. each member state to which such aid is to be granted should establish a strategy at national or regional level and give the necessary publicity to the intervention in the school scheme and to the grants to be used. in addition, member states will give priority to the distribution of fresh food.
