this report contains many of the amendments tabled by my group to give value to and give priority to small-scale fishing as a key economic activity for maintaining coastal areas and to recognise the role of women and the need to improve their working conditions. i have nevertheless abstained because i am not at all clear as to the intentions behind the inclusion in this report of paragraphs 34 and 35 concerning the exploitation of other resources in the sea and public-private partnerships of a transnational nature. in my view, the aspects covered in these two paragraphs represent a threat to small-scale and traditional coastal fishing. that is why i have abstained in this report.
we are glad, mr president, that a report is finally supporting and encouraging small-scale fishing and we are glad that it also includes a strengthening of the role of women, whose work has always been consistently invisible and who continue to suffer from large wage gaps. the commission cannot, of course, deviate from what is considered sustainable, especially in aquaculture. aquaculture must not under any circumstances become an excuse for big business at the expense of the work and effort of fishermen and shellfish farmers. the marine-fisheries resources are not owned by the big corporations. they belong to the whole of the citizenry and especially to those who have a deep link with it, with the sea. the people of the sea, who every day struggle to keep our fisheries sector alive throughout the value chain, those people, their needs and their livelihoods are what should be at the heart of any initiative and any policy. i hope the commission will always be clear on this.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it represents an important and necessary political boost to the maintenance and development of small-scale fishing in the regions dependent on fishing. the report calls on the commission to draw up effective legal definitions to improve support systems for small-scale, traditional and artisanal fishing in relation to the territories where it is carried out and not just in relation to the size and power of vessels. there are many traditional arts that have been considered outside these definitions because of the size of the boats when their relationship with the territory as well as their environmental impact is much smaller, for example arts such as the almadraba. i have decided to vote in favour of this report because it is a commitment to socially and environmentally more sustainable fishing.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour because the report talks about the need for a fairer allocation of quotas that takes into account the protection of the environment and the contribution of fisheries to the local economy. this is something which is already provided for in article 17 of the common fisheries policy, but which spain has been failing to comply with, as we have repeatedly denounced. the commission report also recognises that the recession has hit seafarers hard, further marginalizing the sector, and that diversification and innovation are more necessary than ever for the survival of small-scale fisheries. it is a step forward and in the right direction for europe to recognise and support the development of local communities whose livelihoods depend mainly on fishing and related activities. we also welcome her progress towards the empowerment of women seafarers throughout the fisheries value chain, whose vital work has often been invisible and remains subject to pay gaps.
in writing. ‒ this report highlights the need to define small-scale coastal fishing in a way that respects the specific characteristics of the area and is in line with the new cfp. it proposes a series of measures to encourage innovation and economic diversification in the artisanal fisheries sector. in this context, the capacity of small-scale fishing to provide a social backbone for certain communities is examined in depth, and the economic and social crisis affecting it is taken into account, particularly because of its low level of capitalisation. the development of the fishing tourism segment, the creation of jobs that promote social inclusion, the recognition and visibility of women's work, the promotion of fishing activities outside the informal economy and the need to regulate certain pathologies suffered by women in this sector as an occupational disease have been introduced. this is in view of the importance of ensuring the economic and social stability of coastal communities engaged in small-scale fishing, as well as environmental objectives such as the conservation of fisheries resources and the development of responsible practices and the sustainability of coastal marine ecosystems. i voted yes.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because i am aware of the importance of fishing in many eu countries, since it employs a large number of citizens and is in itself a socially and environmentally sustainable activity. coastal fishing is a traditional form of fishing which is an important source of livelihood, and areas dependent on this type of fishing require specific support measures in order to develop. we must invest in innovation to develop the blue economy. in recent years, more has been invested in systems to control the seas and oceans, but it is still insufficient. similarly, diversification in the fisheries sector needs to be encouraged because of the decline in employment and profitability in the sector.
‒ 80% of european fishermen are small-scale fishermen, but only 20% of the fishing quotas are allocated to them, while the remaining 80% is taken up by industrial fisheries. yet, small-scale fishing creates many jobs in local communities and better selectivity, and therefore better sustainability. to increase the income of fishermen, the tomašić report proposed developing complementary activities: environmental services, tourism, culture and processing of products. but fishing must remain the main activity and the main source of income for fishermen. i therefore tabled an amendment asking the commission and the member states to increase the quotas allocated to small-scale fishermen gradually. this amendment was voted, but the allocation of quotas is at member state level. all the national authorities must now make a major effort to allocate quotas to small-scale fishermen.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour because the report talks about the need for a fairer allocation of quotas that takes into account the protection of the environment and the contribution of fisheries to the local economy. this is something which is already provided for in article 17 of the common fisheries policy, but which spain has been failing to comply with, as we have repeatedly denounced. the commission report also recognises that the recession has hit seafarers hard, further marginalizing the sector, and that diversification and innovation are more necessary than ever for the survival of small-scale fisheries. it is a step forward and in the right direction for europe to recognise and support the development of local communities whose livelihoods depend mainly on fishing and related activities. we also welcome her progress towards the empowerment of women seafarers throughout the fisheries value chain, whose vital work has often been invisible and remains subject to pay gaps.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it represents an important and necessary political boost to the maintenance and development of small-scale fishing in the regions dependent on fishing. the report calls on the commission to draw up effective legal definitions to improve support systems for small-scale, traditional and artisanal fishing in relation to the territories where it is carried out and not just in relation to the size and power of vessels. there are many traditional arts that have been considered outside these definitions because of the size of the boats when their relationship with the territory as well as their environmental impact is much smaller, for example arts such as the almadraba. i have decided to vote in favour of this report because it is a commitment to socially and environmentally more sustainable fishing.
in writing. ‒ the adoption of this report represents parliament's express support for european regions dependent on small-scale coastal fishing. it provides jobs for many european citizens and, moreover, from an environmental point of view, does not entail the usual risks associated with mass fishing. we therefore consider it essential to ensure the continuity of this traditional fishing style. we ask the commission to include all these types of fishing, whose methods and traditions differ considerably from one member state to another, under a common definition and, from there, to focus on promoting innovation and diversification in this type of activity. i therefore vote in favour of this report because of the important support it provides for coastal areas and islands.
in writing. ‒ this report presents the need for a definition of small-scale coastal fishing that respects territorial specificities and is in line with the new cfp. it proposes a series of measures to encourage innovation and economic diversification in the artisanal fisheries sector. in this context, the capacity of small-scale fishing to provide a social backbone in certain communities is examined in depth, and the economic and social crisis affecting it, particularly because of its low level of capitalisation, is taken into account. the development of the fishing tourism segment, the creation of employment that favours social inclusion, the recognition and visualisation of women's work, the promotion of fishing activities outside the informal economy and the need to regulate certain pathologies suffered by women in this sector as occupational diseases have been introduced. this is in view of the importance of ensuring the economic and social stability of coastal communities engaged in small-scale fishing, in addition to environmental objectives with the conservation of fisheries resources and the development of responsible practices and the sustainability of coastal marine ecosystems. i voted yes.

in writing. ‒ for the first time, the basic cfp regulation includes a chapter on the external dimension of the cfp, setting out the minimum conditions for bilateral agreements, the responsibility for cooperation between regional fisheries organisations and the consistency of the measures they take. the report also stresses the need for fisheries agreements to benefit both parties, the eu and third countries, and the importance of supporting the development of local communities. i have therefore voted in favour of the report.

in writing. ‒ the report analyses the external dimension of the common fisheries policy following its latest reform. after the amendments made to this report during the parliamentary procedure, the document is acceptable, although we consider that it still contains some elements which are not related to its purpose - such as charters or joint ventures, which belong entirely to third countries - or which are not adequately covered - the lack of available information. in any case, the current external dimension is well explained in the 2008 regulation on fishing authorisations in non-eu waters and any possible loopholes can be remedied (in particular as regards the granting of licences in the waters of a third country with which there is no agreement on fishing authorisations). spain imposes on its fleet a system of verification of the authenticity of licences and payments to the third country through its embassies which could be extended to the rest of the eu). i voted yes.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because of the need to give the cfp an external dimension in view of the fact that there is intense international competition in all ocean areas and for most species. some have adopted aggressive policies to gain access to increasingly scarce resources, giving them an economic competitive advantage over eu vessels. improving the strategy is therefore essential to achieve the eu's objective of promoting sustainable fisheries by using its influence on the international scene to improve fisheries management and transparency rules and to foster upward rather than downward competition.
in writing. ‒ is european fisheries outside the union's territorial waters environmentally, economically and socially sustainable? in general, yes, but we must improve transparency and not impose unfair competition on fishermen in developing countries. i note with interest that paragraph 67 of the report calls on the commission to cut off trade relations with countries that practice illegal fishing. similarly, the european union is paying less and less access fees in fisheries agreements with third countries. this share has been reduced from 65% to 35% with the shipowners paying the rest. this rebalancing is in the interests of the european taxpayer, but also of small-scale artisanal fishermen in europe and developing countries. the less subsidies for fisheries agreements, the less unfair competition for small-scale fishermen. the latter do not benefit from these agreements, but are nevertheless competing with imported products.

president-in-office of the council.– mr president, regarding the panama papers, i would like to start by saying that all this demonstrates yet again the need to continue our fight against tax fraud and money laundering. it is too early, unfortunately, to have a full analysis of the panama papers, but all of us are – as you are – examining their implications and the responses to be given. national governments have announced investigations. in discussing what the eu can do, i will distinguish between the tax aspects on the one hand and anti-money laundering on the other. on tax, action needs, in particular, to focus on two policy strands – firstly, access to information, and secondly, measures that can be applied to remedy cases of fraud. the commission’s anti—tax avoidance package, presented at the end of january, provides an important basis to implement internationally—agreed standards in binding eu law. as regards access to information, internationally—agreed standards on transparency and the exchange of information have been developed by the oecd. significant progress has been made in recent years. however, not all international players have totally committed yet to playing a fair game, and this is clearly the case for panama. in order to ensure efficient tax transparency, we need everyone on board, and the eu, as a major international player, must speak with one voice to convince its partners on the international stage to adopt the standards agreed by the majority. the eu itself is committed to the issue of the exchange of information. we have gone even further than the oecd standards and many consider us front runners, which is good news. we have adopted a directive on administrative cooperation that was recently complemented to cover tax rulings exchange and which will soon cover country—by—country reporting between tax administrations, as proposed in the commission’s anti—tax avoidance package. the council has already reached agreement on this country—by—country reporting, and i would very much welcome the parliament adopting its opinion as soon as possible. clearly we will not stop here. today the commission adopted a proposal on public country—by—country reporting of multinational accounts to increase transparency, and this proposal will, obviously, receive the full attention of the council. the presidency will definitely strive to have swift progress on this proposal. to come back to the revelations, i would like to speak of what we can do beyond increasing the exchange of information in order to fight tax fraud and avoidance, as well as money laundering. in january the commission issued a communication on an external strategy for effective taxation as part of the anti-tax avoidance package, amongst other things proposing a common eu listing process to respond to third countries that refuse to respect tax good governance standards. the presidency is striving to react swiftly to these proposals, explicitly taking into account the panama papers. also in january, the commission anti—tax avoidance package contained a proposal for a directive laying down rules against tax avoidance practices – the anti—tax avoidance directive – which is currently being examined. some of the rules put forward in the draft directive could be of use, considering that we are also talking about abusive forms of legal tax avoidance. so again, the need for a swift agreement on this directive is stressed. the presidency is striving to reach an agreement on this proposal during this semester, and i hope that we can count on you – parliament – as well. finally, i would like to draw attention to the ongoing work of the code of conduct group on business taxation in fighting harmful tax regimes. the group is committed to promoting the adoption of the code-of-conduct principles in third countries. the group has worked successfully in switzerland and the commission is continuing its dialogue with liechtenstein on behalf of the group. other countries outside the eu should be involved in the near future. let me turn quickly to money laundering. this issue, which is closely linked to the financing of terrorism, is also very high on our agenda. in february, in reaction to the commission’s action plan on the fight against terrorist financing, the council agreed to proceed swiftly with the implementation of a number of measures which will contribute to combating both terrorist financing and money laundering. let me outline the ones which are particularly relevant in the context of our discussion today. firstly, ministers emphasised the need for the identification of third countries with strategic deficiencies in the area of money laundering or countering terrorist financing. as you are aware, in accordance with the fourth anti—money laundering directive, member states should apply enhanced due diligence measures on financial flows from and to these listed countries. in february we called for the identification process to be completed by 1 may. here, however, we are in the hands of the commission. we know that our sense of urgency is shared by the commission, which is working hard on this matter, and we hope that it is also shared by parliament. secondly, ministers underlined the importance of speeding up the implementation of the anti-money laundering package which parliament and the council adopted last year. our shared objective is to aim for completion of this process by the end of this year. thirdly, we have undertaken to further improve the cooperation and exchange of information between member states’ financial intelligence units. fourthly, we called on the commission to propose, by june, certain targeted improvements to the fourth anti—money laundering directive. furthermore, we have asked the commission to explore the possibility of introducing limits to large cash payments and to consider, together with the european central bank, whether appropriate measures might be necessary for high-denomination notes such as the eur 500 bill. as you know, the anti-money laundering directive is very recent and is still being transposed by member states. for certain areas, however, it has already become clear that targeted amendments are needed, for example aimed at strengthening access to information such as access to bank and payments account information by financial intelligence units, operationalising the list of high-risk third countries, and in view of the handling of virtual currencies. the council is ready to work on a commission proposal in this respect as a matter of priority, and i am sure that this would also be the case, again, for parliament. i know that the issue of money laundering and terrorist financing is also very high on our international agenda, particularly in the context of the financial action task force, but also in the g20. let me conclude by saying that the presidency has decided to put the so—called panama papers on the agenda of the informal ecofin meeting in amsterdam on 22 april, where the commission will be invited to give a policy reaction, including an overview of the initiatives on the fight against money laundering and tax fraud. ministers and central bank governors will be invited to exchange views on this issue. i look forward to that specific exchange of views.
member of the commission. mr president, madam representative of the council, madam minister, ladies and gentlemen, the panama papers scandal has given new and increased legitimacy to our programme to combat tax fraud and money laundering. if anyone still needs proof of the importance of our joint work in this area, it is now known to all through the remarkable work, and i want to salute it as such, of the media. if all the measures for transparency and good tax governance that we have long advocated in parliament and the commission had been put in place within the european union and internationally, this huge concealment of funds could not have been so colossal. the indignation i share is therefore not only understandable but also salutary in the face of revelations of such magnitude and such harm. citizens cannot understand or accept these practices which in reality amount to nothing more or less than - let's say the word - stealing from them. we must now turn what we feel, that is, public outrage, into concrete positive action and also seize the opportunity that these revelations offer us, because it is indeed a political opportunity that we have now, and a political duty that we have to do, to deal decisively with tax evasion, tax fraud, aggressive tax or tax optimization practices, corruption and money laundering practices. this is an opportunity to give a boost to our already very ambitious programme to combat tax fraud, tax evasion and money laundering, in particular by getting - i am embarrassed to say this here - member states to turn their political commitment into concrete action and to make new political commitments. it is also an opportunity to reassess our overall framework and identify new measures that can be taken to strengthen the european union's defenses against tax evasion. and finally, it is an opportunity to step up cooperation with our international partners to pressure problematic jurisdictions - let's call them what everyone calls tax havens - to implement reforms for fairer, more transparent, internationally decided taxation, and to adopt our own standards for preventing money laundering. i would like to say a word about what has already been done, because i believe that we should not be constantly beating ourselves up. a lot has been done in recent years. there's a transparency revolution that's started, and i often say that it's not going to stop. i mean it more than ever. we're not starting from scratch. the commission has taken vigorous initiatives to improve the tax environment for citizens and businesses alike. in fact, in the last few months we have introduced no less than three major tax reform packages. this includes, firstly, a proposal containing legally binding measures against tax avoidance. the proposal includes a general anti-abuse rule which would prevent the use of artificial offshore structures, as is too often the case, to avoid taxation, and controlled foreign corporation rules which would allow member states to tax profits which have been artificially diverted through low or no tax jurisdictions. in other words, it would make it possible to grasp a number of situations which were rightly captured by the panama papers. secondly, we have put forward ambitious proposals to advance tax transparency within the union through the world's largest automatic exchange of tax information between states, on the one hand, and between businesses and tax administrations, on the other. thirdly, we are also advancing tax transparency outside the european union, first with european third countries. i am very pleased that we have been able to negotiate and conclude agreements with switzerland, liechtenstein, san marino, andorra and, as will be the case shortly, monaco via bilateral agreements. this has a very concrete meaning for our fellow citizens, that what is called banking secrecy is dying and disappearing in europe; it's a great success. as far as non-european countries are concerned, we have proposed the creation of a common pan-european list of tax havens as part of the external strategy for effective taxation which i presented last january. all this constitutes an anti-tax evasion package which is, for the most part, on the council's table today. we have presented these new initiatives on the basis of the strong transparency requirements of the european union, which are already in place for individual accounts and for the banking sector in the european union. for example, i want to mention here that from 2017 onwards, member states will automatically exchange a large amount of information on bank accounts with each other to prevent fraudsters from hiding their savings and money abroad. just a few minutes ago today, the commission decided to push the boundaries of tax transparency even further by proposing that multinational groups should publish country-by-country reports of their activities. i have participated in enough debates here now for you to know that on the one hand i have been in favour of this publicity from the beginning and on the other hand i am very pleased that the commission is proposing today that the european union should be - i say to those who say that this is not enough - the first economic area in the world to shed light on the activity of companies country by country because, i see you nodding your head, mr lamberts, you know as well as i do that the oecd has proposed that this should be limited - which is not negligible - for the time being to exchanges between tax administrations. in the debate, i imagine, i know, some of you will ask us about the threshold of 750 million euros, which is the same as the oecd threshold; it allows us to understand 90% of transnational activity and also on the perimeter, wondering why we are not going outside the european union. from this point of view, i want to tell you that first we go through aggregated data for the rest of the world, but also - and this will not have escaped you - that we will ask for detailed data for the activity of multinational firms that would work in tax havens. and we can't let that slip away. this is a first step of crucial importance, and i would like the european parliament to welcome it as such, but of course we will continue to work together. while significant progress has been made on some of the tax initiatives, including the swift agreement on two transparency proposals, many important measures are still on the council's table. the panama papers are a signal to the member states that it is time to show the same level of ambition as the commission and parliament in the fight against tax evasion by quickly agreeing on new eu provisions to combat tax evasion. the same applies to our anti-money laundering measures. it is imperative that member states implement their political commitment and transpose the provisions of the fourth anti-money laundering directive by the end of the year. this directive provides, inter alia, for the identification of the beneficial owners of companies and trusts and the establishment of central national registers. and this is, of course, something that parliament knows - and has long called for - is absolutely crucial to preventing the financial system from being misused to launder criminal money. i would like to say that the commission is prepared to provide all the support it needs to facilitate the transposition process and to ensure that these provisions are properly implemented, but let us say that, as you know as well as i do, and i am also addressing the presidency of the council, the primary responsibility lies with the member states. i hope that the message of the panama papers, the message you are sending as a parliamentary institution, the message of the commission, will be heard and that the member states will understand that there can be no excessive caution in these matters and that the revolution of transparency applies to everything and everyone. what else needs to be done? as i said, much has already been accomplished in the fight against tax evasion, against money laundering, but recent revelations show that we still have much to do to reduce distortions between the laws and to be fully cooperative within our own borders. i simply want to mention a number of key areas where we need to do more work. firstly, there are still a number of proposals on the council's table which will have a major impact. i am thinking of the directive on tax evasion, which i know, as does the dutch framework is of course more effective. and that is why we must, in the context of the g20, propose a new stage. it so happens that from thursday onwards all the world's finance ministers will be in give you an overview of some of the additional steps we could take to eliminate opaque structures, offshore arrangements and anonymous financial transactions, such as those that were revealed last week. i know that the commission can count on the european parliament to feed the debate, to support our ideas, to maintain the political momentum that we are instilling in the next steps of this on behalf of the ppe group mr president, commissioner, president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, the citizens are getting tired. it's our responsibility to prevent ourselves from being seen as a problem and to be seen as a solution. and for that we have to act forcefully. the panama papers revelations are further proof of the need to continue to make the progress we have made over the past year towards greater tax transparency. the commissioner said so. we are facing a political opportunity which we cannot afford to miss and you can be sure, commissioner, that we will support you in all the measures you have proposed here today and in all those you propose in the future to fight tax fraud with vigour. because it is absolutely necessary to tackle this problem - as the commissioner has also said - which is not exclusive to the european union. this is a global problem which can only be tackled by a global response involving as many countries as possible. of course, setting up a company in panama is not illegal, but what can become illegal is what you do with it, and it is our responsibility to prevent these companies from being used to defraud. the epp group has always advocated, will always advocate and will continue to advocate greater fiscal transparency. the ppe group wants mossack fonseca and the panamanian government to come and testify to the european parliament, as many companies and other states have already done in the taxe committee. i'm sure the panamanian government will want to cooperate with us. we cannot allow both law firms and states to use fiscal engineering as a business model to live at the expense of other states. the commissioner has defined it well: that is honest theft.

member of the commission.– madam president, i think we just heard in that last debate that it has been a long-standing priority for the commission to work to make sure that taxes are paid more where profits are generated. i think we heard from commissioner moscovici on both the range of the measures that have been taken and the passion with which he is pursuing this. clearly, as we discussed in the last debate, the panama papers have sharpened the focus, but the proposal that the commission has brought forward today, to require all large multinationals operating in europe to publish information on the tax that they pay country-by-country, pre-dates the panama papers. our proposal builds on the work that has been taken forward by the oecd to require the sharing of information related to corporate income tax between tax authorities. but it goes a step further, and we are the first in the world to require the biggest multinationals to make key information public. why? because this greater transparency will shine a light and help us ask whether we indeed have the right laws in place. it can help the public see whether companies are acting in the best long-term interests of their shareholders from a reputational point of view. in working on this proposal in recent months we have been guided by a number of clear principles. first, that we should aim to be consistent, with international work being taken forward by the oecd and endorsed by the g20. then, that we should build on the major reforms already taken forward by my colleague commissioner moscovici and others to increase transparency and to fight tax avoidance. we should bring forward measures that will affect all the biggest multinationals operating in europe, not just the european ones. we should be proportionate in what we do in two main respects: first, we should not undermine the position of european businesses vis-à-vis their global competitors; and second, we should not burden small and medium-sized european businesses – the lifeblood of our economy – which typically operate in one country. indeed, for me it is this wish to protect the competitive position of our smes which lies at the heart of, and is an important part of, this proposal. it should not be the case that smaller companies, which do not know how to shift their profits – they cannot afford the clever tax advice to minimise their bills – should be at a competitive disadvantage compared with the big multinational companies. in some higher-tax countries it is the case that some of the big multinationals can pay up to 30% less tax than would be paid by the smaller companies. i say this as someone who is pro-business, but i would prefer businesses to be concentrating on their customers – on the services they offer, on product innovation, on true competition – rather than the competition of the creativity of their tax advisers. so this legislation that we are proposing would require the biggest multinationals – those with a global turnover above eur 750 million – to publish information in a number of key areas. on a country-by-country basis, they would in future need to publish the nature of their business activities; how many staff they have; their net turnover; their profit before tax; the amount of tax due based on yearly profits; the amount of tax they actually paid in that same year, and their accumulated earnings. they would also be required to report on the total tax they pay outside the eu. in addition – and this links to our last debate on the panama papers – if they pay taxes outside the eu, in countries that do not abide by international governance standards on tax matters – so-called tax havens – multinationals would have to publish the same detailed information as for a european country. we think that, taken together, this information will give a clear idea of whether a large multinational is paying its tax where it makes its profits. the information would have to be made available for five years on the company’s website so that anyone who is interested could see where multinationals are paying their tax and whether there is a level playing field for all businesses. to make sure european companies are not disadvantaged, these rules would apply also to the subsidiaries of non-european multinationals doing business in europe, as well as to large european multinationals. european banks already have to comply with a specific transparency regime in the capital requirements directive that includes country-by-country reporting, so they will not be affected by today’s proposal. the only change would be that large banks established outside the eu but doing business inside it would in future be required to publish a country-by-country report. in preparing this proposal we have looked at the rules already in place for the banks in extractive industries. we have given careful consideration to the ideas that were discussed in this house for the shareholders’ rights directive, and we sought to strike a balanced approach – one that does not harm the competitiveness of european businesses but that is nevertheless ambitious on greater tax transparency. it is now, of course, for the council and parliament to consider our proposal. the commission consulted widely before bringing it forward. we have listened to the views of all interested parties and fed them into our analysis. i think that, as a result of that, the college believes we have a simple, proportionate way to increase accountability. now our ambition is to get this agreed as quickly as possible. with your help and the help of member states we need to seize this opportunity to promote fairer competition and to build trust not just in our tax system but also to build trust again in europe’s businesses.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, commissioner hill, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the commissioner for being here today and for his explanations of his proposal. i agree with the commissioner that we must certainly be committed to the fight against fiscal engineering and above all for a reason which the commissioner has explained to us: we cannot allow our smes, which are the engine of growth and job creation in the european union, to be at a fiscal disadvantage compared to the large multinationals. corporate tax avoidance and harmful tax competition are two of the great challenges we face in the european union. the large companies and large multinationals are protected by the complexity of the tax rules and the lack of cooperation from the member states to transfer their profits and minimise their tax burden, and we cannot allow that, ladies and gentlemen. tax transparency must be one of our objectives to ensure that the mistakes of the past are not repeated. the european commission has presented us with its proposal in defence of the interests of european citizens, smes and transparency; we welcome these proposals. we must be able to demand sufficient data to distinguish the part of the activity of a business with a multinational scope from that which is related to a specific jurisdiction. in short, we cannot allow the resources of the citizens which are so necessary in other fields such as education and health to be avoided.

mr president, it is paradoxical that an initiative for greater fiscal transparency should be tabled the day before the vote to prohibit leaks such as the panama papers, without which debates such as today would not be possible. nevertheless, there are positive elements in this proposal. more information on the taxation of multinational companies will help to make the european people even more aware of how many european governments have protected complex tax avoidance schemes, which legalise the theft from the richest to the poorest. up to 860 billion a year, according to some studies, is lost every year, going from our schools, our hospitals, our town halls to the pockets of the multinationals. however, it is insufficient. if the proposed criteria are followed, we will know nothing about what happens in some tax havens, such as delaware in the united states, and we will also not know what happens to other companies. we will, among other things, call for a simple transparency rule: that tax activity in any state, whether or not in the european union, be reported. we have to be more ambitious.
member of the commission.– mr president, thank you for all the comments that have been made in the debate. i take the general thrust of the comments very much as support for this measure. clearly i hear that there are some parts of the house which understandably want people to go further and to go faster, but i think overall the support for the proposal from the commission is clear. i also think that there was an important set of remarks about balance, and balance is what we have tried to strike with this proposal: the balance between more transparency and wanting to defend and protect and promote the competitiveness of european businesses. i think that links to the questions i have been asked about the threshold in particular, because one of the principles that we have pursued, not just on this proposal but more generally, is to want to take our ideas forward in concert with international work, with the work being done by the oecd and the g20. the reason for that is that this work in international fora has been taken forward over many years, and i think the more we can do it in step, the more we can ensure we can make progress, and the more we can make sure that we can make progress that will be of benefit for europe, european taxpayers and european businesses. this point about competition and the need to make sure that this proposal applies equally to non-european multinationals and to european multinationals lies at the heart of the proposal. so, oecd: why 750 million? yes, because it is consistent with the oecd approach, and i think it is important to preserve an international approach on it. but to be clear: this would capture 90% of the revenues of all multinationals, so that is not an inconsiderable slice of the revenues from the multinationals. i was also asked a question about the aggregated figure. why do we not have a disaggregated figure for outside the eu as well as within the eu? again, this comes back to the point of competition. we do not have the wherewithal to insist that companies outside the eu share, for instance, information between the united states and singapore and publish the same information that we could require companies within the eu to provide. why is it important to try and pursue an approach in parallel? because if our companies were having to provide more information than was the case with companies outside the eu, that could not only be of commercial advantage to their competitors, who would have more information on european businesses to be able to find out, for example, what their strategies might be on r&d to help them with their commercial strategies, but also to third-country tax jurisdictions, so that european businesses might end up being taxed twice. so that was why we have gone for an aggregated figure outside the eu, and i think it was sensible to take that balanced approach. in terms of the questions i was asked about the blacklist and how that process is being taken forward, commissioner moscovici will be responsible for most of that work. he was saying earlier today that he would hope to be able to get that list together in six months. in terms of that process, his intention here is to come up with one which is a fair but careful assessment using all those four criteria on which the list is based. the process, to be clear, is that all third-country jurisdictions would be screened – not automatically just homing in on any particular country or jurisdiction – and then on the basis of that screening we would talk to the jurisdictions in question and ultimately, depending on the severity of the problem in relation to one or more of those criteria, we would put together a list based on that assessment. so it is more of a dynamic process, where we hope to be able to make progress together. i was also asked about what would happen with a non-eu company that might have a smaller subsidiary or branch in the eu. that is subject to our proposal even if the subsidiary is only medium-sized, so we would be able to get those non-eu multinationals through those subsidiaries or branches. finally, a couple of comments on timing. i do not accept that this work has been taken forward by the commission simply because of the panama papers and that that is what has belatedly prompted the commission to ask. as colleagues here will know, we have been working on this proposal for a long time. we have carried out a full impact assessment. we have discussed it over many months. the difference, i think, with the panama papers disclosures is that it has sharpened the focus of the proposal and has made us reconsider how we go about tackling the question of jurisdictions that do not have high standards of governance in terms of their corporate governance over the so-called tax havens, and that element of the proposal has been refined in light of the panama papers. but we had been working on it, and i think we share the sense of urgency that has been expressed by a number in this debate. and so, finally, on timing: how quickly can we take it forward? i agree with the point made by mr hayes that the sooner we can get on with this, the better. i know that parliament will want to make progress as rapidly as possible, and we will be seeking to make progress as rapidly as we possibly can with the member states, so that we can get a measure implemented as soon as possible, because i think that is part of how we can have a system of taxation in which our citizens have confidence, but also so that our businesses can go about the task of rebuilding trust with our citizens. because without businesses in which citizens have trust, we will not have the tax revenues that we all want.

mr president, i would like to congratulate mrs mogherini and the european external action service on the signing of the political dialogue and cooperation agreement, which takes relations between cuba and the european union to a new level. a process that responds to the wishes and demands of civil society. the agreement, which is governed by the principles of reciprocity, respect and mutual benefit, will make it possible to overcome the outdated 1996 common position. it will allow us to normalise relations and to deepen political dialogue, cooperation or collaboration in sectoral policies and trade, but without forgetting the area of fundamental rights, freedoms and democracy on an island where human rights defenders and the opposition are still persecuted and arrested. cuba deserves a better future. it has enormous potential for implementing a sustainable development model with human capital of trained people. a heritage that must be recognized in the recent history of the island and that will be fundamental in this opening. cuba also deserves an end to the embargo and i welcome the fact that the european union considers the effects of this measure on european companies to be illegal. and i would stress that this historic step has been facilitated by a woman, by a high representative who earns my respect and admiration every day. thank you very much, mrs mogherini.

in writing. in the european parliament, the socialists have worked for two decades to get the european union to abandon the so-called 'common position' which prevented relations with cuba. the 1996 common position was an initiative of the spanish right and sought to further isolate cuba. a change in the attitude of the united states now causes a greater general willingness towards these relations. for socialists it is not a matter of joining a fad. it is about working together, to: • complete before the end of the year the signing and ratification of the political dialogue and cooperation agreement between the eu and cuba, which was concluded last march. • and convince the united states of america to lift the blockade, and allow cuba to have economic and trade relations like any other country. we want to see these economic relations develop and all kinds of exchanges, the joint work of universities, scientists and businesses, to the point where the european union becomes a real actor in improving the situation on the island, can take place normally.
mr president, i would first like to congratulate mrs kalniete on her report. it contains important ideas which will be useful in the elaboration of the overall strategy to be presented to the european council in june. since the 2003 security strategy, the strategic context in which the european union finds itself has changed a great deal: it is much more interdependent economically, much more conflicted politically, and it faces very serious security challenges. we need effective common external action - i said that before - external action with the capacity to react to crises, yes, but also with strategic vision and the capacity to anticipate. i think we all know that soft power is not enough to protect our security and to make the european union a true global player. the threats we face require, as the report points out, that we also look into the security and defence dimension. finally, let me stress that in this new international context, the united states remains our main ally. the strengthening of the transatlantic link is paramount, particularly at a time of a certain american external fatigue and the pivot towards asia.

is there any doubt about this when we consider that these are countries which produce energy - oil and gas -; that these are countries which receive substantial investments from a number of member states of the european union; that these are countries of transit and destination for a large flow of goods? no, there's no question of its strategic importance. but there is no doubt that these are also countries which pose serious problems in defining the priorities of european diplomacy: respect for the rule of law, the separation of powers, the dignity of the person, the suppression of fundamental rights, the protection of minorities and, in particular, of women. that is the message that the definition of a european strategy for central asia should convey, and i believe that is the message that they convey in this resolution on which we have worked, the rapporteur - whose work we thank, mr meszerics - and the shadow rapporteurs - because i have had the honour of being the alternative rapporteur for the socialist group. it is precisely to frame the message of the european union in the promotion of the improvement of the rule of law and the separation of powers that the importance of the judiciary, but also civil society and citizens, in the fight against the clientelist practices that define the capitalism practiced there and also, of course, in the fight against corruption. all these messages are top priorities for the european union, and the european union must also frame them in a commitment to prevent jihadism, because these are countries with a significant presence of the muslim religion, which is always a viable terrain for 'jihadisation' and radicalism, which must be prevented intelligently in the combination of the european union's efforts, and do so with a european accent, not competing with russia, nor with the commonwealth of independent states, nor with the importance of the russian-speaking influence in that region, but marking the european accent in the definition of our own diplomacy.
madam president, i am speaking on behalf of the verts/ale group, which is very concerned about the deal with turkey. first, the deal does nothing to solve the refugee crisis. instead of providing a just and humane common european solution, member states are egotistically trying to hide the crisis from the view of eu citizens, pretending that the illegal mass returns of refugees to syria have nothing to do with the union. but we know how terrible the human suffering at the turkish-syrian border is. the union should have proposed an ambitious and united approach in asylum matters based on solidarity and fair sharing of responsibilities. second, turkey is not a safe country for refugees. it does not provide basic guarantees of the status of refugees. moreover, turkey is not a safe country even for its own nationals. turkey is engulfed by violence and repression against kurds and other minorities. the turkish government should put an end to censorship and respect freedom of expression. last but not least, the deal is illegal. by framing it as a statement of the heads of state and government, the eu side is trying to avoid the obligations under eu law, including the charter of fundamental rights. it also circumvents the prerogatives of this parliament to co-decide on asylum and migration matters. we expect parliament to take all necessary steps to evaluate the legality of this agreement, together with the decisions based on it, and contest it in the court of justice. in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report as it allows the mobilisation of eur 1 793 710 following the dismissal of 500 workers at volvo group truck operation emea in sweden following the reductions at the umeå plant, and another 177 from four suppliers and product converters of that company (il logistics ab, lemia, caverion and isringhausen). this mobilization of funds is aimed at mitigating the disastrous social consequences of the economic crisis of the capitalist system. while these funds are not able to solve the problems of these workers in sweden, they at least offer the possibility of alleviating a small part of the human drama. it is for all these reasons that i have decided to vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report, because it calls for funds to compensate and provide for compensatory measures in cases of relocation or closure of companies due to structural changes in markets due to globalisation. they will be used to address the situation of dismissed workers, and aid to young people without education or employment, this time for those affected by the reductions of the volvo group and its suppliers in umeå, sweden. these are measures which, if they were not taken, would leave the workers concerned in a worse position. the vote in favour, however, does not hide the fact that this type of measure is 'bread for today and hunger for tomorrow', while the question of employment and relocations should be approached differently. on the one hand, europe needs an investment plan, different from the one it is pursuing so far, and another employment policy, to act in the field of employment. secondly, this alternative should consist in investing in activities for the future, especially in changing the production model and looking for sustainable outlets for these areas.
in writing. ‒ i supported this report on the european globalisation adjustment fund for volvo sweden which would support the reintegration into the labour market of workers made redundant in five companies operating in the manufacture of motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers. this fund would benefit 500 workers made redundant. as i have done on other occasions in connection with the fund, i voted in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report to approve the mobilisation of eur 1 793 710 from the european globalisation adjustment fund for 500 workers who have lost their jobs at volvo trucks and four suppliers and product converters in sweden as a result of the major structural changes in world trade patterns brought about by globalisation. the production of commercial vehicles is no longer dominated by european and north american manufacturers, as new truck manufacturers are emerging in asia while the production of heavy duty trucks in the union is decreasing. in this context, the truck industry is facing great difficulties in taking on these transformations. the personalised services to be financed by the egf include career guidance, training, retraining and job search activities, as well as grants for setting up new businesses and promoting entrepreneurship. although this aid alone cannot alleviate the drama of growing unemployment in the finnish electronics industry, it does constitute good assistance and makes it possible to provide training for the reintegration of the workers concerned into employment.

in writing. ‒ the union has set up legislative and budgetary instruments to provide additional support to workers suffering from the consequences of major structural changes in world trade patterns or the global economic and financial crisis, and to help them re-enter the labour market, including the egf. these funds are intended to mitigate the disastrous social consequences of the economic crisis of the capitalist system. while these funds are not able to solve the problems of the workers who have been made redundant, they at least offer the possibility of alleviating a small part of the human drama. in particular, this report, which i voted for, is intended to give its approval to the financing of the expert group on egf contact points and the seminars to promote contacts on the implementation of the egf, so that this exchange of information also contributes to providing better and more detailed information on the success rate of measures supported by the egf in the member states.
in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund was intended to provide additional support for workers suffering from the consequences of major structural changes in world trade patterns. the ec must have sufficient resources to manage it properly. i therefore support the request that the commission should mobilise eur 380 000 from the fund for technical assistance. this assistance is intended to finance monitoring and information activities, the creation of a knowledge base/application interface and the provision of advice to member states on the use, monitoring and evaluation of the egf (european globalisation adjustment fund). i therefore vote in favour of the proposal as i consider it important that the above activities be properly covered by the institution.
in writing. ‒ i also support the commission's proposal to use eur 380 000 from the european globalisation adjustment fund to cover technical assistance for the commission. this mechanism anticipates the possibility of using a small part of its resources to improve its operation, and this technical assistance is there to meet that objective, which i am convinced will be to everyone's benefit. the technical assistance is intended to finance monitoring and information activities, the creation of an application knowledge base and the provision of advice to member states on the use, monitoring and evaluation of the fund.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report to approve the mobilisation of eur 380 000 from the european globalisation adjustment fund to provide technical assistance to the european commission. this appropriation is intended to cover the financing of the following activities: data collection, database creation, administrative and technical support, advice to member states on the use, monitoring and evaluation of the egf, communication activities, audit, control and evaluation. activities financed should also contribute to simplifying the egf application procedure and its visibility and to improving the monitoring and evaluation of the effects of egf support on each participant.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of mobilising the european globalisation adjustment fund as this fund is a key tool to mitigate the effects of industrial relocation processes.
in writing. ‒ we are talking about a fund which is responsible for processing transfers of funds to cover maximum redundancy payments for the cessation of different business activities in the member states. any action to ensure the proper functioning of this fund is welcome and necessary. that is why i think it is necessary to vote in favour of this decision.
in writing. ‒ while we share the need to adequately finance the different actors involved in helping migrants and refugees in the european union, this proposal comes from a counterpart to reinforce the fortress europe model. we cannot in any case support an increase in the budget for europol, particularly in the context of migration policy, because that would be to support the closed detention centres and the mass expulsions which are now the norm. we have therefore decided to abstain in this vote, given the urgency of the first point.
in writing. ‒ we abstain from supporting this report because, although we support the urgent dispatch of funds to help with humanitarian aid for refugees, we do not see with good eyes that in the same report items for humanitarian aid are mixed with items for police, border and anti-terrorist control. this is a humanitarian crisis, and in podemos we openly disagree with the measures being taken by the eu, the outsourcing of border control to other countries and the creation of 'stop-gap states', along with the hot returns, without following the legislation itself regarding political asylum requests, and the rise of xenophobic perspectives and the immobility of states in the face of this refugee crisis, leads us to refrain from supporting these funds being diverted in this way to make up the eu's position.
in writing. ‒ the proposed budgetary amendments have two main objectives. on the one hand, to provide funds for emergency aid to address humanitarian needs arising from the refugee crisis: in particular, eur 100 million in commitment appropriations and eur 80,2 million in payment appropriations for the most immediate financing needs. the commission also proposes to increase the number of staff in the european counter-terrorism centre at europol, namely 25 additional staff posts, 5 contract staff and 5 national experts. i have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report with the firm intention of contributing to improving the living conditions of refugees from syria. in view of the current situation, new funding models are needed to provide adequate, rapid and effective assistance to this group so tormented by violence and war. the european institutions, as well as the member states, must bear in mind that the humanitarian crisis we are facing will not disappear until we are able to contribute to restoring peace and security in syria. we must therefore have the mechanisms and the budget to provide aid to people fleeing war.
in writing. ‒ the purpose of this report is to provide additional resources to countries facing the mass arrival of migrants. the commission will also be providing a further €100 million for humanitarian aid and €2 million for the fight against terrorism. it is now common knowledge that the armies of the islamic state are exploiting the flow of migrants to enter our countries and carry out attacks there, but it is irresponsible and criminal to provide the means to continue to welcome migrants. not only are these amounts grossly inadequate, but the union is refusing to take the only real action to stem this crisis: closing our borders as australia has done. i voted against this report, of course.

in writing. ‒ given the massive arrival of refugees and migrants in europe, an exceptional situation has been created where a large number of people are in need of humanitarian assistance on european territory. this situation has brought the member states, especially the countries most affected, to the limit of their capacity to respond. there was no appropriate instrument at union level to provide the necessary assistance in extreme cases such as the one we are in, when people in the eu are affected by a disaster. i therefore support the initiative put forward by the ec to create a budgetary structure which will make available the funds needed to deal with the humanitarian consequences of the current crisis. this project will enable us to accommodate and assist refugees arriving in the territory of the union. i therefore vote in favour of the report.
in writing. ‒ we welcome the proposal to allow the eu budget to provide emergency aid on eu territory to deal with the humanitarian consequences of the current refugee crisis. it is nevertheless desirable that stable mechanisms are established to deal with such situations. a more sustainable legal and budgetary framework should be provided to allow for the future mobilisation of humanitarian aid within the union. i also support the increase in resources to strengthen the european counter-terrorism centre set up by interpol.
in writing. ‒ the proposed budgetary amendments have two main objectives. on the one hand, to enable emergency aid funds to address humanitarian needs arising from the refugee crisis. in particular, eur 100 million in commitment appropriations and eur 80.2 million in payment appropriations for the most immediate financing needs. the commission also proposes to increase the number of staff in the european counter-terrorism centre at europol, namely 25 additional staff posts, 5 contract staff and 5 national experts. i have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ the european parliament hereby declares its readiness to approve draft amending budget no 1/2016 in view of the urgency of the decision to be able to provide assistance in the territory of the union in order to deal with the humanitarian consequences of the current refugee crisis. we are talking about a decision which is necessary because of the urgency of the situation, and i therefore consider it necessary to vote in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the 5 proposed candidates for the court of auditors for various reasons: their lack of independence, the possibility of conflict of interest, the lack of professional knowledge in the field of audit, as well as the lack of gender balance, since they are all men.
in writing. ‒ the procedure for selecting the members of the court of auditors was heavily criticised. however, most candidates lack the appropriate professional skills and have strong indications of a possible conflict of interest. none of the candidates presented the required level of professional knowledge for the post nor were they able to assure that they would be able to perform their tasks with the necessary degree of independence. despite the systematic requests of the european parliament on previous council reports, the court of auditors has an extraordinary gender imbalance which is aggravated by the current nominations, the 6 candidates are men. for all these reasons, we shall vote against all the proposals.

in writing. ‒ the procedure for selecting the members of the court of auditors was heavily criticised . however, most candidates lack the appropriate professional skills and have strong indications of a possible conflict of interest. none of the candidates presented the required level of professional knowledge for the position nor were they able to assure that they would be able to perform their duties with the necessary degree of independence . despite the systematic requests of the european parliament on previous council reports, the court of auditors has an extraordinary gender imbalance which is aggravated by the current nominations, the 6 candidates are men. for all these reasons, we shall vote against all the proposals.

in writing. ‒ i decided to stick to the vote of the greens in the cont committee, meaning that i supported candidates jan gregor, samo jereb and mihails kozlovs. i voted against ladislav balko and janusz wojciechowski. i wanted to stress the need to respect the demands in the tfeu concerning the professional experience and candidates’ complete independence and the need to assure gender balance in the eu’s top positions.
mr president, there has been an attempt to confuse the debate on glyphosate by portraying critics as enemies of science and progress, but it is the commission which is intentionally ignoring the opinion of experts, such as the international centre for cancer research, which has classified glyphosate as a probable carcinogen. on the basis of the precautionary principle and the wording of the regulation itself, the commission cannot give automatic authorization, it cannot take the side of the multinational monsanto and its model of agricultural production, which does not take account of health risks. i regret the lukewarmness of this parliament. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. we ourselves, from united left, have replaced glyphosate in many town halls with less polluting methods, demonstrating that there are alternative solutions. we cannot use any argument to trivialize the use of pesticides. not with our vote, of course.
mr president, we voted against because the amendments adopted do not reflect the outcome of the discussions we have had in committee. it is irresponsible to ask for the renewal of glyphosate for seven years. we call on the competent authorities to apply the precautionary principle. the world health organization report concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans; however, we have ample reason to believe that the european food safety authority has other interests behind it because it reached conclusions contrary to those of the world health organization. we cannot allow a substance with these characteristics to be placed on the market in europe, a substance which is used as fertiliser for our fields and which ends up in food and which also endangers the work of farmers and livestock farmers. we can't gamble with the health of our people.
in writing. ‒ this report contains positive aspects such as it is critical of the authorisation procedures, the impact of glyphosate on fauna and flora and the residues detected. the committee recommends that glyphosate not be used for non-professional purposes, not be used in gardens, public parks or playgrounds or where pest management systems are sufficient. i have voted against it, however, because instead of recommending an outright ban on all products containing glyphosate, it proposes a renewal of its use for seven more years.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution, which ensures greater care for health and the environment by using scientific criteria. the european food safety authority (efsa) assesses the approval of glyphosate on the basis of rigorous scientific criteria. however, there are disparate conclusions between the analyses of this and the study of the international center for cancer research (icrc). efsa considered that some of the studies that had not been assessed by the ciic were of key importance for the final assessment. according to this agency and the bundesinstitut für risikobewertung (bfr), the health risk is unlikely. they both concluded that glyphosate meets the standards required for approval for use and poses no risk to human or animal health or the environment. so we should not be carried away by sensationalism or dismiss its prohibition. we must be responsible to the environment and also to farmers. my position is therefore to reduce the 15-year extension - as proposed by the european commission - to 5 years for future review, clarification by the scientific community and professional use of glyphosate.
in writing. ‒ we voted against because the amendments adopted do not reflect the outcome of the discussions we have had in the commission. it is irresponsible to ask for the renewal of glyphosate for seven years. we call on the competent authorities to apply the precautionary principle in the light of the world health organisation (who) report, which found glyphosate to be 'probably carcinogenic to humans'. however, there is ample reason to believe that the efsa (european food safety agency), whose study came to conclusions contrary to those of the who, is not entirely independent and therefore we should question its recommendations. we cannot allow a substance with these characteristics to be placed on the market in europe, which is used as a herbicide in our fields and ends up in the food we eat.
in writing. ‒ glyphosate is a chemical widely used in pesticides and is the main herbicide used in agriculture. there are conflicting studies from international independent bodies (iarc-who, efsa) on a possible carcinogenic effect, including possible harmful effects on human health, and whether it is the base component or the co-formulants. the european commission has submitted its proposal for an implementing regulation authorising the renewal of the authorisation for a maximum period of 15 years, excluding the use of stem and stem clams for use in plant protection products containing glyphosate among other co-formulants. the commission is also proposing that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of the environment against the emission of gaseous and particulate pollutants from diesel engines. the commission is also asked to ensure that the pesticide is used properly and professionally and that it is limited to public spaces as a precautionary measure.
in writing. ‒ this report contains positive aspects such as it is critical of the authorisation procedures, the impact of glyphosate on fauna and flora and the residues detected. the committee recommends that glyphosate not be used for non-professional purposes, not be used in gardens, public parks or playgrounds or where pest management systems are sufficient. i have voted against it, however, because instead of recommending an outright ban on all products containing glyphosate, it proposes a renewal of its use for seven more years.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution because we were able to amend the original text with the aim of giving both farmers and producers a period of adaptation, while also safeguarding public health. the proposal put forward, which would have meant the abolition of the use of glyphosate products, would have caused great insecurity for farmers, but also for users, and would have been very costly for an already seriously damaged sector, as we discussed yesterday in the house. i believe that the solution proposed is to replace the use of this substance in the medium term, thus guaranteeing the precautionary principle and ensuring that the replacement can be done progressively from the occupational sectors that use it.
in writing. ‒ the objection to the renewal of glyphosate is unfortunately only symbolic: the commission is in no way obliged to act on parliament's requests. in view of the dangers of this herbicide, i supported all the amendments aimed at restricting its use as much as possible: prohibition of use by non-professionals, restriction of agricultural uses, prohibition of certain agricultural uses or prohibition of agricultural use when other methods are sufficient. in 2015, i myself filed an objection to glyphosate-tolerant gmos, in particular because of the risks posed by this product. if the ban on this product is a major public health decision, it should undoubtedly be accompanied by a ban on the import of glyphosate-treated products. the text as voted by parliament finally advocates authorization for a period of 7 years, and suggests only a few provisions of restrictions. it did not, for example, ban the use of glyphosate in public parks and gardens. the text, which is seven years long, leaves consumers and farmers exposed to many risks and fails to take account of the necessary precautionary principle. i therefore voted against this text.
in writing. ‒ we voted against because the amendments adopted do not reflect the outcome of the discussions we have had in the commission. it is irresponsible to ask for the renewal of glyphosate for seven years. we call on the competent authorities to apply the precautionary principle in the light of the world health organisation (who) report, which found glyphosate to be 'probably carcinogenic to humans'. however, there is ample reason to believe that the efsa (european food safety agency), whose study came to conclusions contrary to those of the who, is not entirely independent and therefore we should question its recommendations. we cannot allow a substance with these characteristics to be placed on the market in europe, which is used as a herbicide in our fields and ends up in the food we eat.
in writing. ‒ i agree with this parliament's request to renew the marketing authorisation in the eu for only seven years, instead of the proposed fifteen, and exclusively for professional use. we believe that an independent assessment should also be carried out and the scientific evidence published which led the european food safety authority to give its favourable opinion on the authorisation, given the concerns about the effects of this product.
in writing. ‒ glyphosate is a herbicide marketed by several agrochemical companies and used in fields, gardens and industrial areas. as has been discussed on many occasions, reports published by the european food safety authority (efsa) and the international agency for research on cancer (iarc), which is part of the who, are contradictory, alerting the latter agency to the possible carcinogenic effect of glyphosate. it should also be recalled that several scientific studies show evidence that glyphosate can act as an endocrine disruptor and that the european commission has not yet fulfilled its obligations regarding the regulation of these substances. in the absence of unity in scientific criteria, i believe that the precautionary principle is the right thing to do and have therefore decided not to support the renewal of glyphosate.
in writing. the non-renewal of the extension of the use of the herbicide glyphosate is prudential, when there is evidence that this substance is a possible carcinogen in humans and convincing evidence of being a carcinogen in animals, according to the international agency for research on cancer (iarc), a who agency. in addition, there is evidence of harm to pollinators and the fact that the efsa (european food safety authority) could not rule out the endocrine disrupting effects of this substance are more than sufficient reasons to apply precaution and not to renew its use for a longer period. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover the whole of the eu.
in writing. ‒ glyphosate is an active chemical substance widely used in a range of pesticide products and its use in europe is subject to strict regulation. regulation (eu) no 1141/2010 lays down the procedure for the renewal of the active substances in group ii provided for in directive 91/414/eec. that list includes the active substance glyphosate. in march 2015, the world health organization's international agency for research on cancer (iarc) concluded that glyphosate was 'probably carcinogenic to humans', while the official eu risk assessment, conducted by efsa, reached the opposite conclusion, referring to three studies whose results have not been made public by the industry for free scientific scrutiny. there are also doubts as to its action as an endocrine disruptor. in this context and given the current state of the art, it is not appropriate to renew the approval of glyphosate for the maximum possible period of 15 years and i have therefore voted in favour of a renewal for the minimum period, consistent with the precautionary principle.
