in writing. ‒ we voted against because this report does not reflect the negative and growing role of the union in the current conflicts (southern and eastern neighbourhood countries); and because it advocates the intensification of defence cooperation and greater military integration through the european defence agency. in addition, it proposes further militarisation and the strengthening of eu-nato cooperation, and supports the european defence industrial and technological base (editb) and nato's objective of increasing defence spending. we do not agree with the financing of military expenditure from the union budget, but we also insist on strengthening the european pillar of nato and on the member states of the union living up to their commitments to nato, and we support the union's tactical groups, the nato response forces and their combination, and the permanently grouped multinational military units. we also oppose it because the report emphasizes the merging of internal and external security and the subordination of trade, development and energy policy within the framework of the cfsp/csdp.
in writing. ‒ we voted against an initiative which defends an alarmist, ultra-security and warmongering approach to international relations, which bases eu policies and actions towards peace and security on global arms escalation (making operational precisely the objectives of radicalism and extremism) and on the alliance with countries that have promoted wars and have provoked and fuelled the emergence of the threats they are intended to combat. on the contrary, we advocate a collaborative and humanistic approach to international relations which includes the structural causes of conflict (unequal trade relations, the desire of highly industrialized countries to hoard and exploit the primary resources of developing countries) and a total revision of international relations and its institutions in accordance with international rules, as the main pillars for peace and human security in europe and the world.
in writing. ‒ i would like to thank the rapporteur for her work in bringing this report on the union to fruition in a changing global environment: a more connected, contested and complex world. clear lines are needed on the defence of the peoples of the union, the stabilisation of europe's neighbourhood in the broad sense and the strengthening of multilateral global governance.
in writing. ‒ many of the challenges facing the union, both present and future, are complex and interrelated, originate from state and non-state actors and arise from within and outside common borders, so that it is necessary to connect local, regional and global contexts in order to be able to respond proactively to them. the need for strong solidarity between member states to deal with these threats, as well as strong political will and a common objective between states, is presented as indispensable. we consider it important that arms control and common position 2008/944/cfsp focus on human security. in addition, the eu must play a central role in global climate action and the promotion of sustainable development. on the refugee crisis, we support the need for a joint european approach and for concerted and urgent action and solution. we believe that the member states must work together, developing and pooling their defence capabilities, in order to manage and prevent emerging crises and conflicts and to ensure the security of eu citizens. i therefore voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ we are against this report because it continues to validate the eu's foreign policy, supported by an approach of interference and interference with third countries whose main objective is to achieve conditions favourable to the interests of the big financial groups over the economies and welfare of these countries, particularly in the areas of energy. an interference that forces them to comply with structural reforms. we are voting against this report because it is in line with the eu's ambition to achieve geopolitical and economic dominance in that part of the world as well.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of a report which focuses mainly on the human rights situation in central asia (and not on commercial aspects, as is usually the case in this type of texts), pointing out the major problems to which the eu must contribute: democratic deficit, repression of human rights defenders and journalists, child labour, gender gap, lack of basic services and environmental deterioration. the text also rightly points out europe's responsibility in arms exports and the need for cooperation in the fight against radicalism and drug trafficking.
in writing. ‒ as this report underlines, there is a need to review the framework for relations between the eu and the five central asian countries: kazakhstan, kyrgyzstan, uzbekistan, tajikistan and turkmenistan, which have been increasing their relevance on the international scene in recent years. it is an energy-exporting and energy-producing region, and a transit zone for goods between europe and east asia, and russia and south asia, of great strategic, political and economic interest to the eu, and it is therefore necessary to strengthen our bilateral and multilateral relations. the strategic approach adopted to date has shown only limited viability and success. in addition, respect for democratic norms, human rights and fundamental freedoms is insufficient and the human rights situation remains worrying, although some positive developments have occurred in some countries in the region, through legislative reforms, renewed efforts to prevent torture, and measures aimed at eradicating child and forced labour. all these issues are fully covered in the report which i have supported with my vote.

in writing. ‒ we are against this report because it continues to validate the eu's foreign policy, supported by an approach of interference and interference with third countries whose main objective is to achieve conditions favourable to the interests of the big financial groups over the economies and welfare of these countries, particularly in the areas of energy. an interference that forces them to comply with structural reforms. we are voting against this report because it is in line with the eu's ambition to achieve geopolitical and economic dominance in that part of the world as well.
in writing. ‒ as this report underlines, there is a need to review the framework for relations between the eu and the five central asian countries: kazakhstan, kyrgyzstan, uzbekistan, tajikistan and turkmenistan, which have been increasing their relevance on the international scene in recent years. it is an energy-exporting and energy-producing region, and a transit zone for goods between europe and east asia, and russia and south asia, of great strategic, political and economic interest to the eu, and it is therefore necessary to strengthen our bilateral and multilateral relations. the strategic approach adopted to date has shown only limited viability and success. in addition, respect for democratic norms, human rights and fundamental freedoms is insufficient and the human rights situation remains worrying, although some positive developments have occurred in some countries in the region, through legislative reforms, renewed efforts to prevent torture, and measures aimed at eradicating child and forced labour. all these issues are fully covered in the report which i have supported with my vote.

in writing. ‒ on 1 february 2016, the who declared that the zika virus outbreak constitutes a public health emergency of international concern. sporadic outbreaks of the disease caused by the virus have been detected in two european regions, martinique and french guiana, and cases of contamination in guadeloupe and saint martin. the european centre for disease prevention and control has been monitoring the situation on an ongoing basis, but it is requested that the centre regularly update its risk assessments and epidemiological bulletins and that it establish a committee of experts on tropical communicable diseases. we welcome the commission's decision to allocate eur 10 million to research into the virus, both for prevention with a possible vaccine and for the treatment of the disease. we also call for the establishment of a prenatal diagnosis protocol and the possibility of continuing or not with pregnancy in the event of malformations, as well as the promotion of research for the eradication of the mosquito-carrier, using insecticides that are not harmful to humans. that is why i voted in favour.

madam president, commissioner jourová, i can say without any reservations that this parliament, by striking a new balance this afternoon between freedom and security and, in particular, between the right to security and the confidentiality of personal data, is making history. we are doing this, firstly, because we are confirming the criterion we have held from the outset: that regulation, directive and pnr should form a package. yeah, a whole package. and the regulation makes history because, for the first time, this european parliament is acting as a legislator in the development of the fundamental rights guaranteed by the charter of fundamental rights of the european union with european legislation which is a regulation directly binding on the member states and which can be invoked by citizens before the courts. the directive is a european and homogeneous tool to ensure that police and judicial authorities, who have responsibilities in the investigation of crimes and in the arrest and prosecution of offenders, act subject to a single european legislation. and the pnr, because it is an additional tool in guaranteeing the security of europeans against serious threats, serious transnational crime and terrorism, without being a panacea. but most importantly, we do so by affirming the importance of informational self-determination, the right of citizens to intervene through consent in the handling of their personal data in relation to cancellation and rectification, and also in ensuring the right to be forgotten. so, yes, this parliament is taking a historic step, a legislative step that deserves to be called such.
mr president, i come from a country which has been fighting terrorism for 50 years. we've learned that to win, you have to trust the police. political parties must be united so that society is not divided. and against terrorism, all efforts are small. we have been debating the issue of passenger data for years, and in the meantime there has been the attack on charlie hebdo, there has been the attack on paris, there has been the attack on brussels, and we have been debating it. some say that with a pnr we could not have prevented these attacks. that's a sad thought. who knows if we could have prevented them or not. there are 14 pnrs in europe, they are not connected and they are all fragmentary. and there are 5,000 europeans fighting with daesh, who we do not know when they will return to europe; and i would like to know on what flight they are coming and at what time they are landing, because i am not one of those who care more about the right to privacy of the terrorist than the right to life of the victim who is waiting. through our credit cards, any tax inspector in office can know everything about our privacy. i think it's okay to give up a part of my privacy to pay taxes, but i also think it's okay to give up a part of my privacy to save my life; because privacy is important, but life is more important. because paying taxes is very important, money is very important, but life is much more important. there are some colleagues here who come every day to talk about transparency, except today when we are talking about the transparency of terrorists. the people's group will vote yes to the pnr tomorrow, not because of the attacks that could have been prevented but because of those that we are going to prevent in the future; i hope you will be on the same team. madam president, i am intervening in this debate, which must lead to the adoption tomorrow of this legislative instrument regulating a european pnr, to welcome the work of the rapporteur and also of the alternative rapporteurs, with their conflicting views, but above all to defend the work of this european parliament. because in this european parliament we are a few of those who have had executive responsibilities in government and, in particular and also on the left, responsibilities in the fight against terrorism in a country particularly afflicted by the scourge of terrorism as spain has been. but this parliament has not been dragging its feet and so i am going along with the criticisms that have been heard, which claim that this parliament has unnecessarily delayed the legislative approval of this pnr, because it is not true. this parliament has debated it at length in order to do its job and strike a reasonable balance between freedom and security, delimiting the object, delimiting the serious crimes in which data can be transferred, delimiting the time of retention of such data and ensuring that in no case can it be opened to the drawing up of discriminatory profiles. so, it's not true what i've heard here. it is not true that privacy was an excuse for this parliament to delay approval. i'm not sure. privacy is a fundamental right of europeans, guaranteed as such in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. and privacy is a fundamental right which the european parliament is also legislating on at this session with the final adoption of the data protection regulation. so this parliament has done its job. it is not true that parliament has unnecessarily delayed a tool which is not a panacea - it has been reiterated - but which can be useful in guaranteeing a reasonable balance between freedom and security for the european citizens whom we represent.

member of the commission.– madam president, the commission is aware of the importance of the role played by small- and medium-sized enterprises, which contribute to economic growth and job creation in the european union. the commission is fully committed to identifying the most appropriate policies and tools to address their funding needs. smes face structural financing obstacles – as has been said several times now – as they are largely dependent on bank financing, whereas larger companies have a more diversified source of funding thanks to their access to capital markets. their dependence on bank loans and less-diversified sources of income make smes more vulnerable to downturns in the economic cycle. european smes have experienced huge difficulties in accessing finance in the aftermath of the financial crisis. the problem is especially serious in some member states, which has led to the concerns voiced by this european parliament. in this spirit, the commission has supported the inclusion in the capital requirement regulation of a measure – the sme-supporting factor – aimed at granting loans to smes and giving them more risk-sensitive potential treatment, and thus reducing the potential impact of the tougher capital charges introduced by the capital requirements regulation on lending to smes. the sme-supporting factor has been in force since 1 january 2014. thanks to your and the commission’s efforts, the importance of the issue has also been acknowledged at global level, and the basel committee on banking supervision is now also considering lowering capital charges for exposures to smes. the commission is currently assessing the effects of the sme factor in the context of the review of the capital requirement regulation, which will be published towards the end of the year. in particular, we are looking at its impact on the volumes of sme lending since its introduction, compared to other factors, for example, the macroeconomic environment or the sme’s credit history. moreover, we will be looking to verify whether, according to the available evidence, the sme factor remains potentially sound, taking into account its features in terms of the definition of an sme and the size of the loan. we are drawing on various sources of information for this exercise, such as the recent public consultation on the impact of the capital requirements regulation on banking financing of the economy and the call for evidence on financial regulation launched in september last year. the recently published european banking authority report on smes and the sme-supporting factor has also provided the commission with useful elements for its forthcoming policy recommendations. finally i should stress that, in future, bank lending should not remain the only – or at least the largely dominant – response to the financing gap of eu smes. an appropriate degree of diversification of funding sources should be sought and the dominant role of banks reduced. this is precisely one of the objectives of the capital market union project, which aims at fostering the role of capital markets for the european union economy.

pakistan in its fight against terrorism and in the promotion of our shared values, among which is diversity. we call on pakistan to bring the perpetrators and instigators of these attacks to justice and to take firm action against the organisations that claim responsibility. we are very worried about the rising levels of religious violence and intolerance in some parts of pakistan and we are closely monitoring these developments. minorities in the country, including religious minorities, continue to suffer disproportionately and they are frequently targeted by extremist militants. we call on the government to step up efforts to ensure the security of all members of religious minorities. the 2016 gsp+ report underscores that the human rights situation remains very challenging. we always raise human rights issues in our regular dialogue with pakistan and encourage authorities to address the challenges, including those concerning the situation of minorities. the european union regrets the lifting of the moratorium on the death penalty in pakistan and the large number of executions this has led to. pakistan is now the third largest executor. just yesterday, four more prisoners convicted of murder were hanged. the european union is opposed to capital punishment in all circumstances and has consistently called for its universal abolition. the european union, in all its contacts with pakistan, continues to underline the importance of reintroducing the moratorium on executions and of complying with the minimum standards. the european union is also supporting several projects to improve awareness and protection of human rights, access to justice for vulnerable groups and to strengthen civil society organisations in pakistan. the european union bilateral development cooperation for the period 2014-2020 for pakistan, with a total amount of eur 635 million, has human rights and good governance as one of the three focal sectors. human rights violations remain widespread in the country, despite some of the constructive initiatives underway. pakistan has made some progress in strengthening the institutional framework for human rights, including by establishing a national commission for human rights. furthermore, the government recently adopted an action plan to improve the human rights situation in pakistan. the plan includes various measures, notably the development of a national plan of action for the promotion and protection of the rights of minorities. some action has also been taken to address the widespread problem of hate speech. there have also been some advances on legislation to improve women’s rights. the european union has also been calling for comprehensive action against terrorism, in full compliance with international law, fundamental values and international human rights standards. more emphasis will need to be put on the prevention of terrorism, in particular in the areas of countering radicalisation, recruitment and the financing of terrorism. let me finally underline that the european union has been, and remains, a staunch supporter of democracy and reform in pakistan.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this legislative package because it represents a historic agreement on the protection of personal data of european citizens. it consists of two elements: a regulation, which covers the processing of personal data by private actors, and a directive, which covers the use of personal data by police and judicial authorities. the agreement sets the clock for the protection of personal data in the 21st century and covers all aspects of data storage, processing and deletion. it also gives citizens greater control over a very important aspect of their lives, namely privacy. the way in which judicial and police authorities handle citizens' personal data has a profound impact on citizens' fundamental rights. the new directive will help to bring these exchanges under the umbrella of eu-wide rules, which will improve their effectiveness while protecting fundamental rights. it is the first time that we will have a harmonised system in the eu among the 28 partners.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this legislative resolution on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data by the authorities for the purposes of the prevention, investigation, detection and prosecution of criminal offences or the execution of criminal penalties, and on the free movement of such data. throughout the process parliament introduced important measures to preserve the rights of individuals in the use of such data with limitations on the time of retention of such data, classification of data into categories to determine under which conditions they could be processed and eliminated, among other things, the transfer of information to third countries unless authorised by the competent authorities, as it was not considered to offer the necessary safeguards. that is why we voted in favour of the third reading.

in writing. ‒ the data protection directive negotiations came to an end on 15 december. the agreed text is not perfect but it still provides better data protection rights in the context of law enforcement activities than the current legislation. the main problematic element is the council’s addition of article 36aa which allows transfers of personal data to private entities in third countries. despite this controversial article, i voted in favour of this directive.
in writing. ‒ parliament approves the council's position at first reading on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data. we are talking about an important decision which helps us to take a further step in the fight against crime, and i therefore consider it necessary to vote in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this legislative package because it represents a historic agreement on the protection of personal data of european citizens. it consists of two elements: a regulation, which addresses the processing of personal data by private actors, and a directive, which covers the use of personal data by law enforcement and judicial authorities. the agreement sets the clock for the protection of personal data in the 21st century and covers all aspects of data storage, processing and deletion. it also gives citizens greater control over a very important aspect of their lives, namely privacy. the way in which judicial and police authorities handle citizens' personal data has a profound impact on citizens' fundamental rights. the new directive will help to bring these exchanges under the umbrella of union-wide regulation, which will improve their effectiveness while protecting fundamental rights. it is the first time that we will have a harmonised system in the union among the 28 partners.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of a directive to establish a european register of data on travellers using aircraft as a means of transport within the eu because, as the spanish socialists have been advocating, it is a useful instrument in the fight against the terrorist threat that is hitting us. personal data associated with tickets can be useful in identifying risks. once this instrument is adopted, authorities will be able to exchange information on suspects in a timely manner. in the face of a common threat that knows no borders, the eu must have a common framework for exchanging information handled individually by the police and judicial authorities of each country and even by the national intelligence services of the 28. it is not just a question of increasing uncritically new instruments for combating terrorism, which have an impact on fundamental rights, but of improving the use made of existing instruments. that is why we socialists call for a strengthening of europol, to make it a kind of european fbi that is up to the challenge we face.
in writing. ‒ since the attempt to impose a passenger name record (pnr) in the european union began, we have been opposed to the scant data protection guarantees that exist and this means a further increase in the capacity of the security forces to act in an opaque manner and without guarantees of legality using the fight against terrorism as an excuse. the trialogue process has not reduced the scope of regulation, but on the contrary, with the registration of intra-european flights and without a clear limit on the nature of the data to be stored, so that the police can collect and store information that does not have to be relevant for counter-terrorist intelligence. finally, the possibility of transferring this data to a third party, even outside the european union, remains, which is frankly worrying and deepens the policy of mass surveillance of the population, particularly of social activists, by our governments or by third countries with the complicity of our governments. for all the above reasons, we have voted against the proposal.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report approving the proposal for a directive which will regulate air passenger name record (pnr) data despite my reservations and doubts about its future usefulness as member states are not required to share data. i have done so as a gesture towards the progress and development of a genuine common intelligence system which is effective and facilitates a genuine exchange of appropriate information. but after the hasty adoption in 2006 of a data retention directive that was supposed to serve to improve security, a decade and several attacks later, the regulation has not proved to be effective and has become evident its special gravity in the fundamental rights to respect for private life. the court of justice of the european union (cjeu) overturned it in 2014. i will continue to work to ensure that the european union has a directive guaranteeing the exchange of information between national intelligence services. for europol to become the hub of operations facilitating and coordinating the exchange without having to rely on 28 massive databases and without clear coordination.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this despite the fact that this pnr in the eu was initially proposed by the commission as a way of fighting terrorism and transnational crime. finally, the rapporteur's text shows that the intention goes further. the text was originally intended to harmonise the data collection obligations of airlines and operators operating from third countries. the report, again, went further than the commission proposal, calling for the registration of passenger data to be extended to travellers between eu countries. the text sets out the criteria on the basis of which these authorities may use such data, defined in a vague and broad manner. the proposed mass collection of data is disproportionate and unnecessary in defiance of the ecj recommendations on proportionality in data collection. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the information provided by the member states is not used in a way that would be contrary to the interests of the community.

in writing. ‒ following the tragic events in many european capitals, citizens are calling for action at european level to tackle organised crime and terrorism. at the time of booking an air ticket, passengers provide information held by airlines for operational, commercial and statistical purposes. this data is known as the passenger name record (pnr). the report aims to harmonise the obligation for air carriers operating flights between the territory of a member state and a third country to transmit pnr data. one of the most important measures implemented in the report is the inclusion of internal flights between eu member states, which were not included in the scope of the text, and which will bring major advantages in terms of safety. in my view, the adoption of this report is crucial because it defines the criteria under which law enforcement agencies can use this data to detect, investigate and prosecute both serious and terrorist offences.
in writing. ‒ no european citizen would understand that we would vote against an instrument like the pnr. we need it in these times, because we need to help the police and security services to achieve their objectives. this, of course, must be done head on, by building up the confidence of member states among themselves, and by facilitating the exchange of information between the various national security and intelligence networks so that we can act better and in a more coordinated way. however, we must not forget that this is only one instrument which must be complemented by others, which must be sufficiently balanced to respect the sensitive data of our citizens.

in writing. ‒ pnr data is unverified information provided by passengers, and collected by and held in the carriers’ reservation and departure control systems for their own commercial purposes. it contains several different types of information, such as travel dates, travel itinerary, contact details, the travel agent at which the flight was booked, means of payment used and baggage information. i support the compromise achieved for this pnr report. the recent attacks in europe push us to act and stop delaying the implementation of pnr even further. improved security is fundamental to safeguard democracy and freedom. i support the binding obligation for member states to share and exchange information and pnr processing.

in writing. ‒ we are certainly talking about a priority and a necessary issue on which we had to move forward to demonstrate our commitment to the fight against terrorism and to increased cooperation on these issues by member states. i therefore think it appropriate to vote in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ the recent revelations of the panama papers have once again demonstrated the important role played by informants and the press. it is imperative that individuals acting in the public interest be protected by law. i have therefore voted in favour of this directive because it guarantees the protection of the rights of workers, whistleblowers and the freedom of the press, thus formalising a clear legal framework which ensures that those who expose illegal or unethical activities, in a situation where it is a matter of defending a general public interest, are exempt from the scope of this directive. the s&d group has also called on the european commission to come forward with new proposals to guarantee these measures as a matter of urgency. it has also been possible to guarantee the autonomy of the social partners, the express exclusion of obstacles to the mobility of workers which could be derived from the original text of the directive, the right to information and consultation, and the protection of the right to disseminate information concerning the operation of the undertaking by workers to their representatives as part of the legitimate exercise of the latter's functions.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it represents an arbitrary definition of industrial secrecy which can be reversed in favour of tax evasion, as well as giving more power to private enterprise against potential informants. the need to protect whistleblowers who have made this information public has been demonstrated after the successive luxembourg and panama scandals, but this proposal for a directive does not protect whistleblowers because they did not provide 'illegal' information. in this way, the directive gives tremendous power to private companies which, in the name of competitiveness, can take all kinds of legal action against whistleblowers. the extreme need to protect these contemporary heroes in the fight against tax evasion and avoidance is why i have decided to vote against this report.
in writing. ‒ i am pleased with the recent adoption of the trade secrets directive, a text that encourages innovation and protects freedom of information. legal protection is an indispensable tool to promote innovation, especially for smes investing in r & d & i, against those who want to take advantage of their efforts and talent. the directive offers comprehensive protection, improving on the european commission's initial proposal and favouring a competitive economy of high wages and stable employment. it is a relief for small businesses, which often lack the necessary financial resources. voting would not have been voting for precariousness. the text also stresses the need to guarantee the protection of journalists, another aspect of which must be welcomed. some called for the thorough inclusion of protection for whistleblowers. i shall vote for such an initiative, but it is a separate matter which must be legislated separately. however, for the first time in a text, the protection of whistleblowers is mentioned, an issue which will certainly have to be studied further in the future and which i will certainly support. what is meaningless is to block a directive which combats precariousness using the fight against corruption as an excuse.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this proposal for a directive aimed at protecting companies from the theft of secrets by their competitors in the market. the directive originally drafted by the european commission clearly favoured the protection of economic rights at the expense of the political rights of citizens. unfortunately, despite some improvements, the text resulting from the interinstitutional negotiations and commitments subsequently reached still contains restrictions on fundamental rights which we consider unacceptable.
in writing. ‒ the recent revelations of the panama papers have once again demonstrated the important role of informants and the press. it is imperative that individuals acting in the public interest be protected by law. i have therefore voted in favour of this directive because it guarantees the protection of the rights of workers, whistleblowers and the freedom of the press, thus formalising a clear legal framework which ensures that those who expose illegal or unethical activities, in a situation where it is a matter of defending a general public interest, are exempt from the scope of this directive. the s&d group has also called on the european commission to come forward with new proposals to guarantee these measures as a matter of urgency. it has also been possible to guarantee the autonomy of the social partners, the express exclusion of obstacles to the mobility of workers which could be derived from the original text of the directive, the right to information and consultation, and the protection of the right to disseminate information concerning the operation of the undertaking by workers to their representatives as part of the legitimate exercise of the latter's functions.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it represents an arbitrary definition of industrial secrecy which can be reversed in favour of tax evasion, as well as giving more power to private enterprise against potential informants. the need to protect whistleblowers who have made this information public has been demonstrated after the successive luxembourg and panama scandals, but this proposal for a directive does not protect whistleblowers because they did not provide 'illegal' information. in this way, the directive gives tremendous power to private companies which, in the name of competitiveness, can take all kinds of legal action against whistleblowers. the extreme need to protect these contemporary heroes in the fight against tax evasion and avoidance is why i have decided to vote against this report.
in writing. ‒ the legislative initiative on the protection of trade secrets is based on an assessment of the importance of trade secrets for innovation and the competitiveness of enterprises, the extent to which they are used, their role and relationship with ipr, the economic generation and exploitation of knowledge and intangible assets and the relevant legal framework. the aim of this initiative is to ensure that the competitiveness of european companies and research organisations relying on know-how and undisclosed business information is adequately protected and thus to improve the conditions and framework for the development and exploitation of innovation and knowledge transfer in the internal market. in particular, it seeks to improve the effectiveness of the legal protection of trade secrets against misappropriation throughout the internal market and to have a deterrent effect against the unlawful disclosure of trade secrets without prejudice to fundamental rights and freedoms or the public interest, such as public security, consumer protection, public health, environmental protection and worker mobility.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i consider it very important to create definitions and mechanisms to allow for better protection of trade secrets in the union. i think this is an important step forward, since trade secrets have not enjoyed such protection until now.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because the protection of trade secrets against their unlawful acquisition, use and disclosure is essential if companies are to benefit from a fair trading environment. however, it is important to remember that the circulation of knowledge and information is also essential to the process of innovation and creation. it should also be recalled that according to the approved report, freedom of the press is protected in any case, as well as disclosure in order to reveal improper behavior, fraud, irregularity, fraud or illegal activity, provided that the defendant has acted in the public interest. no one may rely on the protection of trade secrets to act in an opaque or fraudulent manner.
in writing. ‒ the recent revelations of the panama papers have once again demonstrated the important role played by whistleblowers and the press. it is imperative that individuals acting in the public interest be protected by law. i have therefore voted in favour of a directive guaranteeing the protection of the rights of workers, whistleblowers and freedom of the press. in addition, a clear legal framework is formalised to ensure that those who expose illegal or unethical activities, in a situation of public and general interest, are exempted from the scope of this directive. we socialists have also asked the european commission to come forward with new proposals to guarantee these measures as a matter of urgency. the autonomy of the social partners, the express exclusion of obstacles to the mobility of workers which might have been derived from the original text of the directive, the right to information and consultation and the protection of the right to disseminate information concerning the operation of the undertaking by workers to their representatives have also been guaranteed.

in writing. ‒ in the european parliament and in the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, we have always fought to ensure that businesses interact in a fair trading environment. the circulation of knowledge and information between firms is essential to ensure a process of innovation and creation between them. however, this action cannot be carried out in an abusive manner because it has a counterproductive effect. this report seeks to strike a balance so that abusive claims do not arise in relation to the improper acquisition or circulation of trade secrets. it also brings many benefits to both businesses and consumers, as it will encourage the mobility of workers and ensure fair judicial proceedings, especially for small businesses. the definition of 'trade secret' will also be clarified so that large companies do not take advantage of small ones due to the legal uncertainty of the term. i therefore support this report.

in writing. ‒ i voted against the 2017 estimate of parliament's expenditure because i believe that the resources available to parliament are not being used properly. it has increased exponentially in spending on security and cybersecurity, while also increasing the budget with unnecessary expenses such as office renovation. but on the other hand, it has been decided to cut the contribution for interpretation and the proposal to introduce sign language has not been accepted. if cuts are needed, they should be made in the area of members' salaries or travel expenses, as parliament continues to pay for business flights for meps. finally, we continue with the perennial problem of the waste of maintaining the two seats of the european parliament. for these reasons i voted against it.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report on the european parliament's revenue and expenditure forecast for the financial year 2017, because we welcome some of the measures for cutting redundant expenditure proposed by the rapporteur, the broad lines he is moving along are the right ones, and we chose to give our support at this point in the budget construction. it is not obvious that we disagree with several of the statements in this report, to which we are putting amendments, because we believe that the budget of the european parliament, in times of crisis such as this, should set an example of humility and austerity, as long as these cuts do not hinder legislative and parliamentary work and do not endanger jobs.

in writing. ‒ this report welcomes the eu-turkey agreement on migration, which we oppose. it also stresses 'the great humanitarian contribution of turkey' for its role in hosting refugees, when in reality it is crowding refugees fleeing war into concentration camps for people including women and minors, without meeting basic hygiene conditions and violating the most fundamental human rights. with the eu-turkey agreement and the funds given to turkey to turn it into a prison for refugees who want to seek asylum in europe, it continues in the line of an aggressive foreign policy and against human rights, and as this report welcomes this agreement, i decided to vote against it.
in writing. the 2015 report on turkey is characterised by the maintenance of good bilateral relations while calling on the turkish government to move forward on different chapters of the accession negotiations and condemning the deterioration of democracy and human rights that has occurred in recent years. i voted in favour because i believe in a european turkey, and i am also firmly of the view that accession can only come about if turkey meets the copenhagen criteria. i have also rejected some of the gue/ngl amendments because of their partial view in favour of the interests and positions of the pkk. i do not agree with your proposal to remove the pkk from the eu list of terrorist organisations. the latest terrorist acts show that at least one important sector still believes in armed struggle as a solution to the conflict. on immigration and asylum, i support the implementation of our common asylum policy in line with the geneva convention. our obligations can never be outsourced to turkey, a country that has proven to be unsafe for refugees. under no circumstances can the agreements reached with turkey be linked to the accession process.
in writing. ‒ we voted against a text which is appropriately tough in denouncing the systematic violation of human rights by the turkish government against minorities, political opponents and journalists, demanding in terms of the criteria and conditions for turkey's accession to the eu but absolutely opposed to political and legal responsibility in terms of co-management of migration and the protection of the rights of people in situations of forced mobility.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the annual progress report for turkey. the report praises turkey as the country hosting the largest refugee population in the world. the eu and turkey today face many common challenges and we need each other in order to find joint solutions. the report is also critical and shows that there has been a major democratic setback this year, especially in the areas of freedom of expression, freedom of the press, the rule of law and minority rights. the report calls on turkey to resume democratic reforms in line with eu values and hopes that the accession process will speed up these necessary changes. the report addresses the situation in south-eastern turkey, which is experiencing the most significant wave of violence in the last 20 years. it called for an immediate ceasefire and for the resumption of the peace process, since there is no military solution to the kurdish question. a conflict that has tens of thousands of displaced people.

in writing. ‒ in this report, the european parliament underlines the importance of turkey as a strategic partner for the european union. the report highlights certain areas where the country should make progress such as the independence of the judiciary, freedom of assembly, freedom of expression, legal security or respect for human rights. the report also deals with issues of major importance in relation to european energy security, progress in the reunification of cyprus, turkey's participation in the grand coalition to fight daesh and turkey's role in managing the current migration crisis. we are talking about a complete report which deals with the issues that are on the table in relation to this country. i therefore consider it necessary to vote in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the annual progress report for turkey. turkey is one of the countries in the world that hosts the largest refugee population at the moment. the eu and turkey face many common challenges and we must find joint solutions. the report is critical and shows that there has been a major democratic backsliding this year, especially in the areas of freedom of expression, freedom of the press, the rule of law and minority rights. the report calls on turkey to resume democratic reforms in line with eu values and hopes that the accession process will speed up these necessary changes. the report also addresses the situation in south-eastern turkey, which is experiencing the most significant wave of violence in the last 20 years. it called for an immediate ceasefire and for the resumption of the peace process, since there is no military solution to the kurdish question. a conflict that has tens of thousands of displaced people.

in writing. i voted in favour of the 2015 report on albania because of its equanimity and europeanist vision on the situation and future of albania. the document shows the progress made in the country in achieving the commitments set out in the stabilisation and association agreement. the commission is also aware of the backward position it is in as a result of organised crime, the poor judicial system, discrimination against minorities and women, unemployment, etc. i find the trafficking of children in the country particularly worrying. many children are exploited by their families to the point of being financially dependent on the livelihood they get on the streets. albania is the country with the highest number of child beggars in europe. as long as albanian children are slaves to this situation, society will be condemned to remain underdeveloped by mortgaging the lives of the new generations who should be the engine of the country's progress. i am also sceptical about the inclusion of albania as a safe third country. in my view, albania does not clearly fulfil the criteria set out in directive 2013/32/eu. in 2014 it accepted only 7.8% of asylum applications it received.
in writing. ‒ we abstained, despite the fact that the motion for a resolution is in line with the prospect of integration of the balkan countries, for two reasons: the position it maintains on the economic reforms that are being demanded of albania and because the motion for a resolution contains a position on how to fight terrorism that we do not share. in addition, this proposal is quite vague on the orientation in the fight against high-level organised crime, the treatment of the roma minority and on the treatment in the fight against gender-based violence. the report contains positive aspects which we appreciate as a whole, and we shall therefore abstain.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report as it focuses on analysing household expenditure and the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy which has as its challenge to reduce by 20 million people at risk of social exclusion. the report has incorporated four aspects, two of which are included in its general recommendations, which are very positive. first, references to the need to increase investment in renewable energy and energy efficiency to tackle poverty are interesting insofar as they are linked to policies on employment, energy transition, quality and affordable housing and reduction of health spending. secondly, the text refers to an adequate minimum income above the poverty line, which represents 60% of the average national income in all member states. thirdly, a call for better use, dissemination and information on european funds as well as an extension beyond 2020 to the fead is noteworthy and positive. finally, the reference to a moratorium on winter heating cuts to ensure that no household is left without a supply is crucial to our vote in favour.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report on the private sector and development. among other points we reject, the report calls on the european commission to support and finance development cooperation policies which give the private sector a predominant role through so-called public-private partnerships. we are once again faced with a defence of the privatisation of development policies using eu funds for cooperation as instruments to open up new business areas to the private sector with public money. although the report includes some amendments tabled by our political group calling for the involvement and consultation of civil society organisations or the need for member states to implement the un guiding principles on human rights and business in their national plans, we flatly reject the idea that development cooperation should be oriented towards the private sector's profit-making.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report for a number of reasons. the report welcomes the commission's initiative to embrace the private sector as an important partner in achieving development, while recognising that private sector investment in developing countries can contribute to the achievement of the un sustainable development goals (sdgs). the report also calls on the commission to promote support and financing for the private sector-oriented development mechanism, by mixing the private sector with the public sector, in order to take advantage of private flows with public money. these mechanisms are profit-oriented, not aligned with the principles of development effectiveness and do not contribute to poverty reduction and the achievement of the sdgs.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report on the private sector and development. among other points we reject, the report calls on the european commission to support and finance development cooperation policies which give the private sector a predominant role through so-called public-private partnerships. we are once again faced with a defence of the privatisation of development policies using eu funds for cooperation as instruments to open up new business areas to the private sector with public money. although the report includes some amendments tabled by our political group calling for the involvement and consultation of civil society organisations or the need for member states to implement the un guiding principles on human rights and business in their national plans, we flatly reject the idea that development cooperation should be oriented towards the private sector's profit-making.
in writing. ‒ this report is designed to create a strategy for the private sector. it should be noted that the private sector creates 90% of the jobs in the partner countries, accounts for 84% of gdp and provides a sustainable basis for the mobilisation of domestic resources. it is also worth noting that private sector investment in developing countries has achieved high rates of return. the report insists that public-private partnerships should be exploited to a greater extent in sectors such as agriculture, education, health care and property rights, among others. it called on the european investment bank and the eu delegations to use their experience and expertise in working with private enterprises to achieve a development policy that takes account of the commitment of the european business sector. i personally think that the report should be adopted because working with the private sector is essential for development.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this report for a number of reasons. the report welcomes the commission's initiative to embrace the private sector as an important partner in achieving development, while recognising that private sector investment in developing countries can contribute to the achievement of the un sustainable development goals (sdgs). the report also calls on the commission to promote support and financing for the private sector-oriented development mechanism, by mixing the private sector with the public sector, in order to take advantage of private flows with public money. these mechanisms are profit-oriented, not aligned with the principles of development effectiveness and do not contribute to poverty reduction and the achievement of the sdgs.

in writing. ‒ the private sector is becoming increasingly important in developing countries, where it already provides 90% of jobs and is thus a key pillar in the fight against poverty. on the other hand, this sector is of vital importance for investment in sustainable agricultural production, especially if we take into account the forecasts made for 2050, when the world population is expected to reach 9 billion. in view of these two arguments, i am confident that the private sector is vital and must be strengthened, and i therefore support this report.
member of the commission.– mr president, i welcome the opportunity to address with you the impact of the immigration crisis on the transport sector in the european union. as you are all well aware, given the unprecedented inflow of refugees, several member states have introduced internal border controls. though temporary, they hamper the proper functioning of the schengen area. because of current security threats, controls are, in addition, being applied to certain means of transportation as well as at borders. the transport sector is particularly sensitive to these measures. consequently, the reintroduction of internal border controls on a broader and more permanent basis would not only impede the mobility of citizens in the schengen countries, it would also undermine the timelessness and seamlessness of the free exchange of goods within the european union. this currently accounts for more than eur 2 800 billion in value and 1 700 million tons in volume. the commission has analysed the consequences of a systematic reintroduction of border controls at internal borders. first results show that, in the short term, increased waiting times at borders and terminals would affect passengers and trade. in the long run, reduced traffic and trade volumes would severely affect the economy. document checking procedures would entail additional expenses for member states’ budgets for equipment, personnel and new facilities. the road freight sector would be particularly exposed, as prompt delivery is one of the important parameters for competitive advantage, and small and medium-sized enterprises, the backbone of the road transport industry, would be the most affected. with many operating on very small profit margins, any increased costs would either be passed to the end consumers or put the survival of many transport companies in jeopardy. expressed in numbers, the commission estimates that full re-establishment of border controls to monitor the movement of people within the schengen area would generate immediate direct costs to the european union economy ranging between eur 5 billion and 18 billion a year. long—term and indirect effects are more difficult to quantify, but available evidence suggests that re—establishing internal border controls would have substantial negative effects on the whole european economy. the volume of intra—european trade would go down, whereas related costs would go up, chiefly affecting member states highly dependent on intra—eu trade. 1.7 billion citizens working across borders would be affected, in particular in those member states such as slovakia, estonia, hungary and belgium where cross-border commuting is very important. the good functioning of the cross-border labour market could thus be hampered. i believe that these initial estimates clearly demonstrate the serious negative impact of a possible suspension of free movement without internal border controls in the schengen area, which is an essential element for economic growth in the european union and, in particular, for the performance of the transport sector. therefore, closing borders between member states should be only a temporary measure, and controls should be lifted as soon as possible. in its communication of 4 march entitled ‘back to schengen, a roadmap’ the commission has outlined its plan and schedule for getting back to a normally-functioning schengen by the end of 2016. the longer internal border controls remain in place, the more difficult and costly it will be to restore the favourable business environment which the schengen area aims to provide. as economic actors adapt to the new reality, a return to the previous situation will not be immediate or guaranteed. please let me assure you that we will work hard to get the schengen system and the internal market functioning normally again by the end of this year. i am looking forward to hearing your views on the matter and on how we can best work together to safeguard the single market.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, i have to say that there are many aspects of this debate which i welcome and others which i am seriously concerned about. on the one hand, i agree that the migration phenomenon needs to be tackled from a multidimensional perspective in order to put in place effective and sustainable solutions in the medium and long term. for example, it is very important to stress the role of merchant vessels, the role they play in the search and rescue of vessels adrift in european waters. according to data from the office of the united nations high commissioner for refugees, the mediterranean is the deadliest sea migration route in the world and - as we know - these vessels are so fragile and so small that it is difficult to detect them with current satellite technology systems. in this context, merchant fleets and their crews play a role of locating, assisting and managing humanitarian aid for which they are not always prepared logistically or professionally, and risk possible economic and legal sanctions both from their companies and from the authorities of the states when they arrive in port. this requires improving the capabilities of member states to carry out humanitarian search and rescue operations and to make available to merchant ships equipment, training and operational protocols. that said, there are many aspects of this approach that concern me. i am concerned that the focus of the debate is limited exclusively to issues relating to competitiveness and the proper functioning of the internal market. i am well aware that these issues are very important to us, but do you know what is really alarming about this debate? what is really alarming is the proliferation and consolidation of refugee trafficking mafias, who pick up their victims at stations and offer transport services at prices of up to eur 1 000 per person, for example, by transporting them in a truck, when they would have much cheaper options, but they do not know about them because no one informs them. it is a criminal network that takes advantage of the desperate situation of these people, and we cannot look the other way when many of them die because of these means of transport, as was the case of at least 50 people who died from suffocation in a refrigerated truck that was found in austria. they are completely unprotected and uninformed. this is a disgrace, your honours, this is a disgrace. there is also a lot of talk about the need to protect the proper functioning of the schengen area. and i ask myself: if we are so concerned about the freedom of movement within the european union, if it is so important, why have we agreed to an agreement with the united kingdom which so outrageously violates the principle of free movement? or is it that in our europe the same problems are sometimes first and sometimes second? we have a responsibility that we are ignoring, that we are ignoring, and this union can only be saved by more democracy and by putting human rights at the centre.
we are here, mr president, to see once again the high price we have to pay in the european union for a historic lack of policy coordination and the demonstration that watertight compartments and national selfishness, combined, are lethal to our citizens and our development. the absent, erratic and erroneous, intergovernmental and horribly fragmented, selfish policy of taking care of immigrants and asylum seekers in the european territory is now paying a small bill, but it can mean the beginning of the end, because schengen is one of the milestones of that more united, more integrated and more social europe that we want from its origin. and yet, madam commissioner, we support today the commission's intention to maintain schengen and to fight for the reopening of the frontiers as soon as possible, while at the same time introducing better formulas for the humanitarian management of migrants and asylum seekers, avoiding the torture of wandering around our territory lost and mistreated. and to think that we, transport, could have been the solution: that we could have established the safe humanitarian corridors that we have been asking for from the beginning, in which transport could have been precisely the solution to avoid death and suffering; that we could also have created a humanitarian air bridge from greece to the countries that undertook to receive the quotas of applicants agreed by the council, instead of throwing them onto the roads and paths of europe, would also have certainly improved the current solution. but the fragmentation of late and wrong decisions puts us in a position of responsibility. we therefore support today the measures to reopen the frontiers as soon as possible and the establishment of coordinated measures to facilitate transport and its service with safety for workers and transporters. we also denounce to the commission the increasing tendency of national governments to impose their own rules to impede the free movement of our carriers and workers. our appeal today is to overcome, in the face of the council's continuing errors, the fragmentation of decisions within the commission itself. commissioner, the development of the european internal market cannot be achieved without taking account of social and human rights.

mr president, commissioner, the apparent reason for this debate in the house is the annual report on access to documents in 2014 and 2015. and there have been contributions which should be welcomed and acknowledged by the rapporteur and the alternative rapporteurs, especially in relation to the transparency of the legislative procedure and the tripartite dialogues, where amendments and relevant documents should be transparent and, in addition, efforts should be made to webstream relevant debates of the legislative procedure. but i insist that this is only the apparent reason, because here a protest has been made, against the danger that some european institutions practice what we in spain say is 'tell me what you boast of and i will tell you what you lack'. because we cannot allow the strongest transparency ever to be proclaimed under the charter of fundamental rights of the european union and be ignored in practice by some institutions. i would therefore like to remind you that it is essential that the commission and the council unblock at once the updating of the general rules on transparency and access to documents, which were blocked for a long time during the last parliamentary term and are still an unresolved issue today.
mr president, we have received many requests from the committee on petitions concerning the problems that arise when an international family is separated. this is logically because there is more mobility and because there is an increasing number of families from different countries. the best interests of the child are indeed paramount. there is a regulation, which is the regulation of 2003, the brussels iia regulation, as the commission has said. after a few years of operation, its shortcomings and, in a way, its illness have been detected. and that is why this debate is very good for a revision of this regulation. and basically it seems that we have to ensure, firstly, what is the authority and the rule so that no one is left without a referent and there is legal certainty; secondly, the free circulation of judicial decisions because, sometimes, a judicial decision in one country is not applied as quickly as in another country; thirdly, that the executions of judicial decisions are real, because now there is also a lot of delay and, in some cases, there are appeal resources - in others not - that delay the procedure; fourthly, that in the case of child abduction there is agility - it will be six weeks, but this deadline should be respected - and, fifthly, that the return is effective and fast. i am fully confident, as mrs mcguinness has said, that the commission has found the key to what we have to do, what we have to do quickly, because the future is at stake here. one comment: some colleagues have used this debate to attack same-sex couples and i want to make a demand that this discrimination never happens.
member of the commission.– mr president, i wish to thank members very much for this debate which, as i expected, brought here many sad and serious true stories which we see in europe and where, as has been said, the children suffer. it is our duty to address the situation with the proper legislative act. several of you mentioned adoptions without parental consent. let me repeat that adoptions are regulated at national and not eu level. adoptions are therefore not also in the scope of the brussels iia regulation. but it can be generally noted that article 21 of the united nations convention on the rights of the child imposes on participating countries to ensure that the best interests of the child is the paramount consideration with regard to adoption. but the convention does not preclude adoption without parental consent. on norway – and yes, i expected to be asked about the situation and about the position of the european union – i can only repeat that due to the fact that norway is not a member state of the european union and moreover, as i said already before, the functioning of child welfare services is not governed by eu law, but by national law, the commission does not have any competence to intervene with the member states and it is even more difficult in the case in norway, when it comes to the functioning of child protection and welfare services. this is the dry answer. from the legal point of view, i can only assure you that i try every time when i am contact with the regional authorities to raise this problem informally, and the answer is always the same that everything is happening according to norwegian legislation. in cases where the right to family life or the rights of the children involved are allegedly violated by the norwegian child welfare services, it is for norway – including its judicial authorities – to ensure that fundamental rights and especially the rights of the child are effectively respected and protected in accordance with their national legislation. the parents concerned can seek redress at the national level only, through the competent national authorities, such as through an ombudsman or through the courts – and at the european court of human rights, once they have exhausted domestic remedies. just a short note on what mrs ward said on the need to cooperate with children’s organisations. i can assure you that we are now in very intensive contact and cooperation with them in trying to ease the situation for children in migration, where we, together with unicef and others, have prepared comprehensive material which addresses the problems from various angles. thank you very much again for this debate. we all agree that the best interest of the child belongs among our highest priorities, and that the brussels iia regulation tries to tackle the situation of cross—border disputes and the cross-border scope and character of the problems, which fully authorises the european union to take further action and well-targeted legislative solutions, as well as other actions like improving the functioning of the judicial systems in the eu member states so as to increase also the trust between the member states and the judiciary. i am convinced that the proposal which we are preparing, and which i will soon submit, on the amendment of the brussels iia regulation provides such a well-targeted solution, which will improve the situation.
president-in-office of the council.– mr president, let me underline once more tonight that it is important to stay true to our founding values. it is our duty to protect those most vulnerable, including adopted children. at the same time – and i repeat – it is important to understand that the issue of the adoption of children is a matter which is not regulated at eu level but by national laws and by some international conventions. as i said earlier, the council awaits with great interest the commission proposal amending the brussels iia regulation. i am convinced that the amendment will further improve the functioning of this regulation, particularly with regard to the rules on parental responsibility. clearly we share the same goal: strengthening the rights of the child in the eu. this is an investment not only in their future but also in the foundations of the union. a reference was made to unaccompanied minors disappearing upon arrival in europe, and i think it is important to stress that as well. first of all, it is important that we get the facts and figures straight and that these things are further investigated, but clearly the thought alone sickens me already. unaccompanied children are among those most vulnerable, and it is deeply troubling that professional gangs might exploit them. the question is: what is the eu doing? i will give you just a few examples. more than eur 200 million is being earmarked to target the protection of children. europol and eurojust are active in helping to dismantle networks involving the smuggling of children. the european asylum support office works on best practice guidance on the assessment of the best interests of the child. the eu helps member states to be better equipped to deal with the specific needs of child victims of trafficking. outside the eu, we earmarked eur 120 million for protection programmes for vulnerable syrian refugee children, working with ngos in, for example, turkey, lebanon, jordan and iraq. to conclude, it is important that eu member states work together to prevent children falling into the hands of criminals. overall there is, i believe, ample opportunity to improve the sharing of information between member states. this is one of the focal points of the netherlands presidency.
