in writing. ‒ i abstained in this resolution as important amendment tabled by the greens failed and because there was no majority for a high-level eu declaration on demonstrating the eu’s commitment to the 2030 agenda in all external and internal policy areas.
in writing. this resolution expresses the european parliament's position on the follow-up and status of the 2030 agenda and the sustainable development goals, highlighting the eu's will to exercise global leadership in eradicating poverty, endorsing the objectives and targets proclaimed in the 2030 agenda statement, urging member states and the union institutions to take concrete actions to achieve the 2030 agenda for sustainable development goals, and calling on the commission and other relevant union institutions to regularly inform the european parliament on the status of the 2030 agenda and the sustainable development goals. we are talking about a report which shows the commitment of the european parliament to the sustainable development goals, and i think it is necessary to vote in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ this resolution proposes to make it compulsory to indicate the country of origin or place of provenance of certain foods. i voted in favour because i think it is important that the place of origin of all foodstuffs should be specified, and so do most consumers in the european union. implementing a mandatory indication of origin would be a major step towards providing adequate transparency in the food chain and towards potential consumers, thus facilitating an increase in conscious and responsible consumption, a necessary step towards transformative consumption.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution which asks the commission for more information so that the consumer knows the country of origin or the place of provenance of the food he consumes. the aim is to restore consumer confidence in food products and to improve transparency and traceability. in this way we are listening to the public, who in a 2013 eurobarometer survey were in favour (88% in favour) of indicating the origin of the food they consume. we must continue to move towards greater supervision in order to combat fraud and avoid a repeat of the horse meat scandal. we also ask the commission to analyse and study the economic feasibility and proportionality of this measure, although according to a study by bord bia in ireland producers who participated in its quality assurance scheme, which includes origin labelling, did not experience an increase in cost.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the motion for a resolution to make it compulsory to indicate the country of origin of meat and milk on the labelling of processed food products in order to combat fraud in the food industry and to improve consumer information. the proposal also calls for the eu to promote the labelling of food products which are produced with animal welfare in mind. the labelling is a necessary tool to provide the consumer with the maximum information when buying food. it is essential for the strengthening of trade in local products.
in writing. ‒ it is necessary to restore consumer confidence after the food scandals of recent years, such as the horse meat scandal in 2013, and i therefore consider it highly important that the indication of the country of origin or place of provenance of certain foods is mandatory. consumers have the right to know where the food they eat comes from, without being misled, to have greater control and to limit the risk of fraud in the product. the country of origin labelling is a measure widely supported by consumers, farmers and consumer organisations, and its cost is low, so it should be mandatory for lightly processed dairy and meat products. i have therefore voted in favour of this resolution.

in writing. – i voted in favour of this resolution because it restates parliament’s position in favour of mandatory indication of the origin in processed food and asks for legislative proposals in that area.
in writing. ‒ i believe that consumers have the right to know where the products they consume come from, so i do think that labelling with this information is an interesting thing. however, i also think that this should be optional for producers. firstly, because labelling would increase the cost of products and could be detrimental to producers. secondly, because i believe that the real importance lies in the state of the product and not so much in its origin. that is to say, it is aspects such as quality, safety and the fact that the product has been produced in accordance with the standards that really have to be guaranteed. i therefore believe that those consumers who are really interested in knowing the origin of their products can do so by buying those which have decided to add this information. in addition, this optional nature would prevent the market from becoming over-bureaucratized.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it calls for improvements in terms of reconciling work and personal life, promoting gender equality and women's participation in the labour market, protecting their labour rights and career development. the report calls for improvements in the transposition of the parental leave directive's eemms by promoting upward convergence of their applications. conciliation measures are proposed, promoting a more equitable sharing of family responsibilities between men and women. it promotes the individualisation of parental leave entitlement by promoting the role of parents (increasing the non-transferable share between parents) and protecting the rights of same-sex couples. finally, it is proposed to improve the rights of fathers and mothers by asking for an increase in the duration of parental leave to 6 months. the commission and the social partners are called upon to increase the age at which children can apply for parental leave and to extend the duration of leave for children with disabilities or long-term illnesses.
in writing. ‒ i agree with the basic points of this report, although not in an absolute way. first, the gender gap in the use of parental leave needs to be addressed, and the current flexibility needs to be reduced, as it encourages the reproduction of the patriarchal division of care in the home. secondly, support for an ambitious maternity directive (after the commission withdrew its earlier proposal, ignoring parliament's vote) and for harmonisation guaranteeing a minimum level of paternity leave. finally, the requirement that member states apply european legislation effectively and that the social partners are fully involved in the whole process. that is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it calls for improvements in terms of reconciling work and personal life, promoting gender equality and women's participation in the labour market, protecting their labour rights and career development. the report calls for improvements in the transposition of the parental leave directive's eemms by promoting upward convergence of their applications. conciliation measures are proposed, promoting a more equitable sharing of family responsibilities between men and women. it promotes the individualisation of parental leave entitlement by promoting the role of parents (increasing the non-transferable share between parents) and protecting the rights of same-sex couples. finally, it is proposed to improve the rights of fathers and mothers by asking for an increase in the duration of parental leave to 6 months. the commission and the social partners are called upon to increase the age at which children can apply for parental leave and to extend the duration of leave for children with disabilities or long-term illnesses.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution because it is a balanced document which in turn advocates a progressive and egalitarian approach to parental leave, setting the best interests of the child as the main priority. the resolution also seeks to achieve greater consistency in the transposition of directive 2010/18/eu in the member states. she also points to other interesting aspects such as the gender imbalance in the use of parental leave. i think it is essential to promote parental co-responsibility here. the text is not as ambitious, but it does contain another positive element, namely the preference for a system in which parents can choose which leave to take. the resolution also advocates facilitating the return of parents to work after taking leave, calls for measures to address the needs of parents with disabled children, and points to the importance of paid and individual parental leave for same-sex couples. achieving a balance between family life and working life is another challenge we must tackle. that is why i welcome the proposal, contained in the text, to draw up an ambitious directive in this respect.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report on directive 2010/18/eu implementing the revised framework agreement on parental leave. the report adopted is a progressive document, an improvement on the existing directives, and aims to extend parental leave, promote a paternity leave directive and also calls on the states and the commission to implement policies to encourage more men to take paternity leave. we believe that these measures are not enough because in order to achieve equality and co-responsibility between men and women in care, and to ensure that this does not have a negative impact on women and discriminate against them in the labour market, we need to broaden our perspective and go to the root of the problem. we can only achieve equality if parental leave for birth or adoption is recognised as an individual right and therefore equal, non-transferable and paid for 100%. despite the shortcomings and the fact that, from our point of view, this is not a report of the highest quality, it is an improvement on the present situation and that is why we voted in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it calls for improvements in terms of reconciling work and personal life, promoting gender equality and women's participation in the labour market, protecting their labour rights and career development. the report calls for improvements in the transposition of the parental leave directive's emas by promoting upward convergence of its applications. conciliation measures are proposed, promoting a more equitable sharing of family responsibilities between men and women. it promotes the individualisation of parental leave entitlement by promoting the role of parents (increasing the non-transferable share between parents) and protecting the rights of same-sex couples. finally, it is proposed to improve the rights of fathers and mothers by asking for an increase in the duration of parental leave to 6 months. the commission and the social partners are called upon to increase the age at which children can apply for parental leave and to extend the duration of leave for children with disabilities or long-term illnesses.

in writing. i agree with the basic points of this report, though not in an absolute way. first, the gender gap in the use of parental leave needs to be addressed, and the current flexibility needs to be reduced, as it encourages the reproduction of the patriarchal division of care in the home. secondly, support for an ambitious maternity directive (after the commission withdrew its earlier proposal, ignoring parliament's vote) and for harmonisation guaranteeing a minimum level of paternity leave. finally, the requirement that member states apply european legislation effectively and that the social partners are fully involved in the whole process. that is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ as set out in directive 2011/36/eu, trafficking in human beings is a serious crime, often committed within the framework of organised crime, which constitutes a serious violation of human rights and is explicitly prohibited by the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. this report seeks to respond to this phenomenon from a multidisciplinary perspective, not only in the criminal law field but also by adopting a set of procedural and preventive measures. the report provides an opportunity to evaluate the measures taken in the implementation of this directive, focuses on the gender dimensions of trafficking in human beings and identifies possible shortcomings and other measures needed to improve its effectiveness. in this respect, the directive was to be transposed into the national legislation of the member states by 6 april 2013 and 27 member states have done so, although the commission has not yet reported on the measures taken by the member states to comply with the directive. in conclusion, it is a positive report which deals with an issue in which the eu must be very committed.

in writing. ‒ the adopted resolution aims to assess the implementation of directive 2011/36/eu on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting victims, in particular from a gender perspective. it is well known that approximately 80% of the victims of these networks are women and specific measures should be considered in this regard. the resolution is positive in this respect in that it shows that the humanitarian crisis with refugees has shown the inability of measures to prevent trafficking in human beings, and calls for improvements in registration and means, for persons who engage in prostitution out of necessity to be included among the victims of trafficking, for specific training of staff in contact with victims to be improved, for funding of organisations and shelters working with victims to be increased, or for the inclusion of forced marriages as a possible form of sexual exploitation. finally, i welcome the adoption of an amendment to require member states to grant victims of trafficking the right to a residence permit. i therefore voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ the report we have adopted today fully addresses the areas for improvement in order to ensure effective implementation of directive 2011/36/eu. 80% of trafficking victims are women, most of whom are deceived with false promises of employment and then raped, drugged, locked up, beaten, threatened and forced into prostitution. cooperation between europol, eurojust and national and third country authorities, with a systematic exchange of information between member states, is essential; also, the commission should evaluate the union strategy for the eradication of trafficking in human beings ending in 2016. in addition, we still do not know the whereabouts of at least 10 000 unaccompanied minors who entered the european union in 2015. it is not unreasonable to fear that many of them may have become victims of trafficking. all these aspects are well addressed in the report and that is why i voted in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ since the european commission has failed to meet certain deadlines set out in directive 2011/36/eu on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and the protection of victims from a gender perspective, the bearder report calls on the commission to implement it effectively. it sets out measures to improve the protection of victims of trafficking in human beings and to reduce the vulnerability of potential victims, taking into account the following aspects: gender dimension, definition of trafficking in human beings, data collection for effective statistical treatment, prevention, identification and assistance to victims. it has a particular impact on the treatment of women, since we must not forget that 80% of the victims of human trafficking are women and children. we have voted in favour of the report.
in writing. ‒ trafficking in human beings constitutes a violation of fundamental human rights, a violation of the personal integrity of the victim and a serious form of organised crime that undermines the rule of law. in 2011, the eu adopted directive 2011/36/eu on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting victims, which established a legal framework aimed at strengthening criminal prosecutions against traffickers in human beings, improving the protection of victims of trafficking and reducing the vulnerability of potential victims. in the light of the commission's failure to submit two evaluation reports in april 2015, parliament has produced this report which emphasises the urgent need to better identify victims, to include a gender perspective in the prevention of trafficking in human beings and in the identification, assistance and protection of victims of trafficking. it also recommends tougher penalties for traffickers and those who exploit victims and greater cooperation across the eu. it calls on the commission to develop a new strategy for the eradication of trafficking in human beings. that is why i voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ the bearder report was supposed to be aimed at combating trafficking in human beings, which particularly affects women and girls. these account for over 80% of the victims. proxenetism, illegal domestic work, slavery, forced marriage and organ trafficking are all unacceptable situations. however, as is often the case, the proposed solutions risk turning against women and girls and being exploited, in particular by illegal immigration networks. if the recommendations of this report are followed, it will be very simple and profitable to force a woman into prostitution to ensure her subsequent legalization. or she may have been forced into a previous marriage to take advantage of the family reunion... in addition, the report only very superficially addresses the case of baby farms, a modern slavery linked to the promotion of pag. yet here is a real issue of human trafficking, both for surrogate mothers and for children, who have become commodities. it is high time that we took this matter more seriously. in reality, the proposals in this report are not intended to fight against traffickers, but to support them. i voted against this report, of course.

member of the commission. – mr president, as a number of colleagues have said, this has been a short debate at a time when the house is not well attended. i regret that, because it is an extremely important subject. in terms of some of the themes that have come out from the debate, perhaps the most important starting point is: what can we do to protect consumers in future? part of the answer, i think, lies – as a number of colleagues have referred to – in the mortgage credit directive, which will put in place a better framework with specific remedies to protect consumers, in case for those who take out foreign currency loans, the rates were to rise sharply in cost. i think, more generally, in terms of what we need to try to do to improve retail financial services for consumers across the european union, we do need to have more transparency. we do need to try to increase the size of the market so that consumers are able to have the best choice of products that is available and, as mr kelly mentioned, if you look at the pricing of certain financial products across the eu, they vary hugely from country to country. one of the ideas behind the green paper on retail financial services that i have launched, and the process we are working on, is to try to strengthen that single market for retail financial services and think about financial services, not from an institutional point of view, but from the point of view of the millions of our fellow citizens who use them. now i start with that point because the importance of trying to build a stronger single market for retail financial services links to the point about having a single market for capital and the free flow of capital, which a number of colleagues have referred to. that, i think, underpins the approach that the commission has taken in the case of these foreign currency loans. as a number of colleagues have said, it is very important that we strike a balance between the interests of consumers – and clearly there it is absolutely and perfectly proper for member states to take action to protect the interests of consumers – but, at the same time, if we want to uphold the single market in capital, if we want to deepen it and strengthen it, we have to uphold the legal framework that operates and we need to make sure that governments, when they take steps – perfectly properly to protect consumers – do so within the framework of that law. that in essence is what lies behind the approach that the commission has sought to develop with a number of member states. in response to a specific question, i was asked how many member states consulted the commission in advance of taking measures, well member states are not obliged to consult the commission before the adoption of the laws in fields of financial services. we are monitoring measures in romania and poland because there member states have provided us with their draft laws. we are also, as i said, in discussions with the croatian government to see if we can find a balanced solution to the challenge that we face. it is not the case, as was alleged, that the commission is seeking to infringe member states who take action to protect consumers. that is far from the point. i hope i have been completely clear, that it is, of course, absolutely proper for governments to take those actions but, as a number of colleagues have mentioned, the issue of retroactivity is extremely important, the question of proportionality is extremely important and the issue where there is no differentiation by governments in the laws they pass between consumers is also a cause for concern. i am hopeful that we will be able to find practical solutions to the problems that we face. i am encouraged by the support i have had from a number of members of parliament for the approach that we are taking. i am personally involved in doing that work; discussing it with ministers. i hope that we will be able to make that progress, in order to provide clarity and legal certainty for financial services, but also for consumers. so as far as croatia is specifically concerned, we are continuing to assess the situation there and to make sure and explore whether the actions they are taking are compatible with the single market and the commitments that croatia has made under european legislation. we will keep up the pressure on that. also, we are following discussions in other countries where possible measures in relation to foreign currency loans are being considered, just to check that they are in line with eu law. but this is an important issue. i will keep it firmly under review and we will take the necessary steps that we need to make sure that consumers are protected but that we have a common framework and we uphold the rule of law, so that businesses are able to invest with certainty, because if we want to get growth and jobs to be encouraged, if we want to encourage investment, and if we want to build a capital markets union, then businesses need to know that they have certainty and that they are able to invest for the long term.
mr president, members of the european parliament, it is a special experience for me to be among you during the dutch presidency of the council of the european union. you represent the citizens of the union at european level. their desires and expectations, but also their worries and fears. their ideals and their hopes, but also their disappointments and their anger. everything that moves the european electorate comes together here and can be said and heard here. you have an important job, a difficult job, right now. there's a wind blowing in europe. much of what we europeans hold dear is under pressure. two months ago this city, this district, was hit by extremist attacks which killed 32 people of different nationalities. today we think of their loved ones who have been scarred for life by pain and grief and of those who have been injured and are working to recover as best they can. brussels, the city where europe meets, was struck to the heart. as was paris last year, and so many places in the countries around us. i'm going to name ankara, aleppo, beirut, baghdad, sousse, lahore. violence and oppression dominate the lives of millions of people in the regions around europe. whole societies have been disrupted. for the sake of safety, many feel compelled to flee. that's a lot for the countries that are hosting the largest flows of refugees: lebanon, jordan, turkey and a number of african countries. the european union's member states are also affected by the refugee crisis, some more than others. the social cohesion of the member states and the solidarity within the union are thus put to the test. people need shelter, a place where they can truly feel at home. as the german philosopher rüdiger safranski wrote: "we can communicate and travel globally, but we cannot live in the global. we can only live here or there". it's important to keep in mind this human attachment to a place in the world. for many europeans, their own country is an important anchor point, with its history, traditions and customs which they experience as 'their own'. the same applies to the 17 million inhabitants of the european part of the kingdom of the netherlands. the dutch love their country and are proud of the heritage of erasmus, hugo the great, spinoza, rembrandt, van gogh, cornelis lely and johan cruyff. but in all our attachment and love for our country, we must never forget what we owe to the wider european civilization and to the peoples and cultures around us. and it's not about the smallest values. it was the greeks who laid the foundations for the democratic form of government that we cherish. the italians gave us the renaissance, a burgeoning source of innovation in culture and science. it was the french immigrant christophe plantin who published the very first dictionaries of the dutch language at the end of the 16th century. german and french thinkers like leibniz and voltaire laid the foundation for our enlightenment. and it was our british and polish allies who fought with great sacrifice for dutch freedom in 1944 and 1945. acquisitions are rarely purely national. the deeper you dig, the more closely the root systems of our countries and cultures are knotted and connected. you can define a territory, but you can't define a culture. europe also represents a civilized ideal of personal freedom and human dignity, equality and humanity. my mother spoke at your meeting twice, in 1984 and in 2004. she recalled the high expectations that many young people had of europe in the early 1960s. "what had begun with such prosaic concrete building blocks as coal and steel grew into a movement that would break down the walls of division in europe, preserve peace and give our continent new resilience and energy", she said. i was born in 1967. a defining moment for my generation was 1989, when walls of separation between eastern and western europe that seemed untouchable shook and fell to their foundations. the end of the cold war was the beginning of a new era. it opened up a whole new world of connections. it became clear that the european countries have a common responsibility. gradually, another realization came to my mind. the position of europe and the world has changed in a few generations. europe no longer automatically sets the tone in thinking. we are no longer the center of the world, not economically, not geopolitically, not culturally. the values we hold as universal are not taken for granted everywhere and are under pressure in many places. it is precisely because we believe in these values and in our common tradition that our cooperation is so important. not the past, but the future compels us to do so. in these times, we should ask ourselves: what europe are we representing? what else can we be proud of? the attention is often focused on the problems, the shortcomings and the worries. but these concerns, however great and justified, must be seen in the context of what has been achieved, in part, by european cooperation. there's nothing like peace to get used to. since the schuman plan, no member state has fired a shot at another member state. in our union, power relations are embedded in legal relations. i am one of the first generation of europeans in history to have this good fortune. and i wish future generations the same happiness. (applause from the left) the choice of european integration was a choice for a common anchoring of free and open societies in a common legal order. five hundred million europeans have found each other in a union of shared values. the implementation and enforcement of this policy has been and continues to be a subject of much debate and emotion. the mood can be high, even here in your parliament. the translation of abstract values into concrete laws, rules and plans is hotly debated. the differences of opinion can be great. this is sometimes taken as a sign of europe's weakness, but it is a sign of europe's strength. we are committed to critical reflection, freedom of expression, debate and democratic control in the open. only in dictatorships is there no public discussion. why is it important that we keep moving up together? we answer that question ourselves every day. almost every major challenge we face calls for better cooperation. control of refugee flows. the fight against trafficking in human beings, terrorism and crime. improving our energy supply. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. to enable economic growth and new jobs for the more than 22 million europeans who are out of work. and also: strengthening our position as moral beacons against the forces that threaten freedom. in all these tasks, we need each other. as erasmus wrote five hundred years ago: "nothing is easier than to overcome those who are divided". europe is one in its diversity. everyone's input is essential. the european bouquet is not complete without the spanish carnation, the french fleur-de-lys, the greek acanthus, the danish marguerite, the german cornflower, the austrian noble white, the croatian iris, the dutch and hungarian tulips and not without the english rose. the european union can face the world with its head held high. but that does not absolve us from the duty to be open to criticism and to look critically at ourselves. we often only tackle urgent common issues when the need has become so great that there are no alternatives. this has happened in the banking crisis and, more recently, in the humanitarian crisis caused by the influx of refugees from syria and other conflict areas. anticipation is not europe's strong point. europe cannot move faster than the member states allow. the interaction between the union and the member states, and between this parliament and national parliaments, for example, on new challenges and problems on the horizon is therefore more important than ever. at the same time, it also places demands on the way europe works. this is also true of strengthening our economy. our young people are our future capital. are we doing enough to provide good prospects for the future? the unused potential of our single market is budgeted at eur 1 250 billion. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. economic and social prospects for all are essential. the work involved goes far beyond simply stimulating economic growth through the internal market. our common legal order is also a social legal order. it's also about equal opportunity. the right to study, work, do business and use facilities in another member state is a fantastic achievement. but we must never forget the perspective of those who stay at home. they don't experience the extra opportunities so much as the extra competition. europe now means for some: spread your wings. and for others: settle in. the concern of many people about this europe is easily confused with discomfort about the way the european union is governed. some see brussels as a bogeyman and meddler rather than an ally. the european idea has been tried for a long time. a picture of the ever-expanding european construction. but as with building a stable bridge, the material laws of tension and stretch and the anchoring of the base must always be considered. to prevent a breaking point from being reached. this need for 'strengthening the support structure' is recognised within the european institutions and also within the european parliament. the answer is: not more rules, but rules that work better. concentrating european attention on the main issues which really require a common approach. decision-making as close to the people as possible. this not only strengthens the eu's effectiveness, but also responds to citizens' concerns about losing their grip on developments and their cultural identity. citizens can only become european citizens if they continue to feel at home in their own country, city and village. europe starts at the kitchen table. a proud european is - and should be - a proud finn, frenchman, pole, portuguese, briton, bulgarian, greek, german or dutchman. no political order can exist without a close link with the public. the european union must not be an elite project; all citizens of the member states must feel at home in the union. the european union belongs to all of us. the professor, the truck driver, the small businessman, the jobseeker, the retired factory worker, the refugee with a residence permit, the school dropout. every year, one in three europeans visits another european country. so two-thirds of them don't do this. the european union must have a say in the lives of all these citizens. our union is for the travellers and the fast ones. as a directly elected institution of the european union, you have a special responsibility in this regard. i am not saying that the european parliament should be the only institution in the world that has the right to vote. the outcome of elections and referendums - including in my country - can complicate developments in the european context. but the european story can only be written together. it can only be brought forward if voters and elected representatives are willing to listen to each other, in europe and in their own countries. for 60 years, european cooperation has been a bridge to the future. at first, the bridge was narrow, but over the years the base became wider, the set of requirements broader and the ambitions wider. whether the structure can sustain us is up to us. everything depends on how well we manage to keep the connections strong and the structure stable. the european parliament is the only institution in the world that has the power to make decisions on the basis of the will of the people. but no matter how diverse we are, no matter how different we are from one another, there's more, much more that unites us. i wish you all the best in your important work. costs between them. so we need to keep a careful eye on how the technology is evolving and being in used. in the commission we plan to set up a fintech task force to monitor developments in new increase the financial sector’s competitiveness in europe, it has the potential to improve customer services, and i look forward to working with parliament as we monitor and develop our approaches to this important new area.
in writing. for us, virtual currencies are not a new phenomenon, as the existence of alternative means of payment has a long history behind it. so are the bubbles associated with them, although the technology of cryptocurrencies is relatively new. in this sense, we are concerned that confusion about the safety of their use may be encouraged by considering them a new phenomenon, either by ignoring their speculative potential or their limitations as a means of payment that replicate that of any other private financial instrument or by endorsing their potential monetary nature, despite the fact that it is an instrument of sovereignty that does not depend on technology but on the endorsement of the state. we therefore think that they should be regulated at least as the financial instruments whose functions they replicate, and we would have liked more clarity in this respect. otherwise, we continue with the fallacy that digital services - in this case financial services - are essentially different in nature, instead of ensuring that the regulatory standards achieved in their traditional analogues are maintained.
in writing. digitalisation in many aspects of our daily lives is a reality, as evidenced by the fact that it has been more than seven years since the launch of bitcoin, the first and most important virtual currency. virtual currencies are set to have a significant impact on the financial sector, as well as many other markets, as it offers a decentralised, fast, resilient and fairly secure means of recording transactions of any kind along with the history of previous transactions. in 2015, the european institutions took further steps towards a more digitised payments market by reaching an agreement on the payments package, comprising the payment services directive (psdii) and the multilateral interchange fee regulation (mif). we must continue our efforts to promote electronic payments and continue to work towards creating a true digital single market for european consumers.

madam president, the crisis in the dairy sector is demonstrating how little effective measures are available in the european union today to stabilise agricultural markets after so much futile effort at wanton liberalization. the sector is facing a complex problem, where price volatility, the lack of instruments at european level to deal with this volatility, the fall in demand combined with the increase in supply and the imbalances in the food chain form an explosive cocktail that has finally plunged this sector into a severe crisis that has already cost the community budget eur 500 million. the implementation of concerted production reduction measures by producer organisations, associations and inter-branch organisations, as proposed by the european commission, would only have the desired effect if it were undertaken by the majority of member states, including the countries most responsible for overproduction. i think it should be a joint initiative, supported by community funds, to achieve the desired response. the latest package of measures announced by the commissioner leaves it up to the budgetary initiative of each country to find solutions, and i do not think that this is the most appropriate way forward. i would urge the commission and the council of ministers to seek common solutions, which should involve strengthening contractual relations, not just between farmers and industry, but also in the commercial distribution sector, to put an end to abusive practices, of which the farmer is the main victim.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report, which refers to the recent phenomenon of virtual currencies such as bitcoin. these currencies have the potential to become a structural part of our financial systems. however, they carry important risks such as the ease of generating speculative bubbles, and their use for criminal activities. the report mentions these aspects and calls for greater regulation of virtual currencies.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution on virtual currencies from the econ committee of the european parliament. it highlights that such currencies can contribute positively to citizens' welfare and economic development by reducing the costs of operations and operating payments, the cost of accessing financing even without a traditional bank account, increasing resilience, enabling systems that combine ease of use, systems to develop online micropayment insurance systems and allowing the possibility of merging different types of payment mechanisms traditions and innovations.
in writing. ‒ currently, more than 600 virtual currency systems are in operation. as this report points out, virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology can contribute positively to citizens' well-being and economic development, including in the financial sector, by reducing transaction costs and payment handling costs; by reducing the cost of access to finance, even without a traditional bank account; or by increasing the speed of payment systems and trade in goods and services. however, they also entail risks, such as the absence of flexible and reliable governance structures, their high volatility or the legal uncertainty surrounding them. the report recommends increasing regulatory capacity and developing a robust legal framework that is up to speed with innovation, ensuring a timely and proportionate response if it becomes systemically relevant. it therefore calls for the creation of a horizontal working group led by the commission and composed of regulatory and technical experts to analyse these new systems in depth and support a timely, reasoned and proportionate response to the new opportunities and challenges they bring. it also called on the commission to improve consumer information on them.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this pioneering report on virtual currencies because it correctly identifies the opportunities and risks offered by this technology. virtual currencies are private and decentralised in nature, which allows for cost savings by not requiring a clearing house. at the same time, they should be adequately regulated to prevent their use by criminal and terrorist networks and to inform investors in a timely manner. in future, consideration will also have to be given to the role that the european central bank may play in the field of virtual currencies, since it is the institution, together with the central banks of the countries that have not yet adopted the euro, which has a monopoly on the issuance of legal tender coins and banknotes. the report has been widely supported in committee and in plenary.
in writing. ‒ i have abstained in this report because, although it adequately characterises the risks of virtual currencies, it does not require that they be regulated in a similar way to the financial services they perform. as in the digital agenda, the digitisation of services leaves the door wide open to deregulation, in this case of payment and financial deposit systems: something we are opposed to head-on.

in writing. ‒ this own-initiative report takes stock of the development of virtual currencies and the underlying technology that enables them to operate, distributed ledger technology (dlt). bitcoin, created in 2009, currently represents 90% of the virtual currency market and is currently worth only 5 billion euros. with these virtual currencies, we are seeing the emergence of a market independent of the power of states and central banks. this development goes against one of the main attributes of state sovereignty: the right to mint money. it is possible that the major international banks are investing in virtual currencies precisely in order to implement an interbank market managed exclusively by them. furthermore, virtual currencies also lack transparency. they allow for anonymous transactions, which facilitate, for example, money laundering and terrorist financing. i therefore voted against this report.

in writing. ‒ following the success of the first and most important virtual currency (bitcoin), distributed ledger technology (drt) is having a huge impact on the financial sector. the main advantage offered by both virtual currencies and trd is the reduction of transaction costs and increased privacy of payments made. the report also raises the possibility of incorporating drt into the private sector, for example in intellectual property transfers. we should not ignore the risks of virtual currencies or dth, such as the misuse of certain applications for criminal purposes such as money laundering. to put an end to certain bad practices and to achieve an increase in efficiency, the aim is to implement smart regulation of the trd, based on analytical excellence and proportionality, thus avoiding preventive and rigid regulation. i am very pleased that the commission has taken this step.

in writing. ‒ as stated in the report of the committee on legal affairs, which i supported, the office of the prosecutor of the vercelli court of first instance has requested authorisation from the european parliament to obtain data from telephone companies concerning the telephone records of a number used by mr gianluca buonanno, member of parliament, in connection with criminal proceedings brought before the vercelli court of first instance on behalf of that member of parliament and concerning telephone threats which he claims to have received from an anonymous communicator on his mobile phone on 14 april 2015. while the commission considers that it was not necessary for the public prosecutor's office to request authorisation to order the collection of data relating to the telephone traffic of gianluca buonanno, in the interests of legal certainty, it has recommended that gianluca buonanno's parliamentary immunity be suspended.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which calls for the waiver of the parliamentary immunity of mr buonanno, since it is necessary, under italian law, for the italian authorities to be able to search his telephone in order to clarify the threats he has received.
in writing. ‒ in order to find the author of the telephone threats made to my italian parliamentary colleague gianluca buonnano, the deputy prosecutor of vercelli requested the lifting of his parliamentary immunity, in order to obtain the telephone records from the operators concerned. in accordance with the wishes of my colleague, mr gianluca buonnano, i therefore voted in favour of this request, which, i would remind you, is submitted with the aim of finding the author of the threats and is not directed against mr buonnano.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the request for the waiver of immunity as proposed by the juri committee. we understand that there is no possibility of using the suspension to initiate a political prosecution.
in writing. ‒ this report is due to the fact that the vercelli court of justice has requested information from telephone companies concerning italian mep gianluca buonanno, following a series of anonymous telephone threats received by the latter. any member of the european parliament enjoys the immunities and privileges granted to him in his country of origin and, in the constitution of the italian republic, he is granted a personal registration immunity. however, there is a problem of interpretation in italian law, since there is no national case law specifying whether this guarantee should apply to the alleged victim of a crime (as in the present case) or to the perpetrator of the crime. the report calls for the parliamentary immunity of gianluca buonanno to be suspended, as this is the only way to access his telephone records, which will allow the litigation process to move forward and resolve this particular situation. for the same reason, i am voting in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ we voted against this report on interim measures in the international arena for the benefit of sweden. this is a proposal to amend a council decision adopted in 2015 establishing provisional measures for the benefit of member states in an emergency situation characterised by a mass arrival of third-country nationals in one or more member states, also known as a 'temporary relocation scheme'. this amendment to the relocation scheme was tabled by the commission in december, following the request of the swedish government to benefit from that relocation scheme. the original request from the swedish government in november was to benefit from this mechanism as greece and italy. however, this request was rejected by the commission, which instead agreed to a one-year suspension of the 'obligation' to relocate those applying to sweden (1369 persons).
in writing. ‒ i would like to thank the rapporteur for her work and effort in producing this report. i voted in favour of the green amendment, which called for the rejection of the european commission's proposal to exempt sweden for one year from its obligation to take in refugees from greece and italy under the resettlement programme for 160 000 people approved last year, of whom 3 766 were to go to sweden. i therefore voted against the european parliament's report in the final vote. sweden has made great efforts, but i do not agree with the precautionary suspensions of measures agreed by all in relation to the distribution of refugees.
in writing. ‒ in 2015, a number of measures were adopted for countries in difficulty, due to the increasing number of migrants and asylum seekers arriving, known as the relocation mechanism. greece and italy have so far benefited from this mechanism. sweden is the country with the highest number of asylum seekers per capita, and has been an example of good practice in this field until now. however, the present social democratic government has wanted to take advantage of these measures, an exercise of lack of solidarity given its economic situation. the proposal which the commission has sent to parliament is not the original one on relocation but on the suspension of sweden's obligations under the relocation system. we voted against this proposal because there is a very serious situation at the main points of arrival in the eu, where migrants and asylum seekers are surviving in extremely precarious conditions. the solidarity of all the member states is needed to alleviate this situation, and we cannot allow such exceptions.
in writing. ‒ in the context of the migration crisis, sweden has asked not to honour its reception obligations imposed under the 'resettlement of refugees'. the relocation concerns 160 000 migrants who have arrived in greece and italy and obliges the member states to distribute them. this system therefore only affects a small proportion of those who have arrived in europe, while the vast majority are already moving freely in search of the most welcoming countries. sweden argued that it had already opened its doors to many migrants (over 170 000) outside this system and that it could not fulfil its relocation obligation. the request must be the subject of a decision by the union, which therefore proposes provisional measures to postpone the relocation of sweden by one year. the report by parliament proposes to confirm this decision. the relocation process is irresponsible because it encourages migrants to cross the mediterranean to reach europe. it is also ineffective because schengen allows them to move freely once they are settled. i have of course opposed this report because the decision to postpone it still facilitates the wave of migration we are facing.

in writing. ‒ i voted against. in a context of a significant deterioration of the situation, conditions and erosion of rights for asylum seekers in greece and more generally in europe, coupled with the extremely slow progress of relocations in practice, with only 1 500 people relocated across europe since the launch of the scheme (state of play as at 13 may 2016), member states’ commitment to solidarity and responsibility needs to be renewed and urgently strengthened. supporting the commission proposal to exempt sweden from the obligation to accept people to be relocated from greece and italy would further undermine member states’ commitment to solidarity and responsibility sharing.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this motion for a resolution on transatlantic data flows because we believe that it focuses on the legal certainty of the transfer of personal data between the eu and the us and that the right to information is not balanced with the right to privacy of consumers. our group has tabled an amendment to improve the area of privacy and consumer rights, relating to the protection of personal data. the amendment did not pass, so we did not vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution on transatlantic data flows, which points to the shortcomings in the data protection agreement that the european union is negotiating with the united states, the so-called 'privacy shield'. it assesses the efforts made by the commission and considers that substantial improvements have been made compared to safe harbor, but there are still shortcomings, including the access of the us authorities to the information transferred and the possibility of collecting data on a mass scale in some cases, which does not respect the criteria of necessity and proportionality as set out in the eu charter of fundamental rights.
in writing. ‒ following the complaint by max schrems, the eu court of justice ruled last october that the agreement that regulated the transfer of european citizens' data to the us since 2000 did not offer sufficient protection. last february, the commission presented the new agreement with the us, known as privacy shield, to regulate transatlantic data flows. this new framework represents significant advances over the previous scheme, as it includes strict obligations for companies, clearer safeguards and transparency obligations regarding access by the us administration, greater protection of the rights of eu citizens (the us has passed the judicial redress act, which extends access to european citizens to the us courts) and an annual joint review mechanism. however, as stated in the parliamentary resolution, which i supported, the article 29 working party has expressed its deep concern about the commercial aspects and the access of public authorities to data transferred under the privacy shield, and the commission is therefore asked to fully implement the recommendations of this working party in order to avoid a future repeal.
in writing. ‒ we voted against the resolution because it does not propose any of the measures necessary to safeguard adequate levels of protection of personal data. the european parliament has also called for the eu to take a more active role in the fight against terrorism and to promote the fight against organised crime. the resolution also represents a missed opportunity to defend european data protection standards, which will be significantly reduced if ttip is adopted. we are also concerned about the lack of content on spying by private companies and the transfer of personal data to and between them. the buying and selling of personal data is a growing economic sector that must be strictly regulated and limited or we risk losing the right to privacy.
in writing. ‒ we voted against this motion for a resolution on transatlantic data flows because we believe that it focuses on the legal certainty of the transfer of personal data between the eu and the us and that the right to information is not balanced with the right to privacy of consumers. our group has tabled an amendment to improve the area of privacy and consumer rights, relating to the protection of personal data. the amendment did not pass, so we did not vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution because i believe it is essential that the agreement on the transatlantic flow of data with the united states that is reached be transparent and take account of the recently adopted data protection rules so that a new annulment by the court of justice can be avoided. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the euro against counterfeiting and that the council should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of euro banknotes and coins.
in writing. ‒ the protection of personal data is one of the fundamental rights that the european union is obliged to guarantee, but always bearing in mind that it may be limited to the achievement of the general interest objectives recognised in our treaties. i support this report because data flows between the united states and the european union are of fundamental importance for trade and investment between the two. citizens and businesses benefit directly and on a daily basis from the free flow of data, as it creates new opportunities for them to participate in international trade and improves access to new markets on other continents. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of personal data.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report. following the invalidation of the safe harbour agreement by the court of justice, the commission has proposed a new regime for the flow of data between the usa and the eu. nicknamed ‘privacy shield’, this agreement is very much criticised for the lack of data protection safeguards in the usa. the greens/efa are very concerned about the new privacy shield: we understand the need to provide legal certainty for business to continue between the usa and the eu, but not at the cost of fundamental rights. parliament’s resolution on the privacy shield, however, does not reflect those concerns. our key greens/efa demand – a sunset clause – was rejected and therefore i voted against the resolution as a whole.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of the griffin report because it represents a good opportunity to promote energy self-consumption (stable legal framework, rejection of retroactive measures, removal of administrative and financial barriers), while at the same time providing tools to combat energy poverty and recognising access to energy as a basic social right.
in writing. ‒ i would like to thank the rapporteur for her work. i have supported this report which says, among other things, that the energy union must focus on the interests of current and future generations of citizens, empowering them to produce, consume, store or market their own renewable energy. it calls for a contribution to the eradication of energy poverty through better coordination at union level, through the sharing of best practice between member states and the development of a broad definition of energy poverty.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the griffin report on the establishment of a new energy consumer agreement, ahead of the legislative initiatives that are part of the energy union strategy. i support the rapporteur's approach, which puts citizens at the heart of the energy union, with measures to save on the energy bill. combating energy poverty, which affects more than 50 million people in europe, must be a vital objective and affordable energy must be a basic social right. no one should have to choose between eating and paying for heating/cooling. i regret that the epp voted against the prioritization of energy poverty mitigation measures in future legislative proposals. the same applies to the proposals for self-generation and self-consumption of energy. citizens who produce their own energy should not be penalized by excessive taxes or charges, as my country has done with the tax on the sun. if we do not put citizens at the heart of energy market efficiency, we cannot achieve the climate goals agreed in paris.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the griffin report on the establishment of a new energy consumer agreement, ahead of the legislative initiatives part of the energy union strategy. i support the rapporteur's approach of putting citizens at the heart of the energy union, with measures to save on the energy bill. the fight against energy poverty, which affects more than 50 million people in europe, must be a vital objective and affordable energy must be a basic social right. no one should have to choose between eating and paying for heating/cooling. i regret that the epp voted against giving priority to energy poverty mitigation measures in future legislative proposals. the same is true of the proposals for self-generation and self-consumption of energy. citizens who produce their own energy should not be penalized by excessive taxes or charges as has been the case in my country with the tax on the sun. if we do not put citizens at the heart of energy market efficiency, we will not be able to achieve the climate goals agreed in paris.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because it represents a real step forward in shaping electricity markets at european level in the context of the transition to a sustainable economy. the report focuses on the role that consumers can play in the context of the energy transition and, although the report does not mention the key role that the public sector should play in this transition, nor the importance of involving the social partners, it does make interesting proposals for the functioning of an energy sector that can fight energy poverty. while energy poverty cannot be considered and tackled from the demand side alone, the measures contained in the report provide a good summary of the measures to be taken to combat this growing phenomenon. the report introduces key aspects of the energy debate, such as the involvement of local and regional authorities in the design of energy markets, seeks to promote transparency of information on the functioning of energy markets and calls for the definition of the term 'prospective consumer' in the light of the new laws to be implemented in the energy union.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the griffin report on the establishment of a new energy consumer agreement, ahead of the legislative initiatives part of the energy union strategy. i support the rapporteur's approach of putting citizens at the heart of the energy union, with measures to save on the energy bill. the fight against energy poverty, which affects more than 50 million people in europe, must be a vital objective and affordable energy must be a basic social right. no one should have to choose between eating and paying for the heat. i regret that the epp voted against giving priority to measures to alleviate energy poverty in future legislative proposals and that proposals in favour of self-generation and self-consumption of energy were removed from the final report. citizens who produce their own energy should not be penalized with taxes, as has happened in spain with the tax on the sun. if we do not put citizens at the heart of energy market efficiency, we will not be able to achieve the climate goals agreed in paris.

in writing. ‒ the new deal for energy consumers outlines the way forward making it easier for consumers to compare offers, switch suppliers and find their way around a digitalised energy market while protecting the most vulnerable. it supports people who generate and consume their own renewable energy, as well as enhancing the role of local and regional authorities in the energy transition. if the eu institutions are serious about putting citizens at the core of the energy union, there is a need to empower citizens and create solid rights and opportunities for them to participate in the energy transition. the griffin report is definitely providing clear statements in that sense.
in writing. ‒ i am in favour of this report because i believe that we must ensure reliable and stable sources of energy for european consumers and for the economy of all member states. for this reason, i think it is very important to create an energy system in which decentralization, flexibility and renewable energy are the main priorities. on the other hand, i think it is also very important that, when this question is raised, the problem of the lack of physical integration of some eu members is addressed. in the meantime, i think it is very important that these countries, which are not interconnected with the rest of the european union, should be able to continue to apply national measures.
in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report because it deals with a very relevant issue, which has been exacerbated by the austerity policies implemented in recent years, namely poverty and gender perspective. the report mentions the causes of poverty, precariousness and social exclusion of women. women continue to be more affected than men by the economic crisis and are more exposed to the possibility of social exclusion, with significantly higher poverty rates for women. the wage and pension gap, the glass ceiling, the lack of conciliation policies and the lack of equal and non-transferable parental leave are some of the reasons for this inequality. the report contains several points which make our vote in favour decisive, such as the need to guarantee public services, education and social security to combat poverty, the need to promote conciliation to avoid precarious and 'atypical' contracts, the defence of women's economic independence by fighting for equal pay and pensions, strengthening maternity and paternity leave and the fight against gender violence.
in writing. ‒ the problem of poverty and social exclusion of women has been the subject of special attention by parliament for many years. in the past year, despite efforts made, little progress has been made and there is still a long way to go to successfully address the causes and consequences of the multiple facets of this precariousness. according to the latest available statistics, poverty affects women more than men, and it is still predominantly women who are in the most precarious jobs, which in many cases do not allow them to reconcile their professional and working lives. i have supported this report because it places particular emphasis on improving reconciliation and early childhood education and on access to affordable care services for dependent children and families. the commission is also urged to take further action to further promote women's empowerment and combat gender stereotypes.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because, despite the attempts of the right, we have succeeded in making a clear denunciation of the devastating - and even more virulent - effects on women of the austerity policies imposed by the european commission on the member states. these 'austerity' policies are the clear cause of the increase in the feminization of poverty in the european union, where more than 64.6 million women are now living in poverty. the text we have adopted recalls the right of access to education for the children of migrants and refugees and calls on the european commission and the member states to increase the funds allocated to the fight against unemployment, poverty and social exclusion. i therefore share the diagnosis of this resolution and its call for the promotion of free, quality public services in the areas of health, education and social security. i therefore voted in favour of the text because i am convinced that real and effective policies are needed to achieve the still far-off real equality between men and women.
in writing. ‒ the economic crisis and austerity policies have led to an increase in the number of people exposed to poverty and social exclusion, affecting more women (64.6 million) than men (57.6 million). the fact is that women are still overrepresented in precarious work, are forced to interrupt their careers to take care of their children and other dependent relatives, because of the lack of effective rules for reconciling work and family life, occupy positions of lesser prestige, often as a result of sexist stereotypes, and take part-time jobs, not by free choice, but rather forced by the need to take care of their relatives. in addition, there is a wage gap which persists and is very difficult to close. this means that women receive lower wages than men, which also translates into lower pensions. i voted in favour of this report because it calls for urgent measures to improve conciliation, to combat stereotypes, to reduce the pay gap and to facilitate the integration and retention of women in the labour market.
in writing. ‒ there are more women than men in poverty in europe: 64.6 million versus 57.6 million. the resolution therefore takes a gender perspective on the fight against poverty. however, it mixes very different situations: elderly single women, single mothers, lesbian, bisexual, transgender, disabled, migrant or from ethnic minorities. this confusion does not really help to deal with the problems. the resolution does not propose any concrete solutions, for example, to the effects of austerity policies on women. the same is true of the development of single parent families, rural poverty and the rise of parttime work. the only solutions considered are symbolic: proposing to commit expenditure in all directions or strengthening anti-discrimination legislation, whereas existing legislation is not necessarily applied or even relevant. in reality, the fight against discrimination, especially in favour of migrants and ethnic, religious and sexual minorities, seems to be the only real aim of this resolution. it is therefore not likely to improve the material situation of women.

in writing. ‒ we abstained on this report on non-tariff barriers in the internal market, as it raises balanced and protective elements, together with a number of other problematic elements that encourage the removal of barriers, to improve competition and allow companies to expand, which, from their perspective, creates economic growth. it called on the commission to ensure full implementation of eu single market legislation and to ensure structural reforms in the member states. the report also contains a number of balanced and rights-protecting measures. that is why we propose abstaining in the final vote.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this report on non-tariff barriers in the single market, which stresses that much remains to be done, as the free movement of goods and services is still hampered by non-tariff barriers, in particular, in unjustified national technical standards and regulatory and non-regulatory requirements that apply to goods, service providers and conditions of service provision, or by bureaucracy. urgent measures are needed for the best functioning.
in writing. ‒ the creation of the single market is a significant achievement, made possible by cooperation and a common objective: the removal of barriers to trade across the union. we have succeeded in removing tariff barriers almost 50 years ago, but we still face the challenge of removing non-tariff barriers in our common market. this own-initiative report, which i voted in favour of, calls for the removal of the remaining obstacles to the completion of the single market. while insufficient or incorrect application of existing union rules still hampers intra-union trade and constitutes an obstacle to growth, a clear distinction needs to be made between non-tariff barriers and other rules, both at union and national level, which are legitimately in place and serve public interest objectives. in addition, thanks to the socialist group, a balanced reference has been introduced to the so-called 'over-regulation', which does not affect the right to legitimately adopt advanced legislation in the case of minimum harmonisation directives, and an explicit mention of the importance of public services whose regulation does not constitute a non-tariff barrier.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because although the creation of the single market is a significant achievement, made possible by cooperation and the common objective of eliminating barriers to trade throughout the european union, and although tariff barriers were successfully removed almost 50 years ago, our common market still has an existing challenge: the removal of non-tariff barriers. this report recognises the burden that discriminatory and unjustified actions could have on businesses, but at the same time it fully preserves the right to regulate and pursue legitimate public policy objectives such as consumer protection or labour rights and the environment. it called on the commission to present an ambitious proposal to remove these non-tariff barriers as soon as possible in order to unlock the potential still to be exploited in the single market.
in writing. ‒ the report makes a strong commitment to the liberalisation of services and trade in the single market, even suggesting that both sectors are 'over-regulated'. our view is that the european single market agenda, based on deregulation and the tightening of competition (with the encouragement of forced mobility and double standards for digital services) privileges commercial oligopolies and exacerbates social dumping in sectors such as transport. that is why i voted against.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i consider the commission's desire to make progress in this area to be important and positive. it is crucial in the single market that the principle of mutual recognition is promoted. in general, more consistency is needed in the legislation, as well as greater coordination in order to implement it. i think that the report provides a correct definition of non-tariff barriers in the single market, while recognising the rights of member states to regulate in accordance with their policy objectives.

in writing. ‒ in order to protect their businesses from unfair competition or their consumers from dangerous products, some member states take measures to prevent imports of goods and services. these provisions, which may be labelling standards, technical standards for responding to public tenders or regulations for certain professions, such as notaries, are called non-tariff barriers. for example, the french ban on bisphenol a in food packaging has been denounced by other member states as a non-tariff barrier to the free movement of certain products in the european union. this report ignores national particularities and the need to protect the people. it advocates the abolition of all national protectionism within the european union. the aim is to strengthen the single market by abolishing protectionist national legislation. the states would then only serve to implement the decisions of the commission, which itself would be at the mercy of industrial and financial lobbies. i voted against this report, of course.

in writing. ‒ almost 50 years ago, tariff barriers were removed, creating a single market with no barriers to trade across the european union. however, it is felt that we still have a long way to go and that is why the aim is now to remove non-tariff barriers, that is to say, the laws or political regulations of a country which restrict trade. the rapporteur stresses, however, that not all non-tariff measures should be abolished, but only those which are contrary to the principles of proportionality and non-discrimination, and those which are not based on a legitimate public management objective. the report aims to achieve a more consistent application of existing rules and a slight abandonment of certain protectionist policies still in force in some member states, which will make it possible to establish more open national markets. i believe that this report should be adopted because the removal of non-tariff barriers will benefit businesses throughout the eu, but especially consumers, who will be able to access a single market with lower prices and a wider supply.
in writing. ‒ although we have had a single market in europe for decades now, and this has certainly produced some very positive results, it is true that today there are still barriers that make it difficult to achieve the idea, almost utopian for many companies, that any european can set up his business anywhere in the eu. i would like to say this to the entrepreneurs in the outermost regions, such as the canary islands, where i come from, who have to fight every day not only against the physical barriers imposed by insularity and remoteness, but also against less visible but very present barriers, which affect our smes above all. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's citizens are not discriminated against in the same way as other citizens. so i join the call to the commission to do a thorough job in this direction and to eliminate non-tariff barriers once and for all, which are actually hindering competition and reducing the possibilities for consumers.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report, which reflected a vision based on the a priori idea that member states’ regulatory measures consist mainly of protectionist obstacles preventing cross-border trade, hence having to be urgently eliminated. the greens tabled amendments to underline that regulations which pursue a legitimate public policy goal, such as consumer protection, should not be seen as non-tariff barriers. we also wanted to highlight that upwards harmonisation is preferable to mutual recognition, that public services should be protected from competition and internal market rules, that the rules of the country of destination should prevail as regards the exercise of free movement of services and that the lack of fiscal coordination also represents a non-tariff barrier because it prevents firms from competing on a level-playing field.
in writing. ‒ we are talking about a report that confirms the need to abolish non-tariff barriers in the european single market, which currently prevent the movement of goods and services in the eu from working more efficiently. our great strength lies in our market, so it is always necessary and positive to take measures to help it function better. i therefore consider it necessary to vote in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ i am in favour of this report because i believe that all the barriers and obstacles preventing the creation of a true digital single market must be removed. the end of these will mean the improvement of the eu economy as a whole and the empowerment of innovation, as companies will have no obstacles to enter into competition in other member states, where they can expand their knowledge and acquire new intellectual capital. the provision of digital services will also be clearly improved for all europeans, as it will not vary from one member state to another. i am confident that with concerted effort and work among all eu members we will achieve a thriving and fully integrated digital single market, which will help ensure that economic recovery is a reality in the european union.
