in writing. ‒ this directive on the establishment of a general framework for equal treatment in employment and occupation sets out a general framework to ensure equal treatment at the workplace for people in the european union, irrespective of their religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation. i think an important point of this initiative is that it will apply to all people, whether working in the public or private sector, in relation to conditions of access to employment or self-employment, including selection criteria and conditions of recruitment and promotion; vocational training; conditions of employment and work (including dismissal and remuneration); membership and participation in a workers' or employers' organisation, or in any organisation whose members are in a specific profession. for the reasons outlined above and because we must take all possible measures, both at national and european level, to protect the principle of equal opportunities in employment and occupation, i am voting in favour of the adoption of this report.

in writing. we voted in favour of this report as it is positive in content in that it identifies the main problems and challenges in the implementation of the directive and proposes recommendations to the commission and the member states with which we agree to eliminate discrimination on grounds of sex, religion, belief, disability, age or sexual orientation and to ensure equal treatment in employment. amongst others, some highlights that we find very positive are: the commission's presentation of a directive on carers' leave; an improvement and transversalisation of available data on equality, including harmonised and homogeneous statistics; providing ongoing training for stakeholders on employment legislation; strengthening and supporting civil society organisations working in this area; measures to make the private sector take responsibility for creating an environment free of discrimination; the adoption of a european framework of national strategies to combat anti-semitism and islamophobia; recognising social clauses in public contracts or the effective enforcement of legislation (ged review) to ensure the protection of trans people, amongst others.
in writing. ‒ i voted for, as the eu and its ms must step up their efforts to fight discrimination, including by changing the social and political climate that is more and more tolerant towards extremism, racism and xenophobia, fuelling and exploiting fears about unemployment and the refugee crisis. while the employment equality directive has been transposed in all 28 member states, non-discrimination in the field of occupation and employment is only effective if discrimination is comprehensively combated in all areas of life.
in writing. ‒ this equal treatment directive, adopted 15 years ago, sets a general framework to ensure equal treatment at the workplace for eu citizens, regardless of their religion, beliefs, disability, age or sexual orientation. this report examines the challenges that still exist in the implementation of the directive and looks for possible ways to improve it. i am firmly in favour of the principle of equal treatment at work and aware that there are still, for example, pay gaps between men and women which must be reduced further, so i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it assesses the implementation of the employment equality directive since its adoption and draws up recommendations for further improvements in the future. it takes a balanced approach to the most important aspects, such as discrimination on grounds of sex, racial or ethnic origin, religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation. it also stresses that although some member states have gone further in implementing the requirements of the directive, and that europeans are tolerant of groups at risk of discrimination and are also better informed about their rights, challenges to the implementation of the directive still exist. the socialist amendments strengthened aspects relating to age and disability discrimination, reporting, data collection, multiple discrimination, continuing training and apprenticeship. a paragraph on work-life balance (maternity, carers, paternity leave) was also added, and another defending the 'quality' of employment for people with disabilities and the elimination of discriminatory language against migrants and refugees.
in writing. ‒ i am in favour of this report which analyses the activities, impact and added value of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf). the egf was set up to provide assistance and solidarity to workers made redundant as a result of major structural changes in world trade patterns. the report welcomes the extension of the funding period from one to two years, calls for all possible efforts to speed up the application and approval procedures for the funds, and highlights the concern that the egf has had a very limited impact on smes. i believe that it is a fundamental and very useful instrument and we must continue to improve it and adapt it to the changes taking place in the eu. it is therefore necessary to carry out specific studies of the impact of globalisation by sector, enabling it to draw up proposals that encourage companies to anticipate sectoral changes and to prepare their workers in advance for redundancies, and to counter this with a genuine industrial policy at union level that generates sustainable and inclusive growth.
in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) was set up in 2006 to help workers who have lost their jobs in large-scale redundancies as a result of globalisation, when such redundancies have a significant negative impact on the regional or local economy. the egf has been modified, for example by reducing the number of redundancies in the intervention criteria from 1000 to 500. this means that the egf is more accessible to the regions and to the smaller member states. since 2013, self-employed persons have been included and also, in the regions eligible under the youth employment initiative, ninis. the final report voted in committee, while not perfect, incorporates more progressive measures than the initial draft, including greater accessibility for veteran workers, women, youth and single parents. it recognises that women are disproportionately affected by the crisis and austerity. it also contains some positive points in the increased involvement of local authorities, social partners and civil society in the access, distribution and implementation of the egf. we voted yes.
in writing. ‒ i have supported the report by mrs marian harkin, whom i would like to congratulate on her great work. the report covers the activities, impact and added value of the european globalisation adjustment fund between 2007 and 2014. although i support the whole report, i differed with my group by two votes in my case, because i think women have indeed been disproportionately affected by the crisis and the austerity policies. i also agree that although the rate of reintegration into employment for women is higher than for men, for women it is mostly temporary and unstable reintegration into employment because of the family care obligations they have to meet while looking for a new job or attending vocational retraining courses, as well as the lack of affordable and quality childcare and care for the sick.
in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) was set up to help workers made redundant as a result of major structural changes in world trade patterns. the egf was designed to respond to emergency situations by providing rapid intervention and short-term assistance in response to serious and unforeseen labour market difficulties involving large-scale redundancies. the report examines the activities, impact and added value of the egf between 2007 and 2014 and makes a number of recommendations to improve the functioning of the egf. the committee also called for the commission to take action to ensure that smes, social economy enterprises and cooperatives could also benefit from the impact of trade policies and trade agreements on the european labour market, and stressed the importance of social dialogue based on mutual trust and shared responsibility as the best instrument for finding consensual solutions and common points of view in the forecasting, prevention and management of restructuring processes. i have therefore voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this because it is a balanced assessment of the european globalisation adjustment fund. on the basis that this fund cannot replace the economic and industrial policies necessary to maintain the productive fabric, this fund should be used to alleviate the immediate consequences of the closure of enterprises. the report includes many positive references to the role of trade unions, the impact that the crisis is having especially on women, the role that local authorities should also play, etc. the commission is also calling for an ambitious evaluation and review of this fund to deal with the dramatic situation facing the european economy. it is for all these reasons that i have decided to vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the egf (european globalisation adjustment fund) was initially established by regulation (ec) no 1927/2006 to support workers who have lost their jobs in the context of large-scale redundancies due to major structural changes in world trade patterns due to globalisation, where such redundancies have a significant negative impact on the regional or local economy. the main objectives of the report are to examine its performance in the period 2007-2014, to identify the weaknesses and strengths of the reforms of the egf introduced in this period, and to assess their effectiveness and significance, which could lead to the approval of the use of the fund for the current programming period.

in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) supports workers who lose their jobs as a result of major structural changes in world trade patterns brought about by globalisation. periodic evaluation reports have been produced on the activities carried out in the subsequent years of operation, with very positive results both in terms of the number of people assisted and in terms of reintegration rates. this own-initiative report would now attempt to make a more comprehensive assessment of the years 2007-2014. my country, spain, is reasonably satisfied with the functioning of the fund, because, as in other countries, it has been an important element in responding to the employment consequences of the crises. for the reasons described above, i am voting in favour of the approval of this initiative.

on behalf of the green group, madam president, we are addressing this oral question to the commission, and we should certainly thank mrs costa and her colleagues on the committee on culture for the initiative. it seems timely and necessary. we address it to the commission, i say, but we could also address it to the council and address it to each member state, and certainly address it to ourselves. i am sure that it is also more so for some member states than others, and one in particular: malta. we should therefore begin by feeling a little collective embarrassment that this question is still being raised, that this oral question is necessary and relevant, that we are still awaiting ratification of the convention. we know everything, we have the information, we have a presumed political agreement, we have the will expressed by everyone, but nothing happens and procedural issues are alleged or the well-known question of the opposition of a state. both of these explanations seem totally unacceptable to stop the collective ratification. and we also know that everything is the same or worse, that the reality is the same as when this parliament passed a resolution in 2013 or when the council of europe passed the convention in 2014. in this connection, one might ask whether, for example, the fifa scandals have any direct or indirect, immediate or remote connection with what we are talking about. illegal sports betting is a less and less secondary branch of organised crime and is polluting more and more sports, as just mentioned. this issue - believe me - is a black hole in our collective responsibility. we have worked on tax evasion, we have worked on the luxleaks investigation and now on the panama papers, we have prepared directives on money laundering, and we also know that this activity, this business, this organized crime would be impossible without the necessary activity of financial institutions and telecommunications services that must provide the means of payment necessary to make it possible. it is time to go into it in depth, and i think we should also, in closing, add a dimension to it, which we have not talked about and which is certainly not part of the question and does not have to be, although perhaps this is an opportunity to consider it, which is the tax aspect associated with the sports betting sector. do we know what volume of business we're talking about? should not this european union, this commission, have a well-prepared estimate of what this means and of the fiscal cost to the european union as a whole of the lack of regulation in this sector? could we not include a first effort in the commission's response, in the active response of estimating that turnover of online betting and the tax return that each country and the whole of europe should expect? we could then perhaps propose an appropriate tax treatment, which can only be envisaged, by the way, at least within the european union. i'm finished, chairman. if we do not do all this, i fear that even if we achieve universal ratification of the convention, everything will or may remain more or less the same. we had the opportunity yesterday to congratulate commissioner vestager on her decision in the apple case. the volume of tax fraud associated with the online gambling sector and the resulting movement of money may, and probably does, exceed that in that case. we hope that the commission's answer to the question we put to it today will be the first effective step in the right direction.

member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank the committee on development and the rapporteur, mr neuser, for the report on the future of acp—eu relations beyond 2020. i also thank the committee on foreign affairs, the committee on international trade and the committee on budgets for their opinions. this report is an important milestone. the cotonou agreement binds us with almost 80 countries in the world. we have a unique opportunity ahead of us. let us put the eu global strategy into practice and let us use a future partnership as a vehicle for implementing the 2030 agenda for sustainable development jointly. i am pleased to express support for this report. let me point out some of the features i find most important. we are aiming for a partnership that is flexible enough to cope with a radically, and rapidly, changing international environment. we should aim to address effectively common challenges and take advantage of economic opportunities to deliver peace and prosperity for our people, both in the european union and in the acp countries. we need a partnership that reflects and reinforces eu interests, objectives and means, as well as those of our acp partners. this new partnership should keep what has worked, but we should also use the opportunity to improve, or create new ways of working, where weaknesses have been shown. our main concern should be to keep the essential elements as global safeguards, such as respect for human rights, democracy and the rule of law, as well as good governance. this is clearly fundamental. we should also maintain and reinforce our regular political dialogue with our partner countries. international commitments, such as the 2030 agenda for sustainable development or the paris climate agreement, should be central references in a future partnership. enhancing dialogue with acp countries in order to forge global alliances in multilateral settings offers a new perspective for a future partnership. an excellent case in point was the final round of negotiations during cop 21 in paris. the fight to eradicate poverty and combat inequalities is at the heart of our policies and we know that efforts should be maintained. we also expect strong commitment on the part of the acp countries. any future framework that links the acp to the eu should learn from the positive aspects of cotonou, including its legally binding nature. the world around us is evolving and so are the roles of organisations and institutions. the partnership should recognise this and give due consideration to all levels, both continental and regional. it should equally reflect on how to involve national parliaments and other actors at local level, as well as non-state actors, in our project. the impact of the private sector should also be fostered since it has proven to be an essential motor for development. the report encourages engagement with additional countries as well as our current acp partners. for the sake of geographical and political coherence, this certainly merits consideration. while i trust that many honourable members share most of these opinions, i look forward now to hearing your comments.

i would like to thank mr neuser for the report he has prepared for us, which i believe is a very comprehensive report which will provide a road map for parliament's involvement in the renewal of the cotonou agreement. this is an agreement which has enabled us to have a political dialogue with a number of countries on different continents and which has strengthened the european union's external action. it is also an agreement which has enabled us to take part in preventing conflicts and working for peace once these conflicts have ended. it has also allowed us to participate in the protection of human rights, in providing good governance, in advancing democratic processes. i must point out, however, that the results have been very questionable as far as the economic partnership agreements are concerned, which certainly need to be revised. but times are changing and times have already changed, and the situation now of those countries and of the european union is not the same situation as when the cotonou agreement was first discussed. now is the time to work as equals; it is the time to respect each other; it is the time to rebalance our relations; and it is therefore the time to open up a new horizon for the next 20 years, through collaboration rather than one-way action.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, i deeply regret that this report is a missed opportunity to make a difference in the relationship between the european union and the countries of sub-saharan africa, the caribbean and the pacific, that is, the poorest countries in the world. we should encourage an exit from the cycle of poverty in which the european union is often part of the problem, not the solution. i think it is unacceptable that this report does not focus on the solution of the debt problem, which keeps so many states in a constant state of subordination to their creditors. nor does it try to stop illicit capital flows or tax evasion, which drain domestic resources from their economies. these countries are subject to constant plunder, as large amounts of capital generated in them are returned to europe or tax havens, and that is called stealing. all this has one name: financial neocolonialism. basing development aid on asymmetrical trade relations increases inequality and poverty, condemning these countries to a state of perpetual subjugation and dependence. the sustainable development goals are supposed to be at the heart of the new agreement, and yet they are only a decorative element. the fundamental pillars of acp-eu relations must be the fight against poverty and inequality through endogenous development, respecting the space for states to implement policies that are best suited to their citizens, and not to european companies. we all have our contradictions, but there are some red lines and some unbreakable principles, and that is why i will not be voting for this report.

member of the commission. – mr president, let me start by underlining our 100% commitment to the goal of education for all syrian refugees, in line with our pledge at the syria donors conference in london. it is absolutely essential that we do not lose a generation of displaced syrian children. first and foremost, this is important for the well—being of the children themselves. it is also crucial for regional stability, for the eventual recovery of syria from this crisis as well as – let’s face it – in our own interest over the long term. where there are needs, we are responding and we are ready, if necessary, to do more. our neighbours in the region need to know that we stand by them as they work towards a better future. one of the outcomes of the london conference was a joint commitment to provide access to quality education for all refugee and vulnerable children in host communities. we will make every effort to empower young syrians by investing in their future. education is, and has always been, a key priority of the eu response to the crisis in syria. so far we have made a substantial contribution to education in lebanon, with eur 180 million allocated to this sector since the beginning of the crisis. we have stepped up this approach both through the eu trust fund in response to the syria crisis as well as the compact we have been negotiating with the lebanese and jordanian authorities. this aims to turn the challenges posed by the huge influx of syrian refugees into an opportunity both for refugees and host communities. in lebanon the focus has been on education, where we hope that reforms will have an impact across the entire public education sector. eur 42.5 million has already been allocated to the so-called reaching all children with education strategy, the abbreviation for which is race, which i think is a good one. called the race programme, it was designed by the lebanese ministry of education. a substantial part of this has gone towards the enrolment of syrian children in formal and non-formal education, the supply of educational material and transport. i am pleased to say that this coming school year is already well funded and we will be able to cover school fees for over 168 000 syrian children in formal education. i must stress, however, that money alone will not solve the problem of access to education. there are still serious legal, administrative and technical barriers. this includes the lack of residency status, the distance between where refugees live and the schools that service them but also, unfortunately, harassment and discrimination, which has been documented in last summer’s human rights watch report. the problem of residency status is a serious one and has a clear impact on freedom of movement of refugees and leads to exploitation, including child labour. this is why we have placed this at the core of the eu-lebanon compact. in exchange for the considerable financial support being offered by the european union, lebanon has agreed to provide an appropriate and safe environment for refugees. we are working closely with various un agencies and international ngos in this respect and it should be noted that when we see or hear of the commendable work being done by unicef, unhcr and others, that behind this effort there is a strong european union contribution which should also be acknowledged. although not directly linked with the subject we are dealing with today, i should also mention the humanitarian initiative launched by my colleagues mogherini and against hunger and malnutrition is still a central issue today, in the 21st century. working to end hunger, achieving food security, providing better nutrition, providing the means for sustainable agriculture are, in today's world, goals yet to be achieved. the committee on development, which is putting this question to the vote, would like to point out that some of our development aid has undoubtedly helped to reduce the number of people suffering from malnutrition in the world, but it is far from having achieved the objectives of eradicating malnutrition from our reality. in fact, the proportion of undernourished people in developing regions has been reduced by almost half since 1990, but still 785 million people do not get enough food or the necessary nutrients. chronic malnutrition affects 160 million children, is the cause of almost half of all deaths among children under five, one in six is underweight for his or her age. inadequate nutrition during the first 1,000 days of life will have negative consequences on a child's physical and intellectual abilities throughout his or her life. that's why, in 2012, the world health assembly set a goal of achieving a 40 percent reduction in the number of stunted children by 2025. we urge the commission to step up its efforts to combat malnutrition and for this we need specific interventions in those first 1,000 days of life. i would remind you that at the london summit in 2012, the european union committed itself to reducing stunting by at least 7 million children by 2025 and to contribute 3.5 billion euros to this cause by 2020. we hoped that this year in rio de janeiro we would take stock of progress and renew our commitments. it was not possible. however, action is more urgent than ever today, because development interventions against malnutrition receive only 0.57 per cent of all official development assistance. we need to increase the investment 70 times to meet our targets. in 2013, the european union committed 400 million for specific initiatives. we call on the commission to increase this commitment by an additional 1 billion. we need to put strategies in place, by ourselves and all our partners, to support the important role played by small-scale farmers. they produce 70 percent of the world's food. we must support them, use their potential, increase their yield and productivity, preserve the variety of seeds and the nutritional value of what they produce. commissioner, i would like to hear what the commission intends to do in this field. i'm sure you'll agree with us that we have a lot more to do. the president of the world bank has also said this, and he has even pointed out or said that we have to point out to the governments of the countries that are not meeting their objectives. we also know what needs to be done in food safety and we ask the commission to tell us what it intends to do in the coming years. we would like to hear new initiatives and ask the member states to commit themselves in 2017 to an intergovernmental summit to review the objectives and take stock of the needs ahead.

member of the commission. – mr president, it was actually on human rights day, on 10 december 2015, that we had the first trilogue on this issue of how to reform the so-called anti-torture regulation. thanks to very good cooperation between the commission and the parliament and, of course, the council, we managed to get something i think we can all be very proud of. i welcome this agreement. it is ground—breaking. i would like to thank the rapporteur, marietje schaake, and the shadow rapporteurs and, of course, the rapporteur for the committee on foreign affairs, mrs barbara lochbihler. many countries have, like the eu, abolished the death penalty for all crimes, but we know that the death penalty still exists, and the abolition of the death penalty worldwide remains one of the flagship objectives of our human rights policies. today we show how we can concretely deliver trade’s contribution to this. we are leading the way. it is a ground-breaking revised version of the regulation designed to stop the trade in equipment used for the torture or execution of people. the new reforms of the regulation from 2005 is now a robust export—controlled regime designed to prevent eu involvement in trading goods that are intended to be used for capital punishment or torture in third countries. as the rapporteur said, there are some very important new elements in this regulation. it covers such activities as brokering services, concerning goods located outside the eu, for which an authorisation will now be required, technical assistance, which will also require an authorisation, and also advertising. for the first time, we are introducing a ban on the display of goods in trade fairs in the eu. for those products made in third countries and exported in transit through the eu, we are making it more expensive and more difficult by introducing a ban. we simply cannot tolerate that these torture and execution products are circulated through our ports or through our territory. we know that technology evolves and new products for torture may reach the market. that is why it is imperative that the list of products under export control can be updated quickly. the commission will now have the possibility to use a fast—track – or urgency – procedure to amend the list of goods to which the regulation applies on the lists or the list of countries benefiting from the general export authorisation. let me stress that, if this procedure is applied, it does not in any way deprive parliament and the council of their right to scrutiny of the delegated acts. this regulation sets a high eu trade standard, which takes into account the need to respect human rights. it is an excellent example of the new value—based trade that is so essential for our trade policy. we have shown leadership when it comes to human rights. it is not only an empty statement, but this is a concrete way to contribute to it. with concrete action, through concrete measures, we show that we are taking the death penalty and torture seriously. we want to make it difficult and to remind countries, such as saudi arabia, iran, china and also the us, that we do not tolerate, and we condemn, these practices. it is a message of support to all those people suffering torture and inhumane treatment in prisons and police stations that we care about them and we are listening to them. the original regulation already made the point that restrictions on trade are instrumental in promoting respect for human rights and human life and thus it serves the purpose of protecting public morals in compliance with the wto rules in this respect. in our contacts with third countries, be it with members of parliaments or governments, we should promote our values and explain that these restrictions are justified and proportionate. we should of course continue our fight against abolishing capital punishment for all crimes, and invite countries to apply similar end-use control to their exports. we should also explain that these trade restrictions are not intended to deprive third countries of listed medicinal products, but have to prevent such products from being used for the death penalty. we know that in the past that has actually worked. so authorisations can be granted for exports of medicinal products if it is shown that they are being used for the treatment of patients – i.e. the purpose for which they were originally developed. so i hope that parliament with the vote today will confirm the agreement that we reached last may. it is indeed a very important decision. a strong vote in this plenary will, of course, send a very powerful signal, showing that trade policy is not only about economies, jobs and investment, but is also a way to promote our values. i want again to reiterate my deepest thanks for the contribution and for the good collaboration we have had with this parliament.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, commissioner, i would first of all like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs schaake, on the great work she has done on this highly complex technical and highly political dossier. the abolition of the death penalty and of inhuman and degrading treatment is one of the major priorities of the union's human rights policy. the european union, through this regulation, reaffirms its policy towards the abolition of the death penalty in the world. it is a single instrument, which ensures respect for human rights enshrined in both the charter of fundamental rights of the union and the european convention on human rights, in particular respect for and protection of human dignity, the right to life and the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. this agreement is a very important step in the fight against torture and will set a precedent which i hope will serve as an example to other parts of the world. as the rapporteur has very well explained, in may of this year we reached agreement with the council on a compromise text which includes a large part of parliament's recommendations. i congratulate you on that. a number of products intended to inflict torture or the death penalty, as well as their advertising, promotion or transit through the territory of the union, have been prohibited. for other types of products, a series of controls have been introduced to ensure that they are used correctly and are not used for torture or capital punishment. we must not forget that certain instruments or medicines are used to ensure our safety or to treat our health, so we must find a balance, clearly define their legitimate uses. here's the whole difficulty: the same product, well used, can save lives, and, poorly used, can be used to execute a person. we in the european parliament have also succeeded in getting an anti-torture coordination group set up and guidelines on good practice in the verification of the end use of these instruments adopted. in conclusion, the text resulting from the trilogue seems appropriate to us and contributes to the protection of human rights, and makes the european union a pioneer in the regulation of trade in these products. i hope we can pass it by a large majority.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on her excellent work, on her sensitivity and incorporation of the amendments i have tabled and on the good result achieved in the negotiations, which is also the result of the excellent work of commissioner malmström and her team, whom i also congratulate. and my special thanks to amnesty international and the omega foundation for their commendable work and for their involvement. more than 1,600 people were executed in 2015, while more than 20,000 were waiting on death row. the european union is a world leader in the defence against torture and the death penalty, but it is useless if it is not reinforced by firm and binding actions such as the one we are now discussing. today we are taking a big step forward with the adoption of this new regulation in defence of human rights, against torture and the death penalty. the commission has already made considerable progress in ensuring that no european national or company can profit from this trade within the european union. by extending the prohibition and control to all activities necessary for its use, such as brokering, technical assistance, transport, advertising or display at trade fairs. the commission is also proposing to increase the number of member states that have to comply with the directive by requiring a greater duty of control and reporting from the member states, and also by imposing sanctions. and by defending the prerogatives of the european parliament, by including our expert officials in the coordination group, thanks to the push of our commission president, mr lange. with this new regulation, the european union - as those who have spoken before me have said - is raising the bar for the eradication of torture and the death penalty. and that is why my group is pleased with the agreement; in writing. ‒ the paris agreement is the first legally binding international agreement to be adopted on climate change. it was adopted at the 21st cop of the unfccc, held in paris from 30 november to 12 december 2015. i voted in favour of the union and the seven member states that have completed the ratification process being able to deposit their instruments of ratification at un headquarters in new york on friday 7 october, allowing the paris agreement to enter into force in time for cop22, which will take place in marrakech from 7 to 18 november 2016. the socialist group in the european parliament and the spanish delegation have worked hard to make the paris conference a success, advocating the adoption of an ambitious agreement with rapid implementation. the socialists believe that the union cannot lag behind other world powers when it comes to ratification, and have therefore voted in favour of the resolution empowering the council to formally adopt the ratification decision by urgent written procedure.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of ratifying the paris agreement on behalf of the union, as this is a symbolic gesture of validation of this agreement negotiated by the parties, which then has to be ratified and implemented by each member state of the united nations. i do not share the triumphalist rhetoric about this paris agreement. i voted in favour of this agreement, but i think it is insufficient, since it is based mainly on the voluntary commitments and market mechanisms which i criticise. i voted in favour of this minimum agreement, aware that despite progress, it is still far from being an effective response to climate change.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution, which gives its approval to the conclusion of the paris agreement. at the paris climate conference (cop21) in december 2015, 195 countries signed the first binding global climate agreement, which was signed by all the world's countries. to avoid dangerous climate change, the agreement sets out a global action plan that puts the limit on global warming well below 2°c. the agreement will enter into force in 2020.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which implies the approval of the paris agreement, adopted by consensus at the last cop 21. although this is a symbolic vote, since ratification has to be done at member state level, it is important because it means that the european parliament commits itself to the objectives of the paris agreement by asking each member state of the union to ratify the treaty. the agreement shall enter into force one year after 12 december 2015.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of ratifying the paris agreement on behalf of the union, as this is a symbolic gesture of validation of this agreement negotiated by the parties, which then has to be ratified and implemented by each member state of the united nations. i do not share the triumphalist rhetoric about this paris agreement. i voted in favour of this agreement, but i think it is insufficient, since it is based mainly on the voluntary commitments and market mechanisms which i criticise. i voted in favour of this minimum agreement, aware that despite progress, it is still far from being an effective response to climate change.
in writing. ‒ this recommendation approves the conclusion of the paris agreement on behalf of the european union. the european union has long been a leader in the fight against climate change and the approval of this agreement is a testament to that. the paris agreement is a historic milestone in the fight against climate change that has brought together nearly 200 countries in their ambition to lower co2 emissions to limit global warming through ambitious, balanced, equitable, and legally binding measures. i am voting in favour of this landmark agreement, as it will lead irrevocably and decisively to a climate-neutral world economy and serve as a precedent that collective and effective global action is possible. we must provide future generations with a more stable and prosperous future through a sustainable and healthy world.

in writing. ‒ the paris agreement is a before and after in the fight against climate change at global level, paving the way towards a low greenhouse gas emissions development model. the leadership shown by the european union in paris must be maintained and early ratification of the agreement is key to this. i have therefore supported this decision, which, after the approval of the european union ministers, concludes the paris agreement on behalf of the european union. rapid ratification by its member states will consolidate the union as a leading actor in the fight against climate change.

in writing. ‒ on 17 november 2015, the ionian islands (particularly leucadia and the northern parts of ithaca and kefalonia) suffered earthquakes with damage estimated at more than eur 66 million, or 2,1% of regional gdp. the objective of this report is to mobilise the union solidarity fund to the value of eur 1,7 million in commitment and payment appropriations. although this is only a small amount in relation to the total damage, i have voted in favour of this report to help rebuild the area.
in writing. ‒ this report called for the mobilisation of funds to help the ionian islands region in greece for the damage suffered by an earthquake in november 2015. i vote in favour of these funds being mobilised in solidarity with the people who have suffered the damage caused by this natural disaster.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the mobilisation of the eu solidarity fund to provide eur 1 651 834 in solidarity with the greek regions affected by the earthquake in november 2015. the quakes, measuring 6.1 on the richter scale, killed two people, injured eight, and damaged 120 homes, 20 of which were deemed uninhabitable. infrastructure networks and various buildings and cultural sites were also severely damaged.

in writing. ‒ it is a common objective that greece returns to the path of growth and job creation. to achieve this, a key factor is competitiveness, which in turn can only be achieved through the implementation of the structural reforms recommended by the union as a whole to the greek government. i therefore support this commission statement and its purpose, which is simply to assess the progress made by greece in the agreed reforms, since these are a condition for the outstanding disbursements under the second tranche of the third financial assistance programme that we europeans are giving to greece.

in writing. ‒ finland applied for egf assistance following the redundancies of 2 161 workers at microsoft mobile oy and 8 of its suppliers and product converters. although european aid does not guarantee the continuity of employment in the sector in an area that has been badly affected by the decline of nokia and the finnish electronics industry, it does mean an improvement in the situation of the workers made redundant, which is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ i am voting in favour of this report, since it calls for funds to compensate and provide compensatory measures in cases of relocation or closure of companies due to structural changes in markets due to globalisation. it will be used to deal with the situation of workers who have been made redundant and to help young people who are unemployed and without a job, in this case microsoft in finland, which had already absorbed unemployed people from nokia, but who, by mobilising a large part of their production, are again left unemployed. these are measures which, if they were not taken, would leave the workers concerned in a worse position. such measures have only short-term effects, but do not solve the problem in the long term, since the question of employment and relocations should be approached differently. on the one hand, europe needs an investment plan, which is very different from the juncker plan, and a different employment policy, in order to act in the field of employment. on the other hand, this alternative should consist in investing in activities for the future, especially in a change of production model.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the mobilisation of eur 5 364 000 from the european globalisation adjustment fund to help reintegrate into the labour market 1 441 workers made redundant by microsoft mobile oy and eight of its suppliers in finland. these funds will be used to finance measures for redundant workers, including counselling, employment and enterprise services, training, wage subsidies or grants for the creation of businesses.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the mobilisation of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) in respect of the application egf/2016/001 fi/microsoft from finland. europe and the world are engaged in a profound process of globalisation which, while a source of trade and wealth creation, can also entail risks to which we must be very attentive. as a result of this process, some sectors are more exposed to international competition, and the eu must therefore respond to those citizens who lose their jobs as a result of globalisation. the egf shall support workers who lose their jobs as a result of major structural changes in world trade patterns caused by globalisation or by the global economic and financial crisis.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of mobilising the european globalisation adjustment fund for the application of finland (microsoft) and sweden (ericsson) because i agree with the use of the funds for both cases.
in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) was introduced in 2007 as a flexible instrument through which the union budget provides support, under specific conditions, to workers who have lost their jobs as a result of major structural changes in world trade patterns, brought about by globalisation or the widespread global economic and financial crisis. the european parliament, in its report, supports the commission's proposal to grant finland eur 5.3 million from the egf to help 1 441 former microsoft employees and eight of its supplier companies find new jobs. i am firmly convinced that the union's commitment to unemployed citizens must be translated into concrete action, and i have therefore voted in favour of this decision.
in writing. ‒ finland applied for egf assistance following the redundancies of 2 161 workers at microsoft mobile oy and 8 of its suppliers and product converters. although european aid does not guarantee the continuity of employment in the sector in an area that has been badly affected by the decline of nokia and the finnish electronics industry, it does mean an improvement in the situation of the workers made redundant, which is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund has been set up to provide additional support to workers suffering from the consequences of major structural changes in world trade patterns. the request concerns 2 035 workers made redundant by microsoft. the main company operates in the economic sector of 'programming, consulting and other it-related activities'. the report notes that the main reason for the layoffs at microsoft is the declining market share of its phones running the microsoft windows operating system. it is stressed that the software industry is highly international and that competition in the sector is global, i.e. all market players can compete for the same customers and the location and cultural background of staff have limited significance. the report states that this request is the continuation of a series of cases revolving around nokia's decline in finland. i am voting in favour of this report because we must protect the areas most affected by reindustrialisation in order to move forward and be able to adapt to new economic needs.
in writing. ‒ sweden applied for egf support following the dismissal of 1 556 ericsson workers. although european aid does not guarantee the continuity of employment in a sector which is highly exposed to international competition, it does mean an improvement in the situation of workers who are made redundant, which is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ i am voting in favour of this report, since it calls for funds to compensate and provide compensatory measures in cases of relocation or closure of companies due to structural changes in markets due to globalisation. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. these are measures which, if they did not exist, would leave the workers concerned in a worse position. such measures have only short-term effects, but do not solve the problem in the long term, since the question of employment and relocations should be approached differently. on the one hand, europe needs an investment plan, which is very different from the juncker plan, and a different employment policy, in order to act in the field of employment. on the other hand, this alternative should consist in investing in activities for the future, especially in a change of production model.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the mobilisation of eur 3 957 918 from the european globalisation adjustment fund to help reintegrate the 918 workers made redundant by ericsson in sweden into the labour market. these funds will be used to co-finance personalised services for redundant workers, such as counselling and career guidance; protected and assisted employment and rehabilitation measures; education and training; and job search allowances. in addition, special attention will be given to participants aged 50 and over in the provision of motivation and career planning.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of mobilising the european globalisation adjustment fund for the application of finland (microsoft) and sweden (ericsson) because i agree with the use of the funds for both cases.
in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) was introduced in 2007 as a flexible instrument through which the union budget provides support, under specific conditions, to workers who have lost their jobs as a result of major structural changes in world trade patterns, brought about by globalisation or the widespread global economic and financial crisis. the european parliament, in its report, supports the commission's proposal to grant sweden eur 3.9 million from the egf to help 918 former employees of various ericsson production plants find new jobs. i am firmly convinced that the union's commitment to unemployed citizens must be translated into concrete action, and i have voted in favour of this decision.
in writing. ‒ sweden applied for egf support following the dismissal of 1 556 ericsson workers. although european aid does not guarantee the continuity of employment in a sector which is highly exposed to international competition, it does mean an improvement in the situation of workers who are made redundant, which is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund has been set up to provide additional support to workers suffering from the consequences of major structural changes in world trade patterns. this application concerns 918 of the 1 556 workers made redundant in the period from 11 september 2015 to 11 january 2016. ericsson operates mainly in the economic sectors of computer, electronic and optical product manufacturing and programming, consulting and other computer-related activities. the redundancies made by ericsson are mainly in the stockholm and östra mellansverige regions, in sydsverige and västsverige. the report notes that ericsson is experiencing stagnating growth and competition with asian producers. the commission is asked to detail in future proposals the sectors in which workers are likely to find employment and whether the training offered is in line with future economic prospects and market needs. i am voting in favour of this report because we must protect the areas most affected by reindustrialisation in order to move forward and be able to adapt to new economic needs.
in writing. ‒ although the request for the waiver of the parliamentary immunity of mr giorgos grammatikakis was requested by the greek judicial authorities in connection with events which took place in 1996, when he was rector of the university of crete, the nature of those events, in which there is an allegation of illegal payments by the university to private insurers, has led me to vote in favour of the request for the waiver of the immunity of this mep so that the judicial procedure can continue in greece.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the request for the waiver of immunity as proposed by the juri committee. i understand there's no possibility of using the suspension to initiate a political prosecution.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the waiver of the immunity of mr grammatikakis, given that the person concerned had requested it and in the light of the report drawn up by the committee on legal affairs, which states that the proposed procedure clearly has no connection with mr grammatikakis's status as a member of the european parliament, since it relates to his previous post as rector of the university of crete cloister.

in writing. ‒ the request for the waiver of the immunity of mr giorgos grammatikakis relates to the proceedings brought by the public prosecutor of rethymnon for breach of trust in the performance of his duties, committed jointly in rethymnon, crete, during the period 2000 and communicated to the plenary on 27 april 2016. parliament, expressing its surprise at the fact that the request for the waiver of immunity is made some twenty years after the facts and that the greek judicial system has not been able to act against mr giorgos grammatikakis during this period and intends to do so now, when he is a member of the european parliament, and considering that a slow-moving judicial system will never be truly fair, because the persons involved are no longer the same as they were twenty years ago, decides to waive the immunity of mr giorgos grammatikakis, at the request of the person concerned, in order to put an end to this lengthy judicial procedure.
in writing. ‒ since this waiver of immunity is agreed by mr grammatikakis himself, it was logical to grant his request and vote in favour of this report. furthermore, the case is unrelated to the member's performance of his duties, since the alleged acts occurred in the context of his former professional activity. for these reasons, i voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ i understand that access to justice is a fundamental right, and is thus enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the union. the only way to guarantee equal access to this right is through a free justice system which does not exist in the union today. the original report contained some very positive elements which would go in that direction, but after the negotiations with the council it has been weakened considerably, as many of the member states do not guarantee this right. the text presented would only cover persons deprived of their liberty. we believe that this is an improvement on the current situation of lack of protection, but it is clearly insufficient and in sharp contrast to the position adopted by the european parliament at the time, and i have therefore decided to abstain.
in writing. ‒ the aim of this report is to improve the rights of the accused in criminal proceedings. common minimum standards governing these rights should foster mutual trust between judicial authorities and thus facilitate the application of the principle of mutual recognition. a certain degree of compatibility between the laws of the member states is essential to improve judicial cooperation in the union. thanks to the work of our group's rapporteur, the commission's proposal has been considerably improved, including the extension of the scope beyond deprivation of liberty, allowing for provisional and ordinary legal aid in all circumstances. it is important to note that it covers aspects such as the initial phase of the proceedings, especially when the accused or the accused are deprived of liberty, is the time when they are most vulnerable and when they most need the legal assistance of a lawyer. in the trilogue negotiations, the work of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs suffered some setbacks because of the council's resistance. still, it is a significant advance. i therefore vote in favour of this proposal.
in writing. ‒ i have given my support to the report on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on provisional free legal assistance for suspects or accused persons deprived of liberty and on free legal assistance in european arrest warrant proceedings. the report, which is a proposal for agreement at first reading, takes account of the differences between member states in the quality of legal aid they provide and the need to include guarantees on the quality of legal aid covered by the directive. the report, thanks to amendments by the s&d group, focuses on free legal aid and the expansion of the scope covered to cover all types of legal aid in criminal proceedings.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour, bearing in mind that, in accordance with article 82 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, judicial cooperation in criminal matters in the union is based on the principle of mutual recognition of judgments and judicial decisions. the application of this principle requires that member states have confidence in each other's criminal justice systems, including in the way in which the rights of suspects or accused persons are safeguarded. different interpretation of the right to a fair trial, in particular through legal aid, constitutes an obstacle to fair and effective judicial cooperation in criminal matters. the commission proposal is a positive step towards ensuring a minimum level of legal aid in all member states.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because it states that a rule should be included in the directive that, as far as possible, the preferences and wishes of suspects or accused persons and of wanted persons should be taken into account in the choice of their own lawyer. the same applies to the need for continuity in legal representation, if the suspect, accused or wanted person so wishes. there should also be a rule for the replacement of a lawyer of a lawyer's choice, if the suspect, accused or wanted person has lost confidence in the lawyer and can justify this with verifiable reasons, as such a rule is not even mentioned in the recommendation. the report takes account of differences between member states in the quality of legal aid they provide. it states that, in view of the differences in the levels of revenue and costs between member states, it is not possible to lay down rules on the level of fees. however, the report stresses that this makes it all the more important to include at least some guarantees on the quality of legal aid covered by the directive.

in writing. ‒ the objective of this proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council is to establish common basic rules on the right to free provisional legal aid for suspects or accused persons deprived of liberty in criminal proceedings and on provisional legal aid and legal aid for persons subject to the european arrest procedure. the council and the european parliament have stressed the importance of establishing common basic rules to ensure a minimum level of legal aid in all member states. i am voting in favour of this because these rules would strengthen the mutual trust of member states in each other's criminal systems, which is essential for the application of the principle of mutual recognition of judgments and judicial decisions, a pillar on which judicial cooperation in criminal matters in the union is based.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the directive on free legal assistance for suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings and for persons wanted under the european arrest warrant procedure, as it provides for harmonised minimum standards to ensure the effectiveness and the right of access to a lawyer and to strengthen mutual trust, knowledge and cooperation between member states.
in writing. ‒ the analysis of the european directive on legal aid (presented by the commission in november 2013) was started by parliament in 2014. at the end of june this year an agreement was reached with the dutch presidency to amend certain points of the commission's original proposal. the report covers these amendments, with particular emphasis on the scope of the directive and the inclusion of means and merit tests for becoming a beneficiary. the first extends the scope of the directive to cover not only assistance on a provisional basis but also assistance throughout the judicial process. while it is true that the final text has not been as ambitious as we had hoped - because, despite reaching all free legal aid in criminal proceedings, its implementation is subject to national criteria that are not only based on economics but on merits - it stands as a first step towards future improvements that require more time to be accepted by those countries that would prefer to do without the proposal in its entirety. i therefore considered it appropriate to vote in favour.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the new european regulation against business linked to torture and the death penalty, as it is a pioneering initiative in favour of human rights in the world. it introduces binding executive measures which will prevent any european involvement in this heinous business. it strengthens the export ban and control introduced in 2006, making it more effective. and it extends its application to new products, such as drugs for lethal injection, and to services such as transport, online advertising, technical assistance or commercial intermediation. no foreign commercial agent may again display torture material at trade fairs in the union. the responsibility of the member states in their duty to monitor and report is strengthened. when spain took over the presidency of the council of the union in 2010, the socialist government of rodríguez-zapatero demanded a reform of the union in this regard. today the union has taken another step towards ending torture and capital punishment, and the social democrats have been able to demonstrate that trade policy is and must be a fundamental tool for promoting progress and human rights in the world.
in writing. ‒ this report seeks to regulate trade in certain products which can be used to apply the death penalty or inflict torture or degrading treatment, which i consider very necessary and for this reason i voted in favour of the report. however, although i voted in favour of the report, i do not think that the union has any credibility in the fight against torture as long as it remains subordinate to the united states (for example, there is evidence that torture has been routinely practiced with total impunity in guantanamo for the past 14 years). the report contains many proposals with which i fully agree, such as the call to ensure that union exports to third countries do not contribute to what the union considers to be 'inhuman' practices, such as electric chairs, or cage beds. but unfortunately the union has no credibility in its call to 'fight against torture' as long as we continue to profit from arms sales to saudi arabia, or as long as our partners have legalized torture and the death penalty. if we are really against torture, we should start by reviewing our relations with third countries, until they comply with the universal declaration of human rights.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because we are satisfied with the commission's proposal, and even more so after a very constructive amendment process. although i am aware that the new regulation by itself will not eliminate the death penalty or prevent torture worldwide, i consider it a step forward in this regard.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because i am convinced that eu-wide export controls are an instrument that contributes to the protection of human rights by controlling the items and activities that are used, or that could be abused, to apply the death penalty or to inflict torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. the revision of the eu controls on trade in instruments of torture should have been done long ago, and the updates of the control lists are steps in the right direction. it is important to ensure the appropriate combination of eu legislative, administrative, judicial and external measures to prevent and prohibit the production, trade and use of torture articles and, indeed, control products for inhuman and potentially lethal use.

in writing. ‒ this report seeks to regulate trade in certain products which can be used to apply the death penalty or inflict torture or degrading treatment, which i consider very necessary and for this reason i voted in favour of the report. however, although i voted in favour of the report, i do not think that the union has any credibility in the fight against torture as long as it remains subordinate to the united states (for example, there is evidence that torture has been routinely practiced with total impunity in guantanamo for the past 14 years). the report contains many proposals with which i fully agree, such as the call to ensure that union exports to third countries do not contribute to what the union considers to be 'inhuman' practices, such as electric chairs, or cage beds. but unfortunately the union has no credibility in its call to 'fight against torture' as long as we continue to profit from arms sales to saudi arabia, or as long as our partners have legalized torture and the death penalty. if we are really against torture, we should start by reviewing our relations with third countries, until they comply with the universal declaration of human rights.
in writing. ‒ this proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council introduces new rules to prevent trade in goods and services that can be used for executions or torture. the 2005 trade restrictions regulation was already a success as a key instrument to combat the death penalty. it prohibits the export of products intended for capital punishment or torture and controls trade in products originally designed for other purposes but which may be used for torture or executions. despite this success, the union cannot be satisfied with the 2005 regulation and must continue its policy of eliminating the death penalty worldwide and preventing torture. this is the line taken by the present proposal, which thanks to the efforts of parliament includes a ban on advertising products used to treat people in other countries in a cruel, inhuman or degrading way. i am voting in favour of the new proposal because it is a broad approach which will help to protect human rights.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report. i am strongly opposed to the death penalty and supported the eu proposal of a un moratorium on death penalty. the eu cannot be credible and consistent with its core and fundamental values if the eu and its member states allow to trade goods and products used for capital punishment. these are not normal products that can be traded like any others.

in writing. ‒ the prohibition of torture and ill-treatment is a key pillar of the un human rights conventions to which the union is a signatory, one of whose core values is the promotion of respect for fundamental rights worldwide. in june 2016, the european parliament reached an agreement with the european council on products that can be used for capital punishment or for the purpose of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, with the aim of preventing union exports from contributing to human rights violations in third countries. i voted in favour of this agreement, which will allow regulation (ec) no 1236/2005 to be amended in the light of developments since its entry into force (2006), with particular attention to the rules on export controls, new controls on intermediation services and technical assistance, and the prohibition on advertising for certain products.

in writing. ‒ i am clearly opposed to this type of strategic cooperation agreements in judicial and legal matters, where there is a great lack of transparency that prevents us from knowing how the data of citizens of the union and of migrants and stateless persons residing here are used. in addition, this rejection is increased in the case of countries with poor guarantees of compliance with the most basic judicial rights, as is the case of china. it is remarkable that this agreement was concluded shortly before the adoption of the new europol regulation which ensures much greater transparency and openness, particularly in cooperation agreements with third countries, so i understand that there is a will on the part of the agency to continue to operate in an opaque way. i have therefore voted against the agreement.
in writing. ‒ i vote against this report which states, pursuant to article 23 (2) of decision 2009/371/jha, that the council must consult the european parliament when approving the conclusion of international cooperation agreements with third states and organisations. these agreements cover the exchange of strategic and classified information, as well as the exchange of personal data. i am voting against this because i am against the establishment of such information exchange agreements with a country where there are a significant number of cases of human rights violations that have been properly documented. the position of our group on judicial cooperation with third countries is that it should only take place where there are sufficient guarantees of respect for human rights.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on the draft council implementing decision approving the conclusion by the european police office (europol) of the strategic cooperation agreement between the ministry of public security of the people's republic of china and europol. the information exchanged could include expertise, general situation reports, results of strategic analyses, information on criminal investigation procedures, information on crime prevention methods and training activities, as well as the provision of support and advice in specific criminal investigations. however, the exchange of personal data is excluded from the strategic agreement. as europol warns, china is playing an increasingly important role as a country of origin, destination and transit in the fight against organised crime, in areas such as support for illegal immigration, trafficking in human beings, drug-related crime, counterfeiting of the euro, violations of intellectual property rights or corruption in sport, as well as in other activities related to cybercrime and money laundering.

in writing. – this is yet another one of those agreements signed between europol and third states in order to strengthen their mutual cooperation in preventing and combating organised crime, terrorism and other forms of serious transnational crimes. such strategic agreements involve the exchange of information, excluding personal data. the information exchanged could include specialist knowledge, general situation reports, results of strategic analysis, information on criminal investigation procedures, information on crime prevention methods, training activities, and the provision of advice and support in individual criminal investigations. this time the third state in question is china. we are all aware of the systematic violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms committed by the chinese government, some of which are measures that directly fall under the justice and home affairs area. at the same time, china’s definition of whom constitutes a criminal or a terrorist it is often markedly different from what the eu’s is. therefore, i have voted against authorising any kind of police cooperation with china, as doing so would be tantamount to becoming an accomplice of the chinese government in the curtailment and violation of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
