in writing. ‒ the mandate of europol (decision 2009/371/2009) empowers the eu agency to conclude cooperation agreements with certain third countries to improve police cooperation with a view to preventing and combating organised crime, terrorism and other serious forms of crime. the proposed strategic cooperation agreement with china involves the exchange of operational, strategic and technical information; in no case provisions on personal data. the purpose of the council implementing decision is to authorise the conclusion of the cooperation agreement between europol and china. all the mainstream political groups supported this approach, and i am voting in favour of signing this agreement because i consider the exchange of information to be essential for the fight against organised crime.
in writing. ‒ this report aims to set out what the relationship between the union and the african, caribbean and pacific countries should look like after 2020. it should be noted that association agreements have always had a number of negative impacts on the economies of the acp countries, which is why i believe it is essential to have a new type of partnership, which is fair and equitable, which respects the sovereignty of the countries and which promotes the development of the countries' productive capacities, protects traditional agriculture and fights land grabbing and over-exploitation, while at the same time having legal mechanisms to combat labour exploitation, modern slavery, the illicit flow of capital and the financing of terrorism and armed conflict. i think it is also important to stress the importance of ending foreign interference in the internal affairs of the acp countries, as well as the end of neo-colonial policies and the dismantling of all foreign military bases. however, this report does not propose any of these changes which i consider fundamental for the future of eu-acp relations after the end of the cotonou agreement in 2020, so i voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this resolution because we believe that it does not reflect the main challenges of eu-acp relations today. we believe that the post-cotonou process should provide a fair and balanced framework between equal partners in which to discuss, among other important issues, fair trade issues with all acp countries, but bearing in mind that trade liberalisation is not in itself positive for sustainable development. i reject the fact that there is no call in the resolution for the creation of any binding instrument to detect the responsibilities of the private sector for human rights violations and the impunity of transnational companies. i also stress the importance of respecting, as stated in sdg 17.15, the sovereignty of the associated countries and that they have a democratic political space to regulate and make decisions for the dignity of their people, a principle that is not reflected in the resolution.
in writing. ‒ the current partnership agreement with the african, caribbean and pacific (acp) states (the cotonou agreement) was signed in 2000 and runs until 2020. it proposes a framework for cooperation relations focusing on three main areas: political dialogue; development cooperation and the fight against poverty; and trade cooperation and regional economic integration. the amount of financial assistance for the acp countries for the period 2014-2020 shall be eur 30 506 million. the report - which i voted for - proposes to review the partnership framework with the acp countries to ensure their adaptation to the new risks (terrorism, refugees, good governance, peace and security, climate change, sdgs), to establish joint action in global forums and to achieve better results in the objective of eradicating poverty. the report also stresses the need to ensure monitoring mechanisms with the full involvement of civil society and national parliaments; to maintain the conditionality of the agreement on the basis of respect for human rights and the rule of law; to strengthen and make operational legal procedures for the fight against corruption, and to support the parliamentary dimension of the new agreement through the acp-eu parliamentary assembly.
in writing. ‒ this report aims to set out what the relationship between the union and the african, caribbean and pacific countries should look like after 2020. it should be noted that association agreements have always had a number of negative impacts on the economies of the acp countries, which is why i believe it is essential to have a new type of partnership, which is fair and equitable, which respects the sovereignty of the countries and which promotes the development of the countries' productive capacities, protects traditional agriculture and fights land grabbing and over-exploitation, while at the same time having legal mechanisms to combat labour exploitation, modern slavery, the illicit flow of capital and the financing of terrorism and armed conflict. i think it is also important to stress the importance of ending foreign interference in the internal affairs of the acp countries, as well as the end of neo-colonial policies and the dismantling of all foreign military bases. however, this report does not propose any of these changes which i consider fundamental for the future of eu-acp relations after the end of the cotonou agreement in 2020, so i voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ in march 2016, the commission and the eeas published the results of the public consultation launched on 6 october 2015 on the future of the eu-acp partnership beyond 2020, when the cotonou agreement expires. the aim was to take stock of the agreement and to draw up proposals to make the partnership more effective. this report aims to contribute to the debate by defining parliament's priorities for future eu-acp relations. it is important to stress that the cotonou agreement is still in force, i.e. an agreement on a legally binding framework based on three pillars: political dialogue, cooperation and trade. it then examines a number of possible developments, such as further regionalisation, the edf budget, strengthening political dialogue and greater involvement of civil society and the private sector. it also stresses that the fight against poverty should remain a key objective of acp-eu cooperation, although it notes that a new agreement must be above all a political project and clearly leave behind the donor-receiver mentality.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report, convinced of the need to start planning for the future of acp-eu relations after the conclusion of the cotonou agreement between the european union and the 78 african, caribbean and pacific (acp) states for trade and assistance which will end in 2020. the eu institutions must work to ensure human rights and democracy, as well as the participation of local and regional governments in the decision-making of acp countries. we must bear in mind that 80% of the world's least developed and most neglected countries are in what we know as the acp region. this is why the european institutions must build on the achievements of the cotonou agreement in recent years, with a view to the post-2020 scenario. similarly, we must take advantage of the coincidence of the expiry of the cotonou agreement and the union's multiannual financial framework to integrate the european development fund into the general budget and improve transparency, efficiency and accountability.
in writing. ‒ the resolution on acp-eu relations beyond 2020 is in line with the cotonou agreements, which bring together the european union, its member states and the african, caribbean and pacific states. these agreements are based on three pillars: development, trade relations and political dialogue. the 'trade relations' pillar forced developing countries to lower their tariffs, exposing them to competition they could not compete with. the european development fund (edf), the financing instrument for these agreements, is also a sham: only the member states have access to it. it is a popular communication technique: to create a 'fund', a 'plan', to simulate political action when the allocated resources already exist. this was the case, for example, with the juncker plan for investment in europe or the le foll plan for agricultural aid. i therefore voted against this report which seeks to correct the present situation by strengthening the power of the european institutions and by teaching the acp countries moral lessons. but without questioning a system that has led to failure...
in writing. ‒ i voted against this resolution because we believe that it does not reflect the main challenges of eu-acp relations today. we believe that the post-cotonou process should provide a fair and balanced framework between equal partners in which to discuss, among other important issues, fair trade issues with all acp countries, but bearing in mind that trade liberalisation is not in itself positive for sustainable development. i reject the fact that there is no call in the resolution for the creation of any binding instrument to detect the responsibilities of the private sector for human rights violations and the impunity of transnational companies. i also stress the importance of respecting, as stated in sdg 17.15, the sovereignty of the associated countries and that they have a democratic political space to regulate and make decisions for the dignity of their people, a principle that is not reflected in the resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because the future of the agreement between the union and the african, caribbean and pacific group of states (acp) will expire on 29 february 2020. the agreement proposes a framework for the union's cooperation with the acp countries, which is structured around three main dimensions: political dialogue; development cooperation and the fight against poverty; and trade cooperation and regional economic integration. the report proposes to review the partnership framework with acp countries to ensure: adaptation to new risks (terrorism, refugees, good governance, peace and security, climate change, sdgs), joint action in global forums and the best results in the objective of eradicating poverty. the report stresses the need to ensure monitoring mechanisms with the full participation of civil society and national parliaments; to maintain the conditionality of the agreement on the basis of respect for human rights and the rule of law; to strengthen political dialogue to move from reactivity to prevention of political crises; to strengthen legal procedures and make them operational in the fight against corruption.

in writing. ‒ the eu has and should continue to take the lead and great responsibility with the acp. this report, calls for the 2030 agenda and the sustainable development goals (sdgs) to be placed at the centre of a new agreement, and for the creation of strong monitoring mechanisms to ensure that implementation of the agreement contributes to and promotes the sdgs. it calls for an acp-eu peer monitoring, accountability and review mechanism to scrutinise sdg implementation in member states on a regular basis. calls for the fight against, and ultimate eradication of, poverty and inequalities and the promotion of sustainable development to be the overarching objectives of acp-eu cooperation. the eu can only gain from fighting the root causes of many phenomena that affect all of us.

in writing. ‒ the report maintains the cotonou acquis, a legally binding agreement based on three pillars: political dialogue, cooperation and trade. it examines a number of possible developments, such as further regionalisation, the edf budget, strengthening political dialogue and greater involvement of civil society and the private sector. calls for the 2030 agenda and the sustainable development goals (sdgs) to be placed at the heart of a new agreement so that the fight against poverty remains a key objective of acp-eu cooperation; it reiterated its call for the edf budget to have a guaranteed delimitation of development funds to maintain the level of funding and a permanent solution for the financing of security expenditure related to eu development cooperation. it reiterates that economic association agreements constitute a basis for regional cooperation and should be instruments for development and integration. i therefore vote in favour of this report, since spain is in favour of maintaining the geographical areas of the acp and of preserving and improving the existing legal framework.

deputising for the author. – mr president, the global financial crisis brought the role played by international financial reporting standards in financial stability and growth on to the g20 and eu agendas. in particular, the rules regarding the recognition of losses incurred in the banking system. in july 2014, the international accounting standards board (iasb) issued the international financial reporting standard ifrs 9 (financial instruments), addressing some aspects of the financial crisis and its impact on the banking sector, as its key response. in early 2016, the commission referred the draft implementing measure for international financial reporting standards (financial instruments) to parliament for scrutiny. on 7 october 2016, the three-month scrutiny period for this important financial reporting standard will end. the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ) had started its scrutiny activities already well before this official referral of the measure by the commission. these activities have been conducted very thoroughly. the activities included the commissioning of four external studies on ifrs 9 and public scrutiny events during econ committee time, for example, a public hearing. in addition, the newly established ifrs permanent team conducted several meetings on this issue. the international accounting standards board, the european financial reporting advisory group, the commission and the stakeholders have been invited for an exchange of views on ifrs 9. on 7 june 2016, parliament adopted a resolution on international accounting standards evaluation and the activities of the international financial reporting standards foundation, the european financial reporting advisory group and the public interest oversight board, which also addressed some of the issues. in addition, the econ committee had already written in january 2016 a letter to the chair of the european systemic risk board (esrb) expressing its concern about the lack of reliable quantitative data assessment. the impact of the introduction of ifrs 9 on financial instability in general, and on the amount of loan loss provisioning and banks regulation capital in particular, is of especial concern to the committee. the committee requested further analysis from the esrb of the impact of ifrs 9, especially on financial stability. another letter was written by the econ committee to the commission in june 2016 addressing additional concerns. these related to possible negative effects of the implementation of ifrs 9 on crucial long-term investment and on the misalignment of the effective dates of ifrs 9 and the upcoming new insurance standard ifrs 17, which will replace the current insurance standard ifrs 4. in this regard the iasb published in september 2016 amendments to ifrs 4, addressing some concerns regarding the insurance issue. this oral question on ifrs 9 to the commission and the motion for a resolution which will be voted on on thursday, reflect the various concerns which parliament and the econ committee have brought forward during its scrutiny activities.
mr president, at the beginning of his speech, mr juncker stressed that the state of the union address was held in bratislava for the first time, and that it was important that from now on not only speeches were made but that the measures proposed by the commission were put into practice. i think that the declaration's unsalvageable nature is the last point in bratislava. the time has come to execute what we have already agreed. that is the important thing, because what the council has done so far has been to approve matters which subsequently have been ignored by the member states. this is particularly important in relation to emigration. everything has been moving towards security; everything has been moving towards preventing migrants from reaching our shores or our borders; everything has been moving towards issues that have to do with closing ourselves off to the outside. we must protect the borders, we must respond to the places of origin where refugees and migrants are generated so that they do not have to reach our shores, but we must respond internally, with solidarity, with integration and with the relocation of those who are already with us. as regards the economy, the european council has not been dealing with the economic question for a long time, but a week ago someone said that we are getting used to too little growth, for too long, for the benefit of too few. i'm not quoting anyone out of the ordinary: i'm quoting christine lagarde. yesterday the international monetary fund said that our growth next year will be lower than this year's, and that this year's will be lower than last year's. until we provide answers in terms of job creation, growth and opportunities for our citizens, all crises will have a common background: dissatisfaction with the results achieved by the union.

mr president, i have heard the council representative say that we must reduce the number of 'irregular migrants', and he has used this expression; and then mr juncker saying that the agreement between the european union and turkey is working. what's this all about? it means that the physical barriers, the police barriers, the legal barriers that we have put in place for those who are trying to flee the war, for those who are trying to survive, are working. it means that europe has abandoned them; that it does not recognize them as refugees; that it does not give them asylum, which is one of our fundamental rules. these are not the european values that we hear so much about, the values for which i am here and the values i want to defend. i've heard of trade too. the council representative says that trade always creates profits. benefits to whom? if we don't regulate that trade, what grows, the profits, they go into bank accounts that then show up in the panama papers. trade has to be regulated, and we have to have the same conditions. i was pleased that mr juncker asked for more support for our steel industry. i would also like to remind you of the agricultural producers, those who are faced with products coming from other countries which do not respect our legislation.
mr president, the council has spoken little, but it has spoken very clearly. he uses the words 'irregular migration' to tell us that he has frozen the soul of europe. there is no longer a refugee crisis. mr juncker has told us that the post-dublin era is coming, that the time of flexible solidarity is coming. unfortunately, when we plead for flexible solidarity, we are saying that we will tolerate flexible non-solidarity. mr timmermans, you have the opportunity to rebel against this. for the council, there is no such thing as aleppo, there are no bombed hospitals, there are no children who have not been to school for six years in jordan, turkey or lebanon. 108 million for the bulgarian borders, yes, and only 191 million to school syrian children in lebanon 250,000 not in school. those children from moria, those children from turkey, those children from lebanon and jordan will make us pay. if it's not out of solidarity, let's do it out of self-interest. we must rebel!
mr president, brexit has shown us that the european project is not irreversible. since then, we have been puzzled and have no common answer. some avoid answering by saying that the procedure has not yet been initiated; others try to reduce everything to the european council and return to bilateral relations; others threaten the union, or blackmail the union, with further brexits. you know why, but i don't see european politicians defending the union with the same passion as british populists defending brexit. i think the british populists are taking the political initiative. the european union is not a fact. it's still a process. it's under construction. the truth is, it's a dream that hasn't come true yet, and i ask you at what point this project stopped being exciting. the old distinction between europe and non-europe has been replaced by a distinction between europe and anti-europe. the non-europeists were discussing our solutions. the anti-europeanists argue about our values; the anti-europeanists fight our values; the anti-europeanists defend the values of the other side. you know, but there is only one way out of this crisis, which is to restore european solidarity; solidarity between the countries suffering from the refugee crisis and those that do not; solidarity between those suffering from the russian threat and those that do not; solidarity between those suffering from unemployment and those that do not; solidarity between those who are suffering from the consequences of the euro having an unfinished architecture and those that are not. brexit is the most unsound proposal in contemporary european history. anything that looks like brexit is disunity, even if it only looks like brexit from a distance. only by rebuilding solidarity will we build europe, because, whatever we call it, it is anti-european.
mr president, yesterday we had a surreal debate on greece, in which it was advocated, once again, to go further into the same policies which have led the greek people into the abyss. you continue to insist on the same road map which causes unemployment, insecurity and ruins whole countries and regions, and which forces our young people to emigrate. they threaten spain and portugal with sanctions; they ignore the outcry and the demonstrations throughout europe against the transatlantic free trade agreements and bring us back to an agreement like ceta, which contains the same anti-social logic as ttip. you are presenting the shameful treaty with turkey as a good thing, a treaty denounced by all humanitarian organizations and which has led to more and more people dying in the mediterranean: 24% more this year than last. the xenophobic policies of fortress europe are turning the mediterranean into the world's largest mass grave. who do you think can identify with this bureaucratic rights-crushing machine that you have turned the european union into? less interrail tickets and more change of policy! this is what can change europe and make people stop wanting to leave this european union. it is in our hands: let us change our policies, let us change europe.
mr president, brexit, the paralysis in the face of a common immigration policy - culminating in last week's hungarian referendum - and the rejection of the main trade agreements currently being negotiated by the european union are the key points of the debate at the next european council. and they all have one common denominator, which is also well exploited by populism, both on the left and on the right, which is a protectionist wave that is hitting the european union as a result of inequality and paralysis, of the lack of prospects due to low growth, low wages and the weakening of the social model. i therefore ask the council to use this meeting not to save one particular agreement or another, however important they may be, but to put an end to the causes that are plaguing our societies: fear, inequality and uncertainty; to put an end to inequality by increasing investment and raising wages, as the european central bank has recently called for; to also increase the tax burden on those who have the most, who inherit the most; to make a fair fiscal policy to maintain the social model. we must, as the european union, save the social model, and to do so we must also take advantage of these debates to get ahead of the fundamental issues that today cause fear and uncertainty to european citizens. only by tackling the fundamental issues, as i say, will we be able to save a vision of solidarity and a vision of the future that gives certainty to societies, based on social justice and equal opportunities.
mr president, the commission and the council are running against the clock against a loss of confidence of historic proportions and a point of no return in the european project. borders, fences, populism, referenda against integration, the visegrad group, the agreement with turkey and brexit are all a serious blow to europe's image. but the worst part is that the picture would not be complete without the scandalous conflict of interest that has emerged with former commissioner neelie kroes in the bahamas or with former president barroso at goldman sachs. but not without the threat of an unacceptable fine for spain and portugal, countries which have made immense sacrifices by imposing unthinkable cuts on impossible terms, because these fines go against the sacrifices of countries which have been euro-enthusiasts, against their most vulnerable regions - the outermost regions included - but also and above all against the very idea of europe. so before it is too late, enough, commission and presidency!

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of peru's accession to the hague convention on the civil aspects of international child abduction, because it provides greater protection and guarantees for minors. the hague convention establishes a system that allows for cooperation between contracting states to find a solution to situations of international child abduction. these cases are usually in cases of separation with parents from different countries. the convention provides that the law applicable in such cases is that of the state of residence of the child. it also establishes a system to ensure the immediate return of the child who has been abducted.
in writing. ‒ i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work done on this report on the accession of peru to the 1980 hague convention on the civil aspects of international child abduction. it's a critically important instrument. the accession of peru is good news.
in writing. ‒ the 1980 hague convention on the civil aspects of international child abduction, signed by all eu member states, is an instrument of international cooperation which authorises signatory states to resolve transnational cases concerning the custody and abduction of children by clarifying the national law applicable in cases where there is a conflict of jurisdiction between two or more national legal systems. the scope of the rule covers civil matters, applying in particular to cases of separated parents or other persons who have legal rights over the child. since the aim of the convention is to protect children in situations of legal uncertainty, it is important to get as many states as possible to sign it. although the eu has exclusive external competence in this area, the convention does not allow the participation of international actors, and the eu needs to give all its member states express authorisation to accept the participation of any new state in the convention. i have therefore voted in favour of allowing the two member states which have not yet accepted peru's accession, namely austria and romania, to do so.

in writing. ‒ the hague convention of 25 october 1980 on the civil aspects of international child abduction is a crucial instrument, which has been ratified by all eu member states. this convention establishes a system which allows the contracting states to cooperate in finding a solution to situations of international child abduction. the main problem in these cases is the bias of the legal systems of the states in favour of their own nationals. it is common for the courts of both states concerned to declare that they have jurisdiction and to award custody of the child to the parent of their respective nationality. the convention aims to resolve these situations at international level by providing that the competent courts and the applicable law are those of the state of residence of the child. the convention also establishes a system to ensure the immediate return of the abducted child.

in writing. ‒ this resolution calls on all actors at global, national and local levels, both governmental and private, to coordinate and accelerate their actions to fight malnutrition in order to meet the 2030 agenda and achieve sdg 2 on ending hunger. the report, in paragraph 12, also highlights the need to ensure access to land for all peoples as a fundamental element of food sovereignty and underlines that land grabbing poses a threat to food security and nutrition. it also called on the commission to take measures to combat land grabbing and to draw up an action plan to combat it. some amendments on gmos called for no support for gm crops, which i think is too generic, since we have to analyse their effects and consequences on a case-by-case basis and leave it to the scientific bodies to determine the potential impact on the environment, the economy or health. in the face of such biased dogmas, i call for the use of scientific reason and judgment in assessing the effects of such crops.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution on nutrition and food security which recognises the right to food as a human right. the resolution also refers to the threat to global nutrition and food security objectives posed by land grabbing in developing countries, calling for concrete measures to ensure land tenure security. finally, we also welcome the fact that the resolution emphasizes that the privatization of seeds and gmos is a threat to the food sovereignty of countries.

in writing. ‒ the first 'nutrition for growth' summit was held in london in 2013, where $23 billion and immediate action to address nutrition issues were pledged. the european parliament resolution wants to keep nutrition at the centre of the union's political agenda. in the hope of making a significant impact before the next summit in tokyo 2020, the importance of a high-level meeting on this issue is underlined with the aim of developing responses to nutrition challenges, promoting food to boost the economy at the continental level, africa loses around 11% of its gdp due to poor nutrition; curbing malnutrition, especially during the first 1,000 days of life; and realizing the vision of the decade of action on nutrition (2016-2025) launched in september during the united nations general assembly. i have therefore voted in favour of this resolution.

in writing. ‒ the establishment of a european public prosecutor's office, when there is no legal system at european level, is something on which different organisations of lawyers have expressed many doubts. we believe that, as the institution in this right-wing resolution argues, there is no guarantee of the democratic rights which people accused of a crime in the member states enjoy today. furthermore, the relationship between the public prosecutor's office and the courts of the different states, or with the security forces and bodies, is not clarified. the principle of transparency is fundamental in law, and we cannot accept a model which would deepen the deficits already existing in many countries, including spain. our model requires better articulation of the necessary coordination of the various judicial systems of the union, not the creation of structures that operate in parallel with them, which is why i have decided to vote against it.
in writing. ‒ i have decided to vote in favour of this resolution because i believe that the establishment of an independent and effective european public prosecutor's office is of great help in combating cross-border crime and is in line with greater european integration of justice systems. we also welcome the fact that the resolution calls for judicial cooperation and the classification of the system of powers and duties. i believe that a european public prosecutor's office with the necessary powers and funds is a positive step forward and that is why i am voting in favour.

in writing. ‒ resolution on the reports on the establishment of the european public prosecutor's office, eurojust and the protection of the financial interests of the union, in a context where transnational criminal networks and fraud have increased in recent years. article 86 teu provides for the possibility of establishing a european public prosecutor's office to combat crimes affecting the financial interests of the union, where eurojust has been playing a key role in coordinating the different ways of prosecuting fraud. the resolution also calls for the eu to take action to combat fraud and recover funds in a crisis such as the current one, and stresses the need to strengthen the role of eurojust and the european public prosecutor's office. i have therefore voted in favour of this resolution.

in writing. ‒ since 2012, the european commission has put forward three proposals concerning the creation of a european public prosecutor's office, the fight against fraud affecting the financial interests of the union through criminal law and the european agency for criminal justice cooperation (eurojust), respectively. since the three plans are interrelated, the commission was asked what issues remain and what the expected timetable for their adoption is. the commission has also been requested to provide information on the financial and practical implications of the new european public prosecutor's office (following the council's amendments to its document), in particular as regards the impact on eurojust's budget. finally, the commission was asked to explain the operational, organisational and administrative links between the two bodies and to provide information on the degree of involvement of national parliaments. given the need to clarify these matters, i have voted in favour.

mr president, at the beginning of september the caterpillar group announced the closure of its plant in charleroi, belgium: 2 200 employees of the factory and about 5 000 subcontractors will lose their jobs in the coming months. the decision to close the factory is quite surprising because, in the first quarter of the year, caterpillar had announced that the company was once again competitive. what's the reason for this shutdown? caterpillar has its european headquarters in switzerland, which allows it to pay 30% less tax. and this has a name, this is tax evasion. despite this, despite being a profitable company, we are witnessing a new relocation of one more company, a company that received public funds. we must urgently establish a mechanism to prohibit these predatory practices, which in the end make the workers pay the consequences.
mr president, a small sample of the state of industry in the european union this year is: caterpillar in belgium, 2 200 workers laid off; ericsson, 1 556 in sweden and 350 in spain; valladolid, lauki, closure for good and 200 jobs lost; and asturias, already, so to speak, with the scheduled closure of absolutely all the mines. we are all victims of the deindustrialization of a large part of europe, and this commission, with the support of governments that are submissive to the financial markets, tells us that it is committed to competitiveness, and i ask them: how can we be competitive if there is no productive fabric and no stability? in the face of this question, we say that reindustrialisation must be linked to new employment niches such as the sector of renewable energy strategies, the defence of the role of mining in the energy transition, the commitment to the public sector and public banking for investment and control of the economy and, above all, also the revision of free trade agreements towards countries which practice social and environmental dumping.
in writing. ‒ i abstained in this resolution because, while it contains positive elements (the improvement in the use of european funds and public procurement in support of european industry, the role of the social partners, the recognition of the importance of industrial policy, the need to reform competition policies to promote employment, etc.), it contains hardly any critical references to how european policies, from deregulation and privatisation to its aggressive foreign trade policy, are responsible for the industrial crisis europe is experiencing.
in writing. ‒ i would like to thank the negotiators of this report for the work they have done to reach a common resolution on such an important issue; it has been a tough day of negotiations. i voted in favour of this report but i do not agree that every time a company closes it should be the subject of a resolution. the tragedy of unemployment is unfortunately very visible in our society and a general resolution would have been much more objective than one focused on two companies.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution, which was initiated by the s&d group, in which the european parliament calls for the adoption of a strategy for the reindustrialisation of europe in the wake of the announcements of the closure of caterpillar plants in belgium and alstom in france, and the laying-off of thousands of workers. situations such as those in these plants reveal the need to develop a genuine european industrial policy which must be based not only on the development of investment but also on the implementation of a new competition policy and a new trade policy to curb social dumping. and they also reveal the need to be demanding of companies which, even though they are making profits, decide to close their plants, leaving thousands of workers stranded. today parliament has raised its voice to demand sanctions, such as the reimbursement of public aid or the suspension of access to certain eu programmes.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the grounds that caterpillar and alstom, despite the fact that the reduction in production costs between 2013 and 2015 made the products from these plants more attractive than those from outside the union, have decided to close their plants in order to move production to other centres with lower social and environmental protection standards than those applicable to european industry. the rail industry is the backbone of european industrialisation, directly employing 400 000 people across the union. the commission should work towards establishing a genuine long-term european industrial strategy with a view to achieving the target of 20% of gross domestic product coming from industry, as set out in the europe 2020 strategy, and to establishing a union trade policy in line with its industrial policy objectives, ensuring a level playing field for operators from inside and outside europe, thus ensuring a level playing field for all.
in writing. ‒ podemos strongly denounces the policy of relocations and mass layoffs carried out by some large companies to benefit from lax legislation on labour, environmental and safety at work guarantees, especially when these companies, as in the case of alstom and caterpillar, are leaders in their sector and record millions of profits every year. our group, the gue/ngl, drew up its own resolution in line with this position. we have also voted in favour of the joint resolution because, although we believe that it could have been more forceful in denouncing these practices, some important amendments have been incorporated into the text on unfair competition from third countries, including china, on the excessive short-term financialization of the economy, on the limited impact on employment of policies to support the union's banks and markets, or on the need to review trade and labour legislation to protect workers and subcontractors affected by these unjustified business decisions.
in writing. ‒ in trying to find agreement for a jmr, strong references to workers’ rights were watered down. moreover, the right wing not only managed to remove the workers as central, but they shaped the motion in a way which put employers and shareholders as central. we always have had, and always will have, workers, their families, and their communities at heart when we vote on motions in relation to employment and social affairs. in our opinion, there are issues around aspects such as: point 12 calls for ‘the restructuring of the major european manufacturers to be enabled in order to allow the emergence of players with sufficient critical mass to cope with international competition’. this would without doubt create an industrial policy which squeezes out cooperatives, micro businesses, and smes; point 24 looks for the market to dictate how education systems should operate: ‘underlines the importance of fostering better synergies between education systems, universities and the labour market, including exposure to the workplace and cooperation with businesses in the creation of innovative ‘clusters’’. there are many other issues with the jmr, and with some of the amendments; hence, eh bildu has abstain on supporting the jmr. this decision has as much to do with what it left out as what was put in.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution because it deals with the industrial and international trade policy aspects and focuses on the main aspects concerning workers and employment; the resolution focuses on the need to strengthen the legislative package empowering workers in decision-making related to business restructuring. in the case of caterpillar and alstom, restructuring includes redundancies and relocations due to plant closures such as caterpillar's in monkstown, northern ireland, and alstom's in cornellà, barcelona. the commission is therefore asked to draw up, after consulting the social partners, a proposal for a legislative act on information and consultation of workers for the anticipation of change and restructuring, and to submit, after consulting the social partners, a review of the approximation of the member states' legal frameworks on collective redundancies. the report also calls for the reform of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) to improve its coverage of workers directly and indirectly affected by such processes.

in writing. – i voted in favour of this resolution to support the workers of caterpillar and alstom because in the text we managed to add important green wording referring to the green economy (need for investments in energy efficiency and renewable energy, green public procurement, improved social and environmental investment criteria), to the need for stopping tax evasion through increased convergence in fiscal, social and budgetary matters, and the need for trade policy consistent with reindustrialisation objectives to preserve quality employment in the eu.
in writing. ‒ in view of the closure plans threatening caterpillar and alstom's factories in belgium, this non-legislative resolution aims to have the european commission review community legislation on mass redundancies. parliament called on the commission to consult the social partners on the effectiveness of existing legislation, in order to ensure that any corporate restructuring is carried out in a socially responsible manner and in line with both the regulations applicable at regional level and community values. the resolution also stresses the need to put in place a common industrial policy which has real impact and which also ensures the protection of european workers. based on my strong belief that european industry should be treated as what it is - a strategic asset for the competitiveness and sustainability of the union - i voted in favour of this resolution.
in writing. ‒ the report presented calls on the commission to establish a trade policy for the union which is in line with its industrial objectives and takes into account the need to safeguard european jobs and avoid relocation and further deindustrialisation. it called on the commission to ensure a level playing field for market operators inside and outside europe, allowing fair competition for all. it is very important to take into account the social and economic impacts of the closure of these plants on the regions affected, improving the understanding of the impact on employment and european industries. i am voting for this report because we must protect the areas most affected by reindustrialisation in order to move forward and be able to adapt to new economic needs.

president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, honourable members, on 26 september president santos and the leader of the farc, rodrigo londono, signed the final peace agreement at a ceremony held in cartagena de indias at which the european union was represented by the high representative’s special envoy, eamon gilmore. the signature of the peace agreement sent a message of hope after 52 years of armed conflict that has caused 8 million victims, including 260 000 deaths. in times of uncertainty and turmoil, in many regions of the world – including our neighbourhood – it reinforces our conviction that dialogue and diplomacy constitute the best means for resolving conflicts. however, last sunday, 2 october – contrary to forecasts – the colombian population rejected the final peace agreements in a referendum by a very small margin. i think we would all have welcomed a different result, but we respect the sovereign choice of the colombian people. the ‘no’ side in the referendum has defended that the government renegotiate the final agreement with the farc to get a better deal. we can all agree with president santos’s statement after the results were made public, and i quote: ‘all colombians seek peace with no exception. despite the setback, the path towards peace does not end here’. as you are aware, the peace agreement negotiated in havana is a complex agreement. it aims, not only to end a 52-year armed conflict, but also addresses its root causes, supporting rural development and attacking the problem of illicit drugs. it also includes provisions on transitional justice and the political participation of the farc, which are the two aspects most contested by the leaders of the ‘no’ campaign in the referendum held on 2 october. this is a delicate moment for columbia, as the country must now decide on the way forward. it is of great importance that, after the referendum, both the colombian government and the farc have confirmed their commitment to the ceasefire. a solution can only come from politics and from negotiations. for this reason, president santos’s decision to send the negotiators back to havana is a step in the right direction. the eu hopes that all sides – the government, the opposition and the farc – can unite in a renewed effort and continue on the path towards achieving lasting peace. columbia is one of the eu’s closest partners in latin america. our good relations and cooperation is getting deeper and deeper in many areas. we remain fully committed to this partnership. the european union will keep on supporting all efforts towards a sustainable solution and to secure a permanent end to violence. we will continue to cooperate to bring peace and prosperity to all colombians. our commitment to the peace process in colombia goes beyond symbolism. in the last weeks, we have announced two very concrete measures to support peace in colombia. first, the european council has suspended the farc from our terrorist list. this is a decision that the council has taken because of the signature of the peace agreement by the group. it concerns the choice made by the farc to bring the negotiations to a positive end, not the outcome of the referendum. after the vote, farc have not been moved away from the peace agreement they signed. on the contrary, they have confirmed their interest to find a peaceful solution. for this reason, the result of the referendum does not affect the suspension.secondly, we have announced an overall package of nearly eur 585 million to support colombia’s post-conflict and peace-building efforts. this sum includes an eu trust fund for colombia, in which 11 member states have committed contributions. this trust fund is meant to support the implementation of the agreement. so in the current situation we are not moving forward with the launch of the trust fund. the eu’s engagement in supporting peace-building in colombia will continue. the eu has sound experience in peace-building in the country, with flagship initiatives such as peace laboratories, over the past 15 years. lastly, i would like to stress that i share the concern of this parliament in ensuring the effective protection of human rights. it continues to be a priority for the eu, and we will keep on cooperating with the colombian government in this respect. this includes a strong focus on human rights defenders. too often they have been the target of threats and violence. the same goes for minorities, such as the indigenous and the descendant communities and the most vulnerable groups, which have been greatly affected by the conflict, including women and children. i would like to conclude by reiterating that the eu is determined to stand by columbia in its long-term effort in pursuit of durable and lasting peace as well as a brighter future for all colombians. i am sure that we can continue to count on the european parliament’s invaluable and active support for peace-building in colombia.

author. madam president, today we have a new opportunity to make the necessary transition to a more equitable and sustainable way of life. but let us not be deceived, because the paris agreement is totally insufficient to achieve the long-term objective that it sets itself: not to exceed two degrees of temperature increase. if we don't reduce pollution levels, the annual temperature rise will soon exceed three and a half degrees. the world's poorest people, many of whom are farmers, fishermen and herders, are being hit hardest by the rising temperatures. it is urgent that states address this issue in their climate action plans. how did you do that? for example, it is striking that this agreement does not mention industrial agriculture, one of the main causes of climate change. hunger kills 40,000 people a day, yet 60 percent of the food we produce ends up wasted. we spend 30% of all productive land to produce food that ends up in the garbage. this means the production of 3.3 billion tonnes of co2 equivalent; in other words, food waste is the third largest contributor to the world's largest producers of greenhouse gases, behind only the united states and china. this is not in the agreement. we must address the right to food and promote short-circuit agro-ecological production: this will feed the world in a sustainable and equitable way and also mitigate climate change. ladies and gentlemen, this fight is not settled by deals of additions and subtractions. the challenge is great and in it small farmers have to go from being the most vulnerable to becoming the most valuable in history. to do that, we need to refocus agricultural investment towards the needs of these small farmers. as latouche rightly says, "you cannot save the planet and pretend to save an unfair and unsustainable business". we have to choose which side we're on. we're very clear about that.
madam president, i would first of all like to congratulate commissioner arias cañete and his team on the efforts they have made over the years and have been rewarded with this great success, which marks a milestone in their mandate. yesterday, this house voted by a large majority to ratify the agreement reached in paris at the end of 2015. it is the culmination of the leadership that the european union has maintained in successive conferences of the parties and we must congratulate ourselves on that. the european union has committed itself to reducing its emissions by 20% by 2020 compared to 1999 and by 40% by 2030. the first objective is on track to be achieved and i have no doubt that we will also achieve the target we have set for 2030. for many years we have insisted on the need to reach an international agreement so that the countries responsible for emissions all contribute to the fight against climate change under conditions that are at least comparable. not all countries are equally responsible, nor do they face the same social, environmental, energy and industrial challenges. it is therefore logical that there should be solidarity mechanisms to finance investment, research and development. at the same time, a mechanism would be needed to monitor the commitments countries are making and to be able to exert some pressure if efforts are not sufficient. the agreement should have positive consequences for the reindustrialisation of the european union. i also believe that it will allow for rapid progress in renewable energy and energy efficiency in third countries. it is important to speed up further negotiations at international level so that further progress can be made in marrakesh on the paris agreement in terms of transparency, emission control, timetables and compliance.
madam president, when climate change is mentioned, we talk about it as if it were something to be avoided in the future. i'll give you a fact, a very recent fact: on an island in alaska, they recently had to vote in a referendum whether to migrate to the mainland because their island was literally being flooded by rising sea levels. this is just one more example of climate refugee populations around the world. yesterday the chairman of the people's group in this house said that yes, the climate is very important, but it was his group that tabled amendments to parliament's opinion to limit the measures in terms of economic competitiveness. the european commission, mr arias cañete, seems to be very conscious of this too, but the european investment fund has allocated 1.5 billion euros to fossil fuel infrastructure, when, according to the international scientific group ipcc, the electricity sector would not have to produce a single gram of co2 more by 2050.

first vice-president of the commission. – madam president, thank you for allowing me to present our proposal for an interinstitutional agreement on a mandatory transparency register. the register is the key instrument to shed light on lobbying activities. the current register was jointly set up by parliament and the commission in 2011. today it includes slightly over 10 000 organisations and self—employed individuals. it has even surpassed the register they operate in the united states in terms of the number of people and organisations who have registered. all registrants have agreed to adopt a common code of conduct, based on a set of ethical rules and principles, governing interactions with eu political leaders and officials. the current register remains, however, a voluntary system. if we want to fully meet citizens’ expectations for openness and accountability, we need to go further, and the three law—making institutions must act together to make sure that the rules of the register are respected by all lobbyists so that everybody can see who tries to influence the eu law—making process and who they represent. you will see that our proposal has taken on board ideas put forward by you, by the council and by the european ombudsman. the public consultation we organised led to more than 1 700 replies, the majority of which came from individual citizens who expect us to live up to the highest transparency standards. on 2 may, vice-president sylvie guillaume and i chaired a public debate in parliament, bringing together stakeholders from all over the eu. let me briefly highlight the main elements of our proposal. firstly, you need to be in the register before you can have meetings with decision-makers in the three institutions. the commission already applies this rule. not on the transparency register – no meeting. this applies to all meetings of lobbyists with commissioners, their cabinet members, the secretary—general and the dgs of the commission services. over 4 000 organisations and individuals have registered since this rule came into effect. so we now propose to apply it to meetings also of meps as well as the secretary—general, directors—general and secretaries—general of political groups in the european parliament. registration will also be a condition for speaking at committee hearings and for holding events on parliament premises. in the council we propose to apply the rule to meetings with the council secretary—general, directors—general, the ambassador of the current or incoming presidency of the council, as well as their deputies. permanent representations are of course subject to national rules on ethics, but we offer them to join the system voluntarily. last may, we made listing in the transparency register a precondition to sit on our expert groups. this important step forward is also reflected now in our proposal. secondly, we propose to clarify which activities and entities are covered by the register. we propose to keep a broad definition of lobbying activities covered by the register and to set out the exceptions in a clearer way. public authorities, including at sub—national level, and their associations who directly represent a democratic mandate are clearly excluded, for the reasons that this house and the committee of the regions have both underscored. thirdly, we propose changes to improve the quality of the data held in the register and to strengthen monitoring and effective enforcement of the rules. our proposal not only simplifies the data requirements for lobbyists, but also introduces systematic ex-ante checks on new registrations. we propose to streamline procedures with a view to finding quick, effective solutions if compliance with the code of conduct is at risk. if that is not effective, a formal investigation will be opened which can eventually lead to sanctions. those who do not play by the rules risk being temporarily suspended from interactions with the institutions or removed altogether from the register. finally, our proposal creates stronger management structures for the register and increases the resources at its disposal, subject to a commitment by all three institutions. a well-functioning register needs adequate resources, a point repeatedly stressed by this parliament and by stakeholders. we propose a stronger management structure with a management board on top of the secretariat. an agreement between the three institutions would ensure adequate resource allocation to the secretariat, as well as a right means to ensure effective redress for registrars in disputed cases. i have followed with great interest the work of sven giegold and look forward to parliament’s final report on transparency and accountability in the eu institutions. i am convinced that a mandatory register is a major step forward for transparency and accountability. let’s make it happen.
on behalf of the alde group. madam president, i am very pleased to hear you, mr timmermans, and i congratulate you on your enthusiasm at this hour. it's really remarkable. the proposal for an interinstitutional agreement on the registration of pressure groups is a step forward which we welcome. it is timely and appropriate that the european commission, our executive, respond to the needs europe has right now in terms of transparency, and of course the alde group is grateful that transparency is high on the commission's agenda. improvements in data collection should be a tangible advantage in working with the information, and efforts to clarify the definitions and the range of activities and bodies covered should also facilitate the quality and efficiency of this register. we want to thank you for increasing the resources - we want to increase the resources - so that the controls on the activity of the lobbies we seek can be effective. without sufficient means we could have, in fact, a formal but not a material requirement. i mean, if unfounded or incomplete statements can be leaked, we would be making the record worse and perverting the purpose of the record. if we take a decision such as the full achievement of this record, we must be able to make it materialise and not just be in words. i would therefore like to stress that providing sufficient financial and staff cover is absolutely essential if this transparency policy is to be coherent and effective. but let us face it, the european institutions do not enjoy much credibility these days. the scandalous news about revolving doors in the commission does not exactly help people to believe in the project. and we must not forget the most important thing: this reform will require the council to stand shoulder to shoulder and to cooperate. so far, we've been waiting for a move from you that hasn't come. the representatives of the member states must also bear their share of the responsibility. in this situation of common benefit it is in our interest to act with an integrated policy and to be efficient. we have not seen a real move from the council, but we would like to see it cooperating in good faith, soon. i would like nothing more, on behalf of my group of the liberal and democratic group for europe, than to congratulate the commission and the council on the smooth and joint action of the european institutions, if only for once.
in writing. in order to restore citizens' confidence in the legitimacy of the political, legislative and administrative processes in the union, the commission has put forward a proposal for an interinstitutional agreement to increase transparency and accountability for members of self-employed interest groups involved in the formulation and implementation of eu policies. i am pleased that, in the light of the positive experience of the transparency register established by the agreement of the european parliament and the european commission of 16 april 2014, the three institutions have agreed on the need to establish a mandatory transparency register for interest representatives. this establishes the principle that no meeting with policy makers can be held without prior registration and clarifies the activities and data to be entered, increasing quality control. i hope that the new interinstitutional agreement will come into force as soon as possible and i welcome the fact that local and regional authorities have been excluded from the scope of the new agreement, as we had requested.

member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, the european union is founded on law and relies on law to ensure that its policies and priorities are realised in the member states. the effective application, implementation and enforcement of the law is hence a high political priority for this commission. often, it is not the lack of eu legislation that is the source of problems; it is rather the lack of its effective application and redress for citizens. that is why the european commission takes its role as guardian of the treaties so seriously. if member states are breaching eu law, then we need to take steps to address this weakness and, where necessary, we may need to launch formal infringement proceedings before the european court of justice. this unique and essential role of the commission, overseeing the effective and efficient application of union law in the member states, is an integral part of the better regulation agenda. through the annual reports on monitoring the application of eu law, the commission reports on its work and explains how it exercises its powers as guardian of the treaties. i want to thank members for the preparatory work on the 2014 annual report. the commission very much appreciates parliament’s increased interest in implementation issues. the annual report reviews the member states’ performance on key aspects of the application of union law from the point of detection of a possible infringement to the pursuit of the case before the court. we detect problems in the application of law ourselves, but we also rely on petitions and complaints from citizens and business. hence your petitions committee plays an important role. once we have identified a problem we can work with member states to solve it through a system called the eu pilot. if the problem cannot be solved we indicate infringement procedures. the treaty allows us to request financial fines if member states are late in transposition and we have not hesitated to do so. let me summarise the main findings of the 2014 report. citizens and businesses remain active in detecting and bringing forward violations of eu law. more than 3 500 complaints were received from citizens and businesses during the year 2014. we are determined to work with the member states in improving compliance at an early stage and resolving potential infringements quickly, to the benefit of citizens and businesses. about 75% of alleged infringements were resolved at an early stage. as a result, the overall number of formal infringement procedures has continued to decrease. however, there is still a significant gap between what is in the eu rulebook and the rules applied on the ground. how can we improve the implementation of eu law more generally? i strongly believe that we should strengthen our partnership with the member states and support them in their task of timely transposition and correct application of the law. as part of our better regulation efforts, we deploy a wide array of tools, ranging from preventive measures and early problem solving to proactive monitoring and targeted enforcement. you have raised a number of other issues in the hautala report, to which i would like to respond. i note your increased interest as regards parliament’s role in monitoring the implementation of eu law. without prejudice to democratic control by parliament, the commission oversees the application of eu law under the control of the court of justice of the european union. the infringement procedure has a specific bilateral nature. it is conducted solely between the commission and the concerned member state. this being said, the commission will continue to provide parliament with information on infringement proceedings in accordance with its commitments in the current framework agreement. this includes more detailed information, if requested, on specific infringement cases. as regards parliament’s proactive contribution in monitoring the compliance with eu law of accession countries and countries with association agreements, i want to emphasise that the commission will continue its regular reporting on the progress made by these countries. i note your call for a legislative proposal on administrative procedures under article 298 of the treaty. i would like to stress that the commission has already created a strong framework to protect complainants. its code of good administrative behaviour and the communication on relations with the complainant offer a number of guarantees that safeguard complainants’ rights throughout the entire procedure. these include the right to be informed about any decision on his or her complaint, the right to be heard, prior notice before closing a case, and a timeframe for a final decision on complaints. against this background, the commission does not find it necessary to regulate this matter in a legislative act based on article 298 of the treaty. concerning the transparency of infringement procedures, and especially that of eu pilot, the commission is fully dedicated to delivering on the commitments stipulated in the framework agreement. i wish to underline that from the initial phase of infringement procedures, the commission must also respect confidentiality vis-à-vis the member states, as recognised by the court of justice. this means that transparency and access to a specific file has to be limited while the commission conducts its initial investigation in order to clarify the often complex legal and factual background of the cases. i also note your increased interest in better regulation. our aim is to legislate in an open, transparent way, using the best evidence available and valuable stakeholder inputs. we also focus on ways to support implementation and are pleased to see that parliament supports all these efforts.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on economic and monetary affairs. – madam president, every year the commission launches 1 000 new infringement procedures against eu member states due to the bad transposition of eu law. since 2009 there have been 1 000 procedures per year. this is the real sickness of the eu project. this is what is killing the eu and creating political disaffection everywhere: the inability of the eu to maintain the rule of law within its member states. poland and hungary do not want to accept refugees, italy does not want to apply european rules to solve the banking crisis, france is allowed not to comply with the public deficit rules because it is france – as president juncker, incredibly, stated publicly – and spain does not comply with the late payment directive. spain is unwilling to force the big spanish multinationals to pay smes’ bills at 30 days and allows them to pay at 250 days without sanction. in spain one million workers of sovereign smes lost their jobs during the crisis due to these bad practices on the part of big multinationals allowed by the central government. so, in my opinion, bad transposition of eu law, is the silent crisis of the european project. countries in the south of europe, which are the worst offenders regarding eu law, are the countries which most need to implement it to modernise their economy. so, finally, if europe is not able to oblige member states to comply with eu law, citizens will abandon all hope in the european project.
madam president, the implementation of european legislation is not a technical debate, it is a political debate. we all know that european legislation is applied and controlled when it favours big business, but is forgotten when it seeks to protect european workers. it is enough to see how the commission and the european union are busy enforcing every measure of austerity, of cuts, of loss of rights, and deliberately forget to act in the social field. i will give two examples: social dumping. we have directives to require the control of cabotage and letterbox companies in road transport, but the european union does not control their application; on the other hand, when you try to apply a minimum wage to hauliers, you rush to invoke european regulations and prevent the recognition of such a fundamental right as 'equal employment, equal pay'. another example is labour law. you are happy to intervene in the labour market, for example in spanish; two reforms have been imposed, but while you are preaching cuts and others are implementing them, you forget that european legislation is also based on the principle of non-discrimination, and it is the court of justice of the european union that must intervene to recognise the rights of temporary and temporary workers. but for a law to be just, what must be done is above all to apply it for the benefit of all parties, and not as it is being done.
madam president, today we are discussing the 32nd report on the application of european union law in 2014. the commission's priority must be to ensure that this european union law is applied. it will mean that the european union is functioning properly. there are three actors. on the one hand, the commission: it is its responsibility to play an active role in improving the application, observance and enforcement of these rules; but also, the role of parliament, specifically with the committee on petitions, to be able to monitor that this functioning is real - citizens report to us in the committee on petitions cases of malfunctioning and, therefore, it is very useful information for the commission - and, finally, the role of the member states. there is no doubt that conflicts and infringement procedures have decreased - as we have seen in this report - because the structured dialogue between the member states and the commission itself has borne fruit. in fact, the pilot project of this dialogue has resulted in many proceedings not reaching the infringement file, and we think that is good news. it is true that almost all the infringements concern services, the environment, transport and all that is development, but it is equally true that if we make every effort on the part of all the actors - the member states too, to ensure that the transpositions of the directives are carried out in a timely manner, and also if we set deadlines for transpositions that are really objective, we will achieve that citizens really trust the european institutions, and that gap between what we do in the institutions and what citizens receive is shortened, and they believe in us much more.

i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, first of all, our condemnation of the violence, the massacres and the repression of the people in sudan. secondly, to ask the european union to make a real effort to stop the plundering of africa. because we know that behind these conflicts, usually, there are always the interests of the big corporations and the western powers, whether it is land grabbing, whether it is oil, whether it is minerals and, also, logically, behind it is the business of selling arms. that is why, madam commissioner, we ask you to take all the measures in your power to stop the plundering of africa, to stop the sale of arms, and to enable the peoples of africa to develop, to improve the quality of life of their inhabitants and to achieve peace.
author. mr. president, the andy hall case is a joke. how is it possible that a worker rights defender, a citizen of the european union, was sentenced to three years' probation and a large fine just for having collaborated in a report by a non-governmental organisation exposing human rights violations at the thai plant of the natural fruit company? gentlemen, this is a disgrace. so is the human rights situation in thailand. in this regard, human rights watch notes that the human and labour rights of migrant workers, especially from myanmar, cambodia and laos, are violated with impunity on a regular and permissible basis. the european union needs to promote binding systems to ensure that businesses respect human rights. a crucial step in this direction is to support the creation of a binding treaty on transnational corporations and human rights within the united nations. last year our representative tried to block the process: i was there and i saw it. we hope this year will not be like this. in the meantime, what you can do is support our amendments to this resolution.
mr president, we believe that moving from a model in which bank losses are not recorded until they explode to a model in which banks must record, at every moment, their real exposure to financial risks is a positive step, because it will allow a clearer picture of the state of health of banks and will help to avoid excess risk, or what that means, that the people pay for the financial misdeeds. i have abstained on parliament's proposal because it attempts to dilute the effectiveness of these new standards, ifrs 9, by avoiding references to possible regulatory capture and by generally promoting a negative view of the new rules, as if financial speculation had to be encouraged in order to promote economic growth. we cannot understand the enormous instability of the present economic system, the power of big capital over the states and over the workers themselves, not to mention the growing expansion of financial services and the speculative motive.
in writing. ‒ i supported the decision to grant non-objection to the update of international financial reporting standards (ifrs 9) in order to increase transparency in the wake of the financial crisis. i also agree that the commission should be asked to take steps to apply the standards to the insurance sector for long-term investments.
in writing. ‒ i consider, as the report says, that ifrs 9 is an important accounting advance, by moving from a 'loss incurred' model to one of 'expected loss', i.e. by forcing the financial system to provision immediately for risks that are incurred, instead of keeping them under the carpet until the bubble bursts. i have abstained because this motion seeks to postpone its entry into force and to water down some of its proposals in order to protect european finances over and above the general interest.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report, although it contains a number of positive elements which i supported. however, it does not question the process of setting standards as such, which has a number of shortcomings, especially in relation to democratic control and oversight. in addition, the new ifrs 9 has not fully addressed the issues related to the procyclical nature and could have some negative consequences, in particular for smaller financial institutions (e.g. cooperative banks) that use the standardised approach for access to credit risk. while the report does address some of these concerns, i fundamentally question the appropriateness of the new rule, as well as the process by which it has been drafted.

in writing. ‒ the global financial crisis brought to the g-20 and the eu's attention the importance of international financial reporting standards (ifrss), in particular those relating to loss recognition in the banking system, for financial stability and growth. as a key response to some aspects of the financial crisis and its impact on the banking sector, the international accounting standards board (iasb) adopted ifrs 9 financial instruments. considering that the prudential principle should be the fundamental guiding principle of all accounting standards and that ifrs 9 financial instruments constitutes one of the main responses of the ncas to the financial crisis, the european parliament hereby recognises that ifrs 9 is an improvement on ias 39 and points to the importance of fully understanding the interaction between ifrs 9 and other regulatory requirements. it also called on the commission to propose appropriate measures in the prudential framework before the end of 2017 and to ensure that ifrs 9 supports the union's long-term investment strategy. i therefore considered it appropriate to vote in favour of the text.
