in writing. ‒ i voted clearly against this resolution, as i flatly reject the qualification of terrorists as opposition, the same al-qaida terrorists who attacked 11m in spain. in addition, the report 'welcomes the review of the eu restrictive measures against syria' and argues that the union 'should consider all available options, including a no-fly zone', even though this measure is widely criticised and has been described as illegal. we are also opposed to sanctions as a coercive measure, since they affect the peoples in particular. the report also argues that the main culprit in the conflict and the massacres of the syrian people is the "assad regime" backed by "russia and iran", when it is precisely the syrian government and the russian federation that are more effective in fighting terrorism than europe says it feels threatened by. the report also completely ignores the syrian government's efforts to achieve a just peace through dialogue, as shown by the creation of the committee of reconciliation and the reform of the constitution. peace will only come through dialogue between the government and the non-terrorist opposition.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on the situation in syria. i subscribe to the conclusions adopted and support the hr/vp mogherini in her dealings with the key actors in the conflict. cooperation with all of them is essential to achieve a lasting and balanced political solution to the conflict. i therefore support the text in its condemnation of the indiscriminate suffering of innocent civilians as a result of bombing and other military actions, as well as the denial of humanitarian aid, and i consider that the use of incendiary and other munitions against civilian targets and infrastructure amounts to a war crime.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this resolution on the situation in syria, considering it to be biased and warmongering, calling for the establishment of a no-fly zone, and failing to address elements which i consider necessary to achieve a just and lasting peace, such as a call for a ceasefire by all parties, for effective and constructive dialogue between all parties to the conflict 'without external interference', and for fair solutions in line with human rights regarding refugees.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution on the situation in syria to condemn the humanitarian emergency in the country and especially in cities such as aleppo. the continuing fighting and shelling is worsening the already dire situation of the civilians who are directly affected by it. the international community must do everything possible to put an end to this situation. this is unacceptable.
in writing. ‒ the situation in syria is dramatic and complex. the complex reality on the ground, the difficult international circumstances and the endless atrocities committed, make it necessary to support efforts for a new ceasefire and to ensure that humanitarian aid reaches those in need. the union must play a greater role and support the efforts of the united nations, on the idea that there can only be a political solution, where all the parties are convinced that it is the only way forward. the european union must remain committed to achieving a lasting solution to the conflict in syria, where a final military solution cannot be expected. you must continue and continue your diplomatic and humanitarian work. i have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ 33% of european women have suffered some form of violence, family, sexual, harassment at work, etc. a society where half of the population, women, are at continuous risk of being victims of gender-based violence requires us all to take responsibility and work to eliminate this injustice. i voted in favour of this resolution because i believe it is very important that the union should accede to the istanbul convention as soon as possible, because it is the first legally binding instrument adopted and is the most far-reaching international treaty to address violence against women as a serious violation of human rights. it is therefore also urgent that all member states ratify it. a legal act of the union is also necessary to allow the legislative, preventive and corrective measures of the istanbul convention to become part of the legal systems of the member states, so that the court of justice of the union has the power to give judgment. i am aware that legislation is not the only solution but it is the way to engage and compel public institutions in the fight against violence against women.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution, as it calls on the union and its member states to accede to the istanbul convention on preventing and combating violence against women. unfortunately, although all the member states of the union have signed it, only 14 have ratified it. this is very serious, because a determined reaction from the union is essential to put an end to gender-based violence once and for all. every second counts, and we need the european commission and the states to agree and take this problem seriously with real political will. the convention recognises violence against women as a violation of human rights and is undoubtedly a major step forward which the union must take to take political and judicial action against gender-based violence, in the face of the very serious facts such as those in spain where 39 women have been killed by their abusers so far this year.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because it calls for the union's ratification and early accession to the convention. i also want to express my displeasure with the council, because the negotiations are not progressing at the same pace as in the other european institutions. the union's accession will ensure a coherent european regulatory framework to prevent and combat violence against women and gender-based violence. the union must have a binding instrument at its disposal once and for all to crack down on this kind of violence. it is incomprehensible that countries such as germany or the united kingdom, whose women heads of government are among the most powerful on the planet, should still not ratify the convention. the convention recognises violence against women as a violation of human rights and a form of discrimination, holding states accountable if they do not respond appropriately. it is the first instrument of a binding nature at european level on violence against women and domestic violence.
in writing. ‒ 25 november has been designated by the united nations as the international day for the elimination of violence against women, which remains a widespread phenomenon in the union. the council of europe's istanbul convention is the most comprehensive international agreement to date that addresses the issue of violence against women and girls and gender-based violence from a holistic perspective. in march 2016, the commission proposed that the union accede to the istanbul convention. all the member states of the union have signed it, but only 14 have ratified it. the oral question to the council and the commission, as well as to the jrc, aims to speed up accession to the convention and to convince those member states which have not ratified it as soon as possible, to know the state of negotiations on signature, the actions taken by the presidency to speed up signature, the time needed to complete the union's accession to the convention and the role of the european parliament in monitoring it. i consider these to be positive proposals and have therefore voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution, as it calls on the union and its member states to accede to the istanbul convention on preventing and combating violence against women. unfortunately, although all the member states of the union have signed it, only 14 have ratified it. this is very serious, because a determined reaction from the union is essential to put an end to gender-based violence once and for all. every second counts, and we need the european commission and the states to agree and take this problem seriously with real political will. the convention recognises violence against women as a violation of human rights and is undoubtedly a major step forward which the union must take to take political and judicial action against gender-based violence, in the face of the very serious facts such as those in spain where 39 women have been killed by their abusers so far this year.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution, considering that, as recognised by the treaties and the charter of fundamental rights, gender equality is a core value of the union. however, violence against women and gender-based violence remain widespread in the union, and this is something we cannot tolerate in any way. it is therefore essential that the union accede to the istanbul convention, the first legally binding instrument on preventing and combating violence against women at international level.
in writing. ‒ 33% of european women have suffered some form of violence, family, sexual, harassment at work, etc. a society where half of the population, women, are at continuous risk of being victims of gender-based violence requires us all to take responsibility and work to eliminate this injustice. i voted in favour of this resolution because i believe it is very important that the union should accede to the istanbul convention as soon as possible, because it is the first legally binding instrument adopted and is the most far-reaching international treaty to address violence against women as a serious violation of human rights. it is therefore also urgent that all member states ratify it. a legal act of the union is also necessary to allow the legislative, preventive and corrective measures of the istanbul convention to become part of the legal systems of the member states, so that the court of justice of the union has the power to give judgment. i am aware that legislation is not the only solution but it is the way to engage and compel public institutions in the fight against violence against women.

in writing. ‒ the fight to eliminate violence against women and domestic violence is a noble and unyielding goal rooted in fundamental european values, starting with the right to equality between men and women. i have therefore supported this resolution on the union's accession to the istanbul convention. at the same time, i regret that this resolution does not mention at any point that men also suffer from domestic violence, as the preamble to the convention does. although women suffer more domestic violence than men - which may warrant special legal treatment - evidence from international surveys and studies on domestic violence does not, however, support the view that men and boys are forgotten or not sufficiently recognised by our legislation.
in writing. ‒ 25 november has been designated by the united nations as the international day for the elimination of violence against women, which remains a widespread phenomenon in the union. the council of europe's istanbul convention is the most comprehensive international agreement to date that addresses the issue of violence against women and girls and gender-based violence from a holistic perspective. in march 2016, the commission proposed that the union accede to the istanbul convention. all the member states of the union have signed it, but only 14 have ratified it. the oral question to the council and the commission, as well as to the jrc, aims to speed up accession to the convention and to convince those member states which have not ratified it as soon as possible, to know the state of negotiations on signature, the actions taken by the presidency to speed up signature, the time needed to complete the union's accession to the convention and the role of the european parliament in monitoring it. i consider these to be positive proposals and have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ 25 november has been designated by the united nations as the international day for the elimination of violence against women, which remains a widespread phenomenon in the union. the council of europe's istanbul convention is the most comprehensive international agreement to date that addresses the issue of violence against women and girls and gender-based violence from a holistic perspective. in march 2016, the commission proposed that the union accede to the istanbul convention. all the member states of the union have signed it, but only 14 have ratified it. the oral question to the council and the commission, as well as to the jrc, aims to speed up accession to the convention and to convince those member states which have not ratified it as soon as possible, to know the state of negotiations on signature, the actions taken by the presidency to speed up signature, the time needed to complete the union's accession to the convention and the role of the european parliament in monitoring it. i consider these to be positive proposals and have therefore voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ the istanbul convention recognises violence against women as a violation of human rights and as a form of discrimination. on this basis, its objectives are to prevent this type of violence, protect the victims, bring legal action against the aggressors and raise awareness throughout society. it considers physical, psychological and sexual violence to be serious crimes and introduces a number of new criminal offences, such as female genital mutilation or harassment. the european parliament is here to support the commission's proposal for the union's accession to the convention in its entirety, which was launched in march. although the signature of the parties was opened in 2011, latvia, the czech republic and bulgaria have not yet complied with it, and more than ten member states have not yet ratified it. in recognition of the importance of this convention, which is the first binding instrument at european level on violence against women, and the most far-reaching international treaty to address this grave violation of human rights, i voted in favour of this text.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution, as it calls on the union and its member states to accede to the istanbul convention on preventing and combating violence against women. unfortunately, although all the member states of the union have signed it, only 14 have ratified it. this is very serious, because a determined reaction from the union is essential to put an end to gender-based violence once and for all. every second counts, and we need the european commission and the states to agree and take this problem seriously with real political will. the convention recognises violence against women as a violation of human rights and is undoubtedly a major step forward which the union must take to take political and judicial action against gender-based violence, in the face of the very serious facts such as those in spain where 39 women have been killed by their abusers so far this year.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the activities of the european ombudsman's office. the office is the institution which brings citizens closer to the institutions, and its work on transparency in the union is fundamental. mrs o'really works tirelessly to correct the mistakes made by the institutions, to improve the service and the responses given to european society. as a socialist, i believe that we must ensure that the european institutions are transparent and function properly.
in writing. ‒ this report commends the current european ombudsman for her work during 2015, in which in addition to responding to more than 17 000 european citizens who reported cases of maladministration, she decided to open eight strategic investigations into key issues such as the lack of transparency in the atci negotiations, whistleblower protection, revolving doors, limitations to the european citizens' initiative or the violation of fundamental human rights by frontex's forced deportations. the report expresses concern about the flagrant revolving door case, headed by former european commission president josé manuel durão barroso, now a consultant at goldman sachs. i therefore consider this to be a positive report calling for more transparency and i join with it in supporting the work of the european ombudsman.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on the activities of the european ombudsman in 2015. the report contains many of the positive actions of mrs emilly o'reilly, in which we highlight the importance of an institution such as the ombudsman, which looks after the interests of citizens and safeguards their rights against possible misconduct by administrations. it is also important to note that spain is by far the country with the highest number of complaints to the ombudsman and the committee on petitions. the report also takes stock of efforts to achieve greater transparency in the negotiations of the atci and ceta, in decision-making, public access to documents; the problem of revolving doors, violations of rights by frontex and member states in the migrant crisis, or the rights of disadvantaged minority groups; and urges it to safeguard the rights of citizens and the interests of good administration with regard to the ecb and the european commission. for this reason, although improvement is possible, we welcome the ombudsman's accountability and the report that has been presented on how to improve her activities.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this report on the ombudsman's activity 2015. mrs o'reilly's work is outstanding, and she is tireless in her efforts to improve the quality of the service that the european administration provides to citizens. maximum transparency is a key element in building trust and good administration, as highlighted by the high percentage of complaints received in relation to transparency, higher than in any other matter.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which gives a positive assessment of the work carried out by the european ombudsman during 2015 to improve the quality of the service provided by the european administration to citizens. the report particularly praises the ombudsman's work in the area of transparency, highlighting the high percentage of complaints received in relation to it (22,4%), higher than in any other case, and her continued efforts to increase transparency in the negotiations on the atci, by submitting proposals to the commission to this end. in particular, it welcomes the fact that the commission has subsequently published a number of documents and included transparency as one of the three pillars of its new trade strategy. the ombudsman's office carried out investigations into fundamental rights, in particular into unlawful returns. it also investigated how member states spend money on projects funded by union funds, specifically projects related to people with disabilities.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because of the important role the ombudsman plays in helping citizens, businesses and associations who are faced with problems of maladministration by an eu institution. similarly, the ombudsman should ensure that any conflict of interest within the union is addressed, as this is key to ensuring the credibility of the union. in this respect, it is necessary to revise the code of conduct applicable to commissioners, to extend the period of incompatibility from 18 months to 2 years for former commissioners and to 3 years for former presidents.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this own-initiative report setting out parliament's position on the commission's action plan to establish a single european vat area. vat is a tax that raises about €1 billion a year, and is partly an own resource of the union. however, vat fraud is estimated at eur 170 billion, of which eur 50 billion is due to crossborder fraud. the various attempts to update the system have failed because of the lack of consensus in the council. the report is generally positive, calling for greater harmonisation, while the proposal for the vat reverse charge mechanism between businessmen, which the s&d group and the spanish socialists do not share, has been reduced. the psoe also hopes that the next revision of the vat directive will include the proposal to create a european list of products and services that can benefit from reduced and super-reduced rates.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report, despite its many positive points, because it is not possible to talk about vat without understanding its social and redistributive implications. the report contains numerous measures that should be considered for the next vat proposal in 2017; from the signaling of prioritizing the investigation of large fraudsters, to many points on the simplification absolutely necessary for smes. however, the report makes a clear omission of the social impact of this tax, even in a context where the commission 'recommends' that more be raised through this type of indirect tax. this absence is inexplicable when we are debating our political position on it and that is why, despite a good number of logical proposals, i have had to vote against this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because i think it completely ignores the social dimension and impact of indirect taxation. i think that simplification of the rules was necessary, but that does not justify the reduction in rates on luxury goods and other goods. finally, the report ignores the role that multinationals have played in fostering downward tax competition.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on a definitive vat system and the fight against vat fraud. the current system was conceived in 1993 as a transitional system and the commission's communication of april 2016 on action on vat ends the long wait to move towards a single vat area by indicating that the time for reforms has finally come. it's been too many years and it's time to have a performance that goes that way.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report, bearing in mind that the commission presented on 7 april 2016 a communication on a vat action plan, which puts an end to the long wait to move towards a single european vat area. the collection of around eur 1 trillion in 2014 makes vat an important source of financing for the union, as it amounts to 7% of gdp. however, the current vat system was already vulnerable to fraud from the outset, which the commission estimates to amount to some eur 170 billion per year, of which at least eur 50 billion is due exclusively to crossborder fraud. the commission states in its action plan that it will present a legislative proposal to establish a definitive vat system based on the principle of taxation in the country of destination of goods and services. we must put an end to the 23 years of the current system as a temporary measure and make way for a more effective and common system.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because i think it completely ignores the social dimension and impact of indirect taxation. i think that simplification of the rules was necessary, but that does not justify the reduction in rates on luxury goods and other goods. finally, the report ignores the role that multinationals have played in fostering downward tax competition.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report, despite its many positive points, because it is not possible to talk about vat without understanding its social and redistributive implications. the report contains numerous measures that should be considered for the next vat proposal in 2017; from the signaling of prioritizing the investigation of large fraudsters, to many points on the simplification absolutely necessary for smes. however, the report makes a clear omission of the social impact of this tax, even in a context where the commission 'recommends' that more be raised through this type of indirect tax. this absence is inexplicable when we are debating our political position on it and that is why, despite a good number of logical proposals, i have had to vote against this report.

in writing. ‒ this report welcomes the commission's intention to propose a definitive vat system by 2017 that is simple, fair, efficient, robust and less susceptible to fraud. its most ambitious objective is to implement a definitive system of taxation at destination (i.e. in the member state where the consumption of goods or services takes place). it attaches considerable value to the vat action plan presented by the commission in april, which in turn attaches great importance to strengthening existing administrative cooperation and increasing the efficiency of national tax administrations. in order to improve the fight against fraud and modernise the present community vat system, which was introduced provisionally in 1993, i voted in favour of this report.

i was happy to support this report. i am pleased that the protection of other living creatures on this planet is on the ep's agenda alongside the protection of human rights and democracy, and that this report protects wildlife and opposes the illegal and unethical trade in endangered wildlife. i am very pleased that we are clearly criticising trophy hunting, which has led to the critical endangerment of some species, and i am also very pleased that we have adopted support for a total ban on the ivory trade in this text. i think the eu should be a leader in these ethical issues, and it's good that this material has been accepted. now we must do everything possible to ensure that the prohibitions are not only declared but also actually enforced. we must therefore fight against smugglers and poachers.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution, which welcomes the eu action plan against wildlife trafficking, presented by the commission, as it underlines the need for coordinated action to address the causes of wildlife trafficking, to effectively implement and enforce existing rules, and to strengthen global cooperation between countries of origin, transit and destination. the resolution also calls on the commission, the member states, the european external action service, europol and eurojust to recognise that wildlife crime is a serious and growing threat and to address it as urgently as possible. it also stressed the need for global and coordinated approaches across the different policy areas. since the text also urges greater protection for areas designated as vulnerable marine ecosystems, marine areas of ecological or biological importance and natura 2000 sites, i voted in favour, as it supports essential measures to protect and combat wildlife trafficking.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on the eu action plan against wildlife trafficking. wildlife trafficking has become a multibillion-dollar criminal industry run by criminal groups. the union's action plan proposes a series of measures which i consider essential and which seek the cooperation of the actors involved (within and outside the union). the report calls on member states to increase the level of surveillance in this respect. in addition to supporting proposals in the report as an appropriate starting point and human resources needed for the implementation of the plan or monitoring of the evaluation of the mechanisms carried out by the states, we also support those that came out of the envi committee and the gue/ngl shadow committee, such as introducing a point on the import of hunting trophies, ivory, and the participation of ngos and civil society in this process.
in writing. ‒ i would like to thank mrs bearder for her work on this report on the eu action plan against wildlife trafficking. it calls, inter alia, for a total and immediate european-wide ban on the trade in, export or re-export from the union and to destinations outside the union of ivory, including pre-convention ivory, and rhino horn, and for the establishment of a mechanism to assess the need for similar restrictions for other endangered species.
in writing. ‒ illegal trafficking in species is a phenomenon whose scale has increased considerably in recent years. poaching has reached unprecedented levels for some species, such as elephants, rhinoceroses, sharks, tigers, great apes, turtles, pangolins, and corals, and their populations are declining alarmingly. the negative effects of this activity are not limited to biodiversity, but also affect economic growth, law enforcement and, in some regions, political stability because of the financing of militias with these activities. in order to combat these criminal activities, i have supported this action plan (2016-2020) based on three pillars: prevention, implementation and cooperation, taking as a starting point that the main legal instrument at international level and at the level of the union itself is the cites convention on international trade in endangered species of wild fauna and flora. the plan provides an overview of what member states and the commission can do, setting out a comprehensive set of measures for the institutions to take to meet the challenge of halting the rapid decline of some of the world's most valuable and prized species.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report, considering that wildlife trafficking is a serious and growing threat, not only to the survival of many species of flora and fauna, but also to the rule of law, human rights and, most importantly, the very survival of the world's ecosystems. the action plan is part of the union's response to the united nations 2030 agenda for sustainable development and in particular to sustainable development goal 15, which calls for immediate action to end poaching and trafficking of protected species and to address the demand and supply of illegal wildlife products. from 2016 to 2020, the action plan will strengthen the union's role in the global fight against wildlife trafficking through a number of priorities: prevention, enforcement and cooperation, as well as the recognition of the union as a destination market and point of origin and transit for wildlife products.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the parliament's report on the action plan presented by the european commission because it calls on the union and each member state to address wildlife crime with the utmost political urgency. it stresses the need for a structured and coordinated approach across all policy areas, including trade, development, foreign affairs and justice and home affairs. it sets out a series of measures to tackle the root causes of poverty, to make implementation and enforcement more effective and to strengthen a global partnership. only by improving the means of cooperation between all stakeholders, in order to achieve better and more effective implementation and enforcement of existing tools and policies, can a real reduction in wildlife trafficking be achieved. the union and the member states have a shared responsibility to meet the challenge of halting the rapid decline of some of the world's most valuable and prized species. in doing so, biodiversity is preserved for future generations.

in writing. ‒ this eu action plan is made up of 32 broad-based measures designed to improve cooperation between different actors, make more effective use of existing tools and policies and strengthen synergies between them so that wildlife trafficking can be tackled globally. the problem of poaching and trafficking generates annual profits of between 8 and 20 billion euros, making it one of the most lucrative organised illicit activities in the world. these practices have a disastrous effect on biodiversity and threaten the survival of some species such as elephants, rhinos, great apes and tigers. moreover, especially in some regions of africa, they constitute an incentive for corruption and therefore have a certain negative impact on their potential for economic development. in support of those measures which strengthen the mechanisms of control, coordination and cooperation at the border and which provide technical support to the countries of origin in the framework of international programmes, i thought it appropriate to vote in favour of this text.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because i believe that the sharing economy, which is the focus of the report, is not a new opportunity but a label that distracts from the changes in the sectors concerned. the technological opportunity offered by new technological developments should not be confused with their use to make work in the sector concerned more precarious and to circumvent existing fiscal and social obligations, for example in transport: a reality that should not be hidden or disguised.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this own-initiative report because it makes a number of recommendations for transport smes to benefit from the potential offered by new forms of the sharing economy. it also highlights the need to fill several of the gaps in eu legislation, especially in tax and social matters, which are being used to allow some companies, even if they are small at the moment, to escape national regulation in such important matters as social security, consumer rights, quality of service and safety. support for innovation in the transport sector and for more efficient transport initiatives that enable smes to benefit from new technologies. however, i do not agree with deregulation and "anything goes" to provide a cheaper service at the expense of workers' rights, corporate taxation and transport safety. i shall therefore be attentive to the measures announced by the european commission for next year.
in writing. ‒ i have decided to vote against this report because i believe that it does not take a sufficiently firm position on the risks posed by the uncontrolled emergence of certain digital platforms in the transport sector. i understand that the emergence of new operators on the market should not undermine the rights of existing operators, nor the ability of the competent public authorities to define their mobility strategies.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report, bearing in mind that small transport companies are particularly difficult to assess, since their profiles vary widely depending on the mode of transport, the country, the type of service provided and the competitive structure of the market in which they operate. thanks to their better knowledge of the local market, their greater proximity to the customer and often their agility and capacity for innovation, small businesses improve the transport of individual passengers, especially in areas further away from large urban areas. these companies need to take advantage of the digital transition and respond in an environmentally friendly way to the growing mobility needs. however, from the union's institutions, we must accelerate efforts to launch the single european transport area to help create a more competitive and efficient sector.

in writing. ‒ i voted against this motion for a resolution on the political situation in belarus, which was not supported by our group in this parliament, because i believe that, even if i agree with some of the points relating to the protection of human rights and civil liberties, the resolution raises issues which imply changes in the national legislation of that country, which is a clear interference by the union and does not resolve the issues raised by the resolution itself.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution on the situation in belarus, but i voted in the adjournment vote on amendment no 3 by the epr group, which i supported. i think that the policy of the belarusian government to use special forces to interfere in the internal affairs of civil society organisations, including those representing national minorities, such as the independent ngo union of poles of belarus, must be strongly condemned.
in writing. ‒ belarus has resumed the execution of death sentences, being the only european country to do so. there are already 4 convictions in 2016 and 400 since 1991, the date of its independence. this continued implementation contradicts the state's stated intention to introduce a moratorium on the use of the death penalty, a commitment that belarus had made to the union and in response to the universal periodic report of the un human rights council. in september, osce observers noted clear efforts to resolve problems in the electoral process: for the first time since 2000, the opposition won two seats out of 110. however, a large number of recommendations of the council of europe and of the osce itself have not been implemented. electoral reform is needed as part of a broader process of democratisation. belarus must move towards the total abolition of the death penalty. there is a systematic violation by the belarusian state of the right to life, as well as the right to independent legal counsel. i have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because it exposes the current situation in belarus, which has resumed the execution of death sentences. this application contradicts the state's stated intention to introduce a moratorium on the use of the death penalty. this is a commitment that belarus had made to the union and in response to the un human rights council's universal periodic report. belarus is the only european country to apply capital punishment, and it should introduce a moratorium while moving towards total abolition. human rights organizations denounce the widespread use of torture and medical treatment to force defendants into self-incrimination, without access to a lawyer. it is described that there is a systematic violation of the right to an independent defence. the families of the condemned are put under great stress: they are not informed of the date of execution; the bodies are not handed over to them. the burial places of the executed are kept secret.

in writing. ‒ the presentation of this motion for a resolution is preceded by the good example of last year's adoption of a similar resolution by the european parliament following the presidential elections in belarus. in this case, the motion responds to the observations made after the parliamentary elections, which took place on 12 september. the text expresses the community's concern at the irregularities noted by independent international observers and calls on the belarusian authorities to take action to bring about electoral reform and to rehabilitate all released political prisoners, fully restoring their rights. it also urged belarus to sign the international moratorium on the death penalty and called on its authorities to respect democratic principles, human rights and fundamental freedoms. i therefore consider it appropriate to vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ this resolution on belarus is a direct intervention in the country's internal affairs, which constitutes a violation of the basic principles of international law, by calling for political and financial support from the independent opposition, the media and belarusian civil society. the european parliament has also called for the eu to take action to combat terrorism and to ensure that the eu is able to take action against terrorism. it is necessary to recognise the sovereignty and independence of countries in order to define the political, economic and social system which best responds to the interests and aspirations of their people. i also regret that the potential of belarus is not being used to overcome the confrontation between russia, ukraine and the union, but that the logic of confrontation with our neighbouring countries is being continued. that is why i voted against this resolution.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, access to sustainable energy is one of the targets of the united nations' sustainable development goals, and this is because access to it is a key element in the achievement of people's basic rights. energy poverty is a global problem. it is a disease which affects 1.2 billion people in the developed world, including 11 per cent of the population in europe, according to the commission. in spain, more than five million people are cold in winter; the electricity bill has risen by 73% in eight years; and, according to the academy of environmental sciences, more people die each year from energy poverty than from traffic accidents. in europe, we see that energy poverty is the result of deregulation of a strategic sector that has been left to the unlimited greed of the private sector. that is why we must learn from our own experience and not prescribe in africa the measures that have brought europe to this tragedy. in order to ensure access to energy it is essential that the state maintains its political space to regulate and ensure effective access to energy for all citizens. so instruments like budget support and encouraging public investment are the ways to overcome energy poverty in developing countries, not to increase the role of the private sector through blended finance, because we will be exporting an energy model that is proving inefficient and, moreover, indecent.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, i was at cop 22 last week, and we clearly recalled at this climate change summit that access to energy is central to the countries of the south, especially considering that a billion people right now - and half of them in africa - do not have access to energy. but we're not talking about just any kind of access to any kind of energy here, because we know perfectly well that there are types of energy that we can't afford right now, both for poverty reduction and for fighting climate change. and here we are talking, for example, about large projects, large infrastructures, land grabbing and also, for example, monoculture agrofuels: these mean displacement of people, populations; they mean violations of human rights, more poverty, more armed conflict. if we talk about access to energy in the countries of the south, we have to talk above all about access to energy that is sustainable; to energy that is clean; to energy that fights for social justice; that fights for climate justice; that fights to meet people's basic needs; and, also, that fights for human rights, starting with women, who are really the first to suffer from climate change. that said, we are happy with this resolution, because what it does is also talk about a different kind of energy: energy that is decentralized; energy that is small-scale, off the grid. i am referring to energy that is really adapted to the needs of these populations, especially in africa. i would also like to return to two important points. one is funding, and here we are quite critical of the tools of cooperation between the private and public sectors, because experience teaches us that most of these funds go mainly to large projects, large infrastructure that is not at all sustainable. on the other hand, we would also like these funds, at least if there is a public-private relationship, to be funds in line with the sustainable development goals and in line with the paris climate agreements. we also agree on another point: we must divest as soon as possible of all fossil fuels, and that money should be put as soon as possible into the fight against climate change and, moreover, in favour of the objectives of sustainable development. finally, i would like to end by recalling a sentence from this resolution: that policies to combat climate change must be sustainable and must above all be consistent with trade policies; or rather, we must have consistency between agreements such as ceta and agreements such as the paris agreement. and i would like this to be the general tone of all european union policies. i hope that this resolution and what you have said, mr mimica, will be the keynote of all policies, whether those of this resolution or the economic policies of the european union.
mr president, we welcome the fact that the resolution we are debating is promoting european development policies to combat energy poverty in the impoverished countries, but the truth is that this is of little use as long as the european union's current economic and trade policies are maintained. it is useless to continue exporting the european model of turning a basic need - access to energy - into a business and leaving a strategic sector such as energy in private and european hands. we have, for example, what happened in peru: the gas available to peruvians was cut in favour of the export of the resource by multinationals, such as repsol, which get a better price on the international market. this is how european companies operate around the world. we are not in the european union to give lectures on practically anything, but less so on fighting energy poverty. without going any further, last week an 81-year-old woman died in reus, catalonia, because her flat was set on fire by the fire of some candles, because her electricity had been cut off two months ago. in the european union, the number of people suffering from energy poverty is increasing. for example, in spain, since 2008, the number of people in energy poverty has tripled and is now close to five million people, while energy companies have astronomical profits. the three big spanish electricity companies have earned more than 56 billion during the worst years of the crisis: while electricity receipts rose by more than 52%, the electricity companies made 20 million euros a day in profits. they were trading our rights here and plundering the natural resources in impoverished countries. and clearly, as in all types of poverty, women are the ones who are hit the hardest. of the 1.3 billion people in the world without access to electricity, 70 percent are women. it is the result of combining the politics of plunder with oppression.
mr president, we believe that access to energy for people in developing countries is a priority. energy is a right and as necessary to life as water; therefore, it is a global responsibility to ensure it. for many years, the developing countries have been asked to follow the path that the west has followed for centuries: to start their development with a highly polluting industrial era and low labour rights, and gradually to become more technologically advanced and, in principle, less co2-emitting industries and societies. and i say in principle, because the west is still far from this goal. fortunately, the consensus is that we need to transition directly to fair and low-emission developed societies globally, to meet international goals, such as the paris agreement, which set the goal of avoiding global temperature rise above two degrees. it is therefore universal justice and climate justice that developed countries collaborate in the development of the global south, ensuring, among others, access to energy through clean and renewable sources, but also providing tools for adaptation to climate change. the opportunity to do so was marrakech and it has been missed. the developed countries do not want to accept and constantly dilute the shared but differentiated responsibility. and this should not be an invitation to open the door to multinationals and the private sector. a clear example is the effect of biofuels or hydroelectric plants in latin america. multinationals are taking advantage of the renewables boom to violate human rights, as is happening in brazil and central america with hydroelectric dams. in the region of baixo iguazu in brazil, the subsidiaries of iberdrola, a company based in my country, spain, have evicted more than 1 000 families from their land, with no alternative. the protests of these families against this situation were met with police brutality and tear gas, no matter if they were adults or children. energy is not renewable, ladies and gentlemen, if it is stained with blood.
president-in-office of the council. – mr president, today it is my pleasure to attend the european parliament’s debate on the general budget of the eu for the financial year 2017. on behalf of the council, i would like to welcome the positive outcome reached by the conciliation committee in the early hours of 17 november after long and sometimes difficult discussions between, but also within, our respective institutions. we have been able to establish a realistic budget providing, on the one hand, the necessary appropriations to cover the needs expected in 2017 but leaving, on the other hand, sufficient margins to cope with unforeseen situations in the course of next year. i would like to underline the constructive atmosphere during our budgetary negotiations. the agreement on the 2017 budget could only be reached due to the readiness for compromise on both sides of the table, with tremendous help from the commission. thanks to the excellent teamwork, professional attitudes, mutual trust and europeanism, we have managed to avoid another crisis, which our citizens would certainly not have understood – and rightly so. parliament and the council share the same two main priorities for the financial year 2017: to respond to the ongoing migration, refugee and security crisis, and to boost innovation, growth and employment in europe. in the union budget for 2017 we have been able to translate these priorities into concrete figures. almost eur 6 billion will be available for tackling migration issues within the union, for dealing with its root causes and improving living conditions in our neighbourhood, and for reinforcing security in europe and at its external borders. this amount corresponds to an increase of more than 11% compared to the budget of the previous year. furthermore, more than eur 21 billion was agreed for programmes and projects supporting competitiveness for growth and jobs, which translates into an increase of approximately 12% if compared to 2016. successful programmes such as erasmus+ are even increased by 19%, and the european fund for strategic investments will see an increase of 25%. these figures are proof of our joint objective. both parliament and the council want to make europe a better and safer place to live, and to create training and job opportunities, notably for our young people. at the same time, the union budget agreed for 2017 is a responsible compromise in these times of economic and financial crisis, which have led inter alia to major constraints on national budgets. let me underline the importance of our joint agreement on reducing the number of staff in all the institutions, bodies and agencies by 5% by 2017. this signal is of the utmost importance for european citizens, especially in times when anti-establishment political parties are gaining stronger support across europe. the package agreed by the conciliation committee includes a number of joint statements, and the council strongly supports these statements and is fully committed to honouring them. after the successful outcome reached by the conciliation committee on 17 november, the council formally approved the joint text on 28 november, and i am glad to inform you that no member state voted against the compromise reached between our institutions. parliament’s approval of the joint text tomorrow would allow the adoption of the general budget for the financial year 2017 within the deadline foreseen by the treaty. for the first time, as was already mentioned by mr arthuis, for the first time since the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, two consecutive annual budgetary procedures will have then been completed successfully in conciliation without having recourse to a new draft budget to be submitted by the commission and a second round of negotiations. this outcome is also remarkable, as we had an additional challenge this year linked to the mid-term review or revision of the multiannual financial framework. due to the political momentum, the mff revision has been a high priority, both for this parliament as well as for the council. just in the following item on today’s agenda, and state secretary ivan korčok will be clear here on the next steps which are necessary to finalise the mff revision. concerning the eu budget 2017, i would like to thank the chair of the committee on budgets, jean arthuis, and the two rapporteurs, jens geier and indrek tarand – especially for your constructive approach, jean, jens and indrek – during the whole annual budgetary procedure, for your openness to compromise and for the positive atmosphere. i would like to thank all the other colleagues from parliament who during the long and stressful hours on the council’s premises showed patience and a strong spirit of compromise. finally, i would like to thank vice-president kristalina georgieva for facilitating our negotiations. without your support, it would have been far more difficult, if not even impossible, to reach a balanced and timely agreement. i wish you all the best in your future position, and i can say that you will be very much missed here.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, thank you very much for this opportunity to lead you through the process where the slovak presidency was engaged in the council to explore possibilities on amendment to the multiannual financial framework. i would like to lead you through, but we agreed with vice-president kristalina georgieva that she will explain more in detail the components of the package that the council is proposing. instead, i will share with you a few political remarks, but i would like to start by saying that the slovak presidency has a clear guidance for the process of review/revision of the multiannual financial framework, and that was given by the mmf regulation agreed in 2013. i would like to quote what was written there, namely that the review shall, as appropriate, be accompanied by a legislative proposal for the revision of the mmf regulation. so that was a clear guidance for us. i would like to say that we started in the council the work on mmf review/revision with a political debate, so this was not for us, mr president, a technical exercise. on the contrary, we knew that we needed to have a frank and open political debate where we should ensure consensus, or an opinion, on whether the financial perspective, as agreed back in 2013, corresponds to new challenges both outside of the eu and inside the eu, and whether we have sufficient flexibility to react to unforeseen circumstances or events. so these two objectives were at the forefront of our effort. number one: whether we need more in terms of financial resources, and to ensure more flexibility. i can say that the outcome of this political debate that we have had under our leadership in the council was, yes, the council recognised that the events outside of the union and internal challenges in fact require additional resources, and that we need more flexibility to react swiftly to the challenges that i have referred to. so on that basis the commission has proposed, in mid-september this year, a review and revision of the financial perspective that we have agreed in 2013. the second point that i wanted to make is about the process. this was important. of course the substance matters, but the process this time was extremely important. we all know, both parliament and the council and the commission, that we have been working in a framework given by special legislative procedure. nevertheless, we in the council knew that parliament has well-defined expectations when it comes to the need to revise the financial perspective; we were aware of the resolution that you have adopted, and that is why, in spite of this special legislative procedure, we, together with the commission, have engaged in a very open dialogue with you, with parliament. i more flexibility, so i think it is to your credit and your merit that it is included in this package. thirdly, as i said, i will not go into details. i would like to kindly ask kristalina to lead you through, but i would like to say that this package, when it comes to resources, is giving a chance to mobilise more than eur 6 billion to be allocated for the most outstanding priorities until the end of this financial perspective. two, i would like to say that 85% of these additional resources represent fresh money. redeployment is part of it, but it was needed, because you know that the resources of the member states are limited – they are scarce – so redeployment is a legitimate part of it. but 85% of additional resources represent fresh money, and this fresh money will be used in the most pressing challenges, starting with migration, with security, with youth unemployment. and when i speak about youth unemployment, i think that is not an issue of everyday practice that the council has difficult times, and we need to react swiftly to the events outside of the union and inside the eu, and therefore i would just remind you that what the council has agreed on is increasing the vice-president of the commission. – mr president, it is indeed very satisfying that this time, when i talk about the mid-term process, i will no longer use the word ‘review’. i will talk about mid—term revision, because the proposal we have in front of us is a proposal for revision. indeed a lot has been done – also in informal consultations with parliament – to move us towards a place where the job of providing resources to our citizens for the remaining period is well done. i do, of course, fully recognise that there are aspects of this where parliament does not feel completely satisfied. i realise that there will be opportunities today to debate, and perhaps to continue after today. but let me outline the key elements in this broad agreement that the council has proposed. first, a very important element is what we would call top-ups – in other words, additional financial resources towards our top priorities. the total of these additional resources is significant – eur 5.1 billion – of which eur 3.9 billion is for migration and security and eur 1.2 billion for the youth employment initiative. i do recognise that, while it is below what parliament recommended, the proposal is above the original commission proposal, which was for eur 1 billion. we also have to put on record that for heading 1a the council’s broad agreement falls behind the commission proposal and even further behind parliament’s proposal. the council has requested that these top-ups be financed from redeployments within heading 1a. we think that there should be more flexibility regarding redeployments. we accept the fact that we have to squeeze the budget for priorities, but there has to be more flexibility, and they anyway need to be decided in the course of the annual budget procedures. i think that there is some room here for a pragmatic compromise solution that fully respects the prerogatives of the budgetary authority. it is not for the commission but for the council, the budgetary authorities and the parliament to decide, but there may be some space here to reach a pragmatic outcome. the second – and actually the most difficult and therefore the most valuable – part of this package is on flexibility. why? because any amendment of the mff regulation requires unanimity. it requires all members of the council to agree. in that sense i genuinely congratulate the slovak presidency for guiding the council towards that broad agreement on flexibility. what are we talking about? we are talking about sizeable increases in flexibility in terms both of commitments and payments. in very simple terms, if there is no agreement on this proposal – if it falls apart – we will have no funds available under the flexibility instrument in 2017, and that is the eur 740 million that otherwise would be available. secondly, over the years 2017—2020 we would have additional availabilities for special instruments amounting to a bare minimum of eur 1.3 billion. it would definitely be more than eur 1.3 billion. why? because we are calculating only one year of what is left over from the european globalisation fund and european union solidarity fund. it is very unlikely that in the other years there would be nothing left over based on historical evidence, but we have taken a very conservative approach to count only what we are certain would be available. this is critical for us in terms of building flexibilities as, without an agreement, the possibility to use the margins left under the ceilings in the previous financial year for financing additional measures via the global margin for commitments would end next year. if we want to continue, we will have to have unanimously agreed revision. last but not least, the council has agreed to raise the global margin for payments available in 2019 and 2020 when we know that demand for payments will be highest by a total of eur 6 billion at current prices. the council has also agreed to settle in a very pragmatic and positive way the issue of the disputed eur 350 million in payment appropriations which arose in 2014 in relation to the mobilisation of eur 2.8 billion from the contingency margin to reduce the backlog of payments. so, from that perspective, what we see is a chance to expand flexibility that is pretty much exhausted as a result of the crises that have been pressuring us. in conclusion, we have a very valuable opportunity to revise the mff and give us more space. it is a matter of accepting our responsibilities – all of us – to make sure that we have that space to do what is necessary. from the commission side, we would be happy to facilitate further discussions. we believe that we have all been putting our best foot forward in terms of bringing what we believe is right and to end this calendar year knowing that in the future we have more money and more space to do what is necessary.

mr president, this revision of the multiannual financial framework is unfortunately turning into a missed opportunity. we came from a very inflexible financial framework, and above all, a very inadequate one, a framework which was not adapted to the needs of the current emergency we are living in and which requires new investment. and in this sense, it has been decided to do nothing; nothing to provide us with more budget to deal with the social crisis. on the contrary, it has decided to increase the externalization of borders, in violation of the international right to asylum for refugees, as is being done with turkey. we live in a time of urgency and exceptionalism, but unfortunately we have stingy accountants. if the challenge is to have a budgetary framework sufficient for the european union to respond to the needs of the people, you are going in the opposite direction. for the 2017 budget, which we discussed earlier, and for this financial framework, we need a 180-degree turn in budgetary policy to allow, on the one hand, to respond to humanitarian and social emergencies and, on the other, a change in the production model to deal with climate change.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i am deeply touched. we do have a critical task to complete. i heard many voices expressing the wish that it is completed before the end of this year. this is very wise, because we do need to be able to predict how we are going to approach the remaining time of this multi—year financial perspective, and we do need to have the certainty for funds that are going to be absolutely essential for our work to be done. just to give you one example: we have agreed that it is critical for the european union to better protect its external borders. for that reason we have proposed the creation of a new agency, the border and coast guard agency. when we look into the future of implementation, we of course count on having the space to fund it, not only in 2017 – for which we do now have the money – but also in 2018, 2019 and 2020. or when we think about how critical it is to address the needs of young people to have jobs and to be able to benefit from education, it is not good enough to know that we have boosted these funds for 2017. we do need predictability for 2018, 2019 and 2020. so, in that sense, reaching an agreement that allows us to provide these funds in the future so that the money will be there for multi—year programmes of that significance, i believe in my heart of hearts means that we have to find a space for an agreement that allows us to have this predictability. secondly, i agree with those who said that we cannot resolve everything with flexibility. that is very true but, if we have more flexibility in the budget, we can respond when unexpected events occur. i would remind us all that we have generated three times more money to deal with migration and refugees inside europe and in their countries of origin because of the flexibility that parliament demanded as part of the agreement for the mff. but we are now coming close to exhausting the reserves we have had in terms of flexibility. therefore we ought to build more and expand it further. third, is this really fresh money? yes it is, because we are taking money from the margins and we are allocating it predictably. you might say that the margins are part of the mff. yes and no because, if we do not make a commitment and if we do not expand the global margin for commitment and make it available in future years, there will be no commitments to demand further payments from the budget. in fact eur 5.1 billion extra is eur 5.1 billion extra. it would have not been there without that revision. is it true that we are facing more demands than we have resources? yes; since 2012, every year we have been struggling to cope with the demands on the eu budget. however, we also need to be honest with ourselves. unanimity is required to go above the ceilings, and this unanimity is not being met. it is quite simply not there. should we continue – and i look at the parliament – to advocate for the needs of european programmes? yes. maybe that moment will come when this unanimity to go above and beyond the ceilings is there, but it is not there today. if we do not tell ourselves the truth, we will not be able to do what we are here for, namely to serve our people. it is as simple as that: to make sure that everything is done to get the resources to them in a predictable and secure manner. do i have regrets? yes. i thought we had come up with a very good proposal to create a crisis reserve using the commitments. we put it forward, we lobbied for it and we argued for it, but neither net payers nor net recipients liked it. they didn’t like it. they didn’t accept it – and, yes, i am looking at mrs thomas, who wants to have a second bite of this particular apple, bon appétit, hein? but i think, if i am to respond to what people have been saying, that we should continue to work – of course we will continue to work. the work is done only when it is done. i think, with goodwill and determination, the work will be done. we will play our part as sincerely as we have been doing up to now.
thank you very much, mrs georgieva. we wish him well.

member of the commission. – madam president, as you know, parliament and the commission have been working side by side on internet governance issues in support of the multi—stakeholder model for many years. both institutions actively supported the completion of the iana transitions, as well as the extension of the internet governance forum (igf) mandate, which was part of the successful outcome of the review of the world summit on the information society one year ago in december 2015. recently a historical milestone for internet governance was finally achieved. the iana contract has expired. as of 1 october 2016, the multi-stakeholder community is responsible for the overview of the iana functions. in parallel, a series of improvements in economic accountability have come into force. this is a major step in making internet governance truly global and i warmly welcome it. parliament, our member states and the commission have long called for the globalisation of the iana functions. we have all worked together with the rest of the global multi—stakeholder community for it to happen. indeed the european input into this process has been substantial. however, the transition is not only the end of a process. it is, much more importantly, the beginning of a new phase. the multi-stakeholder model will now be put to the test. it is now up to all of us to live up to our new responsibilities. my message to you is that it is even more relevant now for europe to have a strong presence and voice in international discussions. while the united states has stepped back from its previous role, the continued threat from more authoritarian countries means that the eu must remain vigilant and play an even bigger role in the stewardship of the internet and defence of the multi-stakeholder model. next will be the internet governance forum in mexico. it is a very good sign of parliament’s engagement that, as i understand it, 18 meps will be participating in this global meeting. now that the igf’s mandate has been extended, the challenge is to make it even more relevant and helpful for the whole multi—stakeholder internet community, which will face an ever—changing technological landscape. the internet of today is very different from the internet we will have in 10 years’ time. europe can, and should, be a more active and powerful player in internet governance in line with the importance of the internet for the european economy and society. the role of the internet and digital has never been so high on the political agenda. in europe we are working hard to deliver on the digital single market. a fundamental building block for our success is ensuring that the internet continues to function in a reliable and stable way and its governance is balanced, inclusive and transparent. i look foward to your contributions.

commissioner for human rights. i would also like to stress the importance for the governance of the country of our now completed csdp missions in the police and military fields, namely eupol and eusec. i wanted to emphasise this commitment in the drc, even though the political situation has led us to re-examine the usefulness of our partnership. today, the only way to ensure stability in the drc is to guarantee a democratic transition for the first time in its history. a clear easing of the situation could be achieved if president kabila confirmed unambiguously that he would respect the term limits and that the current constitution would remain in force during the transitional period, without amendment. the constitutional deadline can only be waived on the basis of a truly inclusive agreement, which can lead to a peaceful transition period that is as short as possible. the european union has therefore supported a dialogue framework facilitated by the african union. the political agreement reached on 18 october may not, however, meet these expectations. the risk of violence on december 19 is high, especially after the bloody crackdown on september 19 and 20, which left more than 50 dead on the streets of kinshasa. a report by the united nations office for human rights clearly points to the responsibility of the state security apparatus. together with other international partners, we have called for an independent investigation into these events. since the council conclusions of 23 may and 17 october, which were also in line with parliament's resolution of march, the european union has stressed the individual responsibility of those responsible for the institutions responsible for justice and security to act in strict compliance with the rule of law and human rights. unfortunately, the crackdown on dissidents and members of civil society, including largely unjustified arrests, the closure or jamming of radio broadcasts, including rfi, has continued in recent weeks. the council will announce its decision on the first restrictive measures in the coming days. but our work will not stop there. first, we will continue to fully support the efforts of the congolese bishops' conference to make the political agreement more robust and inclusive. we call on both the government and the opposition to cooperate constructively in this regard. the european union also calls on the new government to respect human rights and fundamental freedoms and to ensure security without repression. the european union also commits itself to working with its partners to strengthen the electoral cycle, and in particular the electoral commission. an electoral commission that enjoys neither the confidence of congolese actors nor that of its partners will not be able to fulfil this role. only in such a context, and on the basis of a truly inclusive agreement, can the european union consider providing financial support for the elections. the european union will continue to consult closely with the region, the african union and the drc's neighbours. i have spoken with several of these representatives recently, and i know that they share the same concern and the same goals for a democratic and peaceful transition. finally, the role of the un security council and monusco will remain crucial. we encourage the government to engage more in effective collaboration on the ground between the drc armed forces and monusco. the democratic republic of congo has perhaps a special connection with europe. it is our history, it is our interest in the stability of the whole great lakes region, it is the relations between our peoples that are at stake. this country has seen violence that cannot be forgotten. only a return to dialogue and compromise can prevent further violence. the people of the drc simply want to be involved in the future of their country. only a true democracy can meet this demand. the future of the democratic republic of congo is inseparable from that of the whole region and the continent as a whole.
i would like to begin by condemning the repression in the democratic republic of congo of peaceful demonstrations and of people who are fighting for their political rights, and also condemning the european union's responsibility for the plundering of the natural resources of the democratic republic of congo. we call for the immediate and unconditional release of all those arbitrarily detained, and for respect for freedom of expression, assembly and demonstration. we call for an end to all violence and violation of human rights, an end to the mass rape of women as a weapon of war and an end to the recruitment of children. we call on the european union to put an end to the exploitation of resources and to allow the country to develop on the basis of them. we also call for increased support in the form of donations to meet the urgent needs of the population. we also call for an international inquiry to investigate allegations of collusion between the structural adjustment plans, the financial support of the international financial institutions... in writing. ‒ relations between the european union and the republic of the marshall islands are governed by the association agreement between the members of the african, caribbean and pacific group of states, of the one part, and the union and its member states, of the other part, the so-called cotonou agreement. the signed agreement provides for visa-free travel for citizens of the union and citizens of the republic of the marshall islands when travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a period of 90 days in any 180-day period. the visa waiver covers all categories (holders of ordinary, diplomatic, service, official or special passports) travelling for any reason other than the pursuit of a paid activity. the agreement signed provides for a deepening of relations between the union and the republic of the marshall islands. the agreement could also have positive effects by simplifying travel conditions for entrepreneurs and facilitating investment and tourism. i have therefore voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the recommendation providing for a visa-free travel regime for citizens of the union and marshall islands for a maximum period of 90 days. this is an important agreement in terms of its political significance in the framework of the cotonou agreement, as well as being a supplementary means of strengthening economic and cultural relations and intensifying political dialogue, including human rights and fundamental freedoms.

in writing. ‒ the european union solidarity fund is a tool to respond to natural disasters that directly affect the lives of people, the natural environment or the economy of a given region, and in particular to support public authorities in their emergency and recovery operations. since its creation, it has mobilised a total of eur 3.8 billion in more than 70 disasters in 24 member states and accession countries. i voted in favour of the report because it responds to the observation that natural disasters have increased in number, severity and intensity and supports measures aimed at improving the mechanisms of operation of the instrument (simplifying procedures, gaining agility, raising the threshold for advance payments and increasing transparency) and at improving the capacities of the member states in relation to the prevention and management of disasters and emergencies.
in writing. ‒ i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report on the evaluation of the european union solidarity fund which i supported. this fund has been a very important source of funding for local and regional government, mitigating the consequences of natural disasters occurring across the european continent, ranging from earthquakes or forest fires to floods, and has been a demonstration of european solidarity with the affected regions. the fund is also one of the most concrete and tangible representations to citizens of the support that the union can provide to local communities.
in writing. ‒ the european union solidarity fund (eusf) was set up to respond to major natural disasters and to provide european solidarity to the disaster-stricken regions of europe. it was established in response to the major floods in the summer of 2002 in central europe. since then, it has been used in 72 disasters of many different types, such as floods, forest fires, earthquakes, storms, and droughts. 24 european countries have been helped with over eur 3.8 billion. in view of the use of the eusf in its early years and the commission's specific situation report on the eusf, i have supported this own-initiative report which addresses the three specific aspects of improving the management of the fund: rapid reaction, prevention and complementarity with the cohesion funds; and transparency and cooperation between the different levels of decision-making.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the grounds that the eusf can help member states when the total direct damage caused by a natural disaster exceeds eur 3 billion or 0.6% of the country's gross national income (gni). although it is impossible to foresee all emergencies, the management of their consequences can always be improved. we must avoid situations where victims feel abandoned between the emergency response and the arrival of eusf funds, so speed in mobilising those funds is of the utmost importance.
