madam president, i consider the issue of human rights and democracy to be a very important agenda for the european union. it's also a whole series of points where we're talking about the state of human rights and democracy in individual countries around the world. i agree with most of the report. however, in the end i did not support it and abstained because there are also points in the report which are, in short, very politically volatile, and on which we do not have a unanimous opinion here in the european parliament. it is a pity that there are things in this recapitulative report which may have led me to conclude that i could not support the report, even though i agree with the absolute majority. these are things like trying to push for a uniform asylum system or to speed up the relocation process and so on. we know very well that this is a subject which divides this house and european politics. i therefore state that this is the reason why i did not endorse the report, although i agree with the principles of monitoring human rights and democracy in the world.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because, in the face of an increasingly critical global situation in respect for human rights, parliament is sending a strong message that the union must remain firm in its promotion and defence of human rights, through all its external policies. especially in times of insecurity and crisis, the union must be true to the fundamental values which inspire it. in this sense, the socialists have succeeded in introducing into the text a clear call for effective protection of the rights of refugees and asylum seekers - because we believe that europe has not lived up to its commitments in managing the arrival of hundreds of thousands of people entitled to protection - and for consistent and long-term solutions to the migration phenomenon in accordance with respect for human rights. we are also deeply concerned by the continuing shrinking space for civil society in many countries - with a serious deterioration in fundamental freedoms of association and expression - often under the pretext of the fight against terrorism, and we also call for improvements in the mechanisms for protecting human rights defenders and activists.
in writing. i voted against because the annual report on human rights calls for greater european military integration and improved readiness and flexibility of the european armed forces, to enable them to respond to threats and cases of serious human rights violations, which is a total nonsense; that is, it aims to increase the guarantees of fundamental rights through increased security and defence. an excuse to justify the increase in military capabilities.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it is very balanced and comprehensive.
in writing. ‒ the international community has been unable to stop the armed conflict and killings beyond its borders, and to support democratic processes that have prevented the displacement of thousands of refugees and the death of thousands of people during the annual period covered by this report. the european guidelines on human rights seem to us to be insufficient and the union's policies have been complicit in the most serious humanitarian crisis of recent decades. i have not found any defence of social rights in this report, but i have found articles which use the defence of human rights as a strategy for commercial penetration into third countries. voluntary principles for the control of multinationals are not enough. i am obviously against further european military integration. if we really want to work to maintain consistency with the defence of human rights, as advocated in this report, we must firmly confront xenophobic reactions, rethink our trade policies, and not allow the entry of people without rights into our territory. in the interests of the rights of all and of our duty to defend them, i have abstained on this report.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this annual report on human rights and democracy in the world and the eu's policy on the matter. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on his work. i also supported the amendment calling for the fundamental rights of the people of western sahara to be respected and for the release of all political prisoners from western sahara and for access to the territories to be granted to members of parliament, independent observers, ngos and the press. it also calls for a just and lasting solution to the conflict based on the saharawi people in accordance with the relevant un resolutions.
in writing. ‒i voted in favour of this report because, in the face of an increasingly critical global situation in respect for human rights, parliament is sending a strong message that the union must remain firm in its promotion and defence of human rights, through all its external policies. especially in times of insecurity and crisis, the union must be true to the fundamental values which inspire it. in this sense, the socialists have succeeded in introducing into the text a clear call for effective protection of the rights of refugees and asylum seekers - because we believe that europe has not lived up to its commitments in managing the arrival of hundreds of thousands of people entitled to protection - and for consistent and long-term solutions to the migration phenomenon in accordance with respect for human rights. we are also deeply concerned by the continuing shrinking space for civil society in many countries - with a serious deterioration in fundamental freedoms of association and expression - often under the pretext of the fight against terrorism, and we also call for improvements in the mechanisms for protecting human rights defenders and activists.

in writing. ‒ i voted against because the annual report on human rights calls for greater european military integration and improved readiness and flexibility of the european armed forces, ‒ to enable them to respond to threats and cases of serious human rights violations, ‒ which is a total contradiction; that is, it aims to increase the guarantees of fundamental rights through increased security and defence. an excuse to justify the increase in military capabilities. this partial and reductionist view of the concept of protecting the human rights of the population ignores the impact and importance of economic and political measures for the protection of the social and economic rights of citizens. it is also intrusive and aims to emulate the interventionist us policy of policing the world, as it underlines the need to consolidate in international law the concept of 'responsibility to protect' and to give the union the possibility to 'lead meaningful initiatives and actions to protect civilians, even when they are under threat from their own state'.
in writing. the international community has been unable to stop the armed conflict and killings beyond its borders, and to support democratic processes that have prevented the displacement of thousands of refugees and the deaths of thousands of people during the year period covered by this report. the european guidelines on human rights seem to us to be insufficient and the union's policies have been complicit in the most serious humanitarian crisis of recent decades. i have not found any defence of social rights in this report, but i have found articles which use the defence of human rights as a strategy for commercial penetration into third countries. voluntary principles for the control of multinationals are not enough. i am obviously against further european military integration. if we really want to work to maintain consistency with the defence of human rights, as advocated in this report, we must firmly confront xenophobic reactions, rethink our trade policies, and not allow the entry of people without rights into our territory. in the interests of the rights of all and of our duty to defend them, i have abstained on this report.

in writing. – i voted in favour of this report as it presents a sobering picture of the current situation regarding human rights: promotion and protection of human rights is under threat worldwide and the universality of rights is being challenged; civil society space is shrinking globally, and human rights defenders, notably on indigenous peoples’ rights and environmental rights, are increasingly subjected to violence and harassment.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament's opinion on the thematic issues set out in the annual report on human rights and democracy in the world 2015, presented by the council on 20 june. the report describes the efforts made by the union over the past year to promote the universality of human rights. it highlights, for example, the adoption and progress in the implementation of the new action plan on human rights and democracy 2015-2019, which underlines the community's priorities for the next five years. the report indicates that the union's external policy focused over the past year on promoting priorities such as the empowerment of human rights defenders and civil society, freedom of expression and association, the rights of women and children, the fight against torture and the abolition of the death penalty, non-discrimination and the promotion of accountability for human rights violations. it also explains how relations with third countries have progressed in this area, with particular reference to morocco, azerbaijan and cuba. i therefore voted in favour of this document.
in writing. ‒ the spanish socialists voted in favour of this annual report because it deals with the most relevant issues and developments relating to the cfsp during the past year and sets priorities for the future. it reflects the changing geopolitical context in which the union operates. it stresses the need for a strengthened integration of the union, including steps towards a 'defence union', and the need for the union institutions and the member states to revive this aspiration. the report also calls for the cfsp to play a more visible and effective role in conflict resolution, in particular in syria, by taking advantage of the union's influence over all key regional actors, such as turkey, saudi arabia and iran. by our s & d amendments, it also offers a possibility of more constructive relations with russia and outlines areas of common interest. we have also included the importance of the control of arms exports from the union, i.e. refraining from selling arms to countries which do not meet the criteria for eligibility under the union's common position on arms trade.
in writing. i voted against this report because it is based on a security and militarist view which also draws conclusions without really analysing the causes of the current conflict situation. it is proposing increased arms spending and the increase of all military capabilities, but not in order to seek non-aggressive deterrence or an independent union, but on the contrary, it is taking positions in which it remains subordinate to the interests of the united states. the text also celebrates the warsaw summit and therefore the role of a global nato which seems to be competing with the un and which is taking increasingly aggressive actions and positions with our eastern neighbour, generating greater tensions and conflicts by continuing to opt for unilateral sanctions. this vision of the common foreign and security policy leads to more conflict, reveals a union that continues to misunderstand geopolitical changes, and raises the question of increasing military spending in disregard of the severe economic and social crisis that seriously affects the european population. we reject the allocation of budgetary resources to military financing and call for a union which stops contributing to military escalation in and around the region.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it is in line with my europeanist position. i believe that in the present context a common, ambitious and coordinated foreign and security policy is even more necessary. this policy must be useful in meeting the important challenges ahead. in an increasingly globalised world, where power is increasingly shared between the various world powers, the union must remain united and adopt a common position on foreign and defence policy, with the aim of being an influential actor capable of defending european values on the international stage.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report on the union's common foreign and security policy, because it calls for a strengthening of the union's military structures, which would require an increase in the contributions of the member states. the report endorses the policy of cooperation with turkey in managing the flow of asylum seekers.

madam president, i wanted to explain my positive vote on this report on price volatility on agricultural markets. it is perhaps one of the problems that most concerns our european agriculture and it must be tackled. here very interesting measures are being taken, for example, that there should be european legislation covering all farmers and prohibiting unfair trading practices in the food chain, and thus resolve this serious problem for our farmers. the second point i would like to make, and for which i have supported the report, is that the objectives of the common agricultural policy must prevail over the competition rules. and thirdly, it is absolutely unbelievable that as the european union we do not protect our agricultural model. while we are reducing our strategic support in the budget, our competitors, such as the united states, china or brazil, are doing the exact opposite. i want a better future for farmers and european agriculture. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. i voted against this report because, while we agree that price volatility is a very serious problem in the agricultural sector, it fails to identify the real causes of this volatility, linked to the current agricultural model driven by the union, the liberalisation of this market, excess production and the promotion of exports and new markets. the solutions proposed in this report are based on risk management tools, in particular the different types of insurance and mutual funds, as well as public-private partnerships within the cap crisis management tools. but these are not a long-term solution, they are not effective and they are created almost exclusively to benefit the larger farms, thus reversing the agro-industrial model.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report. i believe that the problem of price volatility on the agricultural market is not reduced to a problem of balance between supply and demand as the report insists. price volatility can affect global food security and is a problem we must end in a decisive way. i do not think this report is sufficiently conclusive. the report looks for solutions in the wrong place, in my view. price volatility is also related to many other macroeconomic variables besides political will, environmental legislation and speculation in agricultural products, in food. the problem that the report deals with is a structural problem given the model of the agricultural market that exists in the union, introducing more risk management tools does not solve the problem in the long run, it only hides it.
in writing. ‒ i supported this report on cap instruments to reduce price volatility on agricultural markets. i have also supported the call for the european commission to create a european legislative framework to prohibit unfair trading practices in the food supply chain which can cause price volatility in agricultural markets.
in writing. ‒ as this report, which i supported with my vote, points out, price instability and volatility due to disturbances in demand, supply and prices have become a structural element of agriculture in recent years, both at european and global level. unfortunately, the european union does not have a real safety net to curb market volatility, which is a strong disincentive to maintain agricultural activity in the union. in view of this, the report calls for strengthening sectoral organisation and contractual arrangements and for farmers to have more negotiating power. the committee also called for risk management tools adapted to price volatility and with sufficient resources to be promoted, and asked the european commission to provide new instruments. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competition' in the definition of the term 'competition' in the definition of the term 'competition'.

in writing. ‒ ms delahaye, elected lr, is the author of a european parliament own-initiative report on agricultural price volatility. it is thus the alpha and omega of the many successive agricultural crises that have put farms in difficulty. the report does not therefore indicate that the real cause of the distress of our farmers is the stabilization of prices at the lowest possible level, which is incompatible with the profitability of farms and which is driving our farmers to bankruptcy or even suicide. the report also gives the wrong impression of productivity and agricultural policy. the broad guidelines of the cap have led our country to specialise in sectors which face fierce global competition and our farmers have to face crises of overproduction. they owe it in particular to the european union and its geopolitical choices which serve no interest of ours, as was the case with russia, whose decision to impose an embargo on our agricultural products has revealed the fragility of our positions. in the absence of a reliable basis, this report cannot make any serious proposals to improve the situation of our farmers. i voted against this own-initiative report.

in writing. ‒ agricultural activity depends on natural factors, such as biological processes and climatic conditions, which are outside the control of farmers, creating a significant degree of uncertainty in the performance of farms. in addition, the volatility of agricultural prices is one of the factors responsible for the dire situation facing many european farmers today. i therefore support the definition in the next cap reform of instruments to reduce price volatility on agricultural markets by strengthening sectoral organisation and contractual arrangements. i also believe that farmers' incomes need to be better protected by introducing risk management tools adapted to price volatility and by increasing market transparency through the creation of price observatories.

in writing. ‒ prices in agriculture suffer from higher levels of volatility than in other sectors. while supply cannot be adapted quickly to changes due to the nature of agricultural production itself, external factors such as oil prices, adverse weather conditions or pests have a substantial influence on food prices. in a context of increasing market volatility, this paper considers that the tools provided by the cap for risk management are inadequate. it therefore recommends further development of these tools, adaptation of competition laws and the inclusion of price observatories. since the ultimate aim of this report is to provide solutions to the difficult situation faced by many of our farmers as a result of the volatility of agricultural product prices and to provide ideas to stimulate reflection on the next reform of the cap - one of whose challenges will be to end price volatility in order to secure the future of farmers, stabilise markets and ensure viable production - i have strongly supported its adoption by voting in favour.

madam president, in recent years we have seen how, 'under the logic of the power of creditor countries', aggressive labour reforms have been imposed on debtor countries, leaving behind poorer, more unequal, less protected and more precarious societies. and to do all that, it has been fundamental to weaken collective bargaining. the extreme case was undoubtedly greece, where we have seen how in a few years it went from having a coverage of contracts of 83% to 42% and a decline in gross wages of 24% during these years of crisis. and now we have to see how the president of the european commission not only recognizes that we suspend part of democracy when we impose these reforms, but we also suspend the charter of fundamental rights in the countries where we apply memoranda because, of course, they are outside european legislation. this is absolutely intolerable and, moreover, it conceals a huge economic and political failure whose consequences we are seeing in election after election on this continent. inclusive growth that thinks about people is the only way out for this continent.
madam president, the attacks on labour rights in greece are obviously the result of the 2010 memorandum. two extremely negative things were done. first, the ability to fix the minimum wage for social workers was withdrawn in order to transfer it to the executive, so that the creditors could implement an effective reduction in the minimum wage. and secondly, individual company agreements were allowed to prevail over sectoral agreements, which obviously caused the fall in collective bargaining from practically 80% to a coverage rate of, at present, 40%. this is intolerable. moreover, i would like to address the commission in particular, because collective bargaining is recognised in european law (article 156 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, article 28 of the charter of fundamental rights, article 6 of the european social charter). what cannot happen is that in certain countries, because they are under a financial intervention programme, european law is suspended. look, no, i'm not going to. the fact that there is a programme in greece does not mean that european law can be suspended. it applies just as much as in any other country and therefore when the greek government is trying to restore rights that have been eliminated for some years what it is saying is the same, by the way, as the current memorandum, which does not speak of adopting more labour measures, what it is saying is: i want to restore european law in my country. and that, commissioners, is something you should be supporting, because you are the guardians of the treaties and it is you who have to ensure that european law is applied throughout the continent.
member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to say a few words after the debate. first, thank you all for the very open and expressive debate. the commission does not agree that there has been any violation of european union or international law and standards. international labour standards are universal instruments adopted by the international community and reflect common values and principles on work—related issues. they are common to us all. the european court of justice has not found that measures adopted in the framework of the economic adjustment programme are in non—compliance with the european union charter. that is also clear. the suspension of the legal extensions of sectoral agreements and the favourability principle does not mean that collective bargaining has disappeared from greece. the workers’ and employers’ organisations are free to negotiate and sign all forms of collective labour agreements at national, general, sectorial and company level. it would therefore be misleading to say that in greece the freedom of collective bargaining has been abolished and needs to be restored. as i mentioned, at the end of september, a group of independent experts delivered a report with recommendations following a thorough assessment of the greek labour market. we all need to see such a thorough assessment of the greek labour market today. the experts made 12 recommendations relating to collective bargaining, collective dismissals, industrial action and the setting of a minimum wage. four of these 12 recommendations were split, reflecting the lack of consensus within the group. these related to the setting of a minimum wage and collective bargaining, extension and favourability of principles. the commission considers the report an important input to the ongoing discussions on possible labour market reforms in greece. in principle, this could entail a revision of some measures which have already been implemented measures. however, simply returning to the pre—crisis status quo is not an option. the greek labour market was already in poor shape before the crisis erupted, not least due to policies and the quality of social partnerships that were dysfunctional and not delivering. the objective of the review is to promote a more responsible social partnership today and ensure sufficient margins for flexibility to allow greek firms still faced with the need to restructure to do so. this process represents a unique opportunity for greece to develop a stable setting that is supportive of social dialogue. we all need such a social dialogue, of course, including job creation and competitiveness, ensuring the right balance between flexibility and fairness and taking into account the very high unemployment and the need to pursue sustainable and inclusive growth and social justice. we have carefully considered the group’s recommendations and discussions with the greek authorities on how to reflect them are still ongoing. therefore i will not speculate on what might or might not be. however, the commission recognises the scope to improve collective bargaining in greece with the goal of establishing a strong and more sustainable social partnership today. for example, extensions would need to be based on reliable mechanisms to measure the level of representativeness for collective agreements, which is something which the experts also recommended. proper consideration should also be given to the design of all functioning systems of possible derogations. as in the past, we will do our utmost to ensure the success of the stability support programme for greece and thus a return to economic, financial and social stability. we are convinced that the structural reforms foreseen, including those in the labour market, are necessary to enable greece to modernise and secure the competitiveness gains of recent years. the goal is to regain the path of sustainable growth and job creation by strengthening the role of effective social dialogue and collective bargaining.
in writing. the labour reforms carried out in greece under the auspices of the troika have damaged the collective bargaining system, leaving millions of people at risk of poverty and social exclusion. this situation is absolutely intolerable because it violates both the charter of fundamental rights of the union and the ilo conventions and the european social charter. the fact that the memoranda of understanding are not specifically regarded as european law cannot serve to undermine the european social model in greece. we ask the commission and the troika, as we did in the cercas report on 'the labour and social aspects of the role and activities of the troika (ecb, commission and imf) in relation to the euro area countries subject to an adjustment programme' and by letter last week, to listen to the ilo, to listen to the european committee of social rights and to take note of the report of the committee of experts which it itself commissioned. this ignominy must be ended by restoring collective bargaining in greece and by taking steps towards a just economic recovery, focused on the well-being of the people.
in writing. the labour reforms carried out in greece under the auspices of the troika have deteriorated the collective bargaining system: marginalisation of sectoral agreements without the promised increase in company agreements, a 40% cut in wages leaving millions of people at risk of poverty and social exclusion. this situation is absolutely intolerable because it violates both the charter of fundamental rights of the union and the ilo conventions and the european social charter. the fact that memoranda of understanding are not specifically regarded as european law cannot serve to undermine the european social model in greece.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, honourable members, i very much appreciate the opportunity to discuss this topic with you today. it is important to clarify what has happened and address concerns. i would like to touch upon the facts regarding the incident and, finally, to draw some conclusions. but first of all, we have to have all the facts straight. on 22 september, a former staff member of europol informed europol that she had been contacted by a journalist earlier that day in relation to europol operational data. the journalist had obtained access to those data via a private storage device belonging to the former staff member. as soon as europol was informed about this possible compromise of data, a security investigation was launched, in coordination with the national authorities of the member state of the former staff member in order to identify the nature of the compromised data. the national authorities also initiated a judicial investigation. in parallel, the member states directly affected were informed by europol in order to establish any possible impact. the security committee of europol, where all member states are represented, received a classified report on the matter. the europol data protection officer was also briefed. later on, the information about the incident became public on 30 november, when a tv programme was announced and then broadcast on dutch television. it was in that context that the europol data compromise was mentioned. immediately, europol circulated a background note about the incident to the relevant stakeholders - the europol management board, the european commission, the europol data protection officer, the joint supervisory body, the eu counter terrorism coordinator, the council secretariat as well as the chairperson of the libe committee. the europol security committee was updated as well. last week, the european data protection supervisor, which will become europol’s data protection oversight body on 1 may next year, was also informed. as regards the content of the compromised data, it is worth noting that we are talking about historical data which are mostly more than 10 years old. according to the assessment of the member states concerned and europol, the data do not jeopardise on-going investigations. let me also make some additional remarks. as unfortunate as this incident might be, the case reported in the media is not a data leak – europol’s information systems and its operational environment were not ‘hacked’ or intruded upon. in fact, europol adheres to the highest standards of data security, including continuous security awareness briefings provided to its staff members. europol operates state-of-the-art databases and secure communication capabilities for processing and analysing operational and classified information. unfortunately, as with any law enforcement agency, the design of a robust system cannot completely eliminate human error. the former staff member clearly did not comply with europol’s security rules, which explicitly forbid the use of private equipment to produce, store, process or transmit europol operational or other sensitive information. this is the first identified case of this kind since europol was established. as far as the parliament is concerned, i would also recall that the new europol regulation, which comes into application on the 1 may 2017, foresees a mechanism to allow enhanced parliamentary oversight. a joint parliamentary scrutiny group will be established by the national parliaments and the competent committee of the european parliament. i therefore sincerely hope that this incident will not undermine our efforts to increase the exchange of information. we all share an interest in this. exchange of information, not least in the framework of europol, is vital in order to address today’s security challenges.
member of the commission. – mr president, thank you. members of the parliament, thank you for the invitation to this session. before sharing with you all the information i have on this security breach, let me stress four key points. 1. it is my firm belief that we need more cooperation on security and effective data exchange. but i am equally clear that this presupposes a high level of data protection and state-of-the-art security rules. 2. this incident could not have happened today, thanks to the technical security improvements that are finally in place. nobody can plug in usb drives and download data from europol computers. 3. it neither affected the private life of european citizens nor any on-going security investigations. 4. with you we have adopted new rules for europol that will impose a different handling of the case today from may 1st 2017. let’s look at facts first. this data breach is a case of human error by a former staff member who broke europol’s security rules. there is no indication that the security breach by the former staff member was ill-intended. still, it is of course unacceptable. our data security rules should prevent human errors from happening. the data compromised involves a limited number of member states. europol received written assurances from the journalist that the data will not be disclosed and that they are stored safely as journalistic evidence for the television programme. i am confident on the basis of information we were given that europol respected all its current security and confidentiality rules. a security investigation was launched with the member state of the former europol employee and to which the employee returned at the end of february 2016. national authorities also initiated a formal judicial investigation into the matter. in parallel, the member states directly affected were updated by europol to establish any possible impact. all member states through the security committee of europol received a classified report for their attention. the europol data protection officer was also briefed at an early stage of the process. it was verified that no current investigation in member states has been jeopardised, because the breach concerns historical data which are around 10 years old. when the case was reported in the media on 30 november, europol provided external stakeholders with a background brief on the facts: namely, an update to the europol security committee, which includes all member states; the europol management board, which includes the commission; separately, the commission, the europol data protection officer, the joint supervisory body, the eu counter-terrorism coordinator, the council secretariat, and the chairperson of the libe committee. last week also the future data protection oversight body of europol, the edps, was briefed with a report. internally, staff were also updated when the incident was reported in the media on 30 november. prior to that, all staff received continuous security awareness briefings. staff members, and in particular staff working in the operational environment, are continuously trained about the expected handling of operational and sensitive information. staff have also been briefed about the implications of the security incident. another security awareness seminar for all staff is scheduled to take place this friday. honourable members of the parliament, as far as i am aware, this is the first real security breach of this kind involving europol data since the establishment of the agency in 1999. the member states concerned confirmed that the compromised data does not jeopardise any on-going investigations. only two people accessed the data. there are no indications that data have been further shared or the lives of private citizens affected. a judicial investigation in relation to a potential criminal offence committed by these two people is ongoing. europol today is a different organisation than the one back in 2009 when the human error occurred. since then, europol has introduced numerous technical measures preventing copying of data, such as prohibiting the connection of external drives i mentioned earlier. staff are constantly trained and informed about security requirements. the case reported in the media is not a data leak. ict systems or the operational environment of europol were not hacked or intruded. handling security breaches is always the primary responsibility of the organisation when data have been compromised. that organisation, europol, is obliged to inform the entities that provide the data, the internal data security bodies and its external data protection supervisor. having said that, we should learn lessons from this case and improve our handling for the future. the europol regulation that enters into application on 1 may 2017 lays down specific rules on handling data security breaches. these rules set high standards on data security. they oblige europol to notify the personal data breaches without delay to the european data protection supervisor and the competent authorities of the member states concerned, as well as the data provider. they oblige europol to inform in certain cases persons whose data have been breached, and they oblige the europol data protection officer to keep a register of data breaches. under the new europol regulation, a new set of security and confidentiality rules is being established. in light of his experience, we look more closely whether any changes are needed there. finally, i would encourage europol in the – hopefully unlikely – event of a future security breach, to share proactively information with the commission and the joint parliamentary scrutiny within the limits of the security rules.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is no secret that i have confidence in europol. i said at the recent interparliamentary meeting and i say again now that europol is an essential tool for the security of europeans, so my commitment is unequivocal. we are looking at an isolated case triggered by a former europol official, which occurred in 2009 and which resulted in confidential information about terrorist investigations ranging from 2003 to 2006 being uploaded to the network, breaking all europol security rules. the prestige of europol should not be affected by this, nor should the confidence of the member states. it is therefore important that europol now asks itself at least three questions: have sufficient measures already been taken to prevent such incidents? secondly, how should europol deal with this fact so that it does not undermine its credibility in the eyes of the member states or third countries with which it has cooperation agreements? thirdly, can it have consequences for the security of the member states? although we know and we affirm that the board of directors meeting on tuesday was very positive. i have also been able to learn from my own experience that a number of important measures have already been improved. network security accreditation has been increased and, as of 1 december, all usb ports on the secure network have been blocked. in addition, as is common knowledge, from may 2017 the new regulation of which i was rapporteur in the european parliament will enter into force, which will strengthen the data protection system. the european supervisor, as mr avramopoulos has said, will be the one ultimately responsible for ensuring that they are used correctly. and finally, there will be a greater and better system of democratic control of the agency through the joint parliamentary control group formed by the european parliament and the national parliaments. this debate is necessary because it is justified, but it must be proportionate and balanced, and help to strengthen and review europol's security protocols.

on behalf of the ppe group mr president, thalidomide was a nazi invention, tested in concentration camps with prisoners of war. in 1954, the pharmaceutical company grünenthal created and marketed this medicine as a compound for pregnant women. during the 1950's and 1960's, 10,000 children were born with congenital physical defects caused by thalidomide. in early 1962, the drug was withdrawn in germany, the united kingdom, and italy. however, in spain it continued to be sold for three more years and continued to appear in the vademécum until 1975, causing more pain. only a few months ago, this house wondered why. why, for fifty years, have governments around the world turned a blind eye to this tragedy? why, 50 years later, are we still waiting for the company that made the drug to apologize? why, 50 years later, have we still not found a solution? i, today, think we should ask ourselves until when. how long are we going to continue to lament our lack of compassion, without solving the problems? how long are we going to allow victims to exist in spain without official recognition and without enough help to live with dignity? thalidomide victims have aged by crying. probably five thousand dead already. the problems they had at birth are compounded by those that have arisen, which could not be expected, with age. we are not asking for any new funds today, because funds already exist. today we do not ask for more resources, because resources already exist. today we are demanding that bureaucracy be reduced and the requirements be eased so that victims, german and non-german, can access the special health fund that exists, created to meet the special needs of victims that have arisen over time. we ask for less bureaucracy, not more money. the money's here. we also demand that the spanish government reopen the process of recognising the victims so that they can qualify for the financial aid they are entitled to. because i am ashamed to admit that spain, my country, is the only one that has not yet recognized its victims. ladies and gentlemen, more is needed. the health of the victims deteriorates minute by minute while many of us do nothing but talk. if we wait any longer, there'll be no more pain to attend to. let's do something right, let's do some justice tonight.

member of the commission. – madam president, first of all i will respond to some questions which were raised in the discussions. ms vallina mentioned the situation regarding the european citizens’ initiative. the commission has already implemented important measures to improve the functioning of the european citizens’ initiative instrument in several areas, such as the european citizens’ initiative register and website, to offer organisers the possibility to use the commission’s own servers for their own online collection system free of charge, and the improvement of the open-source software for the collection of signatures, and many issues which will be addressed in the future. ms hazekamp raised questions about animal welfare. the commission receives indeed many petitions on animal welfare, which shows the interest of european union citizens in this issue. these petitions often refer to article 13 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, on animal welfare, asking the commission to act in various areas. you are right: article 13 obliges the union and the member states to pay full regard to the welfare of animals in formulating and implementing certain union policies. however, it does not itself constitute a legal base for legislative action; therefore actions on animal welfare are only possible if they are at least related to one of the union policies such as agriculture or the internal market. we are listening to citizens’ concerns, but it is not within the competence of the commission to extend its own powers to cover all animal welfare issues. the protection of animals in the eu is subject to detailed rules. the main problems are related to an insufficient level of enforcement and differences in interpretation between member states. as a consequence, the enforcement of existing rules is a priority for the commission. the commission is working with member states to improve the implementation and the enforcement of rules through various actions. against this background, i am pleased to confirm that the commission is preparing to establish a european union animal welfare platform, which should be operational next year. the platform is indeed to improve animal welfare in the eu, in particular through the strengthening of various stakeholder dialogues. mr terricabras touched on questions regarding eu pilot cases. it would be premature to disclose information being examined at eu pilot stage before opening a formal infringement procedure. this is because a possible breach of european union law has been identified, but not confirmed. the complaint has to be investigated and this involves a dialogue with the member states via european union pilot. no commission decision has been taken. this work is preparatory work for the commission services. eu pilot supports the work of the commission services to establish the complete factual and legal background of a case. national authorities must be contacted very often in order to clarify facts and the application of rules. the dialogue between the commission and the member states concerned is confidential, as confirmed by the court of justice. i hope, members of parliament, you will agree with me that the number of speakers and the range of issues addressed during this morning’s debate provides proof, if proof were needed, not only of the importance of the right to petition in our union, but also of the importance of our collective efforts to respond to the concerns that citizens bring to our attention. my choice of the word ‘collective’ in this context is a deliberate one, since both parliament and the commission have key roles to play in this area. the commission very much sees itself as a natural partner of the committee on petitions in its work. on behalf of the commission, i would like to reassure you of our continued and strong commitment to cooperate closely with parliament in the handling of petitions. we are not trying to find possibilities to look at it from a narrow commission approach, rather to be partners and to see how to extend our capacities to solve those petitions. thank you very much indeed for your attention and for your excellent cooperation.

in writing. i voted against the visa suspension mechanism. i believe that mobility is a right of all people and that is why we not only reject the policies of strong europe, but have supported the visa liberalisations that have been taking place. the aim of this mechanism is to create a tool to restrict this visa-free regime, which is not very transparent and is subject to the decision of only one of the two parties to the agreement. i reject the idea of visas becoming a weapon of pressure and blackmail with which the union can conduct its foreign policy, and that is why i have opposed it.
in writing. ‒ this regulation amends regulation (ec) no 539/2001 listing the third countries whose nationals must be in possession of visas when crossing the external borders and those whose nationals are exempt from that requirement. since 2013, there is a provision under which the commission may establish a suspension mechanism for this 'visa-free' status. the report aims to strengthen this mechanism by making it easier and more 'flexible'. although some of our amendments to the text were taken into account in the committee on civil liberties when it was drawn up, relating to the protection of human rights, very problematic aspects remain such as 'the increased risk or imminent threat to the public policy or internal security of the member states related to nationals of that third country' and the substantial increase in 'rejected readmission applications' as a reason for activating the mechanism, which gives it a level of discretion and coercion with respect to the third country concerned respectively. in the negotiations with the council and the commission, (trilogue) the text was strengthened, in line with the 'strong europe' i reject. that is why i voted against.
in writing. ‒ i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr díaz de mera, for his work on this report on third countries whose nationals are subject to the visa requirement or exempt from that requirement with the review of the suspension mechanism. the evolution of the political and migratory situation, especially in the light of successive visa liberalisation processes, requires a review of the suspension mechanism to make it more agile and flexible, and to equip the union with elements to respond to circumstances arising from sudden and substantial increases in third-country nationals residing irregularly on eu territory, unfounded asylum applications by third-country nationals, refused readmission applications or threats to security on european territory.
in writing. ‒ i have supported this agreement reached with the council to strengthen the mechanism for suspending visa waiver agreements with third countries with the aim of facilitating their suspension when a 'substantial' increase in the number of their nationals staying illegally in the european union is detected, in the event of lack of cooperation by the states of origin in the readmission of irregular migrants or when there is a substantial increase in the risk to the security of member states or their public order. these new provisions will reduce reference periods and deadlines, reducing the period for checking for problems that allow suspension from the situation in the year before or prior to visa liberalisation from six months to two months. the suspension mechanism can also be activated by the european commission and not just by the member states, as is the case now. in addition, the agreement introduces a monitoring mechanism to ensure that third countries whose nationals are exempted from the visa requirement continue to meet the criteria they were required to meet in order to be exempted. the commission should send annual reports to the member states and to this parliament confirming that they continue to meet the conditions.

in writing. ‒ i supported this objection because the socialists do not accept any reduction in the phytosanitary controls applied to citrus fruit entering or circulating in the union. in particular, following the recent reform of the union plant health standard, which has strengthened such controls, depending on the risk in the country of origin. we consider the citrus sector to be strategic for valencia and andalusia and we cannot in any way allow the introduction of a measure which unnecessarily threatens the continuity of european citrus production in the face of a certain risk of the spread and contamination of dangerous pests such as 'black spot' or 'citrus canker'. we expect the european commission to ensure, in general terms, for all harmful organisms and origins, the complete traceability of specified fruits for introduction into the union, accompanied by the surveillance documents of the national plant health service. as regards the control of the pest 't leucotreta', we require the 'cold treatment' of imported citrus fruit, as recommended by efsa and eppo.
in writing. with this directive the commission is going in the opposite direction to the legislation adopted on plant pest protection measures, as it is much less stringent than this legislation, undermining the requirements for the introduction into the union of certain fruits susceptible to pests, in particular as regards citrus black spot and citrus canker. the proposed amendment thus directly affects the citrus sector, a strategic sector in southern europe, and underestimates the phytosanitary threat posed by imports of citrus from third countries. the motion for a resolution proposes to amend this directive in such a way as to ensure that appropriate checks are carried out on the entry of fruit, especially citrus fruit, into the union. that is why i voted for it.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution on the draft commission implementing directive amending annexes i to v to council directive 2000/29/ec on protective measures against the introduction into the community of organisms harmful to plants or plant products and against their spread within the community. this resolution directly affects the citrus sector, a strategic sector for southern europe. the resolution calls into question the phytosanitary agreement reached on the import of citrus fruits from third countries. we consider it essential that fruit entering the union complies with the appropriate health processes, detailed labelling and packaging which also complies with the standards set. the european parliament and the council already voted in october to tighten up plant health checks (we support this) and i think the citrus sector should be included in this process.

mr. chairman, i'm going to go with what my colleagues said. i also supported the final resolution. i personally think that when a particular medicine harms citizens of several countries of the european union and each country then compensates those victims in a completely different way and at a different rate, it probably strikes everyone that it is not entirely fair and right. it is here that the european union and the european commission can play at least a coordinating role, acting as mediators and trying to negotiate for all victims equal and, above all, sufficiently substantial compensation to enable them to live in dignity. i therefore supported it, but on the other hand i do not think that the commission should adopt any binding legislation on this. rather, its role should be limited to mediating, negotiating the terms of compensation, rather than adopting new legislation.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution so that the member states and the european commission put in place a european protocol so that survivors of thalidomide are formally recognised, irrespective of the country to which they belong, and receive adequate and fair compensation from the special health fund of the german contergan foundation. the resolution presses the german government to extend the funding available for thalidomide victims in germany to survivors in other affected countries, including spain. in spain, only the socialist government of rodríguez zapatero has taken measures to compensate the people affected, by establishing a disability-related allowance. since last march, the socialists have been encouraging a debate in the european parliament to urge the present government to continue its efforts in this direction, having made ourselves allies in the struggle of the spanish survivors/victims of thalidomide to have their rights recognized in the face of what has been the greatest medical disaster of the 20th century. hundreds of victims have died without recognition or compensation. today we have another opportunity not to condemn to oblivion the survivors of this historic injustice.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution because it calls for the involvement of the german state, the european commission and various member states (including spain) in developing systems of mutual recognition and compensation for the victims of thalidomide, a drug developed by the pharmaceutical company grünenthal to prevent nausea and other side effects of pregnancy, but which nevertheless ended up causing the malformation of thousands of babies across the continent (some three thousand in spain alone). however, i believe that the obligation of the member states is to enforce the protection of the fundamental rights of their citizens, including in the field of health. they should thus oblige the pharmaceutical companies which marketed this product to assume their criminal responsibility and, in the alternative, grant recognition of the status of victims in order to be able to access the corresponding compensation schemes. such schemes should operate with the highest guarantees and facilitate access to compensation for potential beneficiaries in good faith. finally, the spanish state needs to revise royal decree 1006/2010 to grant aid to victims, ensuring affordable deadlines and adequate funding.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this very just and necessary resolution to try to settle the outstanding debt with the victims of thalidomide. the text adopted contains several provisions directly involving the spanish government in order to facilitate the identification of victims so that they can access the special health fund of the contergan foundation. i have led this resolution within my political group, alde. i have won the support of my liberal colleagues to table an amendment to the text which would specify the responsibilities which the grünenthal company must assume. the german pharmaceutical company must therefore compensate and assist the victims who have not yet been compensated and enter into dialogue with them. the amendment was adopted by a large majority in the plenary. i hope that this resolution and this amendment will help to put an end to one of the greatest injustices that i have seen firsthand in my parliamentary career. in particular, it must end the historical discrimination suffered by the spanish victims, the only ones who have not been compensated by the company in more than 60 years.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution which calls on the commission to present the report referred to in article 50 of the paediatric medicines regulation, providing an exhaustive list and a detailed analysis of the current obstacles to innovation in this field. it also urges the commission to consider introducing amendments that take into account: paediatric drug development plans based on the mechanism of action, not just the type of disease; disease and drug prioritization models taking into account unmet paediatric medical needs and viability; earlier and more viable pips; incentives to stimulate research and better meet the needs of the paediatric population, while ensuring an assessment of research and development costs and transparency of clinical outcomes; and strategies to avoid over-the-counter paediatric use where authorised paediatric medicines exist. it also highlights the life-saving benefits of mandatory paediatric drug development based on the mechanism of action of a drug coupled to the biology of a tumour, rather than an indication limiting the use of the drug to a specific type of cancer.

in writing. – i voted in favour of the resolution because it calls on the commission to deliver, as foreseen in the regulation, the report on its application, which should include an analysis of its estimated consequences for public health, by the end of january 2017. it urges the commission, on the basis of those findings, to consider changes, including through a legislative revision of the regulation that gives due consideration to (a) mechanism-of-action-based, and not only cancer-type-based, paediatric development plans, (b) drug prioritisation models, (c) earlier and more feasible pips and (d) incentives that better stimulate research and more effectively serve the needs of the paediatric population, while ensuring transparency of the research and development process and (e) the need to avoid paediatric off-label use where authorised medicines exist.
in writing. ‒ this proposal concerns the current state of the paediatric regulation, which entered into force in 2007 with the aim of improving paediatric health in the union by facilitating the development and availability of medicines for children. it was proposed to ensure that paediatric medicinal products were the subject of ethical and quality research, that they had a specific authorisation for use and that accurate and practical information on their use in children was available. he also wanted to do all of this without subjecting children to unnecessary testing or delaying the approval of drugs for use in adults. among its provisions are the paediatric research plan or the paediatric marketing authorisation to encourage research into off-patent medicines being used outside the indication. in the almost 10 years since its entry into force, the paediatric regulation has led to an increase in the number of paediatric medicinal products in the technical file. however, its assessment shows that the areas of neonatology and paediatric oncology still require specific attention. i therefore voted in favour of this proposal with a view to further improving the regulation.

in writing. ‒ this resolution was negotiated between all members of the tran committee with two main objectives: to ask for greater involvement of the european parliament in the negotiation of international agreements with third countries and to ensure that the main criterion underlying any agreement is to ensure compliance with european safety standards in all its dimensions (material, technical, professional...). we have participated in the drafting of the text as members of the commission and i voted in favour because we fully share both priorities.
in writing. ‒ i supported this resolution of the committee on transport and tourism on international aviation agreements, which was debated at the november part-session. it stresses that in order to be able to take a decision on whether or not to give its consent at the end of the negotiations, parliament needs to follow the process from the beginning, and that it is in the interest of all the institutions to identify and address as soon as possible those issues of sufficient importance which call into question the willingness of parliament to give its consent.
in writing. ‒ in march 2016, the council authorised the european commission to open negotiations on aviation security agreements with china and japan, and on air services agreements with asean, turkey, qatar and the united arab emirates on 7 june 2016. the commission is currently deliberating on draft negotiating directives to open negotiations on union air services agreements with china, mexico, armenia and the four remaining gulf cooperation council member states. these agreements open up eu airspace to some gulf countries, which are competing unfairly by giving massive state aid to their airlines, buying up european companies and operating on european flights with staff from third countries under working conditions that do not respect the minimum european social standards. the resolution, which i supported, calls for greater involvement of parliament, on an equal footing with the council, and for information before and during the negotiations on air agreements with third countries.
in writing. ‒ this motion reminds the commission of the need to keep parliament informed and involved in the negotiations on international aviation agreements. while these agreements may be necessary to ensure minimum standards of social, environmental and consumer safety and protection, they have been used more frequently to force down european standards through competition with third countries. although i share the need for greater transparency and scrutiny, i did not want my vote to be interpreted as supporting this strategy, so i preferred to abstain.
in writing. ‒ this resolution was negotiated between all members of the tran committee with two main objectives: to ask for greater involvement of the european parliament in the negotiation of international agreements with third countries and to ensure that the main criterion underlying any agreement is to ensure compliance with european safety standards in all its dimensions (material, technical, professional...). we have participated in the drafting of the text as members of the commission and i voted in favour because we fully share both priorities.
in writing. ‒ this resolution reminds the commission of the need to keep parliament informed and involved in the negotiations on international aviation agreements. while these agreements may be necessary to ensure minimum standards of social, environmental and consumer safety and protection, they have been used more frequently to force down european standards through competition with third countries. although i share the need for greater transparency and control, i did not want my vote to be interpreted as supporting this strategy, so i abstained.
in writing. ‒ in march 2016, the council authorised the european commission to open negotiations on aviation security agreements with china and japan, and on air services agreements with asean, turkey, qatar and the united arab emirates on 7 june 2016. the commission is currently deliberating on draft negotiating directives to open negotiations on union air services agreements with china, mexico, armenia and the four remaining gulf cooperation council member states. these agreements open up the union's airspace to some gulf countries, which are competing unfairly by giving massive state aid to their airlines, buying up european companies and operating european flights with staff from third countries under working conditions which do not respect the minimum european social standards. the resolution, which i supported, calls for greater involvement of parliament, on an equal footing with the council, and for information before and during the negotiations on air agreements with third countries.
in writing. ‒ this motion reminds the commission of the need to keep parliament informed and involved in the negotiations on international aviation agreements. while these agreements may be necessary to ensure minimum standards of social, environmental and consumer safety and protection, they have been used more frequently to force down european standards through competition with third countries. although i share the need for greater transparency and scrutiny, i did not want my vote to be interpreted as supporting this strategy, so i preferred to abstain.
in writing. ‒ i welcome and support the commission’s mandate to negotiate the future comprehensive aviation agreements and include a strong and clear fair competition clause to make sure airlines can compete on a level playing field and without unacceptable state aid and subsidies. i always insisted and will continue to insist with the commission with the following questions: 1. can the commission clarify whether there is a link between accepting the fair competition clause and financial transparency elements in the future comprehensive aviation agreements, and continuing to operate in eu airspace with a licence granted by eu air carriers that third parties invested in? 2. if a gulf carrier refuses to cooperate or to provide any information about public subsidies or financial support, what are the tools that the commission can use with regard to traffic rights and other european airlines that operate in europe? 3. does not the commission believe that in order to be consistent, there should be a clear link between safeguarding ‘fair competition’, accepting the fair competition clause provisions and checking the origins of money used in eu carriers’ investments ?
in writing. ‒this resolution was negotiated between all members of the tran committee with two main objectives: to ask for greater involvement of the european parliament in the negotiation of international agreements with third countries and to ensure that the main criterion underlying any agreement is to ensure compliance with european safety standards in all its dimensions (material, technical, professional...). we have participated in the drafting of the text as members of the commission and i voted in favour because we fully share both priorities.
in writing. – i voted in favour because it stresses that in order to be able to take its decision on whether or not to grant consent at the end of the negotiations, the parliament needs to follow the process from the beginning.
in writing. ‒ this motion for a resolution assesses a broad initiative covering legislative measures, international agreements and other instruments aimed at developing an aviation strategy for europe. recognising that the sector is essential to the european economy - and therefore vital to its continued competitiveness and sustainability - the text identifies three areas for action. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the labelling, presentation and advertising of foodstuffs for sale to the ultimate consumer. it supports addressing these challenges by maintaining a strong social agenda and creating quality jobs in the sector, as well as protecting user rights, ensuring continuity in innovation and development of digital technologies or contributing to the goals set on climate change and energy market. in order to further strengthen the competitiveness of the aviation sector in the european union, i have decided to vote in favour of this proposal.
